You are a clinical information extraction system. Read ONE outpatient consultation transcript (lines like "[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): text") and return ONE JSON object with the clinical information it contains, in the trained clinical-extraction format. Return only the JSON.

Rules
- Use only what is said. Never invent or infer. Leave out every field and section that has no information.
- Record who said it (doctor, patient, nurse, caregiver, family_member, clinical_staff, unknown), in lower case.
- A denied finding goes in negative_findings, never in symptoms. A doctor's question is not a fact: use the answer.
- A medicine the patient takes is not an allergy. A stopped medicine is not current. Dose, frequency, route and indication belong only to the medicine they were said for.
- Doctor impressions are provisional or differential, and only if the doctor stated one. Do not add a diagnosis the doctor declined to give.
- Use the right status for plan items (planned, completed, recommended, conditional). Do not add a follow-up that was not arranged.
- If speakers disagree or a detail is unclear (dose, date, allergy, name), keep both statements and describe the real doubt in clinical_uncertainties.
- Cite one or two segment ids per item in evidence_ids. clinical_evidence is []. All confidence fields are null.

Transcript (encounter 00692)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I woke up on Tuesday with a stiff neck, and it's not eased. I suspect I slept on it badly.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very common. Which side is it, and what's the movement like?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Right side, running down into the shoulder. I can't turn my head to the right without a sharp pain. Looking left is fine.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you any numbness or pins and needles in your arm or hand?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing in the arm. It's only the neck and a little into the shoulder.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any injury before, a fall, a car accident, lifting something heavy? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I did spend the night on my friend's sofa, which has a pillow like a brick. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, the sofa. That tends to be the culprit. ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I did think so. Is it serious? ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Almost never. Let me check you over to be sure. Temperature first. ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course. ~
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temperature 36.6, pulse 70.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now I'm going to see how far your neck moves, so tell me where it pinches. Look left.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): That's fine. ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now over your right shoulder. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow. That's it. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, no fever and no worrying signs. This is a muscle strain from the awkward position. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): How long will it take to settle? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually three to seven days. It should be a bit better each day. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I rest it? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not completely. Gentle movement is better than keeping still. A warm pack on the muscle for twenty minutes helps.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I have a wheat bag. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. Use one pillow that keeps your neck level, not two. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll get rid of the brick. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care with sudden movements, and avoid carrying a heavy bag on that shoulder. ~
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): And should I come back? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Only if it's still bad after a week, or if you get weakness or numbness in the arm, a fever, or a severe headache.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thank you. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hope the neck loosens up. ~

Transcript (encounter 40246)
[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Naidoo, observations are done. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, heart rate seventy-four, oxygen saturation ninety-eight percent on room air. She's ready, doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, sister. Mrs Naidoo, have a seat. What has brought you in today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. I am forty-six, and I am sorry to trouble you. I found a lump in my left breast while I was in the shower.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Priya, her sister. I came through from Stonehill with her because I didn't want her sitting on it. The robots were out on the highway, absolute chaos, but anyway.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. When did you notice the lump, and does it hurt?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): It was four days ago, doctor. No, it does not hurt at all. I would not have noticed it except for washing.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any discharge from the nipple, whether milky or bloody or clear?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): The water was rather warm, and I only use a plain soap. I felt it on the outer side, um, about the size of a two-rand coin.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, the shower. I still need the other bit. Is there any fluid from the nipple?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): No, doctor. There has been no discharge at all.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has the nipple pulled inward, or has the skin changed colour over the lump?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): No. The skin is the same as the other breast, and the nipple has not changed.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any breast cancer or breast problems in the family? I'm particularly thinking of your mother.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): My mother had breast cancer. I was still in my twenties then.
[SEG0015] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was fifty-five when they found it. I remember the year clearly. She had the operation and she is still with us.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fifty-five, a first-degree relative. That stays on my mind, though it doesn't name the lump. Tell me what medicines you take, even the ones from the chemist or the health shop.
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): I take amlodopine, five milligrams, every morning, for the pressure. The cholesterol one I take at night, I think it is 20 milligrams, but I can never remember the proper name. For my sugar I take metformin, five hundred milligrams, twice a day. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, nothing else from the health shop.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the pressure and the sugar are on treatment, and there's a cholesterol tablet you can't put a name to. I'm not going to open up those conditions today, we'll just keep the tablets going. Sister, does the file match the amlodipine?
[SEG0019] person_1 (NURSE): Ja, the repeat script is amlodipine five milligrams in the morning, that matches. The cholesterol tablet isn't on our list, so I can't help with the name.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): None that I know of, doctor.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just two or three general things, not a full going-over. Have you had any fever?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No, doctor. I have not felt feverish.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble with the breathing?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No cough, and my breathing is quite normal.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And headaches?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really headaches. Sometimes there is a tightness across the forehead, but I am not sure I would call it a headache.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. We'll leave that one. If you're comfortable I'll examine the breasts now, gown open at the front.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Of course. Doctor, I should correct myself before you start. There is a dull ache in the left breast towards evening. I said it did not hurt, and that was not quite true.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): No apology needed, I'd rather have it straight, a dull ache in the evenings. On the left upper outer side I feel a firm lump, about two centimetres, and it moves under my fingers. The skin is not tethered, there's no peau d'orange, the nipple isn't pulled in, the right breast is clear, and there are no glands in either armpit.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, err, you're forty-six, there's a discrete mobile lump, an evening ache, and your mother had breast cancer at fifty-five. My working impression is this may be a cyst or a fibroadenoma, but I cannot rule out a breast cancer. I am not going to pretend I know which today.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): I understand, doctor. I would prefer a proper answer. What do you suggest we do?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll send an urgent referral to the breast clinic, and they should see you within the week. Mammogram and ultrasound will be booked with that visit, and a biopsy only if the pictures look worrying. Please carry on with your tablets as usual, don't keep prodding the lump, and come straight back if the skin reddens or the nipple starts to discharge. If you haven't heard within a week, come back and see me.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the urgent referral through before lunch, Mrs Naidoo, and I'll print you a copy to take home.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Nuala Brennan? Come on in and we'll do the blood pressure before the doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Lovely. Arm out for me. Any pain in the arm?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): That's one fifty-two over eighty-eight, and the pulse is seventy-four. A bit high. I'll stick it on the screen.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was half running in from the car park, so she was.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Sure that wouldn't help it. Doctor O'Shea is just caught with the computer. He'll be in.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry about that. The yoke logged me out again. Mrs Brennan, routine review, is it?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Aye.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Um, one second, it's loading. Right so. The high blood pressure and the cholesterol. How are you keeping?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Are you taking the tablets?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Some.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Some? Say that again, I clicked the wrong bit.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Some.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's after stopping the cholesterol tablet. She still has the blood pressure one.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): You've stopped the cholesterol one, the atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night. Is that it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Aye.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did you stop it?
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was reading this thing online, your man going on about statins and the liver and—
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Months.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Months, is it. Can you get nearer than that, before Christmas or after?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Dunno.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): January, I'd say. Don't write that in stone, she hasn't a clue.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the date open so. What had you worried in the article?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Online.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): I heard online. Was there a particular bit?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Muscles, the liver, and that you'd be better off the statin. I told her ring the surgery, but she had them binned.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to give out. Half the internet is at that. Any muscle pain on you?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sometimes? Sorry, again, the screen hopped.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nothing definite, so. The ramipril for the blood pressure, are you still taking that?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Aye.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not every morning. I missed it with the login. How are you taking it?
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every other day. She's still on the ramipril for the blood pressure, and the box says five milligrams.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams on the box. Nuala, what do you think the dose is?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ten? Say it once more, please.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She might be mixing the boxes. I have the diabetes myself. Metformin, five hundred milligrams, morning and night. Those are mine, not hers.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hold on. The metformin is your husband's, Tom, not yours. I'm not putting that on your list, Nuala. And I still can't tell if the ramipril is five or ten, so the dose stays blank till I see the box.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): His.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): His, yes. Any chest pain, Nuala?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): What did they say about the last blood test, do you remember?
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They told her the cholesterol was—
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Borderline.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Borderline. That was the cholesterol result?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Aye.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cholesterol test from before she stopped. They said it was borderline. No actual number.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): No number, then I won't invent one. The old report isn't up on this thing anyway. Any allergies to tablets?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She gave the cigarettes up years ago.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Let me listen in. Deep breath... Chest is clear, and no swelling around the ankles.
[SEG0062] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's something, anyway.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Ellison. Morning ran long, so thanks for waiting.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): 46 doesn't change the plan. Hold off on sex until the burning eases. Your wife doesn't need testing based on this visit.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Cup today, no script in my hand, you call only if I need a different antibiotic. Am I missing a piece?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the whole of it. Lab's down the hall on the left, they'll take the sample on your way out.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I walked in sure you were keeping me overnight. One last thing, is coffee gonna make the burn worse?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee can poke at an irritated bladder, so skip it for a couple of days if you can stand to. Water's the better move.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Water, then the cup. Thanks for not rushing me out confused.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, the chair by the desk is grand. What brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor I'm really worried. It's the cramps and the bloating, my bowels are all over the shop.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. How long has this been going on, and what actually happens?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): A year, um, a full year. Some days I'm bunged up for ages and then it goes loose, the cramp eases once I pass a stool, and the stress in work sets the cramp off. Is that serious? Be honest with me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, playing that back, cramps that ease when you open the bowels, bloating, and the stool alternating between constipation and loose, for a year.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes that's it. And the stress in work is making it worse. Could it be cancer? I need you to tell me.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't dodge it, we'll get there. Any blood in the stool, red or black?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None. I check every time.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight without trying?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No weight loss. The jeans are tighter but that's the bloat, not weight.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I take buscapan as well, 10 milligrams when the cramp hits, usually twice a day. Is that making the loose stools? Should I stop it?
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Unlikely to be the cause of a whole year of this. Stay on the 10 milligrams for the cramps for now. Anything else you're taking?
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Err, the nurse wrote sertraline fifty milligrams on the sheet this morning. Once a day, she said.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah no, that's not right. I'm on a hundred milligrams every morning. She has the old dose. It's for the anxiety, I've had the anxiety for years.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, two different doses on the table and I won't pick one. We'll check it with the chemist. The anxiety we know about. Tell me the family history, since you were fretting about cancer.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my brother is grand, and another sister has pressure but no sugar. No bowel cancer in the family, not that I know of anyway.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Father with the diabetes, your sister with pressure, and your mother did not have it. Day to day now, the job, the hours, what you eat, the exercise and the drink?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I work in the accounts office in the county council, 37 hours a week, mostly stuck at the desk. The diet is sandwiches and tea, I don't get any exercise, I don't walk or anything, and I'll have a glass of wine most nights and two glasses at the weekend.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a feel of the tummy. Soft, tender low on the left, no lumps that I can find.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): With that pattern over the year, the cramp settling after you go, no blood and no weight loss, my working impression is irritable bowel. I still can't rule out coeliac or some inflammation until the bloods are back.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): So not cancer? Will the bloods show if it is? When are they, I can't wait months, I'm not able for the worry.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing in the story screams cancer. Bloods won't prove or disprove a growth. I'll book them this week, full blood count, coeliac screen and a crp.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): And a scan? Please can I have a scan. I read about it online and I can't let it go.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might do a scan if it does not settle. I'm not arranging one today.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She'll only half hear the food advice, she's that wound up. Can you say it plain?
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smaller meals, a bit more fibre, ease off the white bread and the fizzy drinks, and keep the wine to a couple of nights rather than most nights. That's for you to try yourself.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): If I do all that does it actually settle? Do I come back? And what if I'm worse at the weekend, do I go to the hospital?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks with the results. If you pass blood, or you can't keep fluids down, then you go to the hospital.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Ok. Umm, and the hundred milligrams, you're sure that's not wrecking the bowel?
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think the sertraline is behind this, whatever the dose turns out to be. You were right to come in.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello doctor, sorry, I took a wrong turn on the way here.

[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the timeline, when did it begin?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): I'd say three days, maybe.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was closer to five days, doctor.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, so roughly three to five days. Is that right?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, roughly.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How troublesome is it day to day?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Mild, really.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How frequently does it come?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, it's, um... not exactly... well, hard to explain, I mean—
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me put it another way: how many times in a typical day or week?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): It happens all the time.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, is it accompanied by anything?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, when it starts I tend to get night sweats as well.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, and the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell the doctor about the other thing, that's what worries me.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I was getting to that! The night sweats? That's been for about four days.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it a lot or only a little?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Mild, I'd say.
[SEG0023] person_4 (UNKNOWN): Mm, that's what happened, yes.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed weight loss, chest pain or cough?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, no, no weight loss, no chest pain, no cough. I did have small painful spots on my fingers at one point, but that went away on its own.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your urine normal, no changes?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, that's normal as far as I know.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, how are your joints, any aches elsewhere?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing else aches.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your routine, work, habits, that sort of thing.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing, I'm teetotal. No, I've never smoked in my life. Not much, I mostly stay in these days. I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any previous surgeries?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing, I haven't had any operations.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think I have any, no.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone in your family had anything serious?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): My cousin has psoriasis.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Erm, I'm on hydrocortisone cream, when needed for the eczema.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): It's a... um, I can't remember what it's called. It's a small white one.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): For the anxiety, I believe. My son sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given. Alendronate, 70 milligrams, once a week for my bones.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, I think the last prescription for the alendronate was 140 milligrams. We changed it at the last visit.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm. Do you have the latest prescription with you?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I left it at home. I'm on Seretide inhaler, twice a day.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone ever diagnosed you with something?
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, eczema.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, I have anxiety, for five years. I didn't want to make a fuss, you know. I've had thin bones, yes.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): I've had asthma for five years now.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so eczema and anxiety are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today.
[SEG0053] person_5 (NURSE): Doctor, I've got the readings for you. Weight 68 kilos, SpO2 97 percent on room air. Temp 39.3 degrees, blood pressure 121 over 66, height 174 centimetres, BMI works out to 22.5, pulse is 102 beats a minute.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, noted.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, over here please and I'll take a look.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a deep breath for me.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is a new murmur, small splinter lines under the nails and a tender spot on the finger pad.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check. Putting it all together, it's hard to say. Possible infective endocarditis is one possibility and a viral illness another, and I'd rather not commit yet.
[SEG0059] person_1 (PATIENT): Is there something to worry about?
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with possible infective endocarditis do well once it's treated properly.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): We should do blood cultures for possible endocarditis. I'll request blood tests, it'll help with prolonged fever. The result will help us decide whether anything more is needed. I think an echocardiogram makes sense here, for new murmur. That will help us see what's going on underneath and decide the next step. You need admission today for blood cultures and a heart scan. I'll also refer you to the cardiology team.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0063] person_1 (PATIENT): Actually, okay, I'll look out for that.
[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): One warning sign to remember: the symptoms get worse. In that case don't wait.
[SEG0065] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, okay, I'll look out for that.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please come and see me straight away. Have I covered everything you wanted?
[SEG0067] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, that's helpful.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Left breast. Little lump. Painless. Size of a pea, maybe a bit over. I noticed it in the shower.

[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stuff coming from the nipple? Blood, milk, clear fluid?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing out of the nipple. It's grand.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sore at all, or tender when you press it?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. Not even when I press it. I told you it's not a bother.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the other breast, or under the arm, any other lumps?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just that one. I had a feel. Nothing else.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Our mother had breast cancer. She was only fifty-five. Siobhan's forty-six now, you should say that.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah she did. She was fifty-five. She's years out the other side of it. Doesn't mean I've it.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fifty-five, was it? Sorry, say that again, I'm half on this referral screen.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty-five. Mother. Breast cancer. That's the whole of it.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weight dropping off, night sweats, or are you wrecked tired?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Weight's the same. No sweats. Energy's fine. I'm well able.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tablets. What are you taking? The list on here looks ancient.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the water tablet. Little white one, for the blood pressure and the ankles. And Nurofen the odd time if I've a headache.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet, which one? Dose? Say it again, I've lost the cursor.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Bendrofluzide. Two point five milligrams. Once in the morning. A year or more now.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She has the purple inhaler as well. She leaves it in the drawer and pretends she doesn't.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I hardly touch it. I don't even know the name of it. Purple thing for if I get wheezy rushing about. I'm not asthmatic.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Purple inhaler. What's printed on it? I need the name.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't a notion. It's just purple. I use it the odd time. Hardly worth writing down.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Hop up on the bed there. One second, this alert won't clear.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. Small firm lump, left breast, upper outer part, about a centimetre and a half, moves under the fingers. Skin over it is normal, no dimpling. Nipple isn't pulled in. Nothing in the armpit and the right breast feels clear.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Tiny. I said ye'd find nothing worth worrying about.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's still a lump, Siobhan. Let him talk.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not calling it nothing. Feeling it, I can't tell a cyst from something we'd need to rule out. With your mother having it at fifty-five, it goes to the breast clinic urgent.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Urgent? For a pea? That's a bit much.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's the pathway. I'll send the referral today. They see the urgent ones inside 2 weeks.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And what about tests here?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, eight o'clock. Kidney function and a full blood count, because of the water tablet. Take the tablet after the bloods, not before. No need to fast.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday? I'm working Thursday. Sure can it not wait till after the weekend?
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thursday morning is the slot that's booked. Eight o'clock, in and out. If those bloods are borderline we'll do a third test, the liver profile. Not booking that now.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the wheeze. If it does not settle, a scan, just a chest x-ray. Only if it doesn't settle.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): It always settles. I don't need an x-ray.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine. It's only if. And I'll see you back here in two weeks, with the clinic and the bloods. Reception will book it on the way out.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll make sure she goes. She'll try to cancel, you watch.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't cancel. I just think ye're all going overboard. It's a little lump.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back sooner if the skin changes or it gets bigger before then. Otherwise two weeks, and Thursday for the bloods. Mind yourselves.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Please sit, I will note your vitals before doctor sees you. Blood pressure is 138 over 86, pulse 78, temperature 36.8, and oxygen is 98 percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 138 high? I don't know, sister, these numbers confuse me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): A bit on the higher side, doctor will tell you. Your husband was waiting outside — he said you snore very loudly and you are tired, dozing off in the evening.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I am not tired, and I don't snore. He likes to complain, that's all.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come. Headache, is it? Sit.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes doctor. Well, actually I am having headache from many years. Maybe eight years. Migraine, they told me.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Same pain, or has it changed?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It has changed. Now it is worse in the morning. I wake up and it is already there. Before, it used to come afternoon time, one side.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Since when, the morning one?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't know, doctor. Could be three weeks, could be a month. I cannot put a date.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Two times this week, morning only, with the headache. Not daily.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vision — blurred, double?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, vision is okay.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Weakness of hand or leg? Any fit?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. No fits.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Neck stiff? Neck pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, neck is fine. Pain is in the head, more on the right side.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which tablets?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Crocin — I thought the 500, no, actually the 650 one. And sumatriptan when the pain is very bad.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Crocin how often? By mouth?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, by mouth, 650 milligram. Two times a day, sometimes three. Almost every day now. I don't know, doctor, is that too much?
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sumatriptan — what strength, how many a week?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The chemist calls it Suminat. Fifty mg, one tablet, maybe three times in a week, only if Crocin doesn't touch the pain.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other tablet? BP tablet, sugar tablet?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else. No sugar tablets. I don't have sugar, I think. I don't know, nobody checked recently.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergy?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergy.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Surgery any time?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No surgery.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your husband told sister you snore and you doze in the evening. True or not?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired, no, I am sure. Snoring I don't know — I am asleep, no — but I don't accept it, he exaggerates. Maybe I sleep late because the head is paining, that's all.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Look straight. Pupils equal, reacting to light. No neck stiffness.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grip my fingers — power full in both arms and both legs. Reflexes normal. Walk — gait is steady. That is enough.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): My neighbour uncle had some brain problem last year, everyone in the colony was talking. But that is not family, and I am not like that, no? Also the ceiling fan in your room is making a noise, sorry.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): I am not calling it a tumour. Most likely your migraine pattern has changed. With morning pain and vomiting I cannot fully rule out a secondary cause.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So what to do? Should I stop everything? The Crocin I am taking too much, I feel.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't stop the sumatriptan on your own. Cut the Crocin — not more than three times a day, and avoid taking it daily. Too much painkiller can itself make the headache worse.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): And scan? My husband will ask the minute we reach home.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): We might do a brain scan if this does not settle. I am not booking it today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): If it settles, then no scan, correct?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Correct. Let's see you in two weeks. If the vomiting gets worse, or there is weakness or a fit, come earlier, don't wait for the date.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks... I don't know if office will give leave, but I will manage. The bus was so crowded today, I almost turned back.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sister at reception will put the date. Till then write down the headache days and which tablet you took. We are done.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Frequently the burning. At other times I am simply awake. My mind is not especially troubled.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No black stools. I swallow perfectly well.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your weight, over this time?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, before I forget, the jacaranda out the front is lovely this week. Um, the weight, I have lost a little, though I have not been on the scales.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ha, they are lovely. A little weight down, without a number, that's fine. Are you on any medicines?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I do not take those. They have never suited my stomach.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Any allergies to medicines, foods, anything?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): None at all. No known allergies.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): How about alcohol? Where does that sit for you?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Only socially.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Arthur, come on. It's a bottle most nights. I'm the one picking it up from the bottle shop.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): No apology needed, and no judgement. I'm glad you've told me. That much wine can stir up the stomach, and I'd like to know how your liver is coping. Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. Not even as a young man.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. And at home it's you and Sandra?
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Just us. I do the cooking and the shopping, and I stay over. It's a live-in arrangement.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. It has suited me very well.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mind if I have a feel of your tummy? Hop up on the couch when you're ready.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly. Shall I lie flat?

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Putting this together, it may be gastritis, or it may be reflux. I can't tell those apart today. The evening meals and the wine could both be feeding it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. I had wondered if it was simply indigestion.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): It might sit in that family, yes. I'd like to start pantoprazole, forty milligrams, one tablet by mouth, every morning, half an hour before breakfast, for the burning.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall take it exactly so. Do I get it from the chemist?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, I'll write the script. And I'll order liver blood tests today, because of the wine, to see how the liver is travelling. Jess can take the blood after we're done.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I'll do the bloods straight after, no worries. Tubes are ready out the back.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, smaller evening meals, ease back on the wine if you can manage it, and stay propped up after dinner rather than lying flat. If you vomit blood, or the pain becomes severe and sudden, don't wait on me, go to emergency.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I will be careful, and I will go to emergency if that happens.
[SEG0050] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll keep an eye, and I'll cut the wine down in the shopping.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): That would help. Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through the blood results. You're both welcome.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear, and very kind.
[SEG0053] person_4 (CAREGIVER): We'll book it on the way out. Thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Have a seat, both of you. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I have had headaches for many years, but the pattern has altered, and I felt I should come in.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Altered in what way?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): They are worse in the morning. I wake with the pain, and on some mornings I have vomited, which is quite new.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about the—
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I was coming to the tablets, but it can wait. The vomiting, as I said, did not happen with the old headaches.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have the original headaches been with you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifteen-ish years. I was told they were migraines, though I could not name the precise year I was given that label.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And this morning pattern — can you put a time on when it changed?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I am afraid I cannot. Last winter, or perhaps the winter before that. It crept in, and I never marked the date.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, we'll leave the date open. Before the pain, do you get lights, or a warning—
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, he snores. Terribly. And he's wrecked in the daytime, asleep in the chair after tea.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not snore, and I am not especially tired. With respect, it is the headaches I have come about.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted, and we'll park that disagreement. Back to what I asked — any flashing lights or a visual warning nowadays?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no flashing lights. Not with these. The older headaches sometimes had a little shimmer, but that has gone.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any neck stiffness, weakness in an arm or a leg, or a fit?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness, and I have never had a fit. My neck is not stiff.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does look dreadful some mornings, just before he's sick.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often is the vomiting?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Perhaps two mornings in a week. Not daily. I had started to say, about the medicine, that lately it is less—
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He lives on those tablets.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Less what? Finish that thought for me.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Less reliable, I was going to say. I take sumatriptan, fifty milligrams, by mouth, when a migraine starts. And paracetamol, a thousand milligrams, rather often.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's the hundred milligram sumatriptan, I've seen the packet. And the Panadol is every single morning, two tablets, before he's even dressed.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, but the sumatriptan is fifty milligrams. I do sometimes take a second tablet if the first has not worked, which I know was not what was intended.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm. I'm hearing fifty from you and a hundred from your partner, so I'm not going to invent a dose. Bring the box and we'll settle it. The second tablet means you're not really on the plan you were given.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That is fair. I take nothing else. I do not smoke, and I drink very little — a glass of wine at the weekend.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We nearly turned around, you know. The Monash was a car park from Chadstone out.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): It was grim this morning, wasn't it. I only saw the tail of the cricket. Did you catch it?
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most of it. The batter was poking about for an hour and then he middled one, straight to deep midwicket, and the catch stuck. I nearly spilt my tea.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not a cricket person, I confess, but the delay was extraordinary. We were sitting near the exit for an age, watching the weather come in.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Proper Melbourne grey. Anyway, we've used up your time on the freeway and the cricket. Sorry, doctor.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): All good. Let me get a blood pressure and do a quick nerve check while I think this through.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one thirty-six over eighty-four, and your pulse is seventy-six. Pupils are equal and reacting, no facial droop. Power is full in the arms and legs, reflexes are brisk and even, and your gait is steady. I'm not seeing any focal signs.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm turning it over as I go. The long story still fits migraine best, but a new morning headache with vomiting — I can't rule out raised pressure inside the head. And if the snoring your partner describes is real, sleep apnoea could be adding to the tiredness, though you've set that aside.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I would rather we did not make too much of the snoring. I sleep perfectly well, doctor.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. You two don't agree, and I won't force it. I don't scan every migraine, but if the morning headaches and the vomiting haven't settled in a fortnight, I would like a CT of the head.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should he knock the sumatriptan off until then?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it cold if a bad migraine hits, but skip that second dose, and ease the paracetamol back — more than a couple of days a week can feed the headache. I suspect medication overuse is part of this picture.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I shall keep the paracetamol for genuine need only.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any brain tumours or aneurysms in the family, or migraines?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had migraines. No tumours that I know of.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in a fortnight either way, and if it hasn't eased we'll book that scan then. If you get a sudden thunderclap headache, new weakness, or you can't keep fluids down, go to emergency rather than waiting.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I shall do exactly that. I am grateful you explained your reasoning.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring the sumatriptan box next time so you can read the strength yourself. And I'll get him here, freeway or not.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would help a lot. We'll sort the dose off the packet. Mind how you go.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon, David. Have a seat. Reception's scribbled "stomach" and not much else, so you'll have to fill me in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's nothing. Just a niggle in the tummy. I nearly turned round in the car park.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long, and where do you feel it?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a few weeks, maybe longer, I don't really know, I don't keep track. It's up under the ribs, top of the stomach, not bad. Comes and goes, mostly after I've eaten, or when I'm in bed.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's poor sleep on the form too. Yours, or has someone embellished?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Sleep's fine. Well, actually, no, I wake a couple of times, two or three. The pain's there for some of those, then I can't get back off. It's not a problem, people wake up.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, any blood, black stools, weight coming off?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Appetite's fine. I'm not ill.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels alright? Heartburn, or acid coming up?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Bowels are completely normal. Bit of heartburn now and then, usually if I've had a curry. Milk sorts that. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you actually taken for the pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Rennies, from the chemist. Two tablets, when I remember. Not every day, a few times a week. They take the edge off, and nothing's on prescription. I'm not one for pills.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None at all.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations? Diabetes, or anything else I should have on the list?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. No diabetes. Fit as anything. You're making a fuss over a niggle.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a quick feel, if you lie back. Knees bent, that's it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. It won't even hurt, watch.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Abdomen's soft. Mildly tender just under the breastbone. No guarding, and I can't feel any masses.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Can't stand the smell. My brother smokes like a chimney, we had a row about it at the football on Sunday. Dire match, by the way.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, let me play that back. A few weeks, possibly longer, of mild pain at the top of the stomach, after food and in the night, a bit of heartburn, waking two or three times, Rennies a few times a week, tummy soft with a little tenderness, no vomiting, no bleeding, no weight loss, bowels normal, no drug allergies, you don't smoke. I was going to leave blood tests out and just carry on with the Rennies plus a few tweaks around meals.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Good. I don't want a pile of tests. Tests are for people who are actually sick.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I do need a straight answer on drink, though. How much alcohol are you having?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Socially. The odd glass. Nothing to write home about.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Socially covers a lot of ground. A couple of nights, or most nights?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually... most nights. A bottle of wine, perhaps. Just to switch off after the shift. I'm not drunk, loads of people do that.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for putting it plainly. I'm not going to have a go. A bottle most nights is more than an odd glass, and it can inflame the stomach and chop up your sleep, so it does change what I want to do.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, this could be acid reflux, or gastritis from the wine. I'm not going to call it an ulcer off the back of a chat, and I won't pin a diagnosis down until we've got something more than a story. We'll see what the tests show.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Tests? You just said no blood tests.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I did say that, and I've changed my mind. With a bottle of wine most nights I want liver blood tests, form goes in today. And rather than leaning on the Rennies, I'll start omeprazole for the acid, twenty milligrams, once a day, by mouth, before breakfast, for a month.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): A month of tablets for a niggle. Bit keen. So I bin the Rennies?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, leave the Rennies off while you're taking the omeprazole. No need for both. And if you can ease the wine down, even towards half a bottle, the pain and the waking have a better chance of settling. That's practical, not a telling-off.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Half a bottle. I'll try. No promises. New rota at the depot's been brutal, that's half of why. When do you want me back?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Book in with me in two weeks. We'll go through the liver results and see how the omeprazole is sitting. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or your skin goes yellow, don't wait for that appointment, come straight down or go to A&E.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yellow. I'm not going yellow. I still think this is a waste of your afternoon.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Maybe it is, and maybe it isn't. Two weeks, with the results. First tablet tomorrow morning.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Tomorrow. Alright. Cheers, then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry doctor, err, the auto got stuck near the flyover. We are a bit late only.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That is alright. Sit, sit. What brought you in today?
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This is Kabir, ten days old today. His skin is gone all yellow, like someone rubbed haldi on him, that is why we came.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Aaah. Mmm.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yellow skin. Hmm. From which day are you noticing it?
[SEG0006] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm, I cannot date it doctor. Third day, or the day after we came home, since Diwali or after, no, that is not right, I just cannot say which day.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, we will not pin a date. How is he feeding, breast or...
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Waaah. Waaah.
[SEG0009] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry. Both, umm, my milk and top feed, the formula. Well actually every four hours, not more than that. He sleeps so much, like he has overdone it, all floppy, I feel he is like a wet rag.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every 4 hours is a long gap for a ten day old. Any fever?
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No fever.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Vomiting? Loose motions?
[SEG0013] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting. Stools are that yellow mustard only, not loose, not white. And at night the relatives are all talking, I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): The noise is just the house, not part of his illness. Are the eyes yellow too?
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, the white part is yellow. And the urine in the nappy looks darkish. He is not...
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not what?
[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not active, just lying there. His elder sister had the same yellow skin when she was a baby, it settled.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with his breathing, or the chest?
[SEG0019] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, breathing is fine only.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies for him?
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nothing. No allergy.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operation so far, or a problem at birth?
[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No operation. Normal delivery, he cried at once. They gave drops, calciferal, we are still giving that.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): You mean cholecalciferol, the vitamin D. What dose and how often?
[SEG0025] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): 400 units, once a day, in the mouth. The hospital sister showed me.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at him a minute. The yellow reaches the upper chest, the sclera are yellow, tummy is soft, and he is drowsy but he responds when I touch his foot.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Mmm. Aa.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse weighed him just now, three point two kilograms. So I am thinking aloud here. A newborn liver is still maturing, bilirubin rises and the skin goes yellow. At ten days this could be physiological jaundice, or it could be breast milk jaundice, and I am not ready to say which.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is it dangerous? He is irritable also na, keeps fussing, what to do.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): We should not guess the danger from the colour alone. I am booking a blood test for the bilirubin today. If the level is high he may need phototherapy, but only if it is high.
[SEG0031] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Today itself? And the feeds, should I be waking him?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, the bilirubin test is arranged for today. Wake him and offer a feed every two to three hours, breast first, then the formula. I will see him again tomorrow morning.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tomorrow morning, okay doctor. We will come.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all, please sit. What seems to be wrong?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It's, It's yellow crusts, mostly.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Probably about a week. Yeah.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it bearing on you a lot?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's severe, honestly.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about scratching at night, have you noticed that?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, about the same, about two weeks.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it a lot or only a little?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, uh, maybe a six out of ten on a bad day.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed high fever, eating poorly or blisters?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, no high fever, eating poorly or blisters, none of it.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything unusual with passing urine?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, that's normal as far as I know.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any previous surgeries?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I've never been operated on.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your routine, work, habits, that sort of thing.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a bus driver, so I sit for long hours. I live with my elderly mother. I hardly move around during the day.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): What conditions have you been treated for in the past?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Eczema, for two years.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you react to any medicines or foods? Any allergies?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Not to my knowledge, no.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, I take hydrocortisone cream, when needed for the eczema. I'm on a moisturiser, twice a day.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll note down your vital signs first.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep your arm relaxed for me...
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: temperature 36.9, pulse is 86 beats a minute, blood pressure 112 over 75, SpO2 97 percent on room air.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that okay?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll look at it together shortly.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the area, I'll be gentle.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay as you are for a moment.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): The eczema patches on the arms have yellow crusts and weeping areas.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, doctor.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can relax now. From what you've told me and what I found, the most likely explanation is eczema with a bacterial skin infection.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it clear up?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with eczema with a bacterial skin infection do well once it's treated properly. I think a skin swab makes sense here, for infected eczema. I'd rather check than guess, and this is the quickest way to know more.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Where would I go for that?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): The treatment will be flucloxacillin, 250 milligrams, four times a day, seven days. It's for infected eczema. I'll put all of this in writing so you don't have to remember it.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, I'll pick it up today.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the nails short and keep using the moisturiser. Let's review you in one week. Does all of that make sense?
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. Um, sorry, I'm not sure how this works. My carer said I should talk to you about my chest. ~
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfectly fine, Mr Okafor. Come in. And this is? ~
[SEG0003] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Tunde, I'm his carer, I'm with him four days a week. He gets tight in the chest on the stairs and he hates making a fuss.
[SEG0004] person_3 (NURSE): I'm Nurse Claire, doctor. I'll do his observations whenever you're ready. ~
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you both. Mr Okafor, tell me about this tightness, when does it happen?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): When I go up the stairs, to the bedroom. It's a squeezing, sort of, in the middle of the chest. It goes if I stop and rest a minute.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many steps before it comes?
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): About half a flight. Then he stops on the landing and holds the banister. I've seen it.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it spread to your arm or your jaw?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no, not to the arm. Not the jaw either.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you get breathless or sweaty with it, or any fainting?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No. It's just the squeezing. I don't faint or anything.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had anything like this before? What's your heart history?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I was told I had angina, back in 2020. They gave me a spray and some tablets.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's go through the tablets, then.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): The spray is, um, GTN, 400 micrograms, under the tongue when I get the pain. And atorvastatin, 40 mg once a day.
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And his aspirin, 75 mg, once a day, with breakfast. I give him that one.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how often are you needing the spray lately?
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Three times this week. It used to be once a month.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a change, thank you for telling me. Anyone in the family with heart trouble?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): My father, he had a heart attack at fifty-eight.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Claire, could you do his observations? ~
[SEG0023] person_3 (NURSE): Of course. Mr Okafor, arm on the table for me. ~
[SEG0024] person_3 (NURSE): Blood pressure 138 over 84, pulse 76, and oxygen 97 percent.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? ~
[SEG0026] person_3 (NURSE): All fine, Mr Okafor. ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Claire. Mr Okafor, the spray use going up is what makes me want to look more closely at your heart. I'd like to arrange an exercise ECG at the hospital, where we record your heart while you walk on a treadmill.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): On a treadmill? At my age? ~
[SEG0029] person_4 (CAREGIVER): They'll go gently, Mr Okafor, it's not a race. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exactly. They watch you the whole time. Until then, carry on with the tablets and the spray as you are. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): And if the pain doesn't go with the spray? ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it's still there five minutes after the second spray, or it's worse, call 999. Don't wait, and don't walk to the phone.
[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll make sure he has the phone by the bed. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And I'd like to see you again in two weeks, before the test, to check how it's going.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Tunde will take me. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Splendid. Look after him, Tunde. ~

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I have.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, has there been any vision changes?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Definitely no vision changes.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any nosebleeds or fever at all?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No nosebleeds or fever, none of it.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your chest okay generally?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Breathing's normal.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are there any allergies I should be aware of?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No known allergies.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any smoking?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I gave up cigarettes last spring.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's your work?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a plumber, lots of bending and kneeling.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you follow any particular diet?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm vegetarian and have been for years.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you get out much?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Not much, I mostly stay in these days.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any previous surgeries?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, nothing, I haven't had any operations.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you list what you take, tablets, creams or inhalers?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Asthalin inhaler. I take it when needed for my asthma. Tamsulosin, 0.4 milligrams, at night for the prostate. I'd been on Seretide inhaler, not any more though, I stopped.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your medical history?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I mean, I have asthma. I didn't want to bother you but it keeps coming back. I kept putting it off, which I know isn't sensible.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I follow.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, an enlarged prostate. I've been reading about it online and it worried me.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): May I examine you now?

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's enough for me.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): So where does that leave us? It points towards nasal polyps. That's my thinking for now, and it may change as we learn more. I'm prescribing mometasone nasal spray, 50 micrograms, two sprays each side once a day, eight weeks. That's for nasal polyps. Rinse with saline and use the spray daily.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cut back on tea, coffee and fizzy drinks for a couple of weeks and see how things settle. The thing that would worry me is if the symptoms get worse. If that happens, go to emergency.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): I understand.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all from me. Any questions?
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, uh, I'll do that. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): All the best.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the screen's having a moment. Right. What's brought you in?

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's the tiredness been going on?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, about three months? Maybe a bit longer. I can't pin the day down, it sort of crept up. I did think it was just the dark mornings.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Two flights up to the flat and I'm puffed, have to stop on the landing. Sitting down I'm fine. The bus this morning was a nightmare, some bloke and a dog, but that's not why I'm here.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry. The stairs bit again? I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Two flights, breathless, stop halfway. Fine once I sit down.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any odd cravings?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Cravings? No. Don't think so.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, um, I've been crunching ice all evening, every evening, a whole tray of it. My flatmate thinks I've lost the plot. We were watching that baking thing and I just sat there with a bowl of ice.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ice, right. You're vegetarian, according to this?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Strict, yeah. No meat, no fish, not since uni. Eggs and cheese are fine, I'm not vegan. I nearly went vegan after a podcast but I couldn't give up cheese.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are your periods heavy?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, they're normal. Regular, every month, about five days, not heavy, same as always.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Heart racing?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Heart doesn't race.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicines? Slowly, I'm typing.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, desogestral, the mini pill, 75 micrograms, one every morning, for contraception. I tried ferrus sulphate last year, the 200 milligram tablets, but I stopped after a fortnight cos my tummy hated it.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to anything?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Family, anyone with anything? It beeped, sorry, go on.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, my dad got diabetes in his fifties, type two I think. Mum didn't have any of that, she's fine. My older sister's got blood pressure but no sugar. And my grandad on dad's side had a heart attack when he was about seventy.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Work, food, exercise, alcohol?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I work in a bookshop, part time, about twenty hours a week, afternoons mostly. Strict vegetarian, no meat or fish. I walk to the shop sometimes but no proper exercise, no gym. A glass of wine on a Saturday, and I don't smoke.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood tests before, for this?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, last year, at the uni health centre. They said my iron was borderline. I never got an actual number, and I can't remember if it was March or later, the date's gone.
[SEG0028] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. Obs from just now, blood pressure 112 over 74, pulse 82, sats 98 percent.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ta. Tiredness, the ice, breathless on the stairs, vegetarian. I think this is most likely low iron. That's a working impression, not confirmed till the bloods are back.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we'll do a full blood count, ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate. The nurse takes the bloods Thursday morning. No need to fast, just don't take any vitamin tablets that morning.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday's alright, I don't start till eleven. I'll bring a book, the queue's always grim.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): If those come back borderline we'll add a coeliac screen. If the breathlessness doesn't settle once the iron's dealt with, then a chest x-ray. Not booking that now.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lentils, beans, dark green veg, and orange juice or vitamin C alongside, helps the iron absorb. I'll see you in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0034] person_3 (NURSE): Thursday, half eight, phlebotomy. Leave the vitamins till after, like he said.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, the bus from Rathmines was a disaster. I was stood there near twenty minutes in the rain.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're here. Sit.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks. Fierce warm in that waiting room, I nearly dozed off.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the problem?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, it's this itching. Between me fingers and around the waist. It's driving me mad.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's worse at night, I can't get a wink, and I'm not sure of the date, maybe after the holiday or...
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. How long.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): About three weeks, between the fingers and round the waist. Started as a small patch and then it spread.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Worse at night. Yes or no.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Fierce at night. I'm scratching till all hours.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone else in the house itching?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I got Eurax from the chemist, tried it a few days and stopped, did nothing, and I'm worried it's...
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone else. Partner. Children.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh. Sorry. My partner's scratching as well, and the little fella, he's 4, itching at night too.
[SEG0016] person_3 (NURSE): I'll grab your readings. Blood pressure one twenty eight over seventy eight, pulse seventy six, temperature thirty six point six.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Shivers?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever, no shivers. I feel grand apart from the itch and the sleep.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Face itchy? Scalp?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not the face or the scalp. Just the hands and the waist.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hands out. Waistband.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Burrows between the fingers. Scratch marks along the waist. Face is clear.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it serious? I was googling at half four and I proper frightened myself.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Looks like scabies. Common. We can clear it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Scabies, God. Will the child be scarred, is it in the mattress for...
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): No scarring. Mites die off the body in a couple of days.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): So what do I put on? Is it safe? I've a hundred questions, sorry.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Permethrin five percent cream. Neck to toes, between the fingers, under the nails, waist, soles. Bedtime on, leave it 8 to 12 hours, wash off in the morning. Repeat in 7 days.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): If I put it on at nine, shower at seven, is that enough? I've to be in the creche early and I'm mortified.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's enough. Bedtime on, morning off.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. And, um, will it clash with me tablets? I'm on amlodopine five milligrams in the morning for the pressure, atorvastatin 20 at night for the cholesterol, and only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning from the health shop.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): No clash. Allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Partner and the four year old, same cream, same night. Neck down. Keep it out of the eyes and the mouth.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Even if they're not as bad as me? He won't sit still, he hates when I...
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Everyone. Same night. Or it circles back.
[SEG0037] person_3 (NURSE): I'll go through the washing, if you want.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Please, yeah. I'll mess it up otherwise.
[SEG0039] person_3 (NURSE): Hot wash sheets, towels, clothes from the last three days, 60 degrees. What won't wash, bag it 72 hours. Don't fumigate the sofa.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): And the teddy? He sleeps with it, I can't just...
[SEG0041] person_3 (NURSE): Bag the toys three days. Hot wash if they'll take it. No sharing towels.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Work after the first treatment, yes. Itch can linger 2 to 4 weeks. Don't use the cream every day.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): 2 to 4 weeks? I won't cope, is there a tablet for the night that won't...
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the itch hasn't eased in two weeks, come back. Chemist today for the permethrin.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing much. Pimples on the face, and the periods are a bit off. She fussed, I didn't want to come.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are the periods off, exactly?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): They come every two months, sometimes three. Since two years. Normal for me only, I don't care.

[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): The weight, over how long has it climbed?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't say when it started. Sometime in college. Clothes are tight, so what. I've overdone the eating, finished.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Energy wise, any other feeling in the body?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): By evening I feel like a wet rag. And if I stand too long in the lab my feet feel dead. Ignore both, everyone gets that.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me think aloud. Spots, late cycles, chin hair, weight up. This can be a polycystic ovary pattern, but I am not confirming it sitting here.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't make pimples into a disease, doctor.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): The ovary can put out a little extra male-type hormone, so acne, hair and irregular menses travel as a set. Tests decide it, not my guess.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. From my side it's still nothing.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): When the period does come, is the bleeding heavy, clots, soaking through pads?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Late, that's all. Not heavy.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about thirst, or passing urine much more than before?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave that fuzzy. On the tummy side, loose motions, constipation, pain as a regular thing?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Tummy is fine. Nothing like that.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you yourself have diabetes, or a thyroid problem?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only my mother has sugar, tablets for many years. I'm healthy.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Her diabetes still counts. With this weight I can't rule out an early sugar issue in you, even if you feel well. That sits separate from the ovary thought.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): She takes the medicine. I don't. Please, no tablets for me.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any tablets or creams just now?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, adapaline gel last year, for two months, then I left it. Face was peeling. Nothing now.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so that gel is stopped, and I am not starting any hormone pill today.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): My friend eats some pill for her skin. I don't want that.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): A combined pill, drospirenone with ethinylestradiol, can settle cycles and help acne. If these reports fit, we might start it at the next visit. Not now.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): We'll see. Maybe never.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Inflamed spots and blackheads on the cheeks and chin, and a few coarse hairs along the chin. May I check the abdomen?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Go ahead. You won't find anything.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft, no mass. So my working impression is possible polycystic ovary syndrome, and I still can't exclude a glucose problem with the gain and your mother's sugar.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Possible only. Don't write it in big letters on the file.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): For this ovary pattern, and to check the sugar side, I'll book fasting bloods, glucose, HbA1c, TSH, testosterone, LH and FSH, plus a pelvic ultrasound. Both are arranged, not a maybe.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Needles and a scan for pimples. If you insist.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): Fasting blood form is with you, and the scan is Thursday at eight in the morning. Come empty stomach, bloods that same morning. The slot is already booked.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday I have a practical. Does it have to be then?
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): Kindly come Thursday itself, the test is fixed. If you are a little late we will still take you.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cut back the laddoos, steady only, not a crash diet. That part sits with you.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. No promises. The canteen is right there.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks with both reports, and we decide about the pill then. If you feel badly unwell before that, call us, don't sit on it.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. My class is starting, I can go, no?

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in. What is the problem.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, my right heel is paining badly. Since two months the first step in the morning is like a nail going in, and if I walk a little it eases itself. I think I've overdone it with the jogging.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which heel.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I got new shoes also, from our own shop, very stiff, and the shop is so noisy I can't hear myself think half the day.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left or right. Answer that.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Right side. Only the right heel. Sorry, when I get nervous I talk all around.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only the first steps, or the whole day.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): First steps are the worst, especially in these new stiff shoes. If I stand long in the shop it comes back a bit, not the whole day.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling or redness.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling, no redness. I checked every morning.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fall or twist.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No no, nothing like that. I run three to four km most mornings, then I am standing the whole day, I work in a footwear shop.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Night pain, yes or no.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Will this need an operation? My neighbour had some heel surgery and she was in plaster, I am really frightened.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): I asked about night pain.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. No. It does not wake me. Only the morning, and a little after long standing.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine 5 mg morning for the pressure, atorvastin 10 at night for the cholesterol, metformin 500 morning and night for the sugar. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, my mother sends it from Pune.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): You miss any of them.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, the night one, the cholesterol tablet, sometimes I forget. The others I take properly. Is that dangerous, doctor?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take it every night. Do not skip. I will book a heel x-ray today, and you stop all running for six weeks.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): X-ray? Is it a crack? These shoes I started the same week the pain started, two months back, sole like a board. And if I stop running fully I will put on weight with the sugar, no?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Same week as the stiff shoes, pain settles after a few steps, no injury, so I am cancelling the x-ray. No test, and no need to stop running fully.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me press. Tender just on the inner side of the right heel. I don't see any swelling.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, yes, that exact spot. Is it something bad inside the bone?
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is plantar fasciitis. Morning first-step pain, stiff new shoes, that tender spot. Not a fracture.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Plantar fasciitis, ok ok. What should I actually do? Kindly tell me the steps, I will forget, and can I still jog?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Calf and plantar stretches, morning and evening, hold twenty seconds, three times. Silicone heel insoles in the shoes. Jog on alternate days, keep it shorter than 4 km.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the stretch tear the heel? Our shop has gel insoles, are those ok? And should I stop the Ayurvedic powder?
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): It will not tear. Gel heel cups are fine. Continue the powder and your usual tablets, they are not for this pain.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, my feet feel dead after standing, is that the nerve? I feel like a wet rag by closing time.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numb, pins and needles, or just tired.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Not numb. No pins. Just dead tired, like a wet rag. Sorry.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): That is fatigue from standing, not a nerve problem. Do the stretches and use the insoles. If it has not eased in three weeks, come back.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks, ok. If it gets worse before that, what to do? I saw ice on the internet and now I am more scared.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ice after standing is fine, ten minutes. If it gets worse, come earlier. Otherwise only if it has not eased in three weeks. No scan, no injection.
