[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining.

[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Dunno.
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was levlin. Little yellow packet.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Levlen, yeah. You were taking one tablet by mouth each day for contraception, and you've stopped it?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.

[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Gone.

[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.

[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How strong would you say it is?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly mild. I've had hot flushes too, uh, for about a month. With hot flushes, yes, warm rooms and caffeine. That makes it worse.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had poor sleep?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, yes. Ah, with poor sleep, mostly severe. I've also had mood swings, for about a month.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check a few things. Any weight loss, bleeding after sex, palpitations or chest pain?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none that I've noticed.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any heavy bleeding or breast lumps at all?

[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any muscle or joint problems besides this?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Actually, I move fine otherwise.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your bowels, any trouble?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No, uh, all normal there.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you work outside the home?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a hairdresser, on my feet all day.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): What does a normal day of food look like?

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there someone at home?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, do you have any chronic illnesses?

[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I have COPD.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so COPD is already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. Do you take any prescribed or over-the-counter medicines?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Alendronate, 70 milligrams, once a week for my bones. I take Tiotropium inhaler, once a day for my chest.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): No known allergies.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Actually, I remember she had some kind of reaction to erythromycin before. I couldn't swear to it.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Really? I don't think so.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough, I'll write down both versions.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll do your observations first.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep your arm relaxed for me...

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure and pulse are fine and there are no breast lumps on examination.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): All finished, thank you.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Having listened and examined, I'd lean towards perimenopausal symptoms. It could also be anaemia, so we'll keep that open.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Is this serious, doctor?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like perimenopausal symptoms, but I'd like to confirm. I want a bone density scan done, that's for menopause bone health. I'd rather check than guess, and this is the quickest way to know more. Blood tests is what I'd like next, for hot flushes. Layers of clothing, a fan by the bed, and cutting down on caffeine and spicy food can help the flushes.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book a review after the blood tests. Have I covered everything you wanted?
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor, goodbye.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late, doctor. The Luas sat at Charlemont for ages and then the car park was full, I was pure mortified coming in the door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand. Sit down.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Desperate rain as well. Left the umbrella on the bus, typical.
[SEG0004] person_4 (NURSE): Notes are here. I did her blood pressure outside.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm I had a whole list in my notebook and then I forgot the notebook on the kitchen table, which is just like me, but anyway that's not why we're here.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Why are you here?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Err I'm pregnant, about sixteen weeks, and I'm worried the baby could have thalasemia. Himself was told at a blood camp that he carries the trait, and I've been sick with the worry.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was the camp?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh I cannot pin the date. It was last summer, or maybe after the October bank holiday, I go over it and I still haven't a clue.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The letter said beta thalassaemia trait. It came to the house after the GAA club session.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No bleeding. Not a spot, I've been checking every day since the positive test, probably more than any sensible person would, sorry.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain. There is a heavy tiredness though, and uh I couldn't tell you when that began, last winter or the one before, it all runs together.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sleeping?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Sleep's been rotten. I lie there going through the what-ifs since the letter came.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's awake half the night. I'm anxious too, but sure I'm not the patient.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Medicines?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I take folick acid by mouth every morning for the pregnancy. I told the midwife five milligrams, that was wrong, it's the 400 microgram bit inside the pregnicare tablet from the chemist.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No drug allergies and no food allergies.
[SEG0023] person_4 (NURSE): My own sister was told she was a carrier and her little lad is in senior infants now and flying it. I only say that so people don't panic in the corridor.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I never smoked. I used to have a glass of wine on a Friday and that's stopped since the test turned positive, not a drop.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): The trait means one haemoglobin gene is altered. The red cells come out smaller. It doesn't make him ill by itself. If both of ye carry it there's a one in four chance of the full condition in the child.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): So he's not sick? I read three websites, they contradicted each other, and my cousin went on about a neighbour's child who needs transfusions, and I spiralled, which I do.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. He's not sick from the trait. Working impression is a possible risk to the baby only if you carry it too. Not confirmed.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They mentioned my haemoglobin was low, something like 12, but that was my old result.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): We won't use his figure. Nurse, today's numbers?
[SEG0031] person_4 (NURSE): Blood pressure 118 over 74, pulse 86, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft. No pallor. The womb feels about right for sixteen weeks.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I say sixteen weeks because it's tidy, but the twelve-week scan was fifteen plus a few days and I always round it up, my mother says I over-explain everything.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your mother's health?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Mam has high blood pressure. Nothing like thalassaemia on my side, that anyone ever said.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book a full blood count and a haemoglobin electrophoresis for you today. That's the screen.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Today, even though I had toast and tea? I always get in a knot about fasting rules and then I end up describing my breakfast, which nobody needs.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): No fasting needed. If the bloods show you carry it as well, we might refer ye to genetic counselling. I'm not booking that now.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if she's clear?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then this doesn't put the baby at risk of the major illness. I'll see ye back in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I stay on the pregnicare?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, stay on it. If you get bleeding or bad pain, come straight in, don't wait.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. The notebook had about twenty questions, half of them daft, but the baby was the only one that mattered.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll come back. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0045] person_4 (NURSE): Reception will send ye to phlebotomy on the way out. I'm off at four, so it won't be me.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks a million. Sorry again for landing in late.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Lord, the rain. The car park is a lake entirely. Anyway, it's the legs has me in, doctor.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Cramps. Fierce ones in the calves, both of them, the left worse. Two months now. Of a night, nearly every night, and they wake me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long, did you say? And does anything ease them?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. Two months, yeah. If I get up and stamp about, or stretch the foot up, they ease, but sure then the night is gone.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): And the terrier next door starts up then. White little yoke, barks at his own shadow.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's up on the landing with it most nights. I stay over a few nights in the spare room, so I hear her.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any swelling of the ankles or the calves?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No swelling. Grand in the daytime.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Redness or heat in either calf?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not red, not hot.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I'm not short of breath either.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Waterworks or bowels, any trouble there?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Bowels grand, waterworks grand.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Operations in the past?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never had one. Of.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me what tablets you're on.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Err. The water tablet, Mizartan for the pressure. I've high blood pressure this years. Metformine for me diabetes, and Omprazole for the acid.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The water tablet is Frusemide. Forty milligram, one in the morning, for the ankles. Every day, she doesn't miss it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): And Mizartan, the strength?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Eighty, I think. White box.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mizartan is eighty milligram, once in the morning. She's spot on with that.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformine dose?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformine, 500 milligram twice a day, with breakfast and with the tea.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the Omprazole?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Omprazole, twenty milligram, mornings. Five-ish years I've been on that one.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything from the shop besides?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Magnesium tablets. The girl in the shop said they're for cramps. I like that shop, they still say hello, not like the big place in town.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The magnesium is maybe four hundred milligram. I wouldn't swear to it. She takes it at night, most nights, though she misses the odd one.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I hardly drink water. Three or four teas a day and a small glass with the tablets. My sister would drink a lake and be in the bathroom for it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Any alcohol?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Never smoked in me life. A small sherry at Christmas, that's all.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I used to walk miles in the post office. I'm retired out of that now. Don't walk much at all these days.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me read what the nurse wrote. Blood pressure one forty over seventy-seven. Pulse sixty-eight.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I misread that. The pressure today is one oh nine over seventy-seven. The sixty-eight was the pulse last time in March. Today's pulse is seventy-four.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your last pressure was one-forty, that was March too. Weight today is fifty-two kilograms.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Fifty-two. I was a stone heavier in the post office days. There was a canteen bun every Friday, that didn't help anyone.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I've had a look at them. Soft both sides. No swelling, no redness. Pulses in both feet are there.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, two months of fierce cramps in both calves at night, the left worse, they wake you, and walking or stretching eases them. No swelling, no redness, no chest pain, no shortness of breath. Frusemide 40 milligram, Mizartan 80, Metformine 500 twice a day, Omprazole 20, plus the shop magnesium. Very little water.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I was going to stop the water tablet today. Often that's what sets night cramps off.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The ankles come up fierce if she misses even a couple of days. The heart doctor told her to stay on it. And in March they said the potassium was a bit low.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. That changes it. We'll keep the Frusemide going. I won't stop it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I had thought of a magnesium blood level and an ECG on top. There's no chest pain, and the shop magnesium would muddy a level, so we'll leave those. Blood tests for the potassium this week. That's the plan.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I stay on the magnesium from the shop?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay on that one, but don't double it. And every night before bed, stretch the calves, the foot up towards you, hold it, both sides.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): And drink a bit more water. A glass with each meal, on top of the tea. Not a flood.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): I can manage a glass with the meal. My cousin swears by bananas, two a day, and she's still driving at eighty-six, fair play to her.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bananas are fine if you fancy them. I'm not starting a potassium tablet. My impression is the cramps are coming from the water tablet and not drinking enough, and the potassium may be low. That's provisional, mind, until we see the bloods.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Will you want to see her after the bloods?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book back in with me in two weeks, when the results are in. They'll have the blood form for you outside.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand so. Two weeks, and I'll do the stretches. Mind yourself in that rain, doctor.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you did. Let's sort this out together. How long has the sleep been bad?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): About three weeks. I lie awake until four in the morning.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): What is the worry about?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): A big project at work, and I've been told there may be redundancies. I can't switch off.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I just need sleep.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you for telling me. Any panic attacks or chest pain?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No panic attacks. No chest pain.
[SEG0010] person_3 (NURSE): Doctor, I've done his observations. Pulse 88, blood pressure 134 over 86, temperature 36.6, oxygen 99 percent, breathing 16.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Those are fine, a little up from stress. Do you drink alcohol or coffee?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): A glass or two of wine to wind down. And plenty of coffee, I'm afraid.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much coffee?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Six cups a day.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): That will be affecting your sleep. Any medical problems?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Just mild asthma.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you tried anything to help you sleep? ~
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. Camomile tea, which did nothing. ~
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me explain what I think is going on. You're under heavy stress, with caffeine and alcohol, and it's keeping your brain on alert. ~
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): That makes sense. ~
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to avoid sleeping tablets as a first step. Cut the coffee to two cups, none after noon, and swap the wine for a non-alcoholic wind-down.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): That's going to be hard. ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know. I'd also like to give you a short course of a mild sleeping tablet, zopiclone, 3.75 mg, at night for five nights.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it addictive? ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not in five nights, but we keep it short on purpose. Don't drive the next morning if you feel drowsy.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): All right. ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd also like you to book a review with your own GP this week, to talk about the work stress and plan the next steps.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. Thank you. ~
[SEG0029] person_3 (NURSE): I'll print the information sheet for you. ~
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you both. ~

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me your medicines, please.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, does your family have any medical conditions?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): My grandmother had dementia.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your medical history?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I have eczema, for five years. I told myself I'd wait and see, and here I am.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I have epilepsy. I told my wife I'd come today. I've got depression. I've been reading about it online and it worried me. I thought it would sort itself out, you know, but it hasn't. I've had anxiety for five years now. I did try to ignore it for a while.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, I can see eczema and depression in your file as well.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check a few things. Any blood in the urine, vaginal discharge or back pain?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I'd have said so.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing like fever?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no fever.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Actually, doctor, I did notice fever. She doesn't always say.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I don't think I did. Maybe a little, I'm not sure.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll note both what you've said and what you've noticed. On the cardiac side, anything I should know?
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's been fine.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed any weakness, or anything odd with your balance?
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing odd there.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me get the readings out of the way.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nearly done with the readings...
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: SpO2 98 percent on room air, pulse 86. And respiratory rate 14, BP is 128 over 69.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Raise your arm for me.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft with slight tenderness just above the pubic bone.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can relax now.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, here's what I'm thinking. My working impression is an uncomplicated urinary infection. I'd also keep vaginal irritation in mind.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): What are the odds it's serious?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's an uncomplicated urinary infection, and we'll know more once the a urine dipstick is back. I'm going to order a urine dipstick, for burning urine.
[SEG0054] person_4 (CLINICAL_STAFF): The earliest is Thursday, 10 am.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll begin with nitrofurantoin, 100 milligrams, twice a day, three days. It's for urinary infection. Drink plenty of water and avoid holding urine. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0056] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, I'll look out for that.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't wait if you get a fever or back pain. That's when to be seen urgently. Come back if it is not better in three days. Can you tell me the plan back in your own words, so I know I've explained it clearly?
[SEG0058] person_1 (PATIENT): So, I take the nitrofurantoin, 100 milligrams, twice a day and come back if it is not better in three days. Is that right?
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, exactly right. Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?
[SEG0060] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, thanks, take care.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care now.

[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. Eating's fine. He's just not sleeping, up scratching for half the night.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the skin weeping at all, or any pus?
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No weeping and no pus. Just dry and flaky. It bleeds a tiny bit sometimes where he scratches.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you putting on it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. The white cream for the itchy bits. The yellow one at night for the dry skin. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I don't know the proper name. It's just an Ayurvedic powder from the grocer. He has a pinch by mouth in his milk every morning. I doubt it does much.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. We'll park that as an unnamed powder. Anyone in the family with asthma?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad has asthma, yeah. Been on a puffer for years.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Daddy's puffer is purple.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's your dad's, not yours. Any cough or wheeze in this little one?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough, no wheeze. He runs around fine.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): How about his tummy or his waterworks, anything there?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. All fine.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. Behind both knees and both elbow creases the skin's dry and thickened, scratch marks, no pus. Couple of small soft glands in the neck.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, breathing's easy, and his tummy's soft.
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry he wriggles. Err, we were late, the carpark was a shocker.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book the nurse to take bloods Thursday morning, a full blood count and an IgE. No fasting, breakfast is fine, just have him here around 8.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, a RAST panel. Not ordering that today. And if the neck glands do not settle, we'll organise an ultrasound.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): nothing, really. spots on my face, and my periods are weird. mum kicked off so jess dragged me. spots and weird periods.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): they disappear for ages, then just show up. i've overdone it with night shifts at the cafe. end of story.
[SEG0011] person_4 (CAREGIVER): there's weight gain as well, and dark hairs on her chin. she shaves before work.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): it's peach fuzz, relax. i have gotten heavier. i feel like a wet rag after a shift. so what.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): how long have the spots and the irregular periods been going?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): umm, six months. no, that's not right. year twelve was two years ago and it had started already. so two years.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): and the weight and the chin hair?

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): if you say so. i'm not keeping score.

[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): any pain low in the tummy, or pain when you bleed?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): nah. no pain.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): could you be pregnant?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): no way. i'm not seeing anyone.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): bowels been okay?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah, fine.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): what about your breathing, or chest pain?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): no. chest is fine, breathing's fine.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): thinking out loud, acne plus irregular cycles plus chin hair and the weight, that can be polycystic ovary syndrome. here's the plan. i'll start you on levlen, one combined pill a day, to settle the skin and the cycle, and we'll send you for bloods.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): i don't want tablets. my feet feel dead after a double shift. that's just standing all day, not something a pill fixes.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): fair. before i prescribe anything, any headaches, zigzags, sparkly vision?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): err, sometimes a headache and the edges go sparkly. i lie down, it passes. it's nothing.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): sparkly edges like that are an aura, so i'm changing the plan. no levlen, i don't start a combined pill with migraine aura. we'll do the tests and decide later, and nothing is started today.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): mum's got type two diabetes, years of it. not me though.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): we'll leave that doxycycline off. do you smoke at all?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): never have. two or three beers on a saturday, max.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): jot down when you bleed. a brand new worst ever headache means emergency, not the clinic. otherwise i want you back in three weeks for these results, that's booked in.
[SEG0041] person_4 (CAREGIVER): i'll make sure she comes. she lives with her mum, i'll text her.
[SEG0042] person_1 (NURSE): i'll lock in the bloods, the pelvic scan and the three week review out the front.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): ta. frog in my throat, your aircon's dry as. just need water, not a diagnosis.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): water's by the desk. see you in three weeks.

[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Aunty Marg and two of the cousins are crook with the same thing. They messaged this morning.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many bowel motions are we talking?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): I didn't count properly, a handful, six maybe eight, watery. Who's counting.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in it, or black stool?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah. No blood. Just water, basically.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the vomiting, sorry, say again how many times?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Once, this morning, in the carpark. Yesterday I dry-retched a bit. I wouldn't call that vomiting.
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He vomited three times yesterday, I watched him. And he goes dizzy when he stands up.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm not dizzy. I stood up quick. Don't turn it into a drama.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever at home? Pain in the tummy?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever. There's some cramping low down, comes and goes. Nothing dramatic.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's hardly drunk a thing. A few sips of water since last night, and he keeps waving the glass away.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): I've had sips. I'm not dehydrated.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, fluids, can you repeat that? I was clicking the wrong tab.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A few sips of water since last night. And he's been taking Imodium.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Loperamide. What dose?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Two milligram tablets from the chemist. Two last night, two this morning. They work. I don't see the issue.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): With a gastro bug like this I'd rather you stopped them. Let it out, especially with other people from the same meal crook.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright, if you reckon. I only took them 'cause the cramps were annoying.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else you take? Regular meds?

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me just read that back. Pantoprazole stopped in March, and a single four milligram ondansetron wafer you didn't continue?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Yep. No allergies, by the way, before you go looking.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Hop up on the bed, I'll feel your tummy. Sorry, one sec, this login's timed out again.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Abdomen's soft, tender low on the left, no guarding. Lips are cracked and the mouth's dry. Chest is clear, heart sounds are normal.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Told you. Can we wrap this up? I've got a shift at the warehouse tomorrow.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Looks like foodborne gastro from that wedding meal. That's my working impression, not nailed down. And you're mildly dehydrated, nothing wild.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sip Hydralyte, little and often, not big gulps of plain water. Leave the loperamide alone. If you're still opening your bowels more than a few times by Friday, or you can't keep fluid down, then we'll send a stool culture. I'm not ordering it today.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Friday's miles off. I'll be sweet.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it's not settling by Friday, come back and see me. Sooner if there's blood, bad pain, you stop weeing, or you feel faint, go to emergency. Your wife can nag you about the drinks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): I've done Graham's obs. Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 74, oxygen sat 97 percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks for that. Come on through, Graham. What's brought you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): It's this cough, doctor. I don't know, it's just been hanging around and it's annoying.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been at it for weeks. Dry as anything, especially in the evening.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you cough, are you bringing anything up?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No phlegm. Just a tickle that won't quit.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I don't think so. I haven't felt hot.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hasn't been feverish. I'd have noticed.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your breathing, any shortness of breath?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No, I'm alright getting around. It's just the cough.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): When do you reckon it kicked off?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe three weeks? I thought it was from a cold.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's been five weeks, easy. It started just after we drove up to my brother in Geelong.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Did it? I had a runny nose for a few days back then and that cleared up. The cough stuck around.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the sniffles settled, and the dry cough carried on, worse in the evenings. The timing's wobbly between you, roughly three to five weeks. I'll come back to that.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're on something for your blood pressure. What are you actually taking?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, they started me on a new one. Ramipril, I think. Or was it enalapril? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0019] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's ramipril, five milligrams once a day for his blood pressure, and he started it a few weeks back. Enalapril was never his, that was Uncle Ray years ago. My brother takes lisinopril, but that's not Graham's tablet.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, ramipril, for the blood pressure. Yeah. I don't know, the cough seemed to turn up around then. Could still be the cold, I reckon.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been taking the ramipril every day?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): I think so. Most days. I might've missed one or two. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's pretty good with it. I see him take it at breakfast.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Speaking of that drive to Geelong, it was a shocker. The ring road was absolutely choked.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about it. I was stuck out that way on Saturday. Took an age just to crawl past the West Gate.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): We had the cricket on in the car. The Aussies were all over them for a bit.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Until that collapse after tea. I nearly turned it off.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): And the weather, stinking hot. Air con on the whole way. You could've fried an egg on the dash.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, probably. Anyway, let's get back to you, Graham.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll have a listen to your chest if that's alright.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear. No wheeze, no crackles. And your throat's not red.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): That's something, I suppose. I don't know what I was expecting you'd find.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): The blood pressure today was 152 over 88, still a bit high for someone already on treatment. Pulse 74, oxygen 97, I'm not concerned about those.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Dry cough, roughly three to five weeks, you don't quite agree on the start, worse in the evenings, no phlegm, no fever, no shortness of breath. A runny nose for a few days that cleared. Ramipril five milligrams once a day for the blood pressure, started a few weeks ago, and you may have missed a dose or two.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's about it. I don't know, doctor, I just want the cough to go. I keep blaming the cold.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had a google and now he's sure the tablet did it. I told him to stop reading that stuff.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can see why you'd both wonder. A dry cough can show up with ramipril, and it can also just be the tail end of a cold. I can't say for certain which this is, and I'm not going to pin a diagnosis on the cough today.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): So you don't know either?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not firmly, no. What I'd like to do is stop the ramipril and switch you to candesartan, eight milligrams, once a day, for the blood pressure. If the cough is from the ramipril it often settles after a change. If it was the cold, it may ease anyway.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is candesartan the same sort of thing? My brother's lisinopril, that's a different one, isn't it?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Different group. Lisinopril sits with ramipril. Candesartan doesn't. We're not putting you on your brother's lisinopril.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I start it tonight? I don't know, doctor, I've still got half a box of the ramipril at home.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the ramipril from today. Don't take any more of those. Start the candesartan tomorrow morning, one eight-milligram tablet, once a day. I'll do the script.
[SEG0044] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if he's still coughing his head off?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Give it time. I'd like to see you back in four weeks, to check the blood pressure and see where the cough is.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the cough gets worse, or you get short of breath, come back sooner, don't wait out the four weeks.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright. What about side effects? I don't know, doctor, new tablets make me nervous.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): If your face or tongue swells, that's uncommon but you go to emergency. And if you feel dizzy the first few days, sit down and let me know.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay. I'll try not to worry.
[SEG0050] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll stick the ramipril box up in the cupboard so he doesn't take both by mistake.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. One tablet only, the candesartan. Not both.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Did you want me to print a path form, or are we leaving bloods?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): No bloods today, thanks. We'll leave tests for now.
[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): So no chest x-ray? I don't know if I should have one.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not on what I've heard today. Your chest is clear and you're not particularly unwell. We can rethink it if the cough is still hanging around when I see you in four weeks.
[SEG0056] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll grab the four-week appointment on the way out.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, four weeks with me. Reception will book it. Look after yourself, Graham.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good evening, doctor, thanks for seeing me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, come in and sit down. What brings you here today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you for fitting us in, doctor.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, I've been having stiff aching shoulders and hips.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Around about four days... no wait, it's more like two days.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Moderate, really. It comes and goes.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had a mild temperature?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I have. As for mild temperature, mostly mild. I'd say a few times a day.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about difficulty getting out of bed, have you noticed that?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I have.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had stiff aching shoulders and hips before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a similar thing a couple of years ago. It went away.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what about visual changes, weight loss, jaw pain on chewing or headache?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I'd have said so.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything unusual with passing urine?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all fine.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about any past illnesses or ongoing conditions.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Low haemoglobin, for five years.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sure.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, for about a year.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so low haemoglobin and high blood pressure are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. Has anyone in your family had anything serious?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother had a stroke.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me ask about allergies, anything at all?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, I don't think I have any, no.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you take on a normal day?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He takes iron tablets, once a day for my blood count.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I was on telmisartan before. I stopped taking it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, have you had any surgical procedures?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I had a varicose vein procedure, last year.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now some background about your lifestyle.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I smoke roughly a pack every two days. I used to drink heavily but I stopped four years ago. I look after my grandchildren most days. I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day. I walk the dog every morning.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shall I check your blood pressure and pulse?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep your arm relaxed for me...
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: pulse 81, blood pressure 111 over 77, temperature is 37.0 degrees.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll interpret them after the examination.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, I'd like to check you over now, if that's alright.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breathe out slowly.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): The shoulders are painful to move but strength is normal and there is no joint swelling.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's enough for me. So where does that leave us? My working impression is polymyalgia rheumatica. The reason I say that is that your story and my examination fit together. Another possibility is rheumatoid arthritis. I'm going to order blood tests, for proximal stiffness. What I'm giving you is prednisolone, 15 milligrams, once a day, reducing course. That's for polymyalgia rheumatica.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I carry on if I feel better?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Report any headache or jaw pain immediately. Don't skip meals, and try to eat smaller portions more often through the day. Please don't wait if you get a new headache or visual changes. That's when to be seen urgently.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, I follow.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book a review in two weeks.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, that's fine with me.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): And if they're fine?

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): You can. Reception will have the Tuesday and Thursday times on a slip.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, I'll grab your blood pressure before Dr. Brennan calls you. Arm out straight for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh god, it'll be sky high. I was white knuckling the whole way in, the M50 was desperate.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Sure we'll see in a second. My sister is the same in waiting rooms, she gets palpitations and has to step outside, but that's her own worry, not yours.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. I just, umm, I keep thinking it's something bad.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): One twenty eight over seventy eight, pulse seventy six. That's grand. He'll be in now.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy six, is that too fast? Should I be worried about the heart as well?
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Not from that number, no. I'll leave ye to it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello there. I'm Dr. Brennan. What's been going on?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the tummy. I've these cramps, and my bowels are all over the shop. Sorry, I'm going too fast. It's been a year now, and I googled bowel cancer at two in the morning like an eejit.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll slow it down. Tell me about the cramps themselves.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Low down, kind of gripey. And err, once I pass a stool they ease off. Nearly every time.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the tummy bloating up as well, between the pains?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh yeah. Especially after lunch. I look about six months gone by the evening, it's mortifying at the desk.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the stools. Are they hard, loose, or swinging between the two?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Swinging. Constipated for a few days, then it goes loose, like porridge, three or four times in a morning, then back the other way. That's been the whole year.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the stool, or black stool?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I actually looked, because I was scared. Nothing.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight, without trying?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. If anything the jeans are tighter with the bloating. I haven't lost weight.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the pain or the loose stool wake you up at night?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I wake for the alarm anyway, so I can't really say.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Is night time the dangerous one? That's what the forum said. Am I not explaining it right?
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): What you said isn't a clear yes or no, so I won't treat it as a night symptom. Tell me only what you're sure of. Any vomiting?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. I feel a bit sick with the cramps sometimes, but I don't actually get sick.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks. Any burning, or going more often?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's all grand. No bother there.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Could it be coeliac though? A girl at work was told she had it and she was bloated. Or an ulcer? Or, uh, cancer, honestly?
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Those are fair questions. Bowel cancer is unlikely with no bleeding and no weight loss, but I'm not brushing you off.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): What this sounds like is irritable bowel. The muscle in the bowel goes into spasm, particularly when you're under stress, and that spasm is the cramp. When you pass a stool the pressure drops and the pain eases. That's my working impression, not a final stamp.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): So the stress is actually doing that to the gut? Work is brutal. I'm a payroll clerk in a hotel and since January I'm there till seven most nights, lying awake thinking about the wages.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can wind a sensitive gut up, yes. Stress isn't eating a hole in you. Let me check what you've already tried.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): The GP gave me mebeverin, one hundred and thirty five milligrams, three times a day. I took it about a month and I'm after stopping it in March, because I wasn't sure it did anything.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): The chemist put a box of Buscopan in my hand as well, but I never took a single one. Still sitting in the press.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the mebeverin is stopped since March, and the Buscopan was never started. Anything else you are actually taking?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Peppermint oil capsules, when I remember. Umm I think they're about two hundred milligrams, maybe twice a day, but I forget half the time. The bottle's at home.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. I'll have a feel of your tummy, if you're alright with that.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. It's a bit sore on the left today. Will it hurt? I tense up, I can't help it.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Soft abdomen. Mild tenderness low on the left. No guarding. I can't feel any mass. Bowel sounds are there.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No mass. So not a tumour you can feel? You're sure?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nothing on examination suggests a mass. I still want bloods, because this has gone on a full year. I'll check for anaemia, inflammation, and coeliac disease before I settle on the irritable bowel.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): So, saying it back. A year of low cramps that ease after a stool, bloating after lunch, stools swinging from constipation to loose, no blood, no weight loss, heavy stress in the payroll job, mebeverin stopped in March. Does that match?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's it. Sorry, I keep leaping ahead with the questions.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the needle be awful? How long do bloods take? And if it is coeliac do I have to give up my mam's brown bread forever?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Quick scratch, results are usually a few days. We only talk about dropping gluten if the coeliac test is positive, not before. For now, regular meals, ease off the fizzy drinks and the big lactose loads, smaller portions, and a simple food diary for two weeks. That often settles the bloating.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I do drink a good bit of sparkling water and the odd Coke, yeah. Is the peppermint oil safe to keep on with?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Peppermint oil is grand to continue if it suits you, take it with food. I'm not adding a new tablet today. Come back and see me in three weeks and we'll go through the bloods and the diary. Reception will book it on the way out.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Ok. If I see blood, or the weight starts dropping, I shouldn't wait though, should I?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): You shouldn't. Blood, weight loss, or pain that turns constant and severe, you ring us or the out of hours the same day. Otherwise I'll see you in three weeks. The nurse will do those bloods now.

[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): That's what the thermometer reads, thirty-eight point three, so I'll chart it. Doctor won't be long.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello. Come through, both of you, that's quite all right. What brings you in today?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you for seeing me. I have come about a pain in my jaw when I chew. It has become rather troublesome.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain on chewing. Um, how long has it been, and where exactly do you feel it?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about three weeks. Well, actually it has been three weeks. It is an ache just in front of the ear, and the jaw clicks when I open. It is worse when I am stressed.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grinds his teeth as well. I hear it at night, most nights, for two or three weeks. He only half believes me.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I do believe you. I simply was not aware of the grinding until it was pointed out. I am sorry it disturbs you.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Pain with chewing, a click, grinding at night. I'm thinking this sits in the jaw joint rather than a tooth, err, the grinding loads the joint and the stress clamps the muscle. Does that match what you feel?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is a fair description. I have had no trouble with the teeth themselves.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Have you felt properly unwell? Any swelling you've noticed?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not had a fever, I have not felt unwell, and I have not noticed any swelling.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does it lock at all, or is it only the click? Any earache, or a change in your hearing?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): It does not lock. I can open fully, it merely clicks. No earache, and my hearing is normal.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your chest, just briefly. Any cough, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing of that kind. My breathing is perfectly fine.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): What are you taking for it? Any regular medicines?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Only paracetemol. One gram, um, four times a day, for the past week, for the jaw. I take nothing else regularly.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His sister keeps on about biotin. She takes high strength biotin herself, for her hair, and she wants him on it. I said no.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I have not taken her biotin, and I would not start it without your advice.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Quite right, that's hers, not yours, and it won't touch a jaw joint. Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have no allergies that I am aware of.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me feel the joint. Open slowly for me... and again. Mm. There is a click in the left joint on opening. The muscle here is tender. I can't feel any swelling.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. That is the tender place. It is uncomfortable, though I can bear it.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, the click, the pain on chewing, the grinding your partner hears and the tender muscle, and you don't feel ill. The chart says thirty-eight point three, a little warm, but there's no swelling and it isn't behaving like an abscess. My working impression is a temporomandibular joint problem driven by the grinding.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you're not giving antibiotics? Does he need a scan?
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): No antibiotics. We might do a scan of the joint if it does not settle. I wouldn't book one today.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd like a soft diet for a fortnight, no crusty bread, no chewing gum, and a soft mouth guard at night. The chemist will have one. It just cushions the grinding.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, yes. Would soup and pasta be acceptable? I shall obtain the mouth guard today, if that is suitable.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Soup, yoghurt, pasta, eggs, all fine. Steer clear of steak. Guard at night only, not in the daytime.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I should mention that work is heavy at present. I am an accountant, and it is year-end, so avoiding stress is not straightforward. I will do my best.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): The stress will keep feeding the grinding, which is why the guard matters more than another tablet. Let's see you in two weeks, and we'll go from there.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. We will return in two weeks. I am grateful for the clear explanation.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure the guard actually gets worn. And no parcels of biotin from his sister.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ha. Leave the biotin with her. If the pain suddenly blows up, or you can't open the jaw at all, come back sooner, otherwise two weeks. Mind how you go.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a minute, this computer's crawling again. Mr Naidoo? What did you come in for today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, Ravi Naidoo. I need the form for the new contract at the depot, HR wants it before Friday. I told the sister my knee's been niggling, but that's not why I booked, it's nothing hectic.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): The form, right. The template won't load, so bear with me. Sister flagged your blood pressure out in the passage, I'm just trying to find her note.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): She pulled a face, hey. I told her straight it's white coat, soon as I sit in these rooms it shoots up. At Clicks in Umhlanga last month the lady said it was normal, she didn't even blink.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm on her note now. She recorded one hundred and sixty-eight over one hundred and two.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No ways. She told me one fifty-four over ninety-six. I repeated it back so I'd remember, because I thought, shame, that's not so bad.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): One fifty-four over what? Say it again, the screen just jumped.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety-six on the bottom. One fifty-four over ninety-six. That's what she said out loud to me.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ag, okay. The printout on the other tab is a second reading, one seventy-two over one hundred and four. So the file's got two pairs and neither is the one you heard.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yoh, these machines. My mother's brother had a stroke at fifty-eight, just dropped at a braai, so I do get nervous about pressure. But nobody's ever put me on tablets for it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, who had the stroke? I was still typing the numbers.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): My mom's brother, my uncle. Only him in the family. My folks are fine, my dad still takes the bakkie down the coast on a Saturday.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. The knee you mentioned to sister. Which one, and how long has it been?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The right one. Since the long weekend when we shifted my brother's fridge, so about three weeks. It aches and it clicks when I take the stairs. Not swollen really, and I still walk the dog round the block.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. It's more just the click.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain today, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and I'm not short of breath. I had a headache this morning in the queue at the robot on the M4, gone by the time I parked. Otherwise I'm lekker.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headache settled, good. Are you taking any tablets, even stuff from the chemist?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Never been given blood pressure tablets. For the knee I take Panado, the five hundreds, two when it's sore. And my wife bought omega capsules at Dischem, big soft ones in a blue bottle, I can't tell you the proper name.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often is the Panado? And the omega dose, I didn't catch a number, the cursor's sitting in the dose box.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Panado maybe twice a week, only if the knee nags, not on a schedule. The omega, maybe a thousand something, I'm guessing. I take one most mornings.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): A thousand what? Repeat that, there was a noise at the door and I lost it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, scratch that, I was making the number up. I think it's fish oil. One capsule most mornings, except I forget about half the time, so don't write it down as every day.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or food? Penicillin, anything like that?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Prawns, peanuts, I'm fine with the lot.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink at all?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped smoking when my daughter was born, that's twelve years now. A beer or two at a braai on the weekend, that's it. My neighbour's Weber packed up and he borrowed my grid, whole story, you don't want it.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twelve years, and weekends only for the beer. Any diabetes, asthma, heart trouble, or operations?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes, no asthma, no heart trouble. They took my tonsils out when I was small, that's the only one. Appendix is still mine.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll just feel the knee while this thing thinks. Bend it for me. No swelling, it bends fully, and there's a bit of crepitus on the right, which is the click you mean.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, that's it. It's a sore ache, about a four out of ten, worse coming down the stairs, eases once I sit. I'm loading at the depot, on my feet the whole shift, so by lunch it's nagging.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not starting any blood pressure tablets today. The readings don't agree with each other, or with what you remember. And there's no chest pain or breathlessness with it.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, I'd rather avoid tablets if I can. The uncle thing still sits in the back of my mind, but if you say we wait, we wait. Should I be checking it at the house?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): It may be white coat, the way you describe it, but I can't properly call it that while the numbers are all over the show. Home readings are what we actually need.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): We've maybe still got my dad's old cuff in a cupboard. Or I can pop into Clicks, they're open late, after I fetch my daughter from netball.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Use a decent cuff, morning and evening, for two weeks. Sit quietly for a few minutes first, write every number down, and bring the list. Nothing from the pharmacy for blood pressure in the meantime.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning and evening, two weeks, write them down. And the form, though? HR is on my case already.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Book back with me in two weeks with that list, and I'll complete the depot form then. No scan for the knee today. If it's still catching you on the stairs when you're back, we'll look at it again.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. The pharmacy technician has left me your repeat list. This is that review, and you've asked for something stronger for the pain?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee, still?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's the pain been?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee worse since when?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Diwali. Or after.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Since Diwali, or after it. You can't pin it down?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't invent a date, then. Is the pain there most days?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walking, stairs, or both?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Both.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it wake you at night?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the knee?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the knee give way?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the knee stiff in the morning?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn, or pain in the stomach?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Quick look. Crepitus on bending the right knee, no effusion, and it's tender along the medial joint line.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry. Notes say osteoarthritis of that knee, for years.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Years.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operation on it, ever?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Working these days?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Retired.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Retired. Filthy weather, isn't it, the bus was late. Anyway, paracetamol one gram, two five-hundred milligram tablets, four times a day, for the knee. That the dose you use?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): And do you actually take all four doses?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes. Not really.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Prescribed four times a day, then, but I can't say you stick to it. Does the naproxen ease the knee?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a suppose. I won't record it as helping. What strength are you on?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Two-fifty.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Naproxen for the knee: you say two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day, and the pharmacy list says five hundred milligrams twice a day. They don't agree.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Two-fifty.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't guess which is right. When did you start the naproxen?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter. Or the one before.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last winter, or the one before. No date on that either. Omeprazole, ten— no, twenty milligrams each morning, for the stomach. Still on it?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine I nearly called ten milligrams. It's five milligrams once a day, for the blood pressure. Yes?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other tablets at home?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): The stronger painkiller, what did you want?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Codeine.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I keep turning over a flare, ordinary wear, or a bit of cartilage catching, and I am not going to conclude any of those today.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Tramadol?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): No tramadol, and no codeine. They'll doze you and bung you up, and they won't fix a worn knee. I'm declining both.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Hmm.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): From what you've told me and from the examination, my working impression is only this: the osteoarthritis is grumbling more, not a fresh injury.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll reissue the paracetamol, the omeprazole and the amlodipine. I'm holding the naproxen repeat until the strength is sorted. Bring the box next time.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take the paracetamol more regularly if you can, not just odd doses. No extra anti-inflammatory on top.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): I might send you for an x-ray of the right knee if it's no better in three months. Not booking it now.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in three months. If the pain gets worse before that, come back sooner.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): Saying it back: right knee pain worse since Diwali or after, most days, set off by walking and stairs, and it wakes you at night. Paracetamol one gram four times a day on the script, not reliably taken. Naproxen dose still disputed, two-fifty against five hundred, both twice daily. Omeprazole twenty each morning, amlodipine five once a day. No stronger painkiller. Anything twisted?
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): And you still can't put a time on the Diwali business, or on when the naproxen started?
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

Rules

- Record who said it (doctor, patient, nurse, caregiver, family_member, clinical_staff, unknown), in lower case.

- Doctor impressions are provisional or differential, and only if the doctor stated one. Do not add a diagnosis the doctor declined to give.

Transcript (encounter 00750)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I'm not sure what I've come about, to be honest. The hospital said to come back and see you after I was in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, you were in for a chest infection three weeks ago. How have you been since you came home? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand, grand. Only I've no appetite. None at all. I push the food around the plate.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Since the hospital? Or before it? Honestly, I couldn't say. I've been off my food a while.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): My trousers are loose, so I must have. A couple of stone, maybe? I don't weigh myself.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you feel sick, or does food stick, or does it hurt to eat? ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none of that. I'm just not hungry. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Mirtazapine, 15 mg, maybe? At bedtime, the little white one. And omeprazole, 20 mg in the morning.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the mirtazapine 15 mg, do you think? You said maybe.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): It could be 30. The chemist knows. I only take what they give me.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll check with the record. What's it for? ~
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): For my mood, after my wife died. Two years ago.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm very sorry. Any operations?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Gallbladder, in the nineties.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me weigh you, and check your numbers. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on then. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 82, blood pressure 118 over 72, temperature 36.6, oxygen 96 percent, and you weigh 64 kilos.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that a lot? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your record says 74 kilos a year ago, so you've lost about ten kilos, which is significant. Any cough or breathlessness left from the chest infection?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): A little cough in the morning. No breathlessness.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd say the main thing is poor appetite after your recent illness, in the setting of low mood, so I'd call it reduced appetite following illness.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Do you think it's my mood? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's likely part of it, but with that much weight loss, I don't want to assume. I'd like to arrange blood tests, to look for anaemia, thyroid, and other causes.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Meanwhile, small meals and snacks, six times a day, and a build-up drink between meals, rather than big plates.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I could manage a milky drink. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the idea. And try to eat with someone, if you can, a neighbour or a friend.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): My daughter comes on Sundays. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'd like to see you again in two weeks, and weigh you again.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Fine. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi. Mum said I had to come on my own, because she's at work and I'm fifteen. I've got chickenpox. At least I think so.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, I'll make sure we talk through everything. When did the spots start?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Three days ago. Now they're all over, but nothing in my mouth.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever or feeling unwell?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, I had a temperature the first day, and a headache. Not now.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what's been done about it so far? Let me go through what you're using.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Calamine lotion, on the spots. Paracetamol, 500 mg, when I'm hot, maybe three a day. Cetirizine, 10 mg at night, so I can sleep. My inhaler, the blue one, when I wheeze. And emollient cream, for my eczema, twice a day.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a lot, and it sounds sensible. Any conditions apart from the chickenpox?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Asthma, and eczema.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Just my tonsils, when I was eight.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you do sport, or go out anywhere?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I play netball. But obviously not now.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None that I know of.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Let me look at your spots. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): They're everywhere.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): There are red spots and blisters in different stages, some scabbed, over your chest, back and arms, and none look infected.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it definitely chickenpox? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, the pattern is typical.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh good. Am I contagious? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Until every spot has scabbed over, usually about five days after the spots began, so stay home.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): When can I go back to school? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): When all the spots have crusted over. Don't go near anyone who's pregnant, or has a weak immune system, or a newborn. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): My auntie is pregnant. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep away from her until you're better.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep taking the paracetamol, but avoid ibuprofen, it can make chickenpox skin infections worse, and with asthma, it's best avoided.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And keep your nails short. Try not to scratch. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): It's so itchy though. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): The cetirizine and the calamine are the right things. Cool baths help too. ~
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Will they scar? ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you don't scratch, most don't. ~
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back if the spots become red, swollen and sore, you get a high fever, breathing problems, or you can't keep fluids down.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. Thanks. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a second, this thing's installing an update. Mrs Kapoor? Have a seat. What brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing, if I'm honest. My daughter fusses over me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm her daughter, I live with her. She slid down twice and I wasn't going to ignore it.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Slid down? Say that again, I was on the wrong screen.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Twice. Once in the kitchen, once getting to the bathroom. She says it wasn't a fall, she slid.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It wasn't a fall. My legs went soft and I sort of sat down. I didn't hurt myself.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you black out at all? Any chest pain with it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I never blacked out, and there's no chest pain. I'm not ill.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about dizziness? Does the room spin, or do you go faint?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't get dizzy. Never have.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, bear with me, it's logged me out. Typical. So you're saying no dizziness?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, when I get up out of the armchair it goes a bit swimmy. A second or two. Not proper spinning. I hold on and it passes.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's every time she stands up quickly. She grabs the doorframe. And both times she went down she was white as a sheet for a minute.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): It passes if I hold the chair. I don't see the panic. I had a biscuit and got on with the crossword.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the swimmy feeling start? I need something for the notes.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't give you a date. Since Diwali, or after. Or last winter, or the one before. It's all a blur.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She won't be pinned down on the dizzy bit. The first slide was about three weeks ago, the second was last Thursday, after tea.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, three weeks or three months? The cursor jumped.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Three weeks. Not months. And last Thursday for the second one.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. I don't sit about counting them.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicines. The list on here is from last year and I don't trust it. What do you actually take?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A few blood pressure tablets, and something for sleep. I hardly take anything.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Three for her blood pressure every morning, and a sleeping tablet at night.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Slowly, please, I'm typing. Start with the amlodipine.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Amlodipine ten milligrams in the morning, ramipril five milligrams in the morning, and bendroflumethiazide two point five milligrams in the morning. Zopiclone three point seven five at bedtime for sleep, and the first three are all for her blood pressure.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The zopiclone I only take if I'm lying there awake. Not every night.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's meant to take it nightly. Some weeks the strip's empty, though, so I honestly don't know.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the sleeping tablet as it is today. Anything else, aspirin, a chemist buy?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just those. Morning ones with breakfast, regular as clockwork.
[SEG0030] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. I've done the lying and standing blood pressures.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Go on, and slowly. I'll put them in the wrong boxes otherwise.
[SEG0032] person_4 (NURSE): Lying, one hundred and forty-eight over eighty-two, pulse sixty-eight. Standing, after one minute, one hundred and eighteen over seventy, pulse eighty-four.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Standing one eighteen over seventy, pulse eighty-four? Lying one forty-eight over eighty-two, pulse sixty-eight?
[SEG0034] person_4 (NURSE): That's the one. She said the swimmy feeling came on as she stood, and it eased once she kept still. She didn't go down.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): See? It eased. You're all making a meal of it.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still a drop of thirty on the systolic when you stand. One forty-eight down to one eighteen.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): So that's why she's ending up on the floor?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think so. My impression is postural hypotension, her pressure falling when she stands, from the blood pressure tablets. Not a definite diagnosis until we see how she does on a lower dose, but it fits the sliding and the swimmy head.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I've had high blood pressure for donkey's years. That's hardly news.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, the hypertension is ongoing. The lying reading is still up, we're not ignoring it.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Cross me off, then, and I'll get the bus.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not yet. I want to change one tablet. Amlodipine down from ten milligrams to five milligrams, once each morning. Ramipril and bendroflumethiazide stay as they are.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Does she start the five tonight, or tomorrow?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tomorrow morning. I'll send the prescription through. Take today's ten as normal.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Five milligrams sounds a bit feeble. I'm not keeling over, you know.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a small step down, and the other two are still there. Get up in stages. Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before you stand, and don't rush for the phone.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is up the second the kettle boils. I'll have to nag.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not rush. I walk perfectly well, thank you.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): And don't let yourself dry out, it makes the drop worse. Tea is fine, within reason.
[SEG0050] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Could the zopiclone be adding to it? The bathroom one was after tea, though, not in the night.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): It might be contributing, but I'm only changing the amlodipine today. Leave the zopiclone dose alone. We can revisit it if the standing pressure is still falling next time.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. I like a proper night's sleep.
[SEG0053] person_4 (NURSE): Do you want another standing pressure, or am I done?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're done, thanks. No more obs today. I'll check it again when she's back.
[SEG0055] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And if she slides before then, do I ring you?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. If she slides again, blacks out, or the swimmy feeling isn't settling, come back sooner, don't wait the fortnight. Otherwise I'll see you in a fortnight.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. I'm still saying I slid. I did not fall. Put that down if you must.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We'll get the prescription on the way out. Come on, Mum, mind the step.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Down, yes. Up is grand. At night if I roll over it catches me fierce.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit puffy some evenings, not every day. My sister says I should be doing the exercises off the telly, but I haven't the patience for that fella on the morning programme.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, a bit, of an evening.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stiff in the morning?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): About twenty minutes, then it eases once I'm pottering in the kitchen.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It doesn't give way, and it hasn't locked.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it?
