[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which tablets? Say that again, I was typing.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, the four hundred milligram ones. One tablet, maybe two or three times in the week.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble with them?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no stomach problems at all. I'm grand that way.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your weight — the last reading on here is 89 kilos. Still about that?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): God. I was twelve stone for years. I'm after putting on with the baking, the grandchildren come of a Sunday and I make the queen cakes.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So heavier than that. Any idea what you weigh now?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't a scales. A few kilos more, I'd say, but I wouldn't know exactly.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): The extra weight loads the knee, especially on stairs.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I know. Easier said than done, with the cakes.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Up on the couch and I'll have a look.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Mind the shoes, they're mucky from the garden.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's crepitus when I bend the right knee. No big effusion that I can feel. Tender on the medial joint line.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the very spot.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Flexion stops around a hundred degrees. No redness, and the foot pulses are fine.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): It won't fold back like the left one. I was worried it was the circulation — my father had the bad legs.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vascular trouble, was it?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): He had the bypass in his seventies. Smoked like a chimney. I never smoked, thank God.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any bother in the other joints, the hips or the hands?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): The hands are grand. The left knee is a small bit achey if I walk the whole way to the shops, nothing like the right.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): How far can you walk?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I can manage the shops. It's the stairs and the night that annoy me. Oh, and I do get heartburn of an evening, especially if I've taken one of those tablets.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn. You said there was no stomach trouble.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I wasn't counting that. It's a burning after the tea, up in the chest, not a pain in the belly. I take Rennies for it.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often is it, and how long has it been going on? The cursor stuck — say that again.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Most evenings lately. A couple of months, maybe. I can't put a date on when it started.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the Rennies, how do you take them?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Two tablets when it comes on. Not every night. They settle it mostly.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, or black stools?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. The stools are a normal colour.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines — blood pressure tablets or the like?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the gel, the ibuprofen and the Rennies. Beaumont put me on a statin years ago and I stopped it, the legs were aching and I never went back.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which statin, what dose? The medication list won't load.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. Twenty milligrams — or was it ten? I think twenty. Stopped two years ago.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll record atorvastatin 20 mg, stopped. We'll revisit that another day, not this morning.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Does the knee need an operation? The neighbour waited ages for her replacement.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't be talking surgery. It sounds like wear and tear, osteoarthritis of the right knee, though I've no x-ray today to confirm it.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it the physio, or one of those injections?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might try physiotherapy, or a steroid injection into the joint, but we won't decide that today.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): And the tablets, and the weight?
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off the ibuprofen while the heartburn is about; if you take one, take it with food. Keep the diclofenac gel two or three times a day, and try to drop a couple of kilos. If the knee is no better in six weeks, come back and we'll choose between the physio and the injection.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, Mr Hale. The slip from the desk just says back, so start wherever you like. Is this your wife with you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sandra. I booked him in, or he'd still be at work pretending he's fine.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Back.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Low back, or higher?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Low.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left, right, or both?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Left.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long now?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Three.
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's rounding it down. We moved house eight weeks ago, and it started that weekend, shifting wardrobes and boxes.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What sort of work is it you do?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Warehouse.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heavy lifting in the warehouse, and that flares the pain?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Score it out of ten.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Seven.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Constant, or on and off?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Constant.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything take the edge off?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Lying.
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sofa every night. The dog's furious about the missed walks, and that animal thinks it runs the house.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dog out of the notes.
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll be glad someone said it. Right, back to the back.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say the pain back to you. Left-sided low back pain, constant, seven out of ten, worse with lifting, eased by lying down. On timing you said three weeks and Sandra said eight, since the move, so I'll call it approximately three to eight weeks, not a precise date.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it travel into a leg?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Leg.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): The leg pain, which leg, and how far down does it go?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Left calf.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Painkillers. What have you actually taken?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength are the tablets?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Two hundred.
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He buys four hundred milligram ibuprofen and takes two of them when it's bad.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So for the ibuprofen I can't tell whether a dose is two hundred or eight hundred milligrams. I won't record a dose.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you taking them three times a day, as the packet usually says?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He isn't taking them three times a day. He forgets, then he has a handful at bedtime.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): So whether he takes them as directed is anyone's guess. Any other regular medicines?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Blood pressure.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you know its name?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): White one.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Little white blood pressure tablet, every morning, for years. I almost called it amlodipine and that's me guessing, so scrub that.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Unnamed blood pressure tablet it is. You've got high blood pressure, yes?
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the legs or feet?
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Problems with the waterworks at all?
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Parking.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not the car park. Passing urine. Hesitancy, leaking, anything like that?
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight down without trying?
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are your clothes looser?
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll treat that as not a proper yes. No weight loss recorded. Fevers, or drenching sweats?
[SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowel accidents, or numbness around the saddle, the groin and back passage?
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the couch, please. Looking at you, lumbar flexion is limited, and you're tender in the left lower lumbar muscles.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise on the left reproduces the calf pain at about fifty degrees. Power at the ankle and big toe is normal, no foot drop, and light touch on the foot is intact.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking mechanical low back pain, nothing alarming in the answers so far. Plan A, then: no scan, stay on the ibuprofen, I refer you to physio now, and I see you in six weeks.
[SEG0065] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hang on. The toes. Tell the doctor what the van does.
[SEG0066] person_3 (PATIENT): Tingle.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said no numbness a minute ago. Which toes, and is it tingling?
[SEG0068] person_3 (PATIENT): Left. Sometimes.
[SEG0069] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Left toes go tingly in the van. And the pain wakes him most nights. He's been up at two again.
[SEG0070] person_3 (PATIENT): Wakes.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): That new bit changes my mind. Scrap the immediate physio and the six-week review. The toe symptoms push this past a simple strain.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the ibuprofen. Start paracetamol, one gram by mouth, four times a day, for the back pain. I did wonder about naproxen five hundred milligrams twice a day and I'm not doing that, not with the blood pressure tablet and an anti-inflammatory already.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange an MRI of the lumbar spine because of the left calf pain and the tingling toes. My working impression is mechanical low back pain with possible left nerve root irritation. A disc prolapse is on the differential, not a diagnosis I'll stamp today.
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the scan is clear, we might refer you to physio afterwards. Keep moving gently, no heavy warehouse lifting until the scan is back, and if you cannot pass urine, develop saddle numbness, or a leg gives way, go to A&E the same day.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in two weeks.
[SEG0076] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will.
[SEG0077] person_3 (PATIENT): Ta.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're late, the tram was a shocker. This is Oscar, he's thirteen.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No worries, come on through. What can I do for him today?
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A kid in his class has measles, and now he's got a rash and he's been really hot.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm not sick. It's nothing.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oscar, I'd like to hear it from you too. How have you been feeling, mate?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Can we get Maccas after this.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll see about that later. Mum, when did this fever actually start?
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Saturday arvo. So, um, four days. I checked him that night and the chemist one said thirty nine, well actually it beeped at thirty nine.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah. It was like one day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, so between the two of you it's somewhere from one day to four days, and we won't pin it harder than that. When did the rash show up?
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yesterday. Started behind his ears and then, yeah, all over the chest by bedtime.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Just a couple of spots. They don't bug me.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or a runny nose, or sore eyes with it?
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough and no runny nose. His eyes have been red though, and the light's been annoying him.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting or diarrhoea? Sore throat?
[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting, no diarrhoea. His throat's been a bit scratchy.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oscar, what have you had for the fever, any medicine?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): I take amladipine for the pressure, five milligrams in the morning, the cholesterol one at night, sugar tablets, and only the ayurvedic powder in the morning.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Those sound like your regular ones. I was asking about something for this fever, Panadol or Nurofen. Mum, has he had any?
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Panadol, yeah. Two tablets, um, two fifty? No, five hundred milligrams each, every six hours, since Saturday. He does take them.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta. Any trouble with his breathing, or pain in the tummy?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): We had pizza last night.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll ask that one again. Any breathing trouble or tummy pain?
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, breathing's been fine and his tummy's fine. He did have pizza, that's true, but no pain.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are the immunisations, the measles one especially?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, I reckon he's had the jabs. The blue book's in the kitchen drawer. He might've missed the one around four, uh I'm not sure.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that as not clear and chase the record. Oscar, just so I know the family background, has anyone in the family had ongoing illnesses?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's useful. And what's a normal week look like for you, school, food, all that?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): I pack shelves at the supermarket on Saturdays, about five hours, I pretty much live on two-minute noodles, I don't exercise, and I don't touch alcohol.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. I'm going to have a look at you now, Oscar. Shirt up if that's okay.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Whatever. Hurry up.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temp is thirty eight point four, pulse a hundred and twenty, breathing twenty two, oxygen ninety eight percent, and blood pressure one hundred and ten over seventy.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a blotchy red rash over the face, behind the ears and across the trunk. Inside the cheeks I can see small white spots, those are Koplik spots. Chest is clear and the neck isn't stiff.
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Those white spots, is that bad?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): They fit with measles, along with the timing. If we go with your four days of fever, today is day four, and the rash came yesterday which is about day three, and that's the classic window. I can't call it confirmed yet. It might still be another viral rash, but measles is the one I'm most worried about given the classmate.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): I said I'm fine.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I hear you, mate, and I still want to be careful. We'll keep you home from school, no visitors, especially no babies and no one who's pregnant, until four days after the rash began.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So that's through the weekend, yeah?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, rash day one was yesterday, so stay isolated until four full days from then. I'll notify the public health unit today, measles is notifiable.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll also arrange a measles PCR swab with pathology today. If that swab doesn't sort it out we might add a blood test later.
[SEG0042] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Do I keep the Panadol going?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, same two tablets every six hours if he's hot or sore, and push fluids. If he's drowsy, struggling to breathe, or not drinking, go straight to emergency, don't wait for me.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Can we go now.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nearly. I'll book a review here in three days, or sooner if you're worried. Can you bring the blue book next time so we can check the measles vaccine properly?
[SEG0046] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yep, I'll dig it out. Thanks for not rushing us.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Any questions before you head off?
[SEG0048] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, I think I've got it. Home, no school, swab today, back in three days.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Finally.

[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, six weeks. No, hang on, it started before the long weekend, so closer to two months.

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. I can still do a full shift though.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mrs Fourie. Shame, long wait hey. Shoes off, on the scale before Dr Naidoo sees you.

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I told her to leave earlier. I stay with her, so I came along. Ag, we're here.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Weight is fifty-four, ag sorry, I misread it, fifty-two kilograms. Last time in March you were sixty-eight. Your last pressure was one-forty, and today it's one oh nine over seventy-seven. Pulse eighty-four, temperature thirty-eight point three degrees.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty-eight? Eish. I don't know, sister. My clothes feel the same to me.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. He's free now. Sharp, in you go, I'll leave the chart.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Howzit. Dr Naidoo. Sit, please. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this pain, doctor, up on the right of my stomach, under the ribs. Quite bad, it comes on after fatty food and then it lasts for hours. The antacid takes the edge off a bit, not all the way.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me about an episode, from the start, what sets it...
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. It comes after fatty food. Vetkoek, boerewors, the fried chicken. Then it sits there for...
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): For hours. She holds her side half the night.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Hours. Sometimes the whole evening. I don't know the number.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): And when did it all begin?
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): About three weeks. Since the braai at Uncle Piet's. She was alright before that.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, no, Lindi, it was longer than that braai. I don't know, doctor, maybe two months? I can't say the day, I really don't know.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Somewhere between three weeks and two months, then, and nobody can give me the date. We'll leave it. Do you vomit when it comes?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Once. That night I brought everything up. Not again since.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the vomit?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. There was no blood.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yellow eyes, or a yellow colour in the skin?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I looked in the mirror. Not yellow.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does it travel to the shoulder, or through to your back?
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She said it goes...
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, let me. Not the shoulder. The back I don't know, doctor. I sit all day doing admin at the primary school, so maybe I'm just stiff.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain, and my breathing is fine.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about the waterworks?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No trouble there. That's fine.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Dark urine, pale stools, anything like that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I don't look. Sorry.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then I won't write it. Have you had any operations?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never had surgery.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Our mother had her gallbladder out, though. She always said the pain was like this.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Mom had the gallbladder surgery, in Durban. I don't know which year.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Useful. And medicines, what do you take?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Only that antacid liquid from the chemist. Gaviskon, I call it. I don't know, doctor, maybe ten mils when the pain comes. It takes the edge off, not completely.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Gaviscon, you mean. You drink it when the pain comes. Is ten mils definite?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Maybe ten mils. The little cup confuses me. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the dose is uncertain, we'll say maybe ten mils and not dress it up. Anything else, even a supermarket tablet?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just that.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or food? Swelling, rash?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't have any.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Onto the bed for me, knees a little bent. I'm going to press under the right ribs.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Ow. That's it, right there. Not the left.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tender in the right upper abdomen, and it catches when you breathe in. The rest is soft, no guarding. Your eyes aren't yellow, and there's no rash on the skin.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): So maybe it's just indigestion? I don't know, doctor. I was hoping for something small.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll think out loud. Pain for hours under the right ribs after fatty meals, you vomited once, your mother had the gallbladder removed, and you're sitting at thirty-eight point three. Most likely biliary colic, a stone irritating the gallbladder. I can't lock that in without tests.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): The Gaviscon helping a little keeps a gastritis on the list, though I think it's less likely. Fatty meals pull me toward the gallbladder, not the stomach. Tests will have to decide.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm booking blood tests today, liver functions and a full blood count, and an abdominal ultrasound, the sonar, for the gallbladder. The sonar will be booked within the week. These are arranged, not a wait-and-see.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods today? I have to fetch my boy from soccer at four. I don't know if I make it.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): Lab's just down the passage, Mrs Fourie. I'll take you straight after, it isn't long. Sonar is a different day.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cut the fatty meals for now, the vetkoek and boerewors and fried chicken, and keep the Gaviscon when it bites. Come back in two weeks for the results, whether you feel better or not. If the pain gets savage, or you can't stop vomiting, or you turn yellow, go to casualty and don't wait for that visit.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Two weeks. If the sonar is normal, then what? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then we rethink, simple as that. And Lindi, before you ask, no operation talk today just because mom had one. Far too early. Sister, she's ready for the bloods.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I can't smell anything. It's the strangest thing. Nothing. I had a cold in September and it never came back.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Eleven weeks. I counted, because I'm a chef, and it's a nightmare. I can't taste, either. Everything tastes of cardboard.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your nose blocked as well?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit, on the left, on and off. And a bit of post-nasal drip.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or pain in your face?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever, and no face pain.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bang on the head before this started?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I'd have remembered that. Oh, did I mention I've lost my keys?
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's stick with the nose for now. What do you use for it?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): A steroid nasal spray, fluticasone, two sprays each nostril once a day, and cetirizine, 10 mg, for my hay fever.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any other conditions?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Hay fever, as I said, and asthma.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any previous nose operations?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, my septum was straightened. Septoplasty. In 2015.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I gave up four years ago. Twenty a day, for years, before that.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me take your pulse, pressure and so on. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 70, blood pressure 124 over 80, temperature 36.6, oxygen 99 percent, breathing 14 a minute.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm all right then. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze or breathlessness, with the asthma?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, the asthma's quiet. No wheeze.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to give this a name just yet. A cold can damage the smell nerves for a time, and mostly it comes back, but at eleven weeks, I want to look properly. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange a smell identification test, where you sniff a set of scratch-and-sniff cards.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): That sounds fun. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'd like to arrange a CT scan of your sinuses, to check there's no blockage.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Is it permanent? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Often not. Smell training, sniffing four strong scents twice a day, like rose, lemon, clove and eucalyptus, helps nerves recover.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got those in the pantry. Cloves, lemon. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. Keep using the nasal spray, and make sure your smoke and gas alarms are working, since you can't smell a leak.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, that's a good point. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in four weeks, after the tests.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Right. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I notice it more with movement.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): It happens on and off. There was pain spreading all over yes but that went away.

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I take Asthalin inhaler when needed for my asthma. It's ibuprofen 600 milligrams three times a day. Erm I had pantoprazole at one point but I'm off it now.

[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): have you been to theatre before?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Let me think uh yes I had a bunion operation six years ago.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): do you have any long-term conditions?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Asthma, for about ten years. Actually, I have acid reflux, for about ten years
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): okay I can see acid reflux in your file as well

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I hardly move around during the day
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What does a normal day of food look like?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Lots of rice, lentils and some fruit
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you get blood in the vomit, fever or diarrhoea?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So, no, no blood in the vomit, fever or diarrhoea.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): good you can sit up again. So based on the the history and the examination this is probably a perforated stomach ulcer. I can't rule out pancreatitis yet

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi, doctor, I came as soon as they called me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright, take a seat. What can I do for you?
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I mean, doctor, I'm just here to help with the details.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, doctor, it's a band-like headache. It's getting on my nerves now.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me take your readings now.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, this won't take long...
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: temperature 36.6, blood pressure 115 over 81, pulse is 86 beats a minute. How long has it been like this?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): It's been three weeks now.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Would you say mild, moderate or severe?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, it's... hard to say, it's kind of... I don't know—
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take your time. Mild, moderate, or severe, if you had to pick?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly moderate.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, you know, and the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Actually, tell the doctor about the other thing, that's what worries me.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I was getting to that!
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been a tight scalp too?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, uh, about the same, six months.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been a bit of nausea too?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, yes.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Would you say mild, moderate or severe?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): A eight out of ten, I suppose.
[SEG0022] person_5 (UNKNOWN): Yes, that's right, that's how it was.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any fever or vomiting?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no fever, no vomiting. I did have trouble sleeping at one point, but that went away on its own.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check a few things. Any blurred vision, weakness, head injury or jaw pain on chewing?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none of those at all.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): On the cardiac side, anything I should know?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, you know, no, that's been fine.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's on your current medicine list?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, it's a... um, I can't remember what it's called. It's a little pink tablet.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, for my migraines, I believe. My wife sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given. It's, It's escitalopram, 10 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0033] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, I think the last prescription for the escitalopram was 5 milligrams. We changed it at the last visit.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, I see. Is the most recent prescription on you?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think I have it with me. I take something called carv... carvedilol, 6.25 milligrams, maybe, twice a day.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you got the box or the prescription on you?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, um, so no, it's at home. I'm on paracetamol, 500 milligrams, most days. Diclofenac I don't take anymore.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your medical history?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): I have migraines. I have anxiety.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): I have heart failure. I've had arthritis in my knees for two years now.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay. Alright, migraines and anxiety, that matches what I have here. Anything surgical in your history?
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): I had my tonsils removed as a teenager. A neighbour of mine said I should see someone about it. Work has been very busy so I kept ignoring it.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): I only drink at family occasions.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, do you follow any particular diet?
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm vegetarian and have been for years.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): How active are you?
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): I hardly move around during the day.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to tablets, food or anything in the environment?
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Plasters. I come out in... well, a red itchy rash. Yes, erythromycin. I get bad stomach cramps.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Listening to the whole story, I think we're dealing with tension-type headaches with possible medication overuse at this stage. I want to be honest that this is an impression, not a final answer. I can't rule out a posture-related neck problem yet. It could also be migraine, so we'll keep that open. I want blood tests done, that's for headache.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's get a headache diary, for frequent headaches. The result will help us decide whether anything more is needed.
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): Does it hurt?
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short breaks from the screen every hour and some neck stretches. Try to limit painkillers to two days a week and keep a diary of the headaches. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0056] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, will do.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's plan a check in four weeks. I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0058] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, uh, I think I understand everything. Thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. You're a bit early, the doctor's still busy. I'll take your blood pressure while you wait.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, whatever. This is a fuss over nothing.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): One forty eight over eighty six. Pulse seventy eight, regular. Your daughter phoned the desk as well. She says one morning last week you were confused, couldn't find the kettle, talking all over the show.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish. I was half asleep. I was not confused. She dramatises everything.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in. Sit. What's the problem today?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): My daughter made the booking. She fusses. I told her it's nothing.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): What is the nothing?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): In the mornings I get a bit clammy, sweaty, and my hands go shaky. Before I eat. It's minor.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. A few weeks. Maybe a month. I don't count.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Most mornings, ja. Not if I sleep late and I actually eat. So, nothing really.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any dizziness?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not dizzy.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough, tight chest, or short of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you lost any weight?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mmm. Hard to say. Maybe. The trousers still fit, so no, not really. I don't know.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're diabetic. Still on the tablets?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. The gliklazide and the metforman.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Gliclazide, what dose?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighty milligram. One tablet in the morning when I get up.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): With food?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): With rooibos. I skip breakfast. Porridge sits too heavy, so I eat later, a pie at the shop.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Metformin, dose and how often?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Five hundred milligrams, twice a day. Morning, and with supper. I do eat supper, so that one I don't miss.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Vitamins from the chemist, sitting in the cupboard. I never take them.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Last blood test, what did they tell you?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): At the day hospital, a good while back. They said the H B A one C was borderline. I don't remember a number, I threw the paper out. So I'm fine, hey.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long diabetic?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Twelve years, about. From when I retired off the railways.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Living alone?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Flat in the complex. My girl is in Alberton, she pitches up uninvited. Load shedding killed the gate motor last week, that's the actual problem.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): When the sweats come, hungry or just shaky?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Hungry, not really. Shaky, and sweaty on the chest and the back of the neck. Tea and a biscuit, I sit, it eases.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blacked out?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): She reported confusion. Did that happen?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag no. I found the kettle, I was just tired and slow. Not confused. I'm seventy two, not ninety.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pouring the tea, hands steady?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, well, actually, no. The kitchen goes swimmy and I grab the counter, the cup spills. So ja, dizzy, a little, seconds only, and something sweet and it's gone. I didn't reckon that counted.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): It counts. Arms forward, steady now, skin dry and not clammy. Pulse regular, no extra beats. Chest clear.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Morning sweats and the shakes, on gliclazide, no breakfast. Sounds like a low blood sugar. Working idea only, not confirmed.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Low sugar. Ag, I doubt it. I feel lekker right now.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Doses stay as they are. Gliclazide eighty milligrams every morning, metformin five hundred twice a day. Eat something proper before the gliclazide, not just the rooibos.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you get shaky, take sugar or juice, sit, and don't drive until it has settled.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bloods are booked. HbA1c, a glucose, and kidney function because of the metformin. Come back in two weeks for the results, that visit is booked as well.
[SEG0051] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sharp. I'll put the bloods on for Thursday morning at the lab, and the review in two weeks.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Thursday for the bloods, review in two weeks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. She's still making a big thing of a small thing.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through. I'll get that dressing off before Dr Okonkwo sees you, so we're not faffing about.

[SEG0008] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Pauline, her mum. She sent a photo at tea time and I said we're not sitting on that till next week.

[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the wound hurt?

[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Deeper pain in the tummy? Stinging when you pass urine?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Wee's fine. Tummy's just the usual ache from the section, I think. I don't really know what's normal.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, or diarrhoea?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No sickness. Bowels have been slow since the op, the whole time. No diarrhoea.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the discharge smell of anything?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Can't really tell. Yellow patch on the pad, about a fifty-pence piece.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll say it back. Ten days after the caesarean, lower wound redder since yesterday, small yellow discharge, tender to touch and on standing. Temperature 38.2 last night with a short shiver, and you still looked flushed this morning. Urine normal, no vomiting, bowels sluggish since surgery, no diarrhoea. Fair?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. That's all of it, I think.
[SEG0022] person_1 (NURSE): For the record, skin was warm and red about three centimetres around the lower third. Upper half dry and healing. Small yellow serous ooze, no pus pocket, edges still held together.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Did they send antibiotics home with you?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Co-amoxiclav, the big ones, 625, three times a day. Five days... or was it seven? I don't know, doctor. I finished the packet.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): 625 three times daily, packet finished, no missed doses — but five versus seven days, you can't say.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The midwife did say. It's just gone out of my head.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Letter's in the nappy bag. I skimmed it in the car park and thought seven days, but don't quote me.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't hang the plan on a car-park skim. Bring the letter next time if you can find it. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Different thing — they've started me on metformin, for my diabetes. Mine, not hers. I only say it in case it runs in the family.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Metformin does not go on her list. I will note mother with type 2 diabetes.
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Found last spring. Tablets, nothing else.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): And you — any illnesses or operations before this pregnancy?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I was fit. First baby. Planned section because she was breech, not an emergency.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are feeding and sleep, aside from the wound?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Breastfeeding, and she's managing. I'm shattered, but that's being up every two hours, not the scar.
[SEG0037] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The ring road was the other problem. Solid from the retail park, rain coming down, forty minutes of brake lights.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Those temporary lights have been awful all week. Same queue got me yesterday.
[SEG0039] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Did you see the cricket last night, sat in the car? England were a shambles.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Last hour only. I still don't know how he held that catch at midwicket. Then the tail folded, predictably.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Had it on between feeds. Couldn't tell you the score, or who was even in.
[SEG0042] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We lost, love. Rant can wait till the drive home.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right — wound and tummy now. I'll be gentle.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lower end red and a little warm, small serous ooze, nothing fluctuant underneath. Uterus feels appropriate for day ten, abdomen soft, not peritonitic.

[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll swab the wound now and send it to the lab, then a fresh dressing. I'll see you back in clinic in three days, swab result or not, to check this is settling.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): And if the fever comes back tonight?
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the fever climbs, the redness races off, you feel properly unwell, or the wound opens up, go to A&E, don't wait for the appointment. A home temperature over 38 is worth acting on, not sleeping through.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Swab first, then I'll redress it. Little scratch and we're finished.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Pop yourself down and I'll grab a blood pressure before he starts. Bit of a queue out there, I'm afraid.

[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Right arm, ta. There we go. One hundred and fifty-two over eighty-eight, and your pulse is seventy-six. I'll stick that on the screen.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not bad, is it. I've had worse at the chemist.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, just logging in, this thing's taking an age. What was the blood pressure again?
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): One fifty-two over eighty-eight, pulse seventy-six. He's all yours. I'll be outside if you want the ECG machine.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Sixty-four, according to this. Sorry, what have you come in for today?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the check-up. You lot sent a letter. I'm fine, honestly. Waste of your time.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the screen's jumped. A check-up, you said?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Routine. Nothing doing.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain at all?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I don't do chest pain.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. And what about when you're walking, any tightness?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I said I'm fine. Bit of a busy morning, the car park was a nightmare, that's all.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the car park?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, some bloke in a van blocked the bay. Not medical. Forget it.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Let me just... the template wants me to ask again. Any pain in the chest when you exert yourself?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Pain, no. I wouldn't call it pain.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): What would you call it, then?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, if I'm honest, going up the stairs at home, or if I walk fast to the bus, there's a sort of tight feeling across the chest. It's nothing, and it goes if I slow down.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again, I was typing. Tight where?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Across the chest. Only if I push it, stairs or walking quick. Stops when I stop. It's not a big deal.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Couldn't tell you. Last winter, or the one before. Somewhere round then. I don't keep a diary.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Last winter or the winter before that?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't know. One of those. It's been a while, not yesterday, put it that way.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you breathless with it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not breathless. I can talk. It's just tight, then it's gone.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does it go down your arm, or make you sweaty or sick?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none of that. No arm, no sweat, no feeling sick. Like I said, minor.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any palpitations, heart racing?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Heart's fine. Steady.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dizziness?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Head's clear.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure one. Ramipril, five milligrams... no, hang on, they put it up, it's ten milligrams. One in the morning.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ten milligrams of ramipril, once a day. Anything else?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin. Seventy-five. I take it on and off, not every day. When I remember, which isn't always.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, aspirin how often? The screen lagged.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): On and off. Some weeks most days, some weeks I forget the packet's in the cupboard. It's the seventy-five milligram one.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): And you've been on the ramipril how long?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Years. The blood pressure's been going on for years, since after I retired, or maybe before that. I couldn't put a date on it, don't ask me the year.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else from the chemist?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just those two. Oh, and last time they did my cholesterol they said it was borderline. Didn't give me a number, just borderline, and that was ages ago.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Borderline cholesterol, but you don't have the figure. When was that test?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea. Not this year. They never started me on anything for it.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Gave up years back. Used to, don't now. Maybe a pint at the weekend, that's it, don't make a thing of it.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, a weekend pint. And you live... sorry, ignore that, a box just popped up. Let me listen to your chest.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on then. I told you it's nothing.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, no crackles. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Pulse feels regular.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): There you are. Fit as anything.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not so sure. That tight feeling on the stairs and when you walk fast, I'm thinking it could be angina, provisional mind you. I need the tests before I'd call it certain.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina. That's dramatic. It's a niggle.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll do an ECG today, the nurse can run it, and I'll send you for bloods: cholesterol, kidney function and a sugar.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): More needles. Fine.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled, or if the ECG is off, we might arrange a scan, a CT of the arteries. Not booking that today.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): So maybe a scan, maybe not. Typical.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): Exactly, only if we need it. Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through the results.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If I remember.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): And if that tightness comes on at rest, or it lasts more than a few minutes and doesn't ease when you stop, ring nine nine nine. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. I hear you. I won't, but I hear you.
[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep taking the ramipril every morning. And try to take the aspirin daily, not just when you remember, same seventy-five.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. No promises. The aspirin routine's never stuck.
[SEG0065] person_1 (NURSE): I'll set the ECG up in the side room when you're done. The bloods form is printing.
[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks. That's us for now.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Cheers. See you in two weeks, I suppose, if the car park lets me in.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ugh, sorry we're late, the elevator got stuck and he would not keep his coat on. Um, we're here because Leo's got a rash and a fever.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, come on in. Hey Leo. Mom, just tell me the story in your own words, no rush.
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. Well, the fever came first. I thought it started Saturday, but actually I don't know, it might've been Friday night. He was hot and super cranky.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was Friday. I had him after school Friday and he was warm, flushed warm, and just wiped out. Not Saturday.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Today's Wednesday, so that lands the fever at about four or five days, and we won't pin it tighter than that. When did the rash show up?
[SEG0006] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sunday morning, for sure. Started on his face, then it, um, crept down his chest and his arms. Three days of spots.
[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): Itchy.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Itchy spots. Leo, does your head hurt as well, or is it just the itch?
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been sleeping on the couch instead of playing. And his eyes went pink yesterday.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, and he keeps scratching his belly. Dana stays with us on school nights, so she's seen more of this than I have.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Leo, have you been coughing at all?
[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm. Oh, his dinosaur backpack is still in the car, I'll grab it after. Sorry.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about his stomach. Any vomiting, or loose stools?
[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. He didn't throw up. He had one loose stool this morning, I don't know if that even counts.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): And ears or throat, anything going on there?
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nothing. No ear pain, and he's been eating popsicles, no sore throat.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has he been on any medicine for this?
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Children's tylenol. Err, a hundred and sixty milligrams, I almost said one-twenty but no, the bottle says 160. Every six hours for the fever, and I stopped it this morning cause I got scared the rash was from the medicine.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh, and my sister would not stop texting me to give him benedryl. We never gave it. Not once.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about, medicines or anything else?
[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing he's reacted to.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright Leo, I'm going to take a look. You can stay on mom's lap. Temp here is 101.4, heart rate 128, oxygen sat 98 percent, and he's breathing about 22 times a minute.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a red blotchy rash on his face, chest, and both arms. Eyes are a little bloodshot on both sides. Throat's mildly pink, no pus. I don't see any Koplik spots inside the cheeks. Lungs are clear.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Honestly I was going to swab his throat for strep today and start amoxicilin, 400 milligrams twice a day. Scarlet fever was sitting on my list.
[SEG0027] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh. Um, before you do that. A kid in his class, Jordan, was out with the measles. That's why I panicked and came in. I don't know if Leo's shots cover it.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The school email said measles, yeah. Confirmed, not just a rumor. And the vaccine card, we couldn't find it. Mom thinks maybe he only had the baby shots.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. That changes things. Let me count it out. Classmate with measles, rash started Sunday, so if he was exposed about ten days before that, we're inside the seven to fourteen day window, and with the MMR up in the air I am not treating this as strep.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): So no antibiotic, and we'll skip the strep swab. What I want instead is a measles igm blood test. The nurse draws it Thursday morning at eight. He can eat a normal breakfast, no fasting.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): If that igm comes back borderline, then we do a PCR swab. Not before. And if the fever and the rash do not settle over the next few days, we might get a chest x-ray. I'm not ordering that now.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in one week either way, so we can go over those bloods. Keep him home, no school and no playdates, through Thursday, that's four days after the rash started. If he gets worse before the blood draw, call us, don't wait.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll notify the health department today about a suspected case. My working read is possible measles, but it could still be some other viral rash. I can't lock it in until the bloods come back. Leo, you were brave.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Give me a sec, this login's spinning again. Right, what's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's honestly nothing. Just a bit of burning when I wee, and I nearly cancelled.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? I was on the wrong screen.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Burning when I wee. Mild. I reckon it'll sort itself.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't listen to her. She's been pulling a face every time she goes to the loo, so I dragged her in. We also spent twenty minutes hunting for a park, absolute nightmare.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's the burning been there?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a couple of days. Not long. It's not like I'm crook.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You brought it up Sunday, before we went to Mum's.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, Sunday. Two days of that burning. Whatever, it's minor.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): First time, or has this happened before?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Third time this year. Same little sting, then it goes.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, maybe the fourth. I forgot the one after Easter. Still nothing dramatic.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Pain in your back, under the ribs?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever, no back pain. I'm fine.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood in the wee? Vomiting?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. No blood, and I'm not vomiting. Just the sting, and it's not even bad.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any discharge or itching vaginally?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Can we not go there, it's embarrassing, it's just the urine.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Sounds straightforward. I'll do you a script for trimethoprim, 300 milligrams at night for three nights, and treat it as a simple waterworks infection.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hang on, you haven't told him about the capsules.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, it's nothing. I took some leftover antibiotic from her cupboard. Stupid, I know.
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Cephalexin. They were mine, left from a boil back in June. I didn't exactly hand them over.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, what did you take? This screen just pinged and I lost the last bit.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Keflex, for the burning. I think they were 500 milligram capsules. One in the morning and one at night for two days, then I stopped. They made me feel a bit off, and I felt silly.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): There was amoxicillin in there as well. Did you take any?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I never took the amoxicillin. Left it shut.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you take regularly? Allergies?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I was on Levlen, the pill. I stopped it in March. No allergies.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hiprex, or Ural from the chemist?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Never taken Hiprex. Didn't touch Ural either.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And you still haven't said the other bit. In the car you told me it was itchy.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): God, okay. A little bit itchy, and a tiny bit of discharge. It's embarrassing and it's barely there, I don't reckon it matters.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that once more? Vaginal itch and some discharge?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. A tiny amount. Can we move on. I've got a shift at the cafe this arvo.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Honestly I don't need a big workup. It'll pass.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's maybe the fourth time and she's already had my antibiotic. You should test it, yeah?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, hang on. Scratch the trimethoprim, I'm not prescribing that now. With someone else's antibiotic already in the mix, and this itch, I want a culture before more tablets. We'll send a midstream urine off today.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Working idea is another lower urine infection, but I can't rule out thrush as well. Come back if it's not better in three days, sooner if you get a fever or pain in the loin. Don't take anyone else's antibiotics, and drink plenty of water.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late. The bus never showed and then the wee one kicked off outside, so.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand, sit in. Err, give me a second, this computer's after freezing again.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We were stuck out there an age. She's wrecked, up half the night.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Right. Sorry, say the surname again, it's hopped off the screen... ah leave it. What has you in today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The itch. Between me fingers and around me waist. It's fierce, worse at night, and I can't sleep with it.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): The waist, say that bit again. I was half looking at this yoke.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Around me waist, where the elastic sits. And in between the fingers. I'm scratching the skin off nearly. It's doing me head in.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long is it going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. About two weeks. Well, actually I can't pin the day, it just sort of crept up.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No, it's three weeks. She was at it before the bank holiday, I mind the Monday.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right so, somewhere between two and three weeks, we'll not row over it. Any fever, were you hot at all with it?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm just tired and cross. Can we move on?
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to creams or tablets? Anything that brought you out in a rash?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you tried on it?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Piriton from the chemist, the 4 milligram ones, at night. I stopped them last week, they made me pure dopey. Someone mentioned prednisolone and I never took that. I put a bit of old hydrocortizone on once, did nothing, so I left it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, 4 milligrams or 10? Screen jumped. Say the Piriton again.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Four milligrams, at night, and I stopped it. I already said that.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Hands out for me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yeh. Scratch marks between the fingers, and a couple of little burrows. Let's see the waist.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Here, this side. Don't poke it, it's sore.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Papules along the waistband. No pus, not infected. I was going to give you hydrocortisone 1 percent cream, twice a day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hold on. It's not only her. The partner is scratching the same, and the small lad. Nights, mostly.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Say that again? The child as well?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yes. The little boy and her fella. Both of them itching.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): It's me, himself and the child in the house. And yes they're at it too. I was too tired to start into all that.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, that changes it. Forget the hydrocortisone, I won't be prescribing that. I think this is scabies. Permethrin, the 5 percent cream, Lyclear.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Whole house, the same night. Cool dry skin, neck down to the toes, between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the soles of the feet. Leave it on eight to 12 hours, wash it off in the morning, and do the same again in 7 days.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Eight to 12 hours, all of me? And it's permetrin, yeah, not another tablet. I'm not able for more tablets.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cream, not a tablet, and yes even the feet. Hot wash at 60 degrees for the sheets, towels and clothes, and bag anything you can't wash for three days, the same day you put the cream on. The itch can hang on after the mites are dead, so don't go back near the steroid.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll do the washing. She's fit to drop, she won't manage it today.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'll send the script for the permethrin now. If it's not settled two weeks after the second treatment, come back to me.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come through and grab a seat. What brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, parking was a pain out the front. Anyway, it's nothing, I'm probably wasting your time. Just a bit of spinning when I roll over in bed.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. How long has that been happening, and how long does each little spin last?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, since last week. A few seconds and it's done. Same if I look up, like at a high shelf. I barely notice it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you feel sick with it? Nausea, or have you vomited?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit queasy, yeah. I haven't spewed. Not a big deal.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has the hearing dropped at all, or is there pain in the ear?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Hearing's the same. Not really sore.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any ringing, or a full blocked feeling?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No ringing. Not that either.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headaches with these turns?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Head's good.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any double vision, weakness, trouble walking, slurred speech?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. I'm fine.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other health problems, or medicines you use?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Asthma, had it for years. Err, since I was a kid or maybe later, I can't date it. I hardly think about it, just the blue puffer, ventolin, two puffs when I need it.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had spinning like this before?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Once. Last winter, or the one before. Can't say which. It went away on its own so I left it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): With the asthma, any wheeze lately?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if the warehouse is dusty. Not a drama.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels, waterworks, anything else playing up?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Gut's fine. I'm not fussed about the rest.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): In the family, diabetes, blood pressure, ear problems, any of that?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Dad had diabetes, came on in his fifties. Mum didn't. My sister's got high blood pressure but no sugar. My brother's fine, far as I know.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And work, plus the day to day, food, exercise, a drink?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I drive a forklift in a warehouse. Umm, early starts, on at five, off around one. Diet's ordinary, meat and veg. I walk the dog most nights, couple of beers on the weekend, and I don't smoke.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, thinking aloud. Brief spins when you roll over or look up, a touch of nausea, hearing spared. That sounds like crystals in the balance canal, benign positional vertigo. First instinct was an MRI and stematil, prochlorperazine five milligrams three times a day, in case this is central.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A scan for this? It's tiny.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me test it before I lock that plan in. Head turned to the right, then I'll lie you straight back. That's a Dix-Hallpike.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yep, there it is. Brief upbeat torsional nystagmus on the right, about 10 seconds, and you spun. Left side stayed quiet. Canals are clear and the drums look normal.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): That changes my mind. No MRI, and no stematil, it would only sedate you and muddy the exercises. This is right-sided benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. I've just done the Epley and it eased on the second go.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So no tablets. Good. It'll sort itself anyway.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do that same Epley at home once a day until the spinning stops, and stay off the forklift if you're mid-spin. I'll see you in a fortnight. If you get double vision, weakness, or the spinning won't stop, go to emergency.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, my mother did not, and another sister has pressure but no sugar. Nobody in the family has had skin cancer, to my knowledge.

[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That black part was definitely not there last year. I keep telling him, but he is busy only.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Please be frank with me, doctor. Is this a serious matter?

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am referring you to dermatology, and they should see you within two weeks. Do not scratch it, and please use a sun cream when you go out.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Chin and along the jaw. Big sore ones, not the tiny ones. Two years of it now and I'm sick of looking at them.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She stands at the mirror for ages covering them before the shop. It's really getting her down.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I can talk for myself, thanks. It's embarrassing, that's all. Can we just get on with it?
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course we can. And the periods, how are they these days?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): They were monthly and grand. Now it's every two or three months if I even get one. Same two years. Um.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain with them when they do arrive?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really pain. They just don't show up. And I've hair on my chin and a bit on the lip, I pluck it in the car like an eejit.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did you first notice that hair?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Maybe a year? I don't know exactly. It crept up.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the weight, doctor. Her clothes are after getting very tight.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah alright. I was going to say two stone, well actually about a stone and a half since last summer. Jeans won't close. I'm wrecked even when I've slept.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a fair bit to deal with on top of work. May I look at your face and feel your tummy?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, so. Your hands are probably cold.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Inflamed spots along the jawline, and coarse dark hairs on the chin and the upper lip. Tummy is soft, no masses. We weighed you on the way in, seventy eight kilos.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been putting anything on the spots, or taking tablets?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Just that benzoil peroxide wash from the chemist, the five percent. Most nights. Barely touches them, waste of money.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her sister is always on about biotin, the one with the pressures. And my husband takes metformin for his own sugar, but that's nothing to do with Aoife.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not swallowing her biotin. Or his tablets. Jesus.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): No, we won't be using anyone else's medicine. Is there sugar or blood pressure or women's troubles in the family?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, and another sister has pressure but no sugar. The older one is grand as far as I know.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the day to day stuff, work and food and that?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I work in a clothes shop on Grafton Street. Nine till half five, five days, and the odd Saturday, so the hours are long enough. Diet is rotten, I skip breakfast and it's wraps and takeaways most evenings. Exercise I don't, I get the bus, and I drink a few glasses of wine at the weekend, maybe four or five.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any bad reactions to medicines, antibiotics, painkillers, anything at all?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. I have taken penicillin and everything, the amoxicillin one, no bother.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your breathing, your chest, any trouble there?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Putting the sore spots, the periods every few months, the facial hair and the weight together, I'd be thinking of polycystic ovary syndrome. Only a working idea, not a firm diagnosis.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): PCOS. Brilliant. So that's why I'm floored tired as well, is it?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can travel with it, but I won't hang the tiredness on that until we see tests. We'll do bloods, a hormone panel and a check of your sugar, and a pelvic ultrasound.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Does she have to fast? She goes woozy if she misses food. Sorry, the bus was a nightmare getting here, we were late.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fasting bloods, yes, water only from the night before. The pelvic scan doesn't need fasting, and we'll book that through the clinic.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Someone said the pill would sort the periods. Should I just start one?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): The combined pill can steady the periods and help the spots, but I'm not starting you on it today. Don't start any pill yourself until we have these results and we talk it through.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I wasn't mad keen anyway. Your waiting room is freezing, I nearly walked out.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll mention the heating, that's not on. Come back and see me in three weeks with the results, whether you're feeling better or not.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. If the shop will let me off. Uh, alright.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll work around the shop hours if we can. Mind yourself going home.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come on through. What brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, g'day doc. Traffic was a shocker, took us ages down the freeway. Anyway, umm, I'm 74 and it's the waterworks, I'm up and down all night for a wee and the stream's gone weak.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Karen, his daughter. I stayed over last week and I counted, Dad, you were up five times.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): No, love, that's not right. It's three, sometimes four. You counted when I got up for a glass of water and stood at the window.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I still reckon it was five, at least one of those nights. I was awake with the dog.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so you two don't quite agree on the number. Ray, you're saying three or four, and the stream is weak. Anything else when you pass urine?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah it dribbles at the end. I stand there like a dill waiting for it to finish. Been like that a fair while.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have the night-time trips and the weak stream been going on?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, I can't pin it. Last winter, or the one before. Maybe around the grand final, maybe after, I honestly don't know.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): And I still have my cuppa in the evening. Two teas after dinner, well actually sometimes it's just one if the cricket's on and I'm dozing. Probably doesn't help the bladder, but I like it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine at all?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never seen any blood. Not once.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): While we're on it, he nicked his shin on the rose bush. That cut healed in five days, no drama.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah that was nothing. Cleaned it, gone in five days. The roses are going mad, I should prune them before they take over the path.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good that it healed up promptly. Separate question, any fevers?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fevers.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Chest is fine, no cough.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your weight, has that shifted at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't think so. Maybe a bit. The trousers feel looser, but I've been walking the dog more, so it's hard to say really.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He doesn't take his blood pressure tablets on Sundays. I've seen the blister pack still full.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not Sundays. It's Saturdays. Bowls day. I get home and I forget the tablet. Every other day is fine.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me get the medicine straight. Which blood pressure tablet, and what dose?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The perindopral, uh, 5 mg, one in the morning. The chemist knows it. I've been on it for years for the blood pressure.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perindopril 5 mg each morning. And you miss it on Saturdays after bowls, not Sundays. I'll note Saturdays.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep, that's the one. My brother Kevin had his prostate out, oh, six or seven years back. He lives up in Cairns now, mad on the fishing.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. You're up three or four times by your count, Karen heard five, the stream is weak with dribbling, no blood, evening tea, and the timing is vague, last winter or the one before. Blood pressure is ongoing, perindopril 5 mg, missed on Saturdays.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That's pretty fair, yeah. Apart from Karen's counting. She means well.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): This pattern fits an enlarged prostate, the benign sort, as a working impression. I can't call it definite today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Righto. Not keen on an operation if I can help it. A mate at bowls had something done and he talked about it for a month.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): No operation on the table today. I'd like a PSA blood test and a urine test, both booked from here, to look at the prostate and to check the urine.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): PSA, yeah, I've heard of that one. Do I have to fast? I had a bacon roll on the way, bit late if I do.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): No fasting for these. And I'd like to start tamsulosin, a capsule by mouth, 400 micrograms at night, for the stream and the night-time wees.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Tamsolosin? Will that make me dizzy? I don't want to fall over at bowls.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tamsulosin. It can make some blokes light-headed when they stand, especially the first few doses, so stand up slowly, and take it after you've eaten.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I'll give it a go.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Also, ease off the tea in the evening, keep it earlier in the day if you can. And please take the perindopril on Saturdays too, even after bowls. An alarm on your phone helps.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, fair enough. The tea will be the hard bit. I can do an alarm, I think. Karen bought me one of those phones and I only use it to ring her.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll remind him Saturday arvo when I ring, if he hasn't already taken it.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in four weeks with the results, and we'll see how the tamsulosin is sitting. If you suddenly can't pass urine at all, that's straight to the hospital, don't wait.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Got it. I'll drag Karen along if she's not on shift. Thanks, doc.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No worries. Reception will have the forms on your way out.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): About one month. I get up three times a night just to drink water.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll take your blood pressure and weight while you talk to the doctor. ~
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Do you have any family history of diabetes?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had it. He was on tablets.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight, or have blurred vision?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't lost weight. My vision's fine.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Ramipril, 10 mg, once a day. A cholesterol tablet, I think it's simvastatin. And a water tablet, which I can't name.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember the dose of the simvastatin?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Forty, I think. Or twenty. I'd have to check the box.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't worry, you can bring it next time. Any other conditions?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure and high cholesterol.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Blood pressure 142 over 88, weight 94 kilograms.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. A bit up on the pressure. I'll check your blood sugar with a finger prick now.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, of course.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): The finger-prick sugar is 14.2, which is high.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that diabetes? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): It strongly suggests it, but I need a proper blood test to confirm.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it need insulin? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not necessarily. Many people start with tablets, diet and exercise. Let's get the tests first. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): What tests? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will arrange a blood test for HbA1c, kidney function and cholesterol, and a urine test.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): When? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse can take the blood today, and I'd like to see you again in a week with the results.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): That's fine. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Until then, drink water rather than sugary drinks, and try to cut back on sweet foods.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you start vomiting, feel very drowsy, or become short of breath, go to the emergency department.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): no, that's the old dose. they bumped the amlodipene to ten. the bottle says ten milligrams, one every morning with my coffee.

[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): tell him about the shoes not zipping, you were going on about that in the car.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): oh. no fever. I checked yesterday with that thermometer from the drugstore, it said 98.4.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): lungs wise, any cough, wheezing, shortness of breath?
