[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): what about your weight, any change?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): umm I don't know. the scale sticks, sometimes it says I'm up a couple pounds, sometimes it doesn't, I really couldn't tell you.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): yeah, don't trust that scale. it jumped six pounds in one day. nonsense.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): mm. right. let me see the ankles. shoes off.

[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think the swelling is from the amlodipine. that medicine does this pretty often.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): but then what about my pressure, the home numbers are decent and yours aren't, and if you stop it won't I just...
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): we're going to stop the amlodipine. I'll start losartan, fifty milligrams, once a day, in its place.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): what about the water pill? she can't be sprinting to the bathroom at the senior center, they have one stall.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): keep the hydrochlorothiazide, twenty-five milligrams, every morning. same as now. don't move it to nighttime.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): so the water one stays with breakfast. and losartan, is that the one that starts with an l, because my sister takes something and she never stops talking about it...

[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): I can draw that before you leave. lab's still open.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): good. put your feet up in the afternoon. if you get dizzy, or the swelling suddenly gets a lot worse, call us.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): and the peeing, is that just my life now? eight times in a morning, I timed it, I was late to my hair appointment last tuesday and she gave my slot away.

[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): bring the notebook, yes. sorry, what was that home reading again? I never typed it.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): 132 over 80. this morning.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I had 130 over 82 in my head, but she was watching, so she's probably right.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): okay. we'll use today's clinic pressure for the chart. reception will book the two weeks.

[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll take your observations before you go in. Sleeve up there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, grand. Is it much longer? The head is pounding and I've been clock-watching outside.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): He's nearly ready. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight, temperature thirty-six point seven, oxygen ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one thirty-eight bad? Could the blood pressure be what's driving the headache?
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Only mildly up. The doctor will go through it. In you go.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit down. What's brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The headaches. I've had migraine for years, but it's changed, and I'm really frightened about it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Changed how?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse in the morning. I wake up and it's already pounding, the whole head, and I've been getting sick with it.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A month at least. I'm awake with him from about five.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not a month. It's a fortnight, two weeks. I'm nearly certain.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll call it a few weeks and not fight over the day. Vomiting every morning?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not every morning. Only a few times. I can't tell you when the vomiting started, it crept in, maybe last week, I genuinely don't know.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in an arm or a leg?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. If I did get weakness, what would that mean? Should I be checking?
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): It would mean the emergency department. Speech slurred? Seeing double?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Speech is normal and there's no double vision.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stiff neck?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the neck is fine.
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He snores the house down as well, and he's tired all day. Asleep on the couch after the tea.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not snore. She's exaggerating. And I'm not tired. I'm grand once the headache lifts.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do snore, loud, most nights, and you are tired. I've watched it.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not having that row in here. Can we stay on the headache? I was googling tumours half the night.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have the migraines been there?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Since my twenties. I'm forty-two, so about twenty years. My dad had migraines too, the same sort of thing.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you taking?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Sumatriptan, fifty milligrams, when one starts. I've been taking it nearly every day lately, which is too much, and that worries me as well.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box at home says a hundred milligrams. He keeps telling people fifty.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I thought it was fifty. Maybe the chemist changed it. I haven't checked the new box, so I can't swear to the dose.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else for the pain?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two of the five-hundred milligram tablets, maybe three if it's desperate, most days. Is that dangerous? Could it be causing the morning headache?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Daily paracetamol can keep a headache going. Were you on a preventer?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Propranolol, forty milligrams twice a day. I stopped it in March, it had me wrecked. They offered topiramate after and I never took a single capsule.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): This might sound stupid, but my sister takes biotin every day for her hair. Would it help if I tried some? She also wants me to ask about her mother's tablets.
[SEG0035] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My mother takes metformin for her diabetes. I only wondered if that kind of thing did anything for headaches.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. The biotin is your sister's and the metformin is her mother's. Neither is yours. Anything else you're on?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else. So do I stop the paracetamol today? Am I allowed any sumatriptan at all?
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cut the paracetamol right back, not every day. Keep the sumatriptan for a proper attack, not every morning. I'll have a look at you.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pupils are equal and reacting to light. There's no swelling at the back of the eyes.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the pressure thing, isn't it? So that's clear? Does that mean I'm alright?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): It makes very high pressure less likely. It doesn't close it. Power is normal in both arms and both legs, and the reflexes are present.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Coordination is fine, finger to nose is accurate. No neck stiffness. Your gait is steady.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do you think it actually is? Don't soften it, please.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working impression is a change in the migraine, with medication overuse likely on top. I wouldn't rule out raised pressure, given the morning vomiting.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're scanning me today, then?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it hasn't settled in two weeks, or the vomiting gets worse, we might arrange a brain scan.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Might, so it's not booked. If I wake up worse on Sunday, do I just wait?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): New weakness, confusion, or a sudden terrible headache, you go to emergency, you don't wait. Otherwise I'll see you in a fortnight.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if I feel a bit better? And would the scan be an MRI or a CT? I'm awful in tight spaces.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): The fortnight visit stands either way. If we do a scan it would be an MRI, and only if things haven't settled. Nothing is booked for imaging today.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the two-week review in the book at the desk. Mornings are easier.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning, please. Is there anything else I should watch for, or am I overthinking it?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting that won't stop, confusion, a thunderclap headache. Don't start the biotin, and leave the metformin alone.
[SEG0054] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And you're not going to touch the snoring at all?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): There is no snoring, and I am not exhausted. I wish you'd drop it.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sleep can wait. Emergency if anything sudden happens. Otherwise two weeks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through. Sorry to keep you, the clinic's been hectic.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was getting ratty out there. That telly doesn't help.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I can't hear myself think with it on. I'm shattered. Can we start.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): The waterworks. Up and down all night, and I feel like a wet rag by morning.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many times a night, roughly?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, five. No. Three or four. I lose count half asleep.
[SEG0008] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Four, most nights, and he...
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Let me speak.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. How's the stream itself?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Weak. Stops and starts, then dribbles. Takes an age.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any burning when you pass water?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No burning.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No blood. I'd have come in shouting.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm, I was going to say...
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not a fortnight. Don't let him say that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Six months. No, scratch that. It's a year of getting up three or four times a night, and the weak stream the same. A full year.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Through the day, any sudden urge where you've got to go straight away?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Not the whole day, but when it comes I don't hang about.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you drink in the evening?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Tea. Pot after the news, two or three mugs. Strong.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does that late tea make the nights worse?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Probably, yeah.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any backache, fever, or weight coming off?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Just the tiredness.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels and appetite all right?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Normal. No change.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Ramipril, for the blood pressure. Two and a half milligrams... no, five. Five milligrams every morning.
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And atorvastatin forty milligrams, with his tea... with his dinner, sorry.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Dinner. Yeah, forty milligrams.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Gave up twenty years ago. No, thirty years. Was twenty a day back then.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's let the allotment go. Used to be down there every day.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): I've overdone it down there for years. Anyway. Frog in my throat trying to get the words out, it's not a throat thing. Stick to the peeing.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll check your blood pressure. One thirty six over eighty four, and your pulse is seventy two.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Last time the nurse reckoned one fifty something. Made a right fuss.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll go with today's. Your abdomen is soft, no tenderness, and the bladder isn't palpable. I'll leave the prostate exam for another day.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Not today.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is lower urinary tract symptoms from a benign enlarged prostate. That's not a confirmed diagnosis, just where this is pointing.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): You're not calling it cancer, then.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not, but I can't properly rule a prostate cancer out until the PSA is back.
[SEG0049] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His brother had prostate trouble. Had an operation. Wasn't cancer, they said.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you. We'll do a PSA blood test, and a urine test for blood and infection. Both are booked at reception before you go.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): What, a sample today? I'll try. No promises.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine. I'm also starting tamsolusin, tamsulosin, sorry. Two hundred micrograms, no, four hundred micrograms, once a day, after food. Should help the stream and the dribbling.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Another tablet. Will it flatten me? I feel like a wet rag as it is.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): It shouldn't make you drowsy. It can make you light-headed on standing, more so with the ramipril for your blood pressure. Stand up slowly. If you feel faint, leave it off and ring the surgery.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): And what about the tea, then?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last mug around seven in the evening, not a pot after the news. That often knocks off one night-time trip.
[SEG0057] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if he can't pee at all before we're back?
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you can't pass urine, or you see blood, don't wait, same day here or A&E. I'll see you in clinic in six weeks with the results, to see how the tamsulosin suits you.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks. I just want some sleep.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll aim for that. Reception will sort the forms. Take care, both of you.

[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She nearly cancelled on you. I had to walk her to the car.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): My mum had breast cancer and she was in bits, and I don't want to waste a whole appointment if it's just a cyst.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you. When did you first feel this lump, though?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Sorry. About two weeks ago. Well, actually, might be a bit over, but about two weeks. Soapy hands in the shower and there it was.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any nipple discharge, blood or clear?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. Nipple looks the same as ever.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest's fine.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your weight, any loss?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't know really, jeans fit the same I think. Scales at home are ancient. Haven't been trying.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Any regular medicines?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Hasn't got bigger, if that's what you mean. Same little pea.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's handy, but I meant tablets. Anything every day?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, err, just the blood pressure one. Ramepril, five milligrams, I swallow it in the morning.

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Came off the cerazette about a year back. Didn't suit me. Nothing else.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. Comes out in a rash. Years ago, and I stay away from it.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your mum's breast cancer, how old was she?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty five. She had the op and the chemo. Still about, still nagging.

[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Getting here was the hard bit, mind. Rain like stair rods all down the ring road.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha. Catch who was bowling?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): They'll be playing in wellies at this rate. We just sat there watching it bucket down.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Typical. Right, pop behind the curtain and I'll have a look.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Arms up for me. Skin on the left looks normal, no dimpling, and the nipple isn't pulled in.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): See. Barely there.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two centimetres is nothing. People have bigger peas than that.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Small, yes. Thinking aloud, plenty of lumps like this are a cyst or a fibroadenoma, both benign. I still can't exclude a cancer, though, not at forty six with your mum diagnosed at fifty five.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh please. She was fifty five, I'm not, and mine doesn't hurt.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain's a rotten guide. Most early breast cancers don't hurt, so I'm not sitting on this.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm referring you today on the urgent two-week breast clinic pathway. They usually do a mammogram and an ultrasound when they see you. I won't start any tablets.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Fine. If I absolutely must.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the skin goes red or the lump suddenly grows before they see you, come back and see me. And don't talk yourself out of going.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning doctor, just done Mr Jacobs. Creatinine is 168, eGFR 38, blood pressure 152 over 88, pulse 74. Chart has ramipril 5 milligrams daily.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag shame. Last time they told us 150 for the creatinine. The ramipril though, no, the box at home is 10 milligrams, not 5.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks, sister. Mr Jacobs, howzit, come sit. What's today about then?
[SEG0004] person_4 (PATIENT): Sugar. Kidneys.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ja, diabetes and the kidneys. Wife's with you, that's fine by me. Any fever lately?
[SEG0006] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the chest side, any cough, wheeze, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the weight, up or down since last time?
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Umm. Sort of. Don't know.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hmm, not much to go on, we'll park the weight. Creatinine 168 with an eGFR of 38, that's stage 3b, err, on the background of the sugar. You still on the metforman?
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): Ja.
[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Metformin 500, morning and night. He skips the night one sometimes. I don't always see.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so 500 milligrams twice a day on paper, evenings hit and miss. Ramipril, chart says 5, you're saying the box is 10 in the morning?
[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ten. Every morning. I put it out.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't guess between 5 and 10 till I see the box. We carry on with the ramipril either way, it protects the kidney even if the creatinine ticks up a little.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): eGFR is 38 so the metformin can stay, we'd only stop that under 30. You've been getting ibuprofin from the shop, haven't you?
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Dis-Chem. Ibuprofen, the 200 milligram ones. Two when the knee is sore, so 400, not every day. You told him no.
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): Knee.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): The right one?
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): Ja.
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Months now, that right knee.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. Shop ibuprofen with ramipril and diabetic kidneys, I'm not happy. I'm thinking the creatinine of 168 is the ibuprofen sitting on the diabetic kidney disease.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Could also just be the kidney disease moving on by itself. I can't separate those two today.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): So ibuprofen stops. Paracetamol instead, one gram, two 500 milligram tablets, by mouth, up to three times a day for the knee, not more.
[SEG0026] person_4 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His sister Joyce takes biotin, the hair gummies. Hers, not his. I've got my own pressure tablets too, don't put those on him.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not his. Family, Mr Jacobs, any sugar or pressure in the relatives?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties. Mother did not. My brother had a stroke at sixty. Another sister has pressure but no sugar.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): And an ordinary day, the job, hours, food, exercise, a drink?
[SEG0031] person_4 (PATIENT): I drive a bakkie for the municipality, six till three. Pap and meat most nights. I walk the dogs round the block. A beer on a Friday, that's it.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep it to the Friday beer, hey. Looking now, no swelling at the ankles. Right knee's a bit bony, no heat. Chest is clear.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): So. Repeat creatinine and eGFR in two weeks, sister books that. Back here in six weeks with the ramipril box, then we settle 5 or 10. Paracetamol from today, and the ibuprofen stays in the cupboard.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the bloods for two weeks, and the six week review at the desk.
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): Sharp.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, acid reflux is known to us, good to have that clear. Before we go further, any allergies?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, you know, I think I reacted to some antibiotic once, years ago. I don't remember which one, or what happened exactly.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the examination finished. From what you've told me and what I found, it's hard to say. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is one possibility and a ruptured ovarian cyst another, and I'd rather not commit yet.

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have a good day.

[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mr Pryce, the booking says a painful big toe. Come in, sit, and I'll help you with that foot. Is this your wife? ~
[SEG0002] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Gwen. He's been up all night. I told him to ring last week. ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It's my big toe, doctor, the left one. It came on suddenly two days ago and it's the worst pain I've ever had. Is it broken? Is it infected? Is it going to be amputated?
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's very unlikely to be any of those. Describe the pain.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Throbbing, severe, ten out of ten. Even the bedsheet on it is agony.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it swollen?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Swollen like a plum, and hot.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you limping?
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He couldn't get his shoe on this morning. He's hopping about the kitchen.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you knock it, or drop something on it?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I didn't hurt it.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever or shivers?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit warm last night, but no fever, no.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain in any other joints?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, just the toe.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any rash?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No rash.
[SEG0018] person_3 (NURSE): Doctor, would you like him on the couch with the foot up? ~
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes please, nurse. Mr Pryce, what medicines are you taking?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Allopurinol, 100 mg, once a day. And naproxen, 250 mg, I took one last night, it did nothing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Penicillin, when I was a boy. I had a rash.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Medical history?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Gout, from years ago. High blood pressure. And I'm overweight, I know.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Surgery?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Gallbladder, in 2016.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Gout in the family?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had it terribly.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you do?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I drive a bus. Twelve hours. It's my foot on the pedal, doctor, I can't work like this.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Four pints on a Saturday, and wine with dinner.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what do you eat?
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Red meat, and he loves shellfish at the weekend.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check you. Pulse 86, blood pressure 150 over 94, temperature 37.4, oxygen 97 percent, breathing 16, weight 104 kilos.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Is the pressure dangerous? ~
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): High, from the pain. Now, the toe. I'll be gentle.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow! Stop! ~
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): The base of the left big toe is red, hot and swollen, and it's extremely tender to touch.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): I told you. ~
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): The other toes look fine, and the ankle moves normally.
[SEG0042] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is it infected? ~
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your chest or breathing, Mr Pryce?
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, I'm fine in that way.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): This looks like a gout flare, the classic big toe.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Not broken then? ~
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't think so, but I'd like to arrange a uric acid blood test, a kidney function test, and an X-ray of the foot.
[SEG0048] person_3 (NURSE): I'll book the X-ray for this afternoon. ~
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Keep taking the naproxen with food, rest the foot, and drink plenty of water.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I go to work? ~
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not on the pedal for a few days. I'd like to see you again in two weeks.
[SEG0052] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks, I'll make sure he comes. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I've noticed a new mole on my shoulder, and my husband insisted I get it looked at.
[SEG0002] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm the husband. I spotted it in the summer when she was in her swimsuit. It looked different from her other moles.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you both for coming. Where exactly is it?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): On the back of my left shoulder. I can't see it, so I only know what he says.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has it changed in size or colour, according to your husband?
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's gotten bigger, I think, and darker at one edge.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It does sometimes itch a little, and once it bled when I scratched it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other moles that have changed?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, the rest are the same as always.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had skin cancer, or does it run in the family? ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Neither. My mother had lots of moles, but never cancer. ~
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blistering sunburn in the past? ~
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): As a child, in the south of France. We've avoided the sun a lot more since.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking, if any?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): A multivitamin, a thyroid tablet, levothyroxine, 50 micrograms, and the contraceptive pill.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines or plasters?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Penicillin, when I was a baby, my mother told me I had a rash. I've avoided it since.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Noted. Any other conditions?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Underactive thyroid. That's all.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Doctor, I've taken her pulse and pressure, and weight, they're on the screen. ~
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Pulse 72, blood pressure 118 over 74, weight 66 kilograms, I see. Perfect.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it all right? ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Now let me look at the mole with the dermatoscope. Please turn around. ~
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's an irregular brown mole, about seven millimetres, with an uneven edge and two shades of colour.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is it dangerous? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't say from looking, and I don't like the irregular edge and the change that you describe.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): What should we do? ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to remove the whole mole under local anaesthetic, and send it to the laboratory.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): When? ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): My colleague will book you for two weeks' time. You'll have a small scar, and the stitches come out after a week or so.
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll be there. ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the area covered from the sun until then, and don't scratch it.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I won't. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come through. I've just put him on the scales, today he's 3.51 kilograms. Birth weight in the book was 3.46, so he's up a touch.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh that's a relief, I was sure he'd dropped off. The pram wheel squeaked the whole way from the car park, I nearly turned around.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, just logging in, this screen's crawling. What brings you in with him?
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's gone yellow. Face and chest, proper yellow, not just a bit sallow from the light.
[SEG0005] person_4 (PATIENT): Ah.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yellow, right. How old is he?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ten days today. Vaginal birth, no drama, home on day two. My sister reckons he already looks like my husband, which is, um, generous.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the colour start?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm I can't pin the day. I properly saw it yesterday, but it might've been coming before that. I really don't know the start.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? An email just jumped over the notes.
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah I can't tell you when it started. Noticed it properly yesterday. Anything before that I'm guessing.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. Tell me about the feeds.
[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Breast milk, and we top up with formula, the Aptamil, roughly every four hours. He'll do a good twenty minutes then the bottle if he's still rooting.
[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): Mmm.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every four hours, breast plus formula. Any vomiting?
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No spews at all.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He feels warm sometimes but not hot, not feverish.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the nappies? Any pale poos, or dark wee?
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Wee's yellow, not dark, plenty of wet nappies. Poos are that mustard colour, not pale.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is he hard to wake, floppy, that sort of thing?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nah he wakes himself for the feeds, cranky till he's on, then he's out. Not floppy.
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): Wah.
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I know, I know, shh. Random, but my sister's been on biotin, she says bioten, for her hair, and she keeps telling me to give it to the bub, which I have not done. And my husband takes metforman for his diabetes. Nothing to do with Arlo, sorry, I go off.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the screen refreshed. Your husband is on what?
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Metforman, for his diabetes. Not the baby. Arlo's on no medicines at all.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies for him? Medicines, milk, anything?
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. Pop him on the cot if you can.
[SEG0030] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hates being unwrapped, just so you know. We had a shocking night too, the neighbour's dog went off at about two.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sclera are yellow, and the skin's yellow down to about the nipple line. Fontanelle's soft, not sunken. Belly's soft, and he looks well hydrated.
[SEG0032] person_4 (PATIENT): Eh.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): So, day ten, yellow to the chest, feeding every four hours, weight up on birth, and I'm turning over ordinary physiological jaundice, breast milk jaundice, not enough intake, with haemolysis further down if there was a blood group issue. I am not going to conclude this is liver disease. My leaning is physiological jaundice, and I can't rule out breast milk jaundice. Let's see what the tests say before I go any further.
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is breast milk jaundice a bad one? My cousin stopped breastfeeding over something and I really don't want to, the lactation lady was lovely but hospital parking is a joke.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not stopping the breast milk today. Sorry, the feed interval, say it once more?
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every four hours. Breast, then a formula top up.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. We'll do a bilirubin blood test today, before you leave. And I'll book a repeat bilirubin for Thursday morning. No need to fast him.
[SEG0038] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can take today's one in the treatment room in a few minutes. Thursday I've got half eight.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. If Thursday's result is borderline we'll do a third blood test. If the yellow does not settle, we'll organise an abdominal ultrasound.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A scan, is that like urgent? My head goes straight to the worst thing.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Only if it doesn't settle. Not booked now. I'll see you back in two weeks with the numbers either way.
[SEG0042] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks, yep. Do I keep the formula top ups or is that making it worse?
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the breastfeeding and the formula top ups as you are. Wake him if he stretches past four hours. If he becomes hard to wake or the yellow spreads to his legs, bring him straight in.
[SEG0044] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hard to wake, or yellow down the legs. Got it. My husband'll panic, he panicked when his own sugar was up before the metforman.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): His diabetes isn't Arlo's problem. Questions about the blood test?
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Will it hurt, he's so tiny. And I left the dummy in the car, typical me.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's a heel prick, quick, he'll grizzle. You can feed him straight after.
[SEG0048] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. Thursday half eight, no fasting, I'll set an alarm. The pram better behave.
[SEG0049] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Thursday at half eight, no fast. I'll write it on the card so it doesn't get lost.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): And just so it's clear, if those Thursday numbers are borderline we do the third test, and the scan only if the colour hangs around. No medicine from me today.
[SEG0051] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank goodness. I can't keep names straight, bioten, metforman, whatever my sister's into this month.
[SEG0052] person_4 (PATIENT): Mmm mm.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave it there. Nurse'll take you for the heel prick, and I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0054] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Come on Arlo. He won't say thanks but I will. Thanks, both of you.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Harlan, come on back. I'll grab vitals before Doctor Shah sees you.

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Dad, please. Sorry, he's short on sleep. I'm Karen, his daughter.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Right. Arm loose for me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 74, oxygen 98 percent on room air. Doctor will be right in.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): 152. Wonderful. Exactly what I needed today.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr. Harlan. I'm Doctor Shah. Karen can stay if you want. What brings you in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The cramps. Both calves, every night. I can't sleep and I'm sick of it.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nighttime cramps in both calves. How long has that been?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Two months. Around when it got cold, I guess. Both of them, down in the calf.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Every night, or just off and on?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every night. Wakes me, I stand and walk it off. Couple minutes and I can lie down.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He paces the hall around two. I've caught it most nights I'm over there.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Both calves, nightly, about two months, and walking helps. Any pain in the legs when you walk during the day?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Walking's fine. Not painful then.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the ankles? Redness or warmth in the calves?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. Not that either.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The water pill. Furosimide, forty milligrams, every morning. That's for my blood pressure.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Furosemide forty milligrams each morning for the pressure. So you've been told you have hypertension?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Years. They've called it hypertension the whole time. That's why the water pill.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hypertension, ongoing, on furosemide. Anything else, from us or from the store?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Magnesium. From the store, bottle says magnesium oxide, 400 milligrams. One at night for the cramps.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grabbed it off the shelf last month. I told him to ask you, but.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): How much water do you drink in a day?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The cramps are what I came for, not a lecture. They hit at like 2 or 3 and I'm up pacing. That's the thing.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll get to the cramps, I promise. The water, though, roughly how much?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A cup with the pill. Maybe one more if I remember. I hate drinking cause then I'm up peeing. Not much.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): A cup or two, on purpose. Were you ever given a potassium pill with the furosemide?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Those horse pills, uh, K-Dur, twenty milliequivalents. I stopped it in March. They made me queasy.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stopped the K-Dur twenty in March because of the queasiness. Did anyone ever give you quinine for the cramps?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Nobody gave me that. I never took it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, never took quinine. About the blood pressure. Any chest pain?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Headaches? With hypertension, some folks get them.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. Mornings, behind the eyes. Not every day.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So not a flat no. Sometimes, morning headaches. Any dizziness, or a feeling you'll pass out?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not that either.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not asking if the hypertension is gone. You already said that's still there. Any blurry vision?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Pressure's still there, yeah. Vision, no. Not blurry.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your stomach lately? Nausea, heartburn, any change in the bowels?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Stomach's fine now. Queasy was just those potassium pills, and I quit those.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me check the legs. Calves are soft, no tenderness, no redness, and I don't see swelling. Foot pulses are present, both sides.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Told you. Nothing in the daytime. Can we wrap this, I've had enough of sitting here.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Almost. Let me read it back. Nightly cramps, both calves, two months, you walk them off. No daytime walking pain, no swelling, no redness. Hypertension on furosemide forty each morning. K-Dur twenty stopped in March. Magnesium oxide 400 at night. A cup or two of water. Occasional morning headache. No chest pain, not really short of breath, no dizziness, vision's okay. Fair?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Don't tack anything else on.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he really does dodge the water. I've watched him slide the glass away.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Furosemide can lower your potassium, and not drinking much can feed cramps like this. I want a blood test for the potassium, a basic metabolic panel. It's ordered, and the lab will draw it before you leave today.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Just the needle, then I wanna go home. Don't hand me a jug in the lobby.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): No jug. Do drink more through the day, several glasses, not one cup. And stretch both calves before bed, hold it about thirty seconds each side.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks to go over the panel. If the potassium is low we might talk about a supplement then, not today. Any drug allergies?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Two weeks, alright, let's just get out of here.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Ag, sorry we're late, doc. The robot by the Spar was out, and then the parking machine wouldn't take my card, so my wife had to dash back to the bakkie for coins.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No stress at all, Mr Dlamini. Come sit. How's the traffic been treating you otherwise?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Shame, it's been hectic this whole week with the school holidays. The N2 was bumper to bumper even at half past nine, and we just sat there.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, I know that feeling. So, what brings you in today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, it's the hand, really. The left one. It's still a bit weak, three months after that mild stroke, and I keep dropping things.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit more about the weakness.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's not terrible, hey. I can still hold a cup of coffee, but buttons are a mission, and when I try to... um, when I try to open a jar my wife has to finish it. It started, well the stroke was in March, so about three months, and the hand never quite came right like the leg did.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the walking?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Walking is okay. I go to the shops most mornings, a bit slower than before, no stick, and I haven't fallen. My wife walks with me on the weekends down by the promenade, which is nice except when the wind...
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): ...comes off the sea and it's freezing. But ja, the legs feel steady enough for that.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about your speech? Any slurring, or words getting stuck?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Speech is fine now. For about ten days after the stroke I was slurring a bit, my brother said I sounded drunk, which was embarrassing at the braai, but that cleared. I don't slur anymore.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any headaches?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no headaches.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or shortness of breath when you walk?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And I'm not short of breath, even up the stairs at home. We live in a double storey in Plumstead, so the stairs are there every day, and I manage them fine.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the medicines, what are you actually taking?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Aspirin, a hundred milligrams, one in the morning with breakfast, the little cardio one from the chemist. Then atorvastin, sorry atorvastatin, forty milligrams at night for the cholesterol. And the blood pressure tablet, amlodopine, five milligrams, also in the morning.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine five milligrams every morning, and the statin at night. Any misses?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think I miss them. My wife sets them out in one of those weekly boxes, Monday to Sunday, so if I forget she...
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): ...she notices before I leave for my walk. So pretty much every day.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any other operations, or is the stroke the main thing in the history?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty two, that's the only operation. And the high blood pressure has been there for, ag, years and years, they picked it up at a work medical before I retired from the railways.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family side, anyone with strokes or heart trouble?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): My older brother, Piet, he had a heart attack at fifty eight. He's fine now, lives in George. My dad died of old age, nothing like this.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink much?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped smoking in two thousand and ten, used to be about ten a day. Now I have a glass of red wine with supper, maybe four nights a week, not more. My wife is stricter than the doctor was, hey.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me just take your blood pressure while we talk. Arm out for me.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): This arm? The right one is easier, the left still feels funny when you squeeze it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, right arm is perfect. Sit quiet a second.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I was saying to my wife in the waiting room, the magazines are all from last year, and the sister at reception was so kind, she...
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's one thirty six over eighty two. Pulse is seventy four.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright? Last time at the clinic it was higher, like one fifty something, but that was when I was stressed after the hospital.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Today's reading is fine for where we are. Let me check the hand. Squeeze my fingers.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Like this? I can do it but it feels softer on the left.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, left grip is a little weaker than the right. No droop of the face, and your speech sounds clear to me sitting here.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief, because I keep worrying it's starting again, especially when I drop the teaspoon in the morning.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is leftover weakness from that mild stroke, not a new one. The fact the leg and the speech came back, and it's only the hand lingering, fits with that.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): So I don't need to panic every time I fumble a button.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Keep doing the hand exercises the physio showed you, little and often, and keep walking like you are.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): She said squeeze a soft ball, twenty times, three times a day. I've been a bit slack on the evenings if I'm watching the rugby, I'll be honest, the Stormers game just runs on.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Try not to skip those. I'll book a cholesterol blood test, the lipids, so we can see if the 40 milligrams is enough.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): At the lab downstairs, or do I go to PathCare?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Reception will book it with PathCare, this week if they can. And we might do a scan of the head if the hand does not settle by the time I see you again.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): A scan. Like the one in the hospital? That machine was so loud I nearly...
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Only if it hasn't improved. I'm not ordering it today. Come back and see me in six weeks, we'll look at the hand and the bloods together.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Should I bring my wife in next time? She remembers the dates better than I do, and she wanted to ask about...
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): She's welcome. If the weakness suddenly gets worse, or the speech goes funny again, or you can't walk properly, don't wait for that appointment, go to casualty.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Casualty at Groote Schuur, ja. I'll tell her. Thanks, doc, I feel a bit less wound up than when I walked in.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. See you in six weeks, Mr Dlamini. Drive safe.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. In you come. Bit of a wait, I'm afraid, the list overran.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh I don't mind. Parking was a nightmare, mind you. I very nearly went home, it's nothing really.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She always says that. I'm her husband, I do the looking-after. I wasn't having her skip it.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. What have you come about, then?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): When I roll over in bed the room goes round for a second or two. Same if I look up to the cupboard. I lie still and it stops. I've overdone it in the garden, that's all.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): The room spins on turning in bed. How long has that been happening?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, last week, Tuesday I think, well actually maybe the Sunday, no, stick with last week. It's nothing.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's not last week, love. Week before last it started, nearer three weeks. I'm in the bed next to her and I hear her gasp and grab the duvet.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not grab the duvet, and it is a week. I just wait and it stops. You're making a meal of it.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'll say you put it at about a week, and your husband puts it nearer three weeks. Both on the note. Does it come on when you're just sitting still, or only with those movements?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Only if I turn or look up. Sat still I'm fine. Of. Hardly worth all this.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sick with it at all?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit queasy. Afterwards I feel like a wet rag, then it passes. Nothing to write home about.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yesterday morning she was sick. Breakfast came straight back up. I cleaned the bowl.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not sick. Felt a bit green, sat on the bed, nothing came up. He's wrong.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. Nausea from you, and a disagreement about actual vomiting. Any ear pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Ears don't hurt.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your hearing, any loss, or any ringing?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No hearing loss. I can hear his telly perfectly, too perfectly. I can't hear myself think in that front room.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The news isn't loud.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the telly. Any headache, double vision, weakness in an arm or a leg, or slurred speech?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. My feet feel dead when I first stand up, cold lino, that's all, ignore it.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dead meaning numb? Both feet, and does it ease?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Both of them. Once I'm pottering it's gone. Oh, and a frog in my throat, croaky, and I can't tell you when that started, few days I suppose.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Croak for a few days, start date unclear. Pain in the throat, or trouble swallowing?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just the croak. It's nothing.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets taken for the spinning?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): For the spinning, out-of-hours gave me stematil, five milligrams. I took one tablet and stopped it, knocked me for six. Never took another.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There was talk of an antibiotic as well, and one of those sickness patches. She never collected the antibiotic. The patch was never actually given.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): So that's prochlorperazine, five milligrams by mouth, a single dose, then stopped. I won't list the antibiotic or the patch, you never had them. What do you take every day?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine. Five milligrams, every morning, for the blood pressure. That's it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me summarise. Brief spinning on turning in bed or looking up, for seconds, with nausea, a croak and morning numb feet, and no ear pain, hearing loss, headache or weakness. Duration somewhere between a week and three weeks. One dose of prochlorperazine then stopped, and amlodipine five milligrams every morning.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. Still feels like a lot of fuss.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 72 beats a minute, blood pressure 136 over 84. I'd like to do a Dix-Hallpike test now, head turned to the right, then I'll lie you back. You may spin for a moment.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. Two seconds of daftness.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. There's a brief rotatory flicker of the eyes on the right, gone in about fifteen seconds. Sit up when you're ready.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ugh. That's the one. Ridiculous, isn't it.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I'm seeing fits benign positional vertigo. Crystals shifting in the right ear canal, that's the working impression. It doesn't look like a stroke from the story or this test.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Crystals. Charming.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No new tablet from me. I'll teach you the Brandt-Daroff exercise. Sit on the edge of the bed, turn your head one way, lie onto that side until the spinning stops, sit up, then the other side, three times a day. Don't drive in the middle of a spin.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll see she does them. She'll tell you she won't bother.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight anyway, booked with me, so we can check it. If the spinning turns constant, or there's a sudden bad headache, weakness, or slurred speech, don't wait for that appointment, go to A&E the same day.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hello, good to see you. Please sit.

[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it constant or in episodes?
[SEG0006] person_4 (PATIENT): It's all the time.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been feeling sick?
[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, about the same, four weeks. Right, as for feeling sick, I'd give it a eight, out of ten.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had severe pain in your left side going to the groin before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Oh, a bit, about six months ago. It settled by itself back then.
[SEG0011] person_5 (UNKNOWN): Yes, exactly like that.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you allergic to anything? Any allergies to medicines or foods?
[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): Hmm, there was some antibiotic, I was told I was allergic. But I couldn't tell you what it was called or what it did.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has anyone in your family had anything serious?
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): Well, my cousin has psoriasis. My father had bowel cancer.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you taking anything regularly, including from the pharmacy?
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's metformin, 500 milligrams, twice a day for my sugar, doctor. Well, he is on escitalopram, 10 milligrams, once a day for the anxiety, I give it to him. He is on febuxostat, 80 milligrams, once a day, I give it to him.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you do any exercise?
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): I swim twice a week.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you work outside the home?
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): I'm a hairdresser, on my feet all day.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been to theatre before?
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): So, you know, yes, I had my tonsils removed, as a teenager.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you have any chronic illnesses?
[SEG0025] person_4 (PATIENT): I've had diabetes, yes.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there anything more?
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): Erm, I've had anxiety, yes.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, right.
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, gout.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah. Yes, anxiety is known to us, good to have that clear. Any fever or vomiting at all?
[SEG0031] person_4 (PATIENT): Let me think, no, no fever, no vomiting. I did have not being able to lie still at one point, but that went away on its own.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any burning when passing urine or passing no urine?
[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): Oh, no, not a single one.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed any weakness, or anything odd with your balance?
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): No weakness or anything.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your heart given you any trouble?
[SEG0037] person_4 (PATIENT): Nothing like that.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll just record a few vital signs.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a little longer...
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: saturation 97 percent, BP is 114 over 70. And pulse 86, temperature is 36.6 degrees.
[SEG0041] person_4 (PATIENT): Is that normal?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll go over that shortly.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Could you come over to the couch, please?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay as you are for a moment.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): You are writhing in pain with tenderness in the left loin but your tummy is soft.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please sit back down. From what you've told me and what I found, this looks most like kidney stone colic. Another possibility is a urine infection.
[SEG0047] person_4 (PATIENT): Okay, um, so is there something to worry about?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like kidney stone colic, but I'd like to confirm. Let's book a CT scan of the kidneys and bladder to look into renal colic. We should do a urine dipstick for haematuria.
[SEG0049] person_4 (PATIENT): How long will it take?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): For this, diclofenac, 75 milligrams, once now, single dose. That's for renal colic.
[SEG0051] person_4 (PATIENT): So, should I take that with food?
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drink plenty of water and strain the urine to catch the stone. Do get help quickly if the symptoms get worse.
[SEG0053] person_4 (PATIENT): Actually, I know what to watch for.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll catch up in one week.
[SEG0055] person_4 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, alright, I'll be back.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?
[SEG0057] person_4 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take care now.

[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not years, Dad. Since August, after the trip. Eight months.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the timing loose, about eight months to a few years. Better a range than a date we made up.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): How bad is it? And I'm wondering about swelling, and about stiffness in the morning.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Bad.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swelling, though?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Morning stiffness?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes. Not really.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it? Gel, tablets from the chemist?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Gel.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Voltaren gel. He's meant to put it on the knee twice a day, but he skips the morning most days. Nagging hasn't fixed it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Diclofenac gel, twice a day on paper, and I'm not sure it actually happens. Tablets as well, from the chemist?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which tablets, what strength?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Voltaren. Twenty-five. Think.
[SEG0029] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Those are the fifty milligram Voltaren, Dad. One when the pain's really bad, not every day.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Strength's not agreed, twenty-five or fifty, so I won't write a dose. By mouth, only on the bad days. Any stomach problems with them? Reflux, ulcers?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Never started, so it stays off the list. And you're still on the amlodipine?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Side note while I remember. I take biotin for my hair, that's mine, not his. Mum, his wife, has diabetes and she's on metformin, five hundred milligrams twice a day. His amlodipine is five milligrams every morning for the blood pressure, ongoing for years, and he lives with me and Mum, retired last year.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your biotin and your mother's metformin do not go on his chart. Her diabetes I'll record as his wife's history. Hypertension ongoing, amlodipine five milligrams by mouth every morning. Now the knee itself.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right knee. Tender along the medial joint line, crepitus when you bend, flexion a bit short of full, and no effusion that I can feel.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Working impression is osteoarthritis of that knee. Going down stairs is mechanical and it fits. Night waking means I can't fully rule out an inflammatory flare, so that stays a possibility, not a firm label.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Weight's ninety-seven kilos, and that's a lot of load through a sore knee. Easing off a few kilos would help the joint. Mechanics, not a lecture.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Heartburn. After tablets.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Twelve weeks and 3 days. LMP was the 14th of March, and both my phone app and the gynaecologist in Koramangala gave the same date, so the dates are not in doubt.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Why today?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I want my blood tested, doctor. I need to know if I carry it too, for the baby's sake. I have been turning it over in my mind every single night.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): At a camp in Jayanagar last month they said I have thalassaemia trait. HbA2 was 5.2 percent on that paper. I got very tensed for her.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Any long-standing illness?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, asthma, since my college days. It is the mild type, I have never been admitted, touch wood, and I manage it with the inhalers only.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any operation before?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. Not even a tooth extraction, nothing like that.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not even spotting. I check every morning because I read too many articles, but there has been nothing at all.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tummy pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. There is a stretching low down sometimes, like a small pull, but it is not pain.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I had vomiting in the first month, mostly mornings, but it has gone completely, and I am eating rice and sambar normally now.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fever? Cough?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. No fever, no cough.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Breathless on walking?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. I climb two floors to the flat and I am alright.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Wheeze at night?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. Two or three nights in a week I wake up a little tight in the chest, and it settles if I sit up.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Alcohol?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoke, never alcohol. I take only one small coffee in the morning, and even that I am thinking of cutting down.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mm. Medicines?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Folic acid 5 mg, one tablet every morning, started when we began planning the pregnancy. The brown inhaler, budecort, two puffs morning and night. Asthalin only when I need it, one or two puffs.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, she misses the night puffs sometimes. I have seen that inhaler not used.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, yes, some nights I forget if I sleep early. Also they gave me ferous sulphate, one tablet a day, but I stopped it in March because my stomach was not agreeing.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): You took the iron, or never started?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I took it for about ten days, then I stopped it in March. They also spoke of a deworming tablet, but I never took that one.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any drug reaction?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, penicilin. At 19, for a throat infection, within one hour I got hives all over and my lips swelled. They told me never to take penicilin again, so I have avoided it completely.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest. Lungs are clear, no wheeze just now. Tummy is soft.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that alright? I was frightened the night tightness means the asthma is worsening in pregnancy, because I read it can change, and my mother-in-law has been saying all sorts of things.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Asthma is stable enough. Today is carrier screening. Nothing is confirmed about the baby.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): I am booking a blood count, HPLC for thalassaemia, and a ferritin, today.
[SEG0040] person_1 (NURSE): I will take her to the lab after this. I can print the forms now.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the HPLC shows you also carry the trait, we might do a detailed scan, and we might send you both for genetic counselling. Not otherwise.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I am negative, doctor? I need it clear in my head, because he is a carrier, so is the baby still at risk of the major disease or only when both of us carry it? I keep circling on this.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): If you are negative, the baby cannot have thalassaemia major. Let's see in two weeks with the reports.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I restart the iron on my own? I will continue the inhalers, I will not stop those, and I always tell doctors about the penicilin.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do not restart the iron yourself. Continue the folic acid and both inhalers. No penicillin-group medicines. Bring the camp report if you have it.
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I have it in the file. I can give a xerox.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, one more thing. My sleep is very broken from the worry, I am up till 1 or 2 thinking about the baby. Do we treat that?
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not with a tablet today. See me in two weeks. The nurse will finish the bloods.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of course. Come in, sit down, catch your breath. Where would you like to start?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): My heart, really. It's been fluttering, like it skips and then races, mostly in the evenings when I finally sit down.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me more about that.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, like I said, it flutters. Sometimes it's a few seconds, sometimes it goes on for a minute or so, and it happens a few evenings a week.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm-hm.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It doesn't stop me doing anything. It just feels odd, and I notice it more than I'd like to.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see. And when did you first notice it?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Ooh. Um. It could have been last month, or the month before that, I honestly couldn't tell you. It sort of crept up on me.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's perfectly all right. I can see in your notes that you take carbimazole. What dose are you on at the moment?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Twenty... maybe 20 mg? It was changed at some point, I think, or I think it was. The box is in my other bag, sorry.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't apologise. How often do you take it?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Once a day, in the morning with breakfast. That's the one thing I never forget, because the alarm on my phone goes off.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Has anything else changed in the last few weeks, anything at all, that you can think of?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. Honestly, I'd just like to know if I need a bigger dose or a smaller one and then get on with my day.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand, but I wouldn't want to change a dose by guesswork. The blood result will tell me far more than the box in your bag could.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): So you can't just put it up today and see?
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): I could, but if your levels are already low that could make you feel worse. Let me keep that thought for a moment.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. It's just that I've done this dance before and it takes forever.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): I hear you. Before I decide anything, are you allergic to any medicines, now or in the past?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I came out in hives when I was about six, my mum always reminds me, and I've avoided it ever since.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's important, thank you. I'll make sure it's flagged. Any other medicine or food that's ever given you trouble?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, just that one. That's the whole list, I promise.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Tell me what the fluttering is like when it happens. Do you feel faint, or does it just feel like a noise in your chest?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): More like a noise. Like a little bird trapped behind my ribs. It gets my attention and then it goes away on its own.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, I'm just thinking. Palpitations like that are very common when thyroid hormone levels are still settling on treatment.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): So it's the tablets not working properly?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not necessarily. It can take a few months for the dose to find the right level, and then it can overshoot or undershoot a little. It happens to lots of people.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't give up the tablets. I'd rather you called me first. What I think is most likely is the thyroid hormone level not being fully settled yet.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): And that's it? That's all you think it is?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's my best working guess, based on what you've told me. I'd like to repeat your thyroid blood test today so we aren't relying on guesswork.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Today? Now? I have to be somewhere by eleven, remember.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse can take it on your way out, it takes about five minutes and you won't need to wait.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Five minutes I can do. Will it hurt?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): A small scratch, nothing more.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Anything I should do in the meantime?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep taking the carbimazole exactly the way you have been. And if the fluttering ever comes with a racing heart that won't settle, faintness or chest pain, ring 999 rather than waiting for us.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I wanted to ask about the leaflet that came with the tablets, it says to report sore throats, which seems a bit dramatic.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's actually quite important with that medicine. A sore throat with a fever should be checked quickly, so do mention it if it ever happens.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh. Then I'll remember that too. Anything else I should be afraid of?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not afraid, just aware. That's the lot from me.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Brilliant. Thank you so much, and sorry again for rushing in late.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Mind the stairs on the way down, the second flight is slippery when it rains.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, um, good evening, doctor, thanks for seeing me.

[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hello, doctor. I'm here with them in case I can help.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that'll be useful. Pull up a chair.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Honestly, you know, it's some chest discomfort when I climb stairs, and my family pushed me to come.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): it's been going on for nearly five years
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): how much does it limit you?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): hmm, a seven out of ten, I suppose
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, have you tried anything for it?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Erm, only resting, and it's not much. Oh, um, and indigestion after tablets. That's been about the same, about a year. I mean, as for indigestion after tablets, I'd say mild.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, have you been feeling tired?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I have.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): would you say mild, moderate or severe?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Pretty severe, if I'm being honest. I've also had bruising easily, for three weeks.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had some chest discomfort when you climb stairs before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a similar thing a couple of years ago. It went away.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): and what about blood in the urine, palpitations or black stools?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, um, none of those, no.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what about breathlessness or fainting?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No, um, none of those at all.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's your breathing otherwise?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Breathing's normal.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything different when you pass water?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): no, that's all fine
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any previous surgeries?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your parents, brothers or sisters, any conditions?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): My grandmother had dementia.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you take on a normal day?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I take metoprolol, 50 milligrams, twice a day for my heart it's simvastatin, at night
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what strength is that?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): 20 milligrams. Glimepiride, 2 milligrams, before breakfast for my sugar.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I mean, uh, that's what's prescribed, but I'm not sure she takes it every day.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): I mean, I was told I'm allergic to plasters, but I don't remember what reaction I had. Tramadol, I'd say.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I have about eight cigarettes in a day.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): I used to drink heavily but I stopped four years ago.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you get out much?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Not much, I mostly stay in these days.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): alright, are you on your own at home?
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): I live with my elderly mother.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your meals?
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone ever diagnosed you with something?
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got heart disease
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, high cholesterol. Yes, diabetes.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll note down your vital signs first.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a a little longer...
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: BP is 119 over 74, respiratory rate 18, temperature 36.7. And pulse 66, saturation 98 percent.
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, uh, what was I saying, is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't worry, we'll discuss it in a second.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you in a second, make yourself comfortable.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Sure thing.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me if that's sore.
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal and your chest is clear.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Look straight ahead.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): There are a few small bruises on your forearms.
[SEG0062] person_1 (PATIENT): sure thing
[SEG0063] person_2 (DOCTOR): All finished, thank you. From what you've told me and what I found, my working impression is stable coronary disease on antiplatelet treatment, with minor bleeding. We shouldn't forget reflux from the tablets.
[SEG0064] person_1 (PATIENT): Actually, do you think it's something serious?
[SEG0065] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's stable coronary disease on antiplatelet treatment, with minor bleeding, and we'll know more once the blood tests is back. Just to be sure I understood. You've had some chest discomfort when you climb stairs for nearly five years, and no breathlessness or blood in the urine.
[SEG0066] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, that's right.
[SEG0067] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange blood tests for bruising and bleeding. I'd like to arrange an ECG for chest discomfort. I'd rather check than guess, and this is the quickest way to know more. I'm going to put you on pantoprazole, 40 milligrams, before breakfast, long term. That's for stomach protection.
[SEG0068] person_1 (PATIENT): is that safe with my other medicines?
[SEG0069] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take your blood-thinning tablets after food and do not stop them on your own. If you pass black stools or have prolonged bleeding, or you feel really unwell, please come to the emergency department. That's all from me. Any questions?
[SEG0070] person_1 (PATIENT): no, that's all thanks a lot
[SEG0071] person_2 (DOCTOR): goodbye for now

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Not a bit, no. My granddaughter was meant to be at the minor hurling in Croke Park on Saturday and they postponed it with the weather. She's only ten and she was raging, texting me all morning.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Ah the poor thing. They'll get it played, I'd say. Doctor's free now, in you go.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, uh, one second, this screen is after freezing on me again. Right. What has you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the ringing, doctor. In the right ear. A high whistle, like a kettle left on the boil, and I'm after having it a month now, umm, maybe a little over, from around the start of last month.
