[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): The right. Only the right, it never swaps. It's there all day but it's desperate when the house goes quiet, night time, telly off, herself asleep. If I've the radio on low I can nearly put it out of my head.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the hearing on that side?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Muffled. Like a wad of cotton wool in it. In the canteen I have to turn the left ear to the lads or I miss the bones of what they're saying. There's a fullness in it too, not a pain exactly, more a blocked feeling, if you follow me.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Do you work in noise?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I do, yeah. I'm a fitter in the packaging plant in Sandyford, twenty-two years this August, conveyors and compressors, wicked loud. And I'll hold my hands up, I don't wear the ear protection, the muffs fog my glasses so they stay on the hook. I don't use the plugs either.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Say that again? No protection at all? The screen jumped.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): None. Five days a week, and a Saturday now and again if the line is behind. Eight till half four.
[SEG0016] person_1 (NURSE): Will I get his weight while the computer's thinking, doctor?
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, leave it, we're grand. Any discharge out of the ear? Dizziness? A spinning feeling?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No discharge, nothing leaking. I check with a tissue in the morning and it's dry. No dizziness and no spinning, the room stays put. I was half afraid it was one of those inner ear things, but no.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. It isn't sore to touch and it isn't sore inside. The fullness is there, like I said, but if you're asking is it sore, it isn't.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Umm, the medicine list hasn't loaded. What are you taking?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): There's a few, now. Amlodipine five milligrams in the morning for the pressure, the cholesterol one atorvastin twenty milligrams at night, and the sugar tablets, metformin five hundred milligrams twice a day with breakfast and tea, for the diabetes. Only the Ayurvedic powder as well, a teaspoon in warm water every morning, from the health shop, for the joints. I was on sertraline fifty milligrams for the low mood but I stopped it in March, and there was a prescription for betahistine that I never collected and never took.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hold on, the cholesterol one, what dose did you say? It blinked.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastin, twenty milligrams, every night after the news. Not the morning, the night.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand. Let me look in that ear, tip your head a small bit.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, the right, yeah. I had wax syringed years ago in the left one, a river of it, but this feels different, this is the noise more than anything.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): The right canal is clear, there's no wax sitting in it, and the drum looks intact. It's not red.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That's what I thought. It doesn't feel dirty, it feels stunned, from the machines I'd say.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd say this is most likely noise-related ringing, with the muffled hearing going along with it. I wouldn't call it for definite until we see a hearing test.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): A hearing test, yeah, I was wondering. My brother had one of his own, a different story entirely, I won't go into it.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you for an audiogram, a proper hearing test. You won't be waiting on me to organise the slot.
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book that with audiology now. They'll write out to you with the appointment.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): And you need to wear the ear defenders at work, muffs or plugs, every shift. I'm saying that straight.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I will, I will, I'll put them on from Monday, fogged glasses or not. Is there a tablet for the meantime or do we wait?
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): No tablet from me today. You never started the betahistine and I'm not starting anything now, we'll see what the test shows.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, no new medicine so. And the powder in the morning, I can keep that? It's only herbs, turmeric and bits, whatever's on the jar.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): You can keep the powder, I'm not stopping it. Come back here in six weeks with the hearing test result and we'll go through it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, right. The ring is the thing that gets me at night, lying there listening to it, but I'll manage. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mind yourself on that N11 on the way home.
[SEG0040] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the audiology request before you go. Take care, Mr. Brennan.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through and sit yourself down. Sock and trainer off the sore foot if you can manage.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Cheers. It's the left ankle. I twisted it yesterday playing football.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Talk me through it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, five-a-side after college, I'm on a sports course, I'm 19. Pitch was soaking, I turned, foot stuck, and there was a pop. Not a crack. Dave thought it was hilarious till I started limping, typical.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight on it right after?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, yeah, I limped off. I can still walk on it, it just hurts, quite bad when I walk. Bus was a nightmare, two changes.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has it swollen?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Came up last night, puffy on the outside. My sister said to strap it. She takes biotin for her hair and thinks she's a pharmacist. Honestly.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave your sister's biotin. Any numbness in the toes?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bruising?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Not a proper bruise.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever, or feeling shivery?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I feel fine. Had a huge pizza after, which was probably stupid.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Notes say asthma. Still a problem?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Had it five-ish years. Blue inhaler's salbutermol, well, salbutamol, two puffs when I need it. Brown one's beclomethazone, no, beclometasone, two hundred micrograms twice a day.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does wheeze wake you at night?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if I've been training in the cold. Not most nights.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough with it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain today?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never had one.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Taken anything for the ankle?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two tablets, five hundred milligrams each, this morning. My mum's on metformin for her diabetes, that's her, not me.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoke?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Couldn't, with the asthma, and coach would lose it. We train three times a week usually.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the couch, please. Tender over the outside ligament, not on the bone. Moderate swelling, and I can't see a proper bruise.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah the bone pressing is alright. Ow, front outside, that's the bit. I can feel your finger.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Foot pulses are good, toes pink, and sensation's intact where I'm touching. Pulse at the wrist is seventy-eight. Temperature's thirty-six point six degrees.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is seventy-eight bad? I was sprinting in the warm-up, heart going mad, but that was before. And my uncle broke his ankle last year, they X-rayed him straight away.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Seventy-eight is a normal resting pulse. Your uncle's break is a different beast.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I know, I'm not him. Go on.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ottawa rules, thinking aloud. You've got malleolar-area pain. I'd want an X-ray if there was bone tenderness at the back or the tip of the lateral or medial malleolus, or if you couldn't take four steps both then and now. You're tender on the ligament, not the bone, and you walked in.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Four steps is easy. It throbs after, that's all. I walked from the waiting room fine, slowly.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I don't think this is a fracture. Working impression is a sprain of the lateral ligament, provisional.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So I dodge the X-ray queue?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No X-ray today. If it worsens, if you can't weight bear, or the pain starts climbing, then we arrange an ankle X-ray.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair. What do I actually do with it, then? Saturday's a cup match, I'm on the wing, Dave will be unbearable if I cry off.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Rest, elevate it when you sit, ice in a tea towel for about ten minutes a few times a day. No football this weekend, and no training until you're walking without a limp, a week at least. Paracetamol, up to two tablets four times a day. If you need more, ibuprofen four hundred milligrams with food up to three times a day.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ice, feet up, no wing wizardry, got it. Keep the inhalers going even if I'm not running?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, salbutamol when you need it, beclometasone twice a day, don't stop them. If it's not clearly better in a week, book back in.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, Kai Pillay's in, six years old, mom with him. I did the observations already, before you called us.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Around Diwali. And the cough itself, is it—
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Wet, Doctor, and it wakes him at night. Sorry, I jumped in.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, you're fine. How many days for the fever? Say it again, I typed in the wrong box.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The fever's newer than the cough. From Monday, so five days, if I've counted properly.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): His dad at the front desk said three days, from Thursday. That's what landed on the triage note.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thursday? Ag, no. Dad's been away for work. I'm the one there. Monday, five days. Well, pretty much.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between three and five days, we won't force it. How high did it get? Repeat that, the fan just roared.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Our thermometer at home said 39 last night. His father tells everyone 40, but he never measured, I did.
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): Triage just now, temperature 38.1, pulse 118, oxygen 97 percent, respiratory rate 26, blood pressure 98 over 62.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): 38.1, thanks sister. Kai, how are you today?
[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): I am not feeling well, Doctor. Thank you for asking.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shame, man. Is your throat sore?
[SEG0016] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. My throat is sore.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He said so before we left. He didn't go to school. And he's been off his food since yesterday.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Off his food. Any vomiting, or a runny tummy?
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting. There was one loose—
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hold on, this popup won't close. Say the tummy part again?
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting, and no diarrhoea. I started to say a loose stool, but it was a normal one, actually.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, good. What have you given him for the fever?
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Panado syrup, by mouth. One medicine spoon, the 5 ml one, every six hours, since the fever started.
[SEG0024] person_1 (NURSE): Dad told me it was Nurofen, two spoons, not Panado. I nearly charted ibuprofen instead.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The Panado was me. He might have given Brufen last night while I was at my sister's. He just said a spoon, I don't know if he meant one spoon or the two he told you.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Panado 5 ml six-hourly is clear. The Brufen, your amounts don't match, so I'm not writing a dose. Any allergies?
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing he's allergic to. No rash from a medicine, nothing like that.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): No known allergies. Asthma? Or has a cough like this happened before?
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No asthma. He had croup once, last winter, or the winter before, I always mix those winters. It settled at home, we didn't come in.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you pin a month on the croup? I lost the sentence, someone walked past.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can't, Doctor. Last winter, or the one before. That's the best I can do.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave it undated. Anyone smoking at home?
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad smokes, but outside by the garage, not in the house. I've never smoked.
[SEG0034] person_4 (PATIENT): Excuse me, Doctor. May I have some water, please?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, of course. Sister will sort that now now. Kai, when you cough, does it hurt?
[SEG0036] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. It hurts.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He keeps tapping the middle of his chest when he says it. Not the tummy.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Middle of the chest. Any wheeze you've heard at home? Pulling in under the ribs?
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No wheeze. No pulling in. He does breathe fast when the fever spikes, and it eases once the Panado kicks in.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Eases after the Panado. Let me listen. Big slow breaths for me, my boy.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, no crackles and no wheeze. Throat is red. Ears are fine. Tummy is soft and it doesn't hurt when I press.
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Shame, that's a relief. I got myself worked up, my brother's little one had a bad chest last year. Sorry, not relevant.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's all right. My working impression is a viral infection, the fever and the cough together. I can't rule out an early pneumonia, but the chest doesn't sound like it today.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no x-ray? The lady at the chemist was pushing me to ask.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If he's not better in three days, come back and I'll send him for a chest x-ray then.
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the Panado, do I just carry on with the 5 ml spoon?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Carry on with Panado, but make it 7.5 ml every six hours, he's six and the 5 is light. Don't add the ibuprofen until dad can say exactly what he gave, I don't want you doubling up.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): 7.5, ja, I'll mark the syringe. He'll drink if I nag him.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Small sips of fluid through the day, and keep him home from school tomorrow. If he goes drowsy, or the breathing gets harder, come straight in, don't wait out the three days.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): I'll stick the obs in the file. Dad's still sitting in the bakkie, parking out there is hectic if you wanted him.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, leave him, we're done with the clash on the dates. Mom's account is what I'm using, we just won't pretend they match.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you, Doctor. Kai, manners.
[SEG0053] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you very much, Doctor.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pleasure, Kai. Off you go. Sister, call the next one when the screen behaves.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late. The bus sat on the bridge for ages, then the rain came, and I nearly turned for home.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Rough. And I'm in foul form, so don't mind me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. What brought you down today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the waterworks. I'm up three or four times every night, the stream is weak, and then it dribbles.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. I couldn't put a date on it. Last winter, or the one before. It just crept up.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): By day, does it take a while to get going?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Ages. I stand there like an eejit. Weak stream, and a dribble at the end. Mortifying.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine at all?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I'd have noticed.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or have you been shivery?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever. I'm just tired from the getting up, that's the height of it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed at all?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah I don't know. The trousers are a bit looser, maybe, or maybe I'm imagining it. I haven't been on the scales.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or tightness in the chest?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Chest is grand. I don't be coughing.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you drinking in the evenings?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Tea. Two mugs, sometimes 3, after the news. Don't start on me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are the nights worse when you've had the extra tea?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Suppose they are. Yeah. It still happens on the quiet nights, mind.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other conditions, or tablets you're taking?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Blood pressure. Amladipine, five milligrams, every morning, for years. I'm seventy one. That's the lot.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the amlodipine as it is. Err, my leaning is a benign enlarged prostate squeezing the pipe, though an overactive bladder is still possible. Infection looks unlikely with no fever and no blood, but I won't rule it out, and I'm not calling this definite today. The late tea is stirring the bladder as well.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange a PSA blood test and a urine test, dip and culture. Reception can book the bloods. Leave the sample today if you can manage it.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I can manage the sample. I just want this sorted. I'm sick of trailing to the jacks all night.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a tablet called tamsulosin, four hundred micrograms, once at night. It relaxes the prostate and can help the stream and the dribble. I won't start it today. If the urine is clear and the PSA isn't concerning, we'll start it when you're back.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Will that make me dizzy? I don't need that on top of the blood pressure tablet.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can drop the pressure a bit when you stand, especially with the amlodipine, so if we start it, take it at bedtime and sit a moment before you get up. We'll only go there if the tests are satisfactory. Ease off the tea after six, and try a decaf for the late mug if you can bear it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll try. I'm not promising I'll be pleasant about the tea.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we'll go through the results and decide on the tamsulosin then. Reception will have the blood form on your way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Evening. Let's get started.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Hi doctor, I got here as fast as I could.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): What would you like to start with today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I wanted to get cramps in my calves at night looked at.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Since when exactly?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): About... well, about a month.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it worse at certain times?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, lying in bed. That makes it worse. As for tired legs by evening, I honestly can't say when that began. It might have been last month or the month before.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does anything help it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Only putting my feet up, and it's not much.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): And there's a dull ache after the cramp as well, two years now. Hmm, with dull ache after the cramp, a five out of ten, I suppose. I've also had tingling in my feet, for about a year.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): How frequently does it come?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd say every other day.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): A few quick ones: weakness in the legs or redness of the leg?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't had weakness in the legs or redness of the leg, no.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any back pain, swelling of the legs, chest pain or shortness of breath at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing to report there.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are your bowels, any trouble?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Erm, no, all normal there.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about alcohol?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll have a glass of wine with dinner.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you live by yourself?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I share a house with my brother.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are your meals?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you work outside the home?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm a hairdresser, on my feet all day.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me your medicines, please.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): It's glimepiride, 2 milligrams, before breakfast for my sugar. Lisinopril, 10 milligrams, once a day. Right, before this I was on gliclazide; that's been stopped.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me ask about allergies, anything at all?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No known allergies.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has anyone ever diagnosed you with something?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I've had diabetes for five years now.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I have high blood pressure, for nearly five years.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): And besides that?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, I can see diabetes and high blood pressure in your file as well.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does your family have any medical conditions?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had a stroke.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll just record a few vital signs.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nearly done with the readings...
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: heart rate 64, temp 36.9 degrees, blood pressure 118 over 80.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that normal?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine, I'll explain it soon.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): From what you've told me, it points towards night-time muscle cramps without a worrying cause. Another possibility is a low salt level or low magnesium.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Is there something to worry about?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's night-time muscle cramps without a worrying cause, and we'll know more once the blood tests is back. We should do blood tests for muscle cramps. We should do a vitamin level for tingling feet.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Does it hurt?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gentle calf stretches against a wall before bed often help. Come back or go to emergency straight away if one leg becomes red, hot or swollen.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): That's fine by me.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's review you in four weeks. How would you describe the plan, so we're on the same page?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): So, I come back in four weeks. Is that right?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, yes, exactly right. Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Great, thank you for your help.

[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): for the stent, I believe my wife sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given i'm on something called an a... an antacid, 10 ml, maybe, when needed

[SEG0039] person_4 (NURSE): Here are the numbers, doctor. Pressure 123 over 75, pulse is 80 beats a minute, temp 36.5 degrees.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does that hurt?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is tender under the right ribs and you stop breathing in when I press.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please sit back down. From what you've told me and what I found, I think we're dealing with gallstone-related pain at this stage. It could also be a stomach ulcer, so we'll keep that open.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Is there something to worry about?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with gallstone-related pain do well once it's treated properly. Let's get an ultrasound of the abdomen, for biliary pain. It's a routine test and it'll give us a much clearer picture. Let's get liver blood tests, for biliary pain
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): let me think, when would that take place?
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): for this, paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day when needed, one week it's for pain avoid fatty and fried foods until the scan we'll refer you to the surgical clinic and please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose

[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, I'll do that. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): All the best.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Iyer, keep the arm relaxed. First reading is one hundred and seventy-two over one hundred and four.

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Appa, sit properly, you were almost running from the auto.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Actually what happened is, near the temple steps I missed one step, not a full fall, um, just a small twist, and from that evening there is this dull pain inside the right knee. It is there from five-ish weeks, not exactly to the day, around that only, and it catches when I climb.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): I will recheck after you sit quietly for two minutes. Any chest pain or giddiness just now?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no, nothing like that. No chest pain, no giddiness, no headache also. Sorry, I talk too much, that is my habit only.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Dr. Menon. Is it the knee you came for?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor, the right knee. This BP, whenever I enter a clinic it shoots up, pure white coat. At home I feel absolutely normal, I am telling you.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Swelling? Giving way? Locking?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling that I have seen, it does not give way, and it does not lock. The ache is worse on stairs, better if I sit with the leg straight for some time.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any tablet for it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I took one Crocin, five hundred milligram, by mouth, the night before last, for the pain, only that single dose, then I stopped. My stomach felt a bit heavy after it, but that settled by morning. I am not on any BP tablet, never have been.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, his father had a stroke, that is why I pushed him to come. I did not want us to ignore a high reading.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Noted. Diabetes? Heart problem?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes, no heart problem. BP was never told high before, except these clinic readings, and even those I do not trust.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Alcohol?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked. Alcohol, only at weddings, maybe twice a year, one small peg, that is all. I am retired from the accounts department at the mill, and I walk to the market most mornings.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Appa, do not start on yesterday's match, the doctor has other patients.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, but it was such a match, doctor, India were fifty for three and I was so tense, then Kohli settled and they crossed two hundred easily. My neighbour was shouting from the balcony the whole evening, very disturbing, but nice also.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the weather was so heavy we could not go to the terrace for the fireworks after the win. Coming back, the auto sat near the flyover for forty minutes.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty minutes, yes, and the driver was playing old Ilaiyaraaja songs, my grandson would have loved it, he is just learning the keyboard, poor boy practices till late.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Back to the knee. Pain on flat walking?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat walking is okay, doctor. Bending is possible, but the last bit on the stairs is where it catches. No fever, no redness, I checked in the mirror this morning, skin looks the same both sides.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me look.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): No swelling, no warmth. Bend and straighten are both full. Tender on the inner side of the right knee. That is all.
[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): Second reading, after sitting, one hundred and fifty-six over ninety-two.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): See, already coming down. If you check a third time it will be one-thirty only, I know my body. The cuff itself makes me nervous, my heart goes fast, then it settles. Classic white coat.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pulse is eighty-four, regular. I am not calling this established hypertension today.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): It may be white coat. It may be early hypertension. I cannot separate them on two readings.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no tablet today?
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): No tablet today. No point starting a BP medicine on clinic numbers alone.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Get a home reading morning and evening, sitting, for seven days. Write every number and bring the paper.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): We can use my wife's machine, she checks her own pressure, she takes telmisartan forty milligram at night, but that is hers, I have not touched those tablets. I will make a full table, date and time, I am very particular with records from my accounts days.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): One arm only, the right, same each time, after sitting five minutes.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Right arm, five minutes, morning and evening, seven days. And the knee, you are not sending me for any scan?
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): No scan now. If it is not better in three weeks, then an X-ray.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Avoid deep squats, take the stairs slowly. Paracetamol five hundred milligram by mouth, up to three times a day if the pain needs it, with food. Skip it on days you are comfortable.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times only if needed, with food, no squats. If the paper shows high BP, which tablet will you give, because my neighbour got a bad cough from one of them and I do not want that kind of trouble.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): We decide after the seven days. I am not naming a tablet now. Come back with the readings in one week.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will bring him. Should he worry about the stroke thing tonight?
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not tonight. Pulse is steady and there is no chest pain. If he gets chest pain, a severe headache, or weakness on one side, go to emergency. Otherwise just the one-week visit.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Understood, doctor. One week, readings written properly, knee advice followed, and I will not borrow her telmisartan, promise. Sorry for the long match story, I get carried away.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): There is no BP medicine to print. Collect the slip for the knee advice at the desk on your way out.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No headaches, no. Dry mouth, yeah, a bit, but no headaches.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you ever wake up choking or gasping?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I don't think I wake up. She says I just gasp and carry on.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your nose blocked at night?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Always. Both sides. I breathe through my mouth.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, to medicines especially?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, something gave me a swollen lip once, years ago, but I don't know what it was. A tablet, I think. Or maybe food.

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of beers, most nights. I know, I know.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): That relaxes the throat muscles and makes snoring worse. Let me look at your nose and throat. Say ahh. ~

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): It won't cure sleep apnoea, but it can help the snoring, and make any treatment easier. Give it a fortnight. ~

[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, you know, I think I understand everything. Thanks.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): See you soon.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh leave it. I'm not hungry at six. The trains were stuffed again, but that's not... anyway.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So the sweating and the shaking are on you before any food. How often is that?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every morning. Some days worse. I'm over it.

[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Settled after the tea. Any chest pain when this happens?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's fine.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is wiped by lunch though. Flat on our couch. She moved in with us last year, so I see all of it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I'm knackered. Couch is lumpy, write that down if you like.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, lumpy couch. The diabetes has been with you a good while though, hasn't it. How long?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifteen-odd years. Umm. Tablets, not the needles. Thank goodness.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets, and what doses are you on these days?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea. The chemist does a Webster pack. Metforman and the other one. Ask her, I'm sick of the questions.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Gliclazide, eighty milligrams, every morning. Metformin, five hundred milligrams, morning and night. She does take them.

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Penicillin, rash and swollen lips. We'll steer well clear of that. Mind if I check you over?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): If you must. Be quick, I want a lie down.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is seventy-six, nice and regular. Blood pressure's one forty-two over seventy-eight. Hands are cool and a bit clammy. Chest is clear, heart sounds normal, and the tummy's soft with nothing tender.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Cold hands. Story of my life.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not losing the plot. Good. I suppose.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not losing the plot. I do want bloods today, the HbA1c and a kidney check while you're on metformin. We'll book both.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The pathology on High Street, same as usual?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, reception out the front will book it. Have some brekky with that gliclazide, even toast. If you get shaky, juice or a few jelly beans and sit yourself down. Come back and see me in two weeks with the results, I'm not changing the dose today.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Toast. Fine. I'm done in.

[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ta. Sorry, drop-off was a mess and then we couldn't find a park.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): All good. Grab a seat. What are we sorting?
[SEG0006] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His eyes. School wants a note or they won't have him back. They've been red and sticky after a cold.
[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): It's nothing. I'm fine.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which eye, and how long has it been?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Left one started about three days ago. Err, actually I can't pin the morning, might've been Friday night or Saturday. Then the right one went red yesterday. Both of them now, sticky gunky lashes in the morning.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the eye painful? The eyeball itself, not just the crust.
[SEG0011] person_4 (PATIENT): No. Doesn't hurt.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Itchy at all?
[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): Nuh. It's fine.
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had a cold all last week. Runny nose, a cough. That's mostly gone now. I've been giving children's panadol, five mils, that's two hundred and forty milligrams, by mouth, morning and night since yesterday, for the temperature.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Is the discharge just mornings, or through the day?
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mostly mornings. Yellow, a bit green. He rubs it and it looks angrier.
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): Well actually it is itchy. When I rub it. Heaps.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. So the itch is there. Are the lids swollen? Is the light bothering him?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Puffy lids in the morning, then it settles a bit. Light's fine, he's not squinting.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Can you see the board at school?
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): Yeah. I can see. Not a big deal.
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He says that about everything. The teacher reckons it's conjunctivitis and wants him off. He just wants his footy.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Both conjunctivae are red, left more than right. Some crust on the lashes.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): The cornea is clear. No real lid swelling just now. Pupils are equal.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm turning it over in my head. After a cold, both eyes sticky and red, with a bit of fever, my leaning is a viral conjunctivitis. I can't fully rule out an early bacterial one, but I'm not going to conclude that today, and allergy doesn't really fit the gunk.
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The chemist mentioned cloramphenicol drops. Should we grab some?
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. I wouldn't start an antibiotic. That sort of drop won't change the usual viral course, and there's no reason for it today.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cooled boiled water, a clean cotton pad, one pad for each eye, wipe from inside to out. Wash his hands, his own towel, no sharing pillows. Bin the pads straight after.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): School-wise, not tomorrow. Once the discharge has dried up, usually a couple of days, he can go back. I'll write the note they want.
[SEG0030] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been tired, and a bit off his food, since the cold. He's drinking, just not loads.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any tummy pain, vomiting, or diarrhoea? Any earache?
[SEG0032] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No tummy pain. No vomiting. No diarrhoea. Ears are fine.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breathing been alright? Any chest symptoms at all?
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Breathing's fine. No chest stuff.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Panadol can continue if he's miserable. Same two hundred and forty milligrams, up to four times a day, at least four hours apart. Don't add nurofen on top unless we've talked about it.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Often three to five days. If it's not settling in three days, or the eye becomes painful, the light really hurts, or his vision drops, come straight back. Sooner if he seems properly worse.
[SEG0037] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the note for school?
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yep, I'll do it before you leave. Viral-type conjunctivitis, keep him home till the sticky discharge settles, likely back in a couple of days. Reception will print you a copy.
[SEG0039] person_4 (PATIENT): So Saturday footy?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the eyes aren't gunky by then, yes. If they're still stuck shut, you sit it out.
[SEG0041] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Beauty. Thanks for that.

[SEG0054] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will come with the reports. Thank you, doctor.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab a pressure and a pulse before you go in, just sit easy there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I will of course, I've been sitting out there an age, the radio was going and some fella talking about the hurling, I wasn't even following it, my mind was on the legs.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Grand so. Blood pressure is one forty two over eighty six, pulse is seventy eight, and your oxygen is ninety seven percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the oxygen the important bit? Years ago in the hospital with the flu they said a different number but that was a whole other story, I was in a ward with six of us.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. That's only today's. Doctor's ready for you now.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): In you come. How are you keeping these days?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure I'm not bad in myself at all, doctor, it's the legs that have me in.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go on so, tell me about the legs.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It's cramps in the two calves, at night. I'm two months at it, nearly every night, and they wake me out of the sleep.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It begins with a little twitch, err, and then the calf just locks, like someone has a fist in there, and I'm out on the landing walking up and down, and then I put the kettle on even though I won't drink the tea.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): What eases it when that happens?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The walking eases it, and if I rub the calf hard with my hand. The hot water bottle was useless, I gave up on that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you get any swelling in the ankles or the legs?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No swelling at all. I check them in the morning and they're ordinary, no puff in them.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or are you getting breathless walking on the flat?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort. Down to the shop and back I'm grand, the breathing doesn't bother me, it's purely the nights.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are the waterworks and the bowels, any change?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No change, they're as they always were. I go regular enough and there's no burning or anything like that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And what tablets are you on at the minute?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Well there's a few. Amlodipine five milligrams with the breakfast, that's for the pressure. I've a long history with that tablet but you don't need the whole saga.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the water tablet, forty milligrams, every morning, the little white one. On the box the chemist has frusemide, but everyone at home calls it the water tablet.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): At night I take the cholesterol one, atorvastin twenty milligrams, for the cholesterol. And my sugar tablets are metformin, five hundred milligrams in the morning and again with the tea, for the sugar.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and only the magnesium from the shop as well. I got it in the chemist on Patrick Street, two hundred milligrams, one at bedtime, for these cramps. I'm about three weeks taking that.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you getting all of those in, the way they're supposed to be taken?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The prescription ones, yes, they're in a box by the kettle and I don't miss them. The magnesium, umm, I forget it. Maybe four nights in the week I actually take it, I couldn't swear to which nights.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about fluids, how much are you drinking?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Very little water, doctor, I'll admit it. Two small cups of tea in the day and that's the height of it. With the water tablet I'm afraid of being up half the night, and the bathroom window doesn't even close properly, there's a draught.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I follow you. May I have a look at the legs?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): You may of course. Don't mind the hole in the left sock, I've been saying I'll mend it since Christmas and I haven't.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Calves are soft, no tenderness there. Pulses are present in both feet. The ankles are a bit puffy, both sides.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Are they now. Well actually, by the evening they do puff up. The shoes get tight and the elastic of the socks leaves a mark, the two ankles, and that's been a few weeks. They're grand again in the morning so I put it out of my head.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. So they swell by evening and settle overnight.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it exactly. Just the ankles, not up the leg.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working thought is these night cramps are linked with the water tablet and how little you're drinking, because the potassium can drop on frusemide. I don't want to call it for certain until the bloods are back.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): So I'm booking blood tests, the kidney function and the potassium, and the magnesium too while you're on the shop one.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put you down for Thursday morning in the clinic. No fasting for those.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday is fine, I have bowls but I'll skip the start. The half eight bus is reliable, Mrs Kearney from two doors down gets it as well, she talks the whole way.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, stretch the calves before bed. Both of them, hold it about half a minute, and do a few on each side.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Half a minute, a few each side, I can do that in the kitchen. Should I stay on the magnesium?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stay on the same two hundred at bedtime for now. Try and sip a bit more water through the day, nice and steady, not buckets of it. And don't start any other bits from the shop.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't, no. There was an ayurvedic powder sitting on the shelf and I looked at it twice, but I never bought it and I certainly never took any.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in two weeks, whether the results are in or not.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, I'll write it on the calendar beside the bins day. Am I to keep the water tablet going the same?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep it the same, forty milligrams in the morning. Don't stop it yourself.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): And say the cramp is desperate on a given night, would you give me something for the pain of it?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't add a painkiller today. Let's see what the tests say before we add anything.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): Your blood form will be at the desk, so Thursday is booked.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Lovely, thanks very much. I'll start the stretches tonight so.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Yoh. Poor kid. Anyway, I'm here.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello. Come through. You look like you'd rather be somewhere else.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ha. My wife made the booking. I'm forty-four, I'm fine, really. It's nothing.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. What's she worried about, what's been going on with you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the jaw. It clicks, and it aches when I chew. Been about two months. But it's not bad.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): You said about two months. Can you place it any tighter than that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Work's mad. I'm an accountant, tax season, everyone's shouting. I just clench.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eish, that sounds heavy. Coming back to the jaw though, when did the ache actually begin?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, I can't say the day. I had a few weeks in my head. Well actually no, more like two months, when the audits kicked off. I just ignored it.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the click there all the time, or mainly with food?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mainly when I chew. Steak's a write-off, I just leave it. Left side, I think. Minor stuff.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And does stress make it worse?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, deadlines make it tighter. But everyone's stressed. It's not a thing.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does your partner notice anything at night?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): She says I grind my teeth, keeps her up. I don't feel a thing, so maybe she's exaggerating.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or have you felt hot and unwell with this?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The click's louder in the morning, then it eases off. That's all.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Louder in the morning. I did ask about fever though. Have you had one?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm not ill.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Pain in the ear?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. Ear's fine. People make a fuss.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for it?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Panado. I take four, wait no, two, when it's annoying, which is hardly ever. Chemist also sold me those yellow muscle tablets, can't remember what they're called. Took like three, they made me dozy, so I stopped.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything you take every day? Pressure tablets, that sort of thing?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't do chronic pills. I'm healthy.
[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry folks, I still need his obs. I got pulled away earlier.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Temperature is 36.4, blood pressure 128 over 76, pulse 74. All decent.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lovely, thanks. Let me feel the joint. Open nice and slow, then close.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Click on the left as you open, and the muscle just in front of the ear is sore when I press. No swelling, and you open fully, no problem.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I reckon is the little disc in the jaw joint slips when you chew or clench, that's your click, and the muscles are overworking from the grinding. Your body's not fighting an infection, the joint's just overloaded.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): So I can tell her to relax then.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's not dangerous, but it is real. Soft foods for a few weeks, hey, no steak, no biltong, cut everything small. And a mouth guard at night so the teeth stop grinding on each other.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): A thin one from the dentist, just while you sleep. I'll write them a note today. Also skip chewing gum, and when you catch yourself clenching at the desk, just let the jaw hang.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the guard and the soft food haven't sorted it in six weeks, we might do an x-ray of the jaw. I won't book that now.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in six weeks anyway, whether or not, so we know where we stand. Reception will book it on your way out.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Fine. And the Panado?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Panado's fine, two tablets when you need them, don't go over eight tablets in a day. Leave those yellow ones, we don't know what they are.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sharp. I'll tell her she was half right. Cheers.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Hale, come on through. I'll grab a blood pressure and a pulse before the doctor sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I hope I have not kept anyone waiting.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Pressure is one forty-two over eighty-eight. Let me repeat that, you just sat down. One thirty-six over eighty-two. Pulse is seventy-eight.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I did come up the stairs rather quickly. The second reading is probably the fairer one.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): She's finishing a note, then she'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr. Hale, thanks for waiting. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I have come about pain in my stomach, Doctor, and I have also been sleeping poorly. I felt it was time to have someone look at it.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Ruth. I live in with him, and I drove. Traffic on Maple was a mess, by the way, we circled the lot twice.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Glad you made it. Ruth, I'll want your view too. Mr. Hale, where is the pain, and what is it like?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a burning pain in the upper part of my stomach, moderately uncomfortable. It comes most days, particularly after I eat, and a little purple pill takes the edge off.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have you had it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): About two weeks. Forgive me, that is not correct. It is closer to five weeks, though I cannot give you the exact date it began.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Most days for about five weeks, burning, after meals. Any vomiting with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not vomited at all.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, black stools, or chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, no black stools, and no chest pain. I am quite certain of that.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Regarding the pill, I have been taking a little purple pill for heartburn, once a day. The dose is, um, maybe twenty milligrams. I am not certain of the number, and I never learned the proper name.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he doesn't take it every morning. Some days I find it still sitting in the Monday slot on Wednesday.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. A little purple heartburn pill, possibly twenty milligrams, once a day, not always actually swallowed, name unknown. We'll leave it described that way.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's lost weight, too. His good trousers hang on him.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I must respectfully disagree. I do not believe I have lost any weight. It has been steady.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll hold both of those and not pretend we weighed him today. Tell me about the sleep.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I lie awake a good deal, and the burning often wakes me. I would say the poor sleep has gone on for about two weeks.
[SEG0024] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Longer. It's been at least two months. He's in the kitchen at two in the morning, lights on, just standing there.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): So two weeks from you, Mr. Hale, and at least two months from Ruth. I'll call it somewhere between two weeks and two months, since you don't agree on a number.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a fair summary. I simply had not counted the earlier nights.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud here. Burning after meals, a heartburn pill that helps a little, this may be gastritis or acid reflux. I was going to suggest an over-the-counter antacid and skip blood tests. Before I settle on that, do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Only socially.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Socially covers a wide range. What does a usual evening look like?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I did not mean to be evasive a moment ago.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Yeah. It's the bottle with dinner, not a splash in a glass. He corks it and it's gone.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you saying it straight. I'm not going to lecture you. A bottle most nights does change the plan I just sketched, because wine can inflame the stomach and it can stress the liver.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Please tell me what you would advise.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me examine you first. Your abdomen is soft. There is mild tenderness in the upper middle, the epigastrium. No guarding and no rebound, and I can hear bowel sounds.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that spot is tender under your hand.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He flinched. I saw it.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I had also been considering an ultrasound this afternoon. Soft belly, no fever, I'm setting that aside. My impression is gastritis or acid reflux, possibly stirred up by the wine. Not confirmed, just the best fit so far.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): An ultrasound did sound rather involved for a stomach ache.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Instead I'll order liver blood tests, a hepatic panel with the enzymes and bilirubin, because of the wine and this upper abdominal pain. For the pain I was going to start omeprazole at forty milligrams. Thinking it through, twenty milligrams is the better starting dose.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Would that be by mouth? And shall I keep taking the purple pill beside it?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): By mouth, twenty milligrams every morning before breakfast, for the stomach pain. Leave the purple pill off while you are on the omeprazole, so we are not stacking two acid medicines.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Very well. I will set the purple one aside.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you can bring the wine down from a bottle toward a glass, or skip some nights, that will help both the stomach and the liver. No scolding in that, just how the organs work.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall try. The evenings are quiet, and the wine has become a habit I am not proud of. There is a biography on the nightstand I keep meaning to finish instead.
[SEG0045] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I can put the bottle in the cupboard instead of on the counter. That helps a little, sometimes.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks to go over those blood results and see if the omeprazole is doing its job. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or your skin turns yellow, do not wait for that appointment. Go to the emergency room.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have explained it clearly, and I am grateful.

[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Sort of. It's odd, really. My back pain gets better the more I do, which my mum says is the wrong way round.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not wrong at all, it's actually a clue. Remind me how long it's been going on?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Let me think. It started gradually, around when we moved flat, so about eight months now.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): And where do you feel it?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Low down, right across the bottom of my back. Sometimes it shoots into my right buttock.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's it like first thing in the morning?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Awful, I'm stiff as a board. It takes me a good hour to loosen up and I can barely get my socks on.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it ever wake you at night?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, I get night pain, usually around four. I have to get up and shuffle about the kitchen.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if you've been sitting a long while, say at work? ~
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Worse. Sitting is the enemy. But a swim or a bike ride and it's far better, so exercise helps it.

[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my eyes have been fine.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any diarrhoea or blood when you go to the toilet?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Nope, nothing like that.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or weakness in your legs?

[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies to medicines that I should know about?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no allergies that I know of.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Now your background. Are you well otherwise?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): I get skin trouble, psoriasis, on my scalp and my elbows. Since I was about nineteen.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, that's worth knowing. Anything else?

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations in the past?

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Noted. And what about alcohol?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Stomach cramps. And my bowels are a mess.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me what the cramps do.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): They're low, more on the left. A grabby pain. When I pass stool they ease off. Been a year.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): The bowels, what's the mess exactly?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I go constipated for days, then it's loose, then constipated again. Whole year, same as the cramps. And I'm bloated most afternoons, worse when work goes crazy.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work, if that's the trigger?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Project manager at a logistics firm. Stress is basically the job. It never turns off.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm 46 and I feel like my body just quit on me. Don't need a lecture, okay.

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I checked more than once. No blood.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss?

[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fevers? Chills?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. I don't know. I get hot sitting at my desk but the vents are broken, and I never stuck a thermometer in, so maybe, maybe not.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, fever's a maybe, we'll leave it. Have you vomited?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. I do get queasy when the cramp hits, but it passes.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Top of my list is a sensitive gut, irritable bowel, especially with the stress and the way the pain eases when you go. I will not put that down as final today. I also can't rule out celiac, or a thyroid problem, from the story alone.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Wonderful. So nobody knows. What now, more pills?
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Maybe not more pills. What are you on already?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the pressure, five milligrams every morning.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Next?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): The cholesterol one at night. It's simvastaten, twenty milligrams. And sugar tablets, metformin, five hundred milligrams twice a day.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. Half a teaspoon in water. Label's gone, I couldn't tell you the real name.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister dumped it on me. I take it so she'll stop texting. It's probably nothing.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Easy. I didn't like the taste anyway.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): All of that today? Ugh. Okay. Stick me and let me leave.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the food side, keep a plain diary for the next two weeks, what you eat and what your gut does. And cut back on the usual agitators.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. What if this gets ugly before then?

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah yeah. Just don't poke the left side like you're mad at it.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soft belly. Tender over the left lower side where you said, no rebound, bowel sounds are present.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. Yep. That's the spot. Are we done?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): We're done for today. Labs on your way out, hold the powder, diary and less coffee, and I'll see you in three weeks.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. If the diary is a mess of scribbles don't yell at me.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Scribbles are fine. As long as I can read the pattern. Take care, Ms. Hale.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ice it, and keep the knee moving gently, don't rest it the whole time. Still no nurofen.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah yeah.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in a fortnight with the Thursday results. That's booked.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Fortnight. If I'm still standing.
[SEG0047] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him here.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Knee's not red and it's not hot. The bend's a bit short of full. That's enough for today.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put Thursday at 8 in the book on the way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, Mama. Observations first, then Doctor. Baby can stay put, shame, she's fast asleep.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks, Sister. Load shedding caught us at the robot by the mall, she spat the dummy the whole way, so I'm frazzled already, sorry we're late.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're fine. Blood pressure is one twenty eight over eighty four, pulse ninety two, temperature thirty six point seven. I'll let Doctor know.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, umm, this machine is crawling. What brought you in? Say it from the top, I only half heard.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the sleeping. She's six weeks on Thursday, and even when she sleeps a proper stretch I lie awake. I watch the monitor, I fold nappies, I check her breathing. My eyes just won't close.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not sleeping even when the baby sleeps. For how long?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The last four weeks. Since she was about two weeks old. I thought it was ordinary new-baby stuff and it hasn't budged.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): How's your mood? Feeling low?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not really. I'm tired, I feel like a wet rag by lunchtime, but I'm not low. The neighbour's dog goes all afternoon and I can't hear myself think, that's just noise, not me being sad.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, that's not right. She cries every afternoon. Three weeks of it, sitting on the bed in tears. I'm scared, hey.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, Thabo. Fine. I do cry most afternoons and I can't stop, and I feel flat, like I'm pretending to be her mother. But not three weeks. It started about ten days after the birth, she's six weeks, so more like four or five weeks.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok, so the low mood is somewhere between three and five weeks. I won't nail the date. Your file says asthma. Still a problem?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, asthma since I was about fourteen, ongoing, it never went away. The blue one is salbutamol, a hundred micrograms, two puffs when I need it. The brown one I can never remember the name of, two hundred micrograms I think, twice a day. I'm breastfeeding, if that changes anything.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Umm, the cursor jumped, sorry. Say the brown inhaler again?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I really can't, err, tell you the name. Brown inhaler. Maybe two hundred micrograms, twice a day.
[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was meant to take it twice a day. She skips it, some days nothing, with the night feeds.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze with the asthma?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. About two in the morning while I'm feeding her I get wheezy. Not every night. Just this last week or so.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cough?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. No cough.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath, like you can't get air?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): The stitches from the tear. Are they painful?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not painful. They've healed, I hardly notice them.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I've had panado plenty of times, no reaction, and nothing else either.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): I have to ask this plainly. Any thoughts of harming yourself?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. I call myself a bad mother in my head, yes, but I have never thought of hurting myself.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): And any thoughts of harming the baby?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not once. I check her breathing because I'm frightened something will happen to her, not because I would hurt her.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, I rabbit on. This past week I can't face food, two bites of pap and chicken and I'm done. And my head's full of cotton wool, I lose the sentence halfway.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): You look tearful, I can see it, but you're following everything. Chest is clear, no wheeze when I listen. I think this is postnatal depression. I can't rule out your thyroid either, so that stays possible.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll book a TSH and a full blood count with Sister before you go. Starting you on sertaline, sorry, sertraline, fifty milligrams, one tablet every morning. It's used in breastfeeding. Come back in two weeks.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): If things get worse before then, phone the rooms and we'll see you sooner. If you feel you might act on those thoughts, go to casualty, don't wait for me. Thabo, take one night feed if you can, and I'm referring her to the postnatal counsellor at the clinic.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello. I've been very tired since the doctor put me on a new heart tablet, and I get out of breath. My daughter thinks I should say something.
[SEG0002] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm her daughter. She's been much slower since the tablet. She naps all afternoon now.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Which tablet is it, Mrs Silva? ~
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): A beta-blocker, I think. It's called bisoprolol.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember how long ago it was started? ~
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Two months ago, after the heart attack.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry to hear that. When does the breathlessness happen?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Climbing stairs, and when I walk to the shops. I used to manage it fine.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, palpitations, or fainting?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No fainting.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze, or swelling in the ankles?
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No swelling. She does cough a little at night.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does anyone smoke at home, or have you smoked?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped when I had the heart attack.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good for you. Do you have any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to your heart and lungs and feel your pulse. ~
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your heart rate is slow, around fifty, and regular. Your lungs are clear, and your ankles are not swollen.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is that too slow? ~
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): A bit slow, which can make people feel tired. It may be the beta-blocker, and her heart condition may also play a part.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I have to stop it? ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't stop it on your own, because it protects your heart after a heart attack. I'd like to check things first. ~
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What checks? ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange a heart tracing today, and a blood test for anaemia and thyroid.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And then? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Depending on the results, I might lower the dose, or discuss it with her cardiologist.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): All right. I'd rather feel less tired. ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll phone you with the results. If you become faint, get chest pain, or are very breathless, call an ambulance.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come in, sir. Err, your wife caught me outside only. She says the mole has turned almost black, it has bled quite a few times, and you have been dizzy with it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): She wasn't asked. I am not dizzy. It bled once, once, and I am tired, so can we get on.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ah, sorry, this screen has frozen again. What did you say about the bleeding, say it once more?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Once. Last week it bled once, a little, then it stopped. She makes a drama.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. And the colour, she was telling nurse?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The colour has changed, yes, darker. Not jet black. Brown and a bit black, on my back, I can't even see it.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long is the mole itself there?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Two years. No, wait, before my son's wedding, that is four years. Four years it is sitting there.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, four? The system jumped. Four years?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, four years. The colour, she noticed it after Pune. Umm three weeks back... no, actually six weeks. Six weeks.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): Sir, vitals while you talk. Blood pressure one thirty six over eighty eight, pulse seventy eight, saturation ninety eight percent.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): One second, I didn't catch the pressure. Cursor was in the wrong box.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): One thirty six over eighty eight. Pulse seventy eight. Sats 98.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Is it paining? Any itch?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Not paining. It itches some nights, not every night. Irritating when I am trying to sleep.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Any loss of weight? I have to ask, you look worn out.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Weight is the same. I am worn out because I drive a taxi at night, not because of a mole.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Uh, your wife told the nurse you get dizzy. Say that again for me?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I said no. I am not dizzy. Don't write dizzy, I am just fed up and I want to go home and sleep.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Any other skin trouble, rashes anywhere else?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only this one thing on the back.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sun, what about sun? You burn?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Badly. Since I was a boy in Kerala, every summer I was burnt. Even now if I am out without a shirt I burn easy.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Medicines? Any tablet daily?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastin for cholesterol. Seventy five milligrams... no, that is wrong, it is forty milligrams, at night. And I stopped the Shelcal, the calcium, two months back.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Forty milligrams at night, atorvastatin, yes. Shelcal stopped. Anything else, blood pressure tablet?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only that. And I don't smoke, if you are going to ask. I just want this finished.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the back. Shirt up. Left side, near the shoulder blade.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): It's cold in here. Just look and tell me, I'm half asleep.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Asymmetric, border not smooth. Colour is mixed brown and black. Diameter six millimetres... no, sorry, the scale says nine millimetres. No open sore today.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): So what is it? Don't give me a long lecture.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I am concerned it is an atypical mole. I cannot rule out a melanoma, so that is not a final word, dermatology has to see it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Melanoma. Fine. What do I do.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): I have booked the skin clinic, Tuesday week, that slot is fixed. And I will see you here in two weeks with the reports.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Two places. More waiting.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nurse will take bloods Thursday morning, full blood count and TSH, because of the tiredness. Come fasting, nothing to eat after midnight.
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning bloods, I will put it in the book. Fasting.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): If those two are borderline we do ferritin, the third test. Only if borderline, not now.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): And the bleeding? It already stopped.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the bleeding does not settle before the skin clinic, we might do an ultrasound of that area. Not booked today.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): So I just wait and don't scratch it, is that the advice.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Don't scratch, don't pick, and keep the back covered in the sun. If it pours blood, press and go to emergency, but the Tuesday clinic stands.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I'm going. Tell my wife it is not an emergency tonight, she will be outside only, worrying.

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's worse with standing. Pretty moderate, if I'm being honest. Honestly, once or twice a day. And I've been feeling tired and weak as well.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any darker skin as well?

[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, did you get severe tummy pain or fainting?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no severe tummy pain or fainting.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been any vomiting?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Not at all, no vomiting.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Actually, doctor, I did notice vomiting. She doesn't always say.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, you know, I don't think I did. Maybe a little, I'm not sure.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll note both what you've said and what you've noticed. Anything unusual with passing urine?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No changes there.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your digestion otherwise okay?

[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, can you list what you take, tablets, creams or inhalers?
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's iron tablets, once a day, doctor.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about smoking?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I smoke roughly a pack every two days.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you work outside the home?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a hairdresser, on my feet all day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you get out much?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Not much, I mostly stay in these days.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there someone at home?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your medical history?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, COPD. I've had low haemoglobin for about ten years now.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so COPD and low haemoglobin are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. Right, have you got any known allergies?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I've never had an allergy.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I've never been operated on.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything relevant on the family side?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): My grandfather had a stroke.
[SEG0040] person_4 (NURSE): Here are the numbers, doctor. Heart rate 100, temp 36.7 degrees, pressure 99 over 66, oxygen saturation is 98 percent.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Raise your arm for me.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check.

I'm going to send a referral to the endocrine clinic. Book a review after the results.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, that's the plan. Do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care now.
