[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're a bit late, the carpark machine ate my card. Archie's six and he reckons none of this is worth coming in for.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not sick. It's just spots. Can we go?
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Just the spots, got it. Hop up on the bed, mate. Mum, how did this kick off?
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): School rang yesterday. Priya in his class has measles. Then he came out in this rash and he's been really hot, like—
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not hot.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the rash start? And the fever, if that's what we're calling it?
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I pick him up after school. He was burning up Monday arvo, shirt stuck to him, and he slept really badly, awake half the night.
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The fever wasn't Monday. I noticed it Wednesday, so three days. The rash only showed this morning, on his tummy.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It was Monday, I wrote it on the fridge. That's six days, not three. He was kicking the doona off the whole night too.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll hold the fever as roughly three to six days, not an exact figure. Rash this morning, so that's day one of the rash. Any cough, sore eyes, runny nose?
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough. Eyes are fine. He—
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): My knee bled ages ago. It's fine.
[SEG0013] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry. No runny nose either. He's drinking ok.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain?
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No to all of that. He managed toast.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you been giving him?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Five mils. Yuck.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Panadol syrup. The nurse at sick bay read it out, 5 mils. He won't take it on Sundays, just clamps his mouth.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not Sunday. Saturday.
[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's got the day wrong. It's Saturdays he skips, over at his dad's for swimming. And it's not 5 mils, the chemist label says seven and a half.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't choose between 5 mils and 7.5. Bring the bottle Thursday, and the green book if your sister can send it. Was there nurofin as well?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Bottle's at home.
[SEG0025] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We stopped the nurofin. Two doses yesterday and he went queasy, so that was the end of it. Only panadol when he actually takes it.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has he had both MMR doses, the measles ones?
[SEG0027] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. The twelve month one, I reckon yes. The eighteen month, I can't say, the green book's in Geelong. Might have missed it.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cuts that took a long time to heal?
[SEG0029] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The bike graze on his knee healed in five days. I thought maybe it was slow, but no, it healed normal.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ta. Temp is 38.2, pulse 118, breaths 22, sats 98 percent.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): See, I'm fine.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're warm, mate, even if you feel fine. Pink blotchy rash on the chest, tummy and a bit on the cheeks. No spots inside the mouth, throat's quiet, chest is clear.
[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Does he go to school tomorrow?
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working idea is a plain viral rash. I can't rule out measles, not with a classmate case and a fuzzy vaccine history. Day three to day six of fever is just when a measles rash can start.
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll hate the needle though.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, measles antibodies and a full blood count. No fasting, breakfast is fine, and no panadol after midnight so the temperature's honest. If those are borderline we do the third test, a throat swab for measles PCR. If the rash has not settled in two weeks, then a scan, an ultrasound of the glands.
[SEG0037] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And till then?
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep him home, away from other kids and anyone pregnant, until I clear him. I'll notify public health today. I'll see you Thursday arvo with the bloods.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to stay home?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yep. Sip drinks, and panadol only if you're miserable.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): I do apologise for being late, Doctor. The bus was held up at the lights, and then the rain came on.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. Do sit down, both of you. Did you get very wet?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Only at the edges, thank you. My coat took most of it.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I did tell him to bring the brolly. He wouldn't.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's quite all right. What have you come about today?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): I should like to ask whether I may drive again. It has been two years since my last convulsion, and I need to know where I stand with the licence.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. So you have epilepsy, and no convulsion for two years. Have I got that?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. I was diagnosed about eight years ago. I take, uh, levetiracitam, seven hundred and fifty milligrams, twice a day.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Levetiracetam, seven hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day, for the epilepsy. Have you been taking it steadily?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): On the whole, yes. When we went away to York I did miss some doses. I was rather thrown by the journey.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He doesn't take them on Sundays. I've watched the box.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Forgive me, that isn't correct. I do take them on a Sunday. It was the Saturday of the trip. I missed both the morning and the evening dose that day, and then I started again.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Let me say it back. One Saturday while travelling, both doses missed, and every other day twice a day, including Sundays.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And, uh, last month, the week we got home, he had a blank spell. Staring, not answering me. It lasted about a minute. Then he was a bit muddled, and then he was fine.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I have no memory of it, but I accept my sister's account. I would not call it a convulsion. There has been no shaking for two years.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): A blank spell of about a minute, not recalled by you, no shaking. Any headache, weakness, or difficulty with speech at the time?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None of those, Doctor.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh, and the little cut on his hand from the suitcase had healed up fine in a few days. Nothing in it.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. I am not going to decide today what that spell was. Umm, it might have been a brief focal seizure, or it might simply have been tiredness. I will not conclude either way until we have a level.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I understand. When they last measured it, err, the year before last, they said it was borderline. I was not given a figure.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): So a previous level, described to you as borderline, with no number. I will not treat that as a confirmed value.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): They did take my blood pressure in the corridor just now. I believe it was one twenty-eight over seventy-eight.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): May I check your pulse as well.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Please do.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Seventy-two, and regular. The nurse has written one hundred and twenty-eight over seventy-eight, the same figure you just gave me.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): That is much as I thought. I work in an accounts office in town, and without a car the commute is rather trying.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He lives with me, so I can drive him in on the days I am free.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Do you drink any alcohol? It can lower the seizure threshold.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): A single glass of wine at the weekend, Doctor. Nothing in the week.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me set out the plan. I will arrange a blood test for the levetiracetam level, and the form will be at reception today. I am not changing the dose now. If the level comes back low, we might consider an increase then.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, that seems entirely sensible.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): On the driving, I cannot clear you today. Please do not drive until we have reviewed this spell and the level, and we will speak about the DVLA at that visit. I will see you in two weeks.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I shall not drive in the meantime, and I will attend for the blood test.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him there. Sorry again about running late.

[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): Cough.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been around?
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Years.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every morning he—
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, let him answer. Is it every morning?
[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does phlegm come up, or is it dry?
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): Brown stuff.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Brown. Only mornings, or through the day?
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): Mornings.
[SEG0018] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It can hang on till lunch, but the bad part is the morning. Been like that since he smoked.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you quit?
[SEG0020] person_4 (PATIENT): Last year.
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): March, last year. Pack a day for about thirty years before that.
[SEG0022] person_4 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Umm, former smoker, about a thirty pack-year history, quit last March. I'm leaning toward chronic bronchitis, but I don't want to call COPD yet. Any chest pain?
[SEG0024] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever? You been feeling hot?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He never lets me check a temperature, I've tried—
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): Uh. Sometimes warm. Not really.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you been losing any?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0030] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He eats like a horse. I cook a full dinner every night.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking? Any inhalers?

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Known high blood pressure, lisinopril ten milligrams daily. Let me listen.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a wheeze on the right. No crackles. Heart's regular, I don't hear a murmur.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Working impression is chronic bronchitis. COPD is still possible, the test will sort that. I'm ordering spirometry.
[SEG0043] person_3 (NURSE): Thursday morning is open for the breathing test if that works.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book Thursday. Then I want you back in about three weeks to go over it.
[SEG0045] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We can do Thursday.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay quit, that's the biggest thing you already did. You should also get the flu shot and the pneumonia vaccine, with this history. Pharmacy downstairs can give both.
[SEG0047] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he actually goes.
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): The brown phlegm in the morning fits that old smoker airway irritation, even a year after quitting. Err, not an emergency, but we shouldn't ignore it.
[SEG0050] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His brother keeps telling him to try some tea thing. I told him no.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Skip the tea. We'll let the spirometry talk. See you in three weeks.

[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No. She cut her thumb last month, it healed in five days only. Normal.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, it closed up quick. Why, you are thinking sugar?
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which medicines?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Pantaprazole, 40 mg, every morning on empty stomach, for the acidity. Two years now.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does not take the tablet on Sundays. I have seen the strip.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, not Sunday. Sunday I take it, we have family lunch. It is Saturday I miss, when I go to the market. Sorry.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other tablet?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No other tablet. I left dairy for one week and the bloating was much less, then ice cream at my cousin's engagement brought it back the same evening. My cousin has coeliac, can I get that? Should I stop wheat?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The test is today itself? Do I fast? The needle is very painful, no?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No fasting. Reception will book the blood test today. Small needle, few seconds.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok doctor. I will write the diary properly. Please make sure it is the coeliac test, I have been so worried.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will sit with her and fill the diary.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Reception is just outside.

[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): There isn't a problem. Umm, just the kidney check. I'm alright.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's not, umm, he's not alright. The knees have been agony, he can hardly get to the corner shop.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh give over. Bit of an ache if I walk to the shops. Nothing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Painkillers.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, ibuprofen from the shop. Four hundred milligrams when it niggles. Not often.
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Most days, if I'm honest.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): It is not most days. Couple of times a week. Hardly counts.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Regular tablets.

[SEG0016] person_4 (CAREGIVER): They offered him alendronic acid for the bones once. He never took a single one.

[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Paracetamol's useless. But yeah, whatever you say.
[SEG0028] person_4 (CAREGIVER): My sister's been on dialysis three years. I can't help thinking of her when they read those numbers.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Different thing entirely. Repeat kidney bloods in one week. Back here in four weeks. If the creatinine hasn't come down we'll refer to renal then, not today.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. And bin that ibuprofen when you get home.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm. Fine.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll see it goes. He tucks things at the back of the cupboard.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Since Saturday. Well, actually Saturday morning, so three days. It's light, not pouring.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): A small bit of cramp, low down, on and off the last day or two. It eases if I sit. I wouldn't even call it pain.

[SEG0018] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in, Doctor. The GP note on the chart says folic acid five milligrams once a day.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, love. You look knackered. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm just tired, alright. It's my stomach. Cramps, and my guts are all over the shop.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): That sounds rough. Tell me what a bad day actually looks like.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I bloat up after lunch, like I'm six months gone, then the cramps kick in low across the belly. If I can pass a stool they ease off. If I can't, I'm stuck for hours.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when you do go, what are the stools doing?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): All over the place. Some weeks I'm constipated, can't go for days. Then it flips and it's loose and urgent, three or four times of a morning. Been like that the whole year.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): A year is a long time to put up with that. How did the cramps themselves start, do you reckon?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): A year. Maybe a bit more. I kept thinking it'd settle and it just didn't.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any blood in the poo, or black tarry stuff?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've looked. Nothing like that.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you dropped any?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Scales haven't budged. Clothes feel tighter but that's the bloating, not weight.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Any fevers, or waking up drenched in sweat?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. I don't think so. Felt a bit hot and bothered last week but I never checked, and the office is a sauna, so yeah nah, probably not.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. We'll leave the fever thing unclear. What about your waterworks, any burning or going more often?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Wee's fine. Can we stick to the gut? I'm running on empty.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. What stirs the cramps up, and what settles them, apart from opening your bowels?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Stress. Deadlines. Big meals, pasta especially. Lying down after tea helps a bit. Sometimes.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Work sounds like it's right in the middle of this. What do you do?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Project manager, logistics place in Footscray. We're short two people so I'm doing their jobs too. Home at eight most nights. I barely eat properly.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a heavy load. Do you smoke, or have a drink through the week?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. Wine, maybe two glasses on a Friday if I even remember. Not every week.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you taking for the gut at the moment?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Buscopan. Little white tablets, ten milligrams when a cramp hits. Maybe three times a week. And the green peppermint capsules for the bloating, one before lunch.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you've tried, or been given and not taken?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I was on mebevureen for a bit, stopped it in March, did nothing, waste of money. And some GP floated amitriptyline, a tiny dose, but I never took it. Not going there.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fair, we won't push that today. Any other regular tablets at all?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Panadol now and then if my head's sore. Not often. That's the lot.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mind if I have a feel of your tummy?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, go on. Just don't poke around forever, I've got to get back.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soft all over. Bit tender low on the left, no guarding, no lumps I can feel. Bowel sounds are ticking along, nothing wild.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, left side. That's where it grabs.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 76, blood pressure one twenty-two over seventy-eight. You're not pale.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): So what is it then? I keep thinking it's something awful and then I snap at everyone.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I reckon this is most likely irritable bowel. Cramp that eases when you go, the bloating, the swing between constipation and loose stools. I can't lock that in until the bloods are back.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods. Course. More waiting.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book a full blood count, a CRP, a coeliac screen and a thyroid test. Pop down to the lab this arvo, no fasting.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Today. Whatever.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Food-wise, smaller meals, ease off the big pasta serves, and jot down what sets the bloating off for a couple of weeks. The peppermint capsules are fine to keep going.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): A diary. On top of everything else. Alright, I'll try, no promises.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the Buscopan, ten milligrams when the cramp starts, no more than three times in a day.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't always remember it. Some weeks I just put up with the cramp.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's alright, it's only for the bad spells. Come back and see me in three weeks and we'll go over the bloods and that diary.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. If I'm still this wrecked I'll be even less charming. Thanks, I s'pose.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Ugh, sorry we're late. Traffic on the beltway was stopped dead, err, a fender bender by the exit, and then every light was red.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I told her to turn the car around. This is nothing. Whole trip was a waste.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're in the chair now. What have you been feeling?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Little burning on the left side of my chest. Hardly anything.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Since Tuesday. He winces when he reaches up. I hid the car keys or he'd still be on the couch.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Burning on the left since Tuesday. Two days, then?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. Well, a day and a half, no, two days. Not a big deal.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blisters, or just the burning?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Couple little spots. Tiny. You'd miss them.
[SEG0010] person_1 (CAREGIVER): There's a cluster on the left ribs, kind of under the arm. I saw them this morning when he got his shirt on.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): One side only?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. The left. Other side's fine.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does it itch?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the itch as unclear. Any fever, chills, or feeling wiped out?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A tiny bit warm last night. I'm not wiped out. I walked out to the mailbox.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath, or pain into the jaw or down the arm?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. It's not my heart.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cough? Pain with a deep breath?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Breathing's easy.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): These are the nurse's numbers. Blood pressure one oh nine over seventy-seven. Temperature thirty-eight point three.
[SEG0022] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Out in the hall she said his pulse was ninety-six. That sounded high to me.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): She corrected that reading. Pulse is eighty-four, not ninety-six. Separate from today, last time in March you were sixty-eight kilograms, and your last pressure was one-forty. I am not using those.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Old numbers. I'm fine. Can we be done.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Almost. Did you have chickenpox as a child?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure did. I was seven, uh, maybe eight. Everybody on the street had it. Ancient history.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which medicines do you take?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, five milligrams, for the pressure, every morning. The cholesterol one at night. Sugar tablets with breakfast. That's the real list.
[SEG0029] person_1 (CAREGIVER): And the powder. He takes Ayurvedic powder every single morning, mixed in warm water, from the shop on Hill Street.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. A spoon. Not a real medicine, just herbs. My cousin got me on it.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): The cholesterol pill, what's it called, and what strength?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember the name. Beige little thing. It's the cholesterol one. No idea the milligrams. At night, when I remember.
[SEG0033] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He skips some nights. I keep finding them in the pill box, Monday and Thursday.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the sugar tablets, the name on the bottle?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Sugar tablets. White ones. Met, umm, something, I always forget. One in the morning with breakfast.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Amlodipine five milligrams every morning for the pressure. A cholesterol pill at night you can't name, dose unknown, and some nights get missed. Sugar tablets, one with breakfast, name unknown. Ayurvedic powder, a spoon every morning. That everything?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's it. Bet the game is already in the late innings.
[SEG0038] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Oh, Marcus, his grandson, had little league on Saturday. Rain turned the outfield into a swamp and he still slid into second like it was the world series. The coach kept them out in that wind, and I was freezing up in the metal stands.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Boy cannot throw a strike, but he cracks me up. Ballpark hot dogs after were terrible, which they should be. Weather was rotten all weekend too, cold and then that weird sun on the drive.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shirt up, I need to see the left side. Small cluster of blisters on a red base along the left ribs. It stops at the midline and does not cross.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Told you. Tiny. Barely even a rash.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Burning on one side for two days, blisters in a strip, and chickenpox as a boy. This looks like shingles, herpes zoster. That's a working impression, and no test has confirmed it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Shingles. Come on. That's an old-person thing and these spots are nothing.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm treating it today anyway. Valacyclovere, one gram by mouth, three times a day, for seven days. Take the first dose today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times a day for a couple of spots. Fine, if you say so.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines before I send it?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm allergic to.
[SEG0048] person_1 (CAREGIVER): His daughter Lisa is pregnant, about six months, and she was over Sunday putting groceries away. Should she stay away?
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Until the blisters crust over, Lisa and any other pregnant people should stay away, and babies too. Keep the rash covered, wash your hands, and don't share towels.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): She'll be perfectly fine. I'll keep a shirt on. Everybody fusses.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the pain gets sharply worse, or the rash spreads past the midline, call sooner. Otherwise I'll see you back in a week. The script will be at the front desk, and finish all seven days even if the burning lets up.
[SEG0052] person_1 (CAREGIVER): I'll tell Lisa to stay home, and I'll stick the week on the fridge calendar.

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Left side. Err, two days, the burning and the blisters both. Like a hot cup held on the skin.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, just a little cluster. I had chickenpox as a kid, terribly, is it that again? Sorry, I'm jumping ahead.

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the rash itchy?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the pressure, five milligrams, in the morning. The cholesterol one at night, um, atorvastin, twenty milligrams. [SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The powder's just a brown tin from his sister in Leicester. I put it by his cup, he does take it.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and I stopped the naproxen in March. That was two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day, played havoc with my stomach. They wanted ramipril as well but I never took it.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): So that's amlodipine five milligrams each morning for the pressure, atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night, metformin five hundred morning and with your tea, plus that powder. Naproxen stopped in March, ramipril never started. With the pressure, any headaches?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if I've been rushing about.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any puffiness round the ankles?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, let's have a look. Shirt up, that's it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's a small crop of blisters on the left chest, stopping at the midline, and a bit of redness round them. Chest is clear and I can't hear a murmur.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 78. Blood pressure today is 136 over 84.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it my heart though? My brother had a heart attack at sixty. I parked on a double yellow I was that worked up, that's not important, sorry.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think this is your heart. One-sided burning, blisters that respect the midline, and chickenpox as a child. My working impression is shingles.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Shingles? Oh god. Is it catching? My daughter-in-law's pregnant, she's meant to come tomorrow. Can she still come? Will I give it to the baby?
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Priya, yes, about six months gone. He was saving her a slice of cake and everything.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Best she stays away while the blisters are weeping. Once they've crusted, the risk is much lower. Keep the rash covered, and don't share towels.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, actually, it does itch. Quite a lot once I'm in bed, round the blisters. I said no before, that wasn't right.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine, itching fits. I'm starting an antiviral today, aciclovir, 800 milligrams five times a day for seven days, by mouth.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Five times a day? Will it clash with the amlodipine? Will it make me sick? And how long does the burning last?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): It doesn't clash with your amlodipine, or the others. Have it with a little food if your stomach's delicate. The burning often settles over the week, though it can grumble on after the spots dry.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to stay indoors the whole time? And what if blisters pop up on the other side? Should I stop the Ayurvedic powder?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): You needn't shut yourself away, just avoid Priya, and babies or anyone very run down, until it crusts. If it spreads across the midline or you feel very poorly, ring us sooner. I'd pause the powder this week, we don't know what's in it, but carry on with the amlodipine, the atorvastatin and the metformin.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. A week of not knowing feels awful, will you actually see me again?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book you back in a week, face to face, so I can check the rash myself.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Sorry for all the questions. I just keep picturing the baby.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're alright. Covered rash, Priya stays away till the blisters crust, aciclovir five times a day for seven days, and I'll see you in a week.

Rules

Transcript (encounter 00949)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, I'm having a hernia repair next month, and the surgeon wants a heart check first, and I'm a bit nervous about it, honestly.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's perfectly normal before an operation. Tell me about your heart. Any problems that you've noticed? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I get a bit puffed on the stairs. Two flights and I'm blowing.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been the case? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): A while now. Since I put on weight, I'd say. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain on exertion?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Not at all.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Palpitations?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No palpitations.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you fainted, or nearly fainted?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Never fainted, no.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Ramipril, 5 mg, once a day. Atorvastatin, 20 mg, at night. And aspirin, 75 mg, in the morning.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any heart history?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure. For ten years.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any procedures on your heart?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): They put in a stent, in 2020.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Let me take your numbers. Pulse 66, blood pressure 132 over 80, temperature 36.5, oxygen 97 percent, breathing 14, and weight 97 kilos.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): All fine. Let me listen to your heart.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Take your time. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal, regular rhythm.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Does that mean I'm okay for the surgery? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise that yet. The breathlessness on the stairs could simply be weight and fitness, but I can't rule out that it's coming from the heart.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh. That's not what I wanted to hear. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know. But it's better to know before the operation than after. ~
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): True. What happens now? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll write to the surgeon with what I've found today and ask them to hold the date until I've seen you again. ~
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it delay the surgery? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possibly by a short time. It's much safer than rushing. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I suppose so. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, keep taking all your tablets, including the aspirin, and keep walking each day.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks, before the date.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Thanks, doctor. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't worry. You're in good hands. ~
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): I hope so. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Pressure outside is one fifty two over eighty eight, pulse seventy eight. He kept saying it is nothing only.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Come, sit. What is the problem.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): No problem as such doctor. I am sixty eight, old age only. My wife dragged me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Urine?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh, getting up in the night. Three times, four times. Everyone does that, no?
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not everyone. Stream is weak?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Little bit weak, yes. Well, actually mornings are worse. I am managing, it is not a big thing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dribbling after you finish?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Few drops in the underwear, sometimes. I don't even look.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, the tea. My wife boils it very strong, two cups after dinner, she will not reduce. And the traffic today was mad, we left the house at seven.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tea later. How long are you getting up at night.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Some months only. Three months, four months, I don't count. Around Diwali maybe. I can't say the date.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood in the urine?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Never.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Burning?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No, it is not painful.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever? Weight down?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever. Weight is the same. I am eating.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): You are on treatment for pressure. Which tablet.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, five mg, morning, since many years. One tablet.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every day?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Mostly. Sometimes I skip, if I am feeling alright. The reading is fine, what is there.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): One fifty two is high. Don't skip it. Giddiness when you stand?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Well, sometimes, if I get up fast from the bed. It goes.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Short of breath?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that either. Nothing of that.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any surgery before.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Never went for an operation.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Drug allergy?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Drink?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Never smoked. One small peg on a Sunday, sometimes only. I am retired now, accounts in the mill, that life is over.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Father or brother, prostate problem?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Father had the same, up in the night. He went to eighty four. So I am not fussed.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any tablet earlier for this, finasteride or dutasteride?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Finesteride, last year. Two months I took, then I stopped it in March. No use. Dutasteride I never took, nobody gave it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): What dose was the finesteride.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Five mg I think, maybe. I threw the strip. Anyway I am not on it.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft. No tenderness over the bladder. No rectal exam today.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Good. All this fuss for a small thing.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): This is most likely the prostate, the night frequency, weak stream and dribbling. Not final until the tests.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Urine test today, give it before you leave. Thursday morning, blood for PSA, sister will take it. No fasting. No heavy exercise, no cycling, no relations for two days before that blood.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): Urine pot is ready. Thursday eight thirty I have kept for the PSA. He need not fast.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the PSA is borderline we do a free PSA. If this does not settle, then a scan of the bladder and prostate. Not booked now.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Starting tamsulosin zero point four mg, one capsule at night. It can increase the giddiness, so get up slowly. And no tea after six.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Another tablet. If you insist. Tea, she will shout, but I will try. It is nothing serious.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will see you in two weeks with the reports. If you cannot pass urine at all, come sooner, do not sit at home.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): Sample before you go sir. Thursday eight thirty. And no heavy exercise, like doctor said.

[SEG0001] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Right, I'll be quick, because I've got two more in the car. It's Sorcha, she's seven, she's got nits again, and she's been scratching for a fortnight.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello Sorcha. Where does it itch?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): My head. At the back.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Behind her ears and the back of her neck, and she scratches in her sleep.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you found any lice or eggs?
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I found two lice last week, and loads of eggs. I did the treatment, but I don't think it worked.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): What did you use?
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The lotion, malathion, I think, I left it on for twelve hours, once. Then a different one, maybe permethrin, I can't remember, and the conditioner and the comb every day. Well, most days.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. So the lotion, you're not sure which one was the second, and the comb most days but not every day. When did you do the first treatment?
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ten days ago. And the second, four days ago. ~
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's useful. Is anyone else in the house affected? ~
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her brother, I think, he scratches. I haven't checked him. ~
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does Sorcha have any other conditions?
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She has asthma, mild. And eczema on her scalp, sometimes, I forgot to say.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does she go to school, or after-school clubs?
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, school, and Irish dancing three days a week, where they share the hair bands.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at her scalp. Sorcha, bend your head forward. ~
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): There are live lice moving at the back of the scalp, and many eggs stuck to the hair near the roots, with red scratch marks at the nape. No sign of infection.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It hasn't worked, then. ~
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): It looks like the first treatment may have been missed, or too early, as one treatment doesn't kill eggs. You need two treatments, a week apart. ~
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I did them four days apart, I think. ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's reset. I'd like you to use dimeticone lotion, coat the whole scalp, leave it on overnight, and wash it out in the morning, and repeat it seven days later.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is it safe with her asthma? ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, it's a silicone oil, not a poison. ~
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Also wet-combing with a fine comb and conditioner every three days for two weeks, and check the whole family, and treat only those with live lice.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her brother, I'll check tonight. ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please wash her pillowcase and hats in hot water, and don't share hair bands.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll tell the dancing teacher. ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see her again in two weeks, to be sure they've gone.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. It is quite sharp, umm, particularly at the finish.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Been abroad lately?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not travelled.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, both sides, low down. A dull ache.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shooting down the leg?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Background conditions?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, for five-ish years. I take amladipine, five milligrams, every morning for it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Operations?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. Err, they did kidney bloods at some stage. They said it was borderline. I could not tell you the date.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I come out in a rash.
[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take your observations. My sister had a kidney infection last winter, two nights in hospital, she was in bits.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I am sorry to hear that. I hope she is well.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Abdomen soft, not tender. A little tenderness across the lower back. Loins are not sore.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): It is more a dull ache than anything sharp, doctor, if that is useful.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): The burning is germs irritating the lining of the water pipe. Track up towards the kidney and you get the back ache. The temperature is your body fighting the infection.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. What happens next?

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Would that be from the chemist, then?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Only if we ring you. Plenty of water in the meantime, and don't hold on. I'll see you back here in a week.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the pain goes sharp on one side or you start vomiting, come back sooner. Don't wait the week.

Transcript (encounter 00975)
[SEG0001] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hello, doctor. I'm Maya, I'm Mr Okafor's carer, I drove him in. He's got a sore lower back since he helped move his daughter's house on the weekend. ~
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks for bringing him, Maya. Mr Okafor, how are you? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Sore, doctor. Right across my lower back. I lifted a lot of boxes.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did it begin?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Saturday afternoon, after the sofa. It's Monday now.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it a dull ache or sharp? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): A dull ache, but sharp when I bend. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it go anywhere? ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Just the back. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me have a feel. Can you stand up for me?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Slowly. ~
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's tenderness in the muscles on both sides of the lower back, and they feel tight.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): That's where it hurts. ~
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been walking about all morning, doctor. ~
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's good. Mr Okafor, does anyone in your family have back trouble?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother had a bad back all her life.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's useful to know. Here's what I'd advise. Keep moving, short gentle walks, little and often.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): I thought I should rest. ~
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bed rest makes it worse. Gentle movement helps it recover. ~
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's what the physio told his sister. ~
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Use a hot water bottle on the sore area, for twenty minutes at a time.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Warm, not hot. ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exactly. And avoid heavy lifting for two weeks, even a bag of shopping.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll carry the shopping. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll try. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most back pain like this settles in a couple of weeks. ~
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): That's good to hear. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't improved in two weeks, or if you get any weakness in your legs, come back and see me.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch for that. ~
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, hi, doctor, I came as soon as they called me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No problem at all, come in. What's troubling you?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hmm, um, doctor, I'm just here to help with the details. We came because of burning pain in the upper tummy.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did this begin?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I'd say two weeks, maybe.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was closer to three weeks, doctor.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, so roughly two to three weeks. Is that right?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): I suppose so, uh, yes.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you describe it a bit more for me? How strong it is, what the pattern is, what helps.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): I'd say every other day. An empty stomach definitely sets it off.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, and the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell the doctor about the other thing, um, that's what worries me.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, I was getting to that!
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about pain at night, have you noticed that?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, for about a month. Let me think, I've also been feeling full quickly, since Monday. And there's indigestion as well, one week now. Uh, about indigestion, I'd give it a six, out of ten.
[SEG0016] person_4 (NURSE): Okay, so the vitals from earlier. Pressure 113 over 75, oxygen saturation is 97 percent. Pulse 68, respiratory rate 16, temp 36.7 degrees.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Raise your arm for me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your upper tummy is tender in the middle with no guarding.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can relax now.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you get difficulty swallowing, weight loss or vomiting blood?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't had any of them.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, nothing like black stools?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Not that I've noticed, no black stools.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your joints, any aches elsewhere?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing else aches.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything in your past medical history I should know?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I've had arthritis in my knees for about ten years now. I've got depression.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm-hmm. Yes, depression is known to us, good to have that clear. Alright, have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing, I haven't had any operations.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are there any illnesses in your family?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had bowel cancer. My uncle has high cholesterol.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you got any known allergies?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): No allergies at all.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm not sure that's right. I seem to recall a problem with amoxicillin.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Really? I don't think so.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll note both of those.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your meals?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's on your current medicine list?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): It's a... um, uh, I can't remember what it's called. It's a small white one.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): For the knee pain, I believe. My wife sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given. It's fluoxetine, 20 milligrams, every morning. It's ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, three times a day.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you start it?
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): For two months.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, here's what I'm thinking. I'm honestly not certain yet. It could be a possible stomach ulcer from anti-inflammatory tablets, or it might be reflux. We should do a stool test for helicobacter for dyspepsia. I'm sending you for a blood count because of dyspepsia. What I'm giving you is omeprazole, 20 milligrams, once a day, eight weeks. You take it by mouth. It's for stomach ulcer.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): How soon will it work?
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the ibuprofen and use paracetamol for the knee pain instead. See me again in six weeks.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, good, I'll return then.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are the next steps as you understand them?
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): So, I take the omeprazole, 20 milligrams, once a day and come back in six weeks. Is that right?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, exactly right. Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, thanks, take care.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Goodbye for now.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit down, you're very welcome. What brought you in today?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just a small bit of a pain, up here on the right under the ribs. Comes on after the fry or cheese, anything greasy.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right side, under the ribs, after the greasy food. What does it feel like when it's there?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): A deep ache, more than a sharp thing. I'm grand between times, so I don't know why I'm fussing.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And once it starts, how long before it lets go?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was going to say all evening. Umm, well actually no, two or three hours and then it eases. It's been about three months, an antacid takes the edge off, and I was sick with it the once. I'm making it sound worse than it is.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three months is worth a look, even if you're playing it down. Anything else you notice when the pain is on you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I just wait it out. Put the kettle on, that sort of thing.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said you were sick the once. Was that vomiting, and did it happen again?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Vomited, yeah, err, just the once, a couple of weeks back after a roast. Nothing since. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been taking anything for it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That gaviscn from the chemist. I thought it was two spoons, well actually it's one spoon, the 10 ml, when the pain starts. My sister keeps pushing her omeprozole on me but that's hers, I don't take it.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So gaviscon, 10 ml, when the pain starts, and not your sister's tablet. Does it do much?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Takes the edge off, that's all. I'm not looking for a miracle.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family had trouble like this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had her gallbladder out, years ago. She was far worse than me. That's the only one.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Your mother had the gallbladder removed. Anyone else?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband John is on metformin for his diabetes, two tablets a day, but that's his sugar, not mine. I don't take a thing of his.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave his metformin well alone. Now, any fever with these pains, or do you feel shivery?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm not shivery either.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And chest wise, any cough, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine. I can walk the length of the town.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed at all?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah no. Well, the jeans feel a small bit loose, or maybe they just stretched, umm I haven't been on the scales. No, I'm the same weight I've always been.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no weight loss, then?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): The thing that actually annoyed me today was the bus. Forty minutes from Salthill in the rain, and the radio hurling cutting out.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was the rain that bad on the coast road?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Sheets of it. And I missed the last ten minutes of the match stuck at the lights. Galway were doing tidy enough before that.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah that's frustrating. Who were they playing?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't even catch the name properly, the reception was desperate. My neighbour's lad is on the under sixteens, he was practising in the garden in all that wet.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Practising in that? Fair play to him.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): His nan knitted him a scarf in the wrong colours entirely. We were in stitches over it. Purple and orange, if you can imagine.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Purple and orange, lord. Did he wear it anyway?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): He did, to please her. He's a good kid. Anyway, that's me rambling, sorry.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't be sorry, it's nice to hear. Let me come back to your tummy, if I may. Lie back and I'll have a feel.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on. It's only a bit sore, I'm not going to leap off the bed.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tummy is soft. Tender under the right ribs, and sore when you breathe in there. No guarding, and nothing rigid.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. That's the spot. Still only mild, though.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely biliary colic, the gallbladder acting up after fatty food. I wouldn't call it certain until we see the tests.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Gallbladder. Sure I'm nothing like my mother was. She couldn't keep a cup of tea down.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book the bloods and the ultrasound. Bloods can be done downstairs today, and the scan as soon as there's a slot. Not a fuss, just a proper look.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Grand, so. If you say so.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off the fry and the cheese in the meantime. Stick with the gaviscon, 10 ml, when it niggles.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I can leave the rashers. I'll miss them, but I can.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, I was stuck on the M50, sat there near twenty minutes. The traffic was desperate.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah you're grand altogether, don't be worrying. Filthy day for driving.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It is yeah. Rain hasn't let up since Tuesday and I left the good coat in the house.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you out in that on Sunday for the match?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I was, up in the stand, soaked through. Dublin were poor in the second half, I thought they'd never score.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah they left it very late. My brother was roaring at the telly the whole time. Sure look, you're here now. What brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, well, um, it's the hands. They go numb at night.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which fingers, and is it the two hands?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly the right. The thumb, the index and the middle one. I do be waking with it and I have to shake the hand to get the feeling back.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, I haven't a clue of the date. A few months anyway. Maybe since the spring, I'm not sure.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how are they in the daytime?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Daytime they're mostly grand, but I've started dropping cups. Dropped a mug of tea yesterday, all over the kitchen floor.
[SEG0014] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry for barging in. I'll just do the blood pressure. My own sister had the numb fingers last year, shaking her hands out at breakfast, her husband was driven demented.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): God, was she alright? Am I going to lose the use of the hand? I keep panicking.
[SEG0016] person_3 (NURSE): She was grand after. Yours is 138 over 86, and the pulse is 74. I'll leave ye to it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Any pain in the neck?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the neck.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in the legs, or pins and needles in the feet?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, the legs are fine, and there's nothing in the feet. Uh, is this a stroke? I was reading things at half two and I frightened the life out of myself.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't think this is a stroke, let me think it through. Numb thumb, index and middle finger at night, you shake it awake, you're dropping cups. Could be the nerve at the wrist, could be a nerve from the neck, could be a bit of arthritis in the hand. I'm not going to call it the neck just yet.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): If I'm right, the median nerve is getting pinched in the little tunnel at the wrist. That nerve looks after those three fingers, so they go dead, and the little finger is usually spared because a different nerve minds it.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): So not the brain? Will I need an operation? How serious is it really?
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working impression is carpal tunnel. A pinched nerve from the neck is still possible, I wouldn't rule that out. There's no operation talk today.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. Sensation is a bit dull over the right thumb and index. Tinel's, tapping at the wrist, sends a tingle into those fingers. The little finger feels normal and the grip is decent.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Is dull bad? I work in accounts, typing all day. Do I have to give up the job?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, don't be giving up the job. A wrist splint at night is the first thing, for six weeks, keeps the wrist straight so the nerve isn't bent up. You can get one in the chemist, no bother.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Every single night? And if I need the nerve test, does it hurt? The neighbour said they stick needles in you and I'm fairly worked up about that.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not booking a nerve conduction study today. If the numbness hasn't settled in six weeks, then we'd arrange the nerve test. It's mostly little electrical taps on the skin, not a big needle job, people are grand with it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): And what if it is the neck after all? Should I be on tablets? I take paracetemol now and again, two tablets, when the hand gets sore. Not every day.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's why I won't lock it down further today, we'll see how the splint goes. Paracetamol as needed is fine, nothing stronger for now. Come back and see me in six weeks.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if the hand goes properly weak, or you can't hold a cup at all, come back sooner, don't wait.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Six weeks. I'll try not to be googling it at half two. Thanks.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Mind yourself on that motorway going home.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): All the best.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, have a seat. What brings you in today?

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Which side is it, and how long has it been bothering you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The right side. It has been three weeks, umm, no, closer to five weeks. After a chewy meal I feel as though I have overdone it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the jaw click, or lock, or is it only an ache?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It clicks when I open wide. It does not lock, I am pleased to say.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry to cut in. I live with him, we are partners. I have heard him grinding his teeth most nights for weeks.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not aware of that myself. I am sorry if it has been a nuisance at night.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think it through out loud. Pain on chewing, a click, and night grinding fits the jaw joint and the chewing muscles, and a cracked tooth can imitate it. I am not going to conclude this is arthritis today.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, and I would rather you did not rush to a label.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no fever. I have felt quite well in myself, apart from being tired.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired how?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): By the evening I feel like a wet rag, if you will forgive the phrase. The days are rather long.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Is the click with every bite, or only when you open wide?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mainly with a wide opening, or with crusty bread. Not with every mouthful.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The grinding gets louder when work has been grim. Nearly every night lately, I would say.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does stress make the pain worse, or only the grinding?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The pain is worse when I am under pressure. At the open-plan office I cannot hear myself think, though that is the building noise and not my hearing.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of. I will not treat that as an ear symptom. Any ear pain, or any swelling you have seen?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No ear pain, and no swelling that I have noticed.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been taking for the ache?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Neurofen. I thought the tablets were two hundred milligrams, uh, but I checked the packet and they are four hundred. I take one by mouth when it is bad, perhaps twice a day.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else regular?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will have a feel. Open slowly. There is a click on the right as you open, and the muscle just in front of the ear is tender. There is no swelling, and you open about three fingers, which is acceptable.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a little tender there, yes. Some mornings I have a frog in my throat, though it clears once I have had tea.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): A rough voice, or pain in the throat?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Only a rough voice, for a few minutes. Nothing more than that.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He also says his feet feel dead after standing about. I am not sure he means it medically.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I would not wish to mislead you. They are not numb. They are simply weary after a long day on my feet.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that is fatigue rather than numbness. Any cough, wheeze, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): What is the work, in that open-plan office?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I am a conveyancing solicitor. The hours have been heavy this quarter, I am afraid.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We share a flat in Carlton, so I hear the night grinding more than he realises.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or, err, take a drink in the evenings?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I have a glass of wine with dinner, perhaps four nights a week.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is temporomandibular joint dysfunction driven by the night grinding. A dental cause is still possible, so I would like a dentist to exclude a tooth problem.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall arrange to see one. What should I do in the meantime?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): A soft diet for the next fortnight, no crusty bread and no steak, and a boil-and-bite mouth guard from the chemist at night until the dentist advises. Keep the neurofen at four hundred milligrams, up to twice a day, with food.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. That is very clear.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it has not eased in a fortnight, come back and see me. If the jaw locks or you develop a fever, do not wait, and reception can give you a dentist's name on the way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm grand, doctor, really. It was only Bridget here who insisted I come in for the check on the leg after the tablets.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good on Bridget, then. This is the second time it's flared up on that shin, so I'd sooner look than guess. Bridget, you're with him at home?
[SEG0003] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I am, I'm his live-in carer, five days a week. He'd never tell you if it was bad, so I tell you for him.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): There's nothing to tell.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough, we'll see. Is it all right if the healthcare assistant takes down the dressing first?
[SEG0006] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Hello Mr Doyle. I'll unwrap the leg and have the dressing pack ready for the doctor, it won't take a minute.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, don't be making a fuss.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): While she does that, a couple of questions. Any fever or shivers since I last saw you?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And any pain in the leg, or is it just a bit tender?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain. Nothing worth mentioning.
[SEG0012] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He doesn't complain, that's the problem. But I'll say he's been walking the garden path every day without limping.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's useful to hear from you, thank you. Now, the tablets. Which antibiotic are you finishing?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): The doxycycline, 100 mg, twice a day. I've two days left.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And you're taking that because of the penicillin trouble, aren't you?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): I am. Penicillin gave me hives years ago. They told me never again.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, penicillin allergy with hives, I'll make sure that's on the front of your notes. Any other tablets I should know about?
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): There's the water tablet for the swelling, the furosemide. It's in the morning. I think it's maybe 20 mg? I'd have to check the box.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Maybe 20 mg, we'll confirm it against the pharmacy list. Mr Doyle, do you remember?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I take what Bridget puts in my hand.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair. Anything long-term behind the swollen legs?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): The heart failure. It's well managed. And I had the hip replaced about ten years ago.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart failure and the hip replacement, thank you. Let's have a look at the leg.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temperature is 36.8 degrees, and your pulse is 76. Now I'm looking at the shin. The redness has faded to a pale pink, and there's no warmth over the skin where it was.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that good or bad?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. It looks like the cellulitis has cleared, which is what we wanted from this course.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I told you it was nothing.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): You did, and I'm still glad we checked. Now let me give you the choices for keeping it from coming back a third time.
[SEG0029] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Please do. I'm tired of the carpet being covered in cotton wool.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): First option, compression stockings in the daytime, which helps the swelling that sets the skin up for infection. Second, moisturise the skin twice a day so it doesn't crack. Third, keep your feet up when you're sitting.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): The stockings are a divil to get on.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): They are. Bridget or the community nurse can help with that. Which of the three would you actually do?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): The moisturiser. I'd do that.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And I'll do the feet up, if I have to tie him to the stool.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then moisturiser every day, feet up when sitting, and finish the doxycycline. We can talk about the stockings another day.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand. Will that be everything?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's everything for today. You look well, Mr Doyle.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll put a light dressing back on, and a clean sock over it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, love.
[SEG0040] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring him in for a cup of tea first, we passed a lovely bakery.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Enjoy it. Take care, both of you.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Good day, doctor.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Ned? Straight through, doctor's free. Second door on the left.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ta. Come on, shoes off.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): G'day, I'm Dr Singh. Sit wherever you like. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): These dry itchy patches. Behind his knees and in the elbow creases. He's four and he's been scratching something awful.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): You poor thing. Ned, does it itch?
[SEG0006] person_4 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which bit is the worst?
[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): Knees.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): When does the scratching really get going?
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): At night. He wakes up scratching. It's better in the day.
[SEG0011] person_4 (PATIENT): Night.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on for?
[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm, about four months. I nearly said since June, after winter, but nah, it's about four months.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weeping or pus in the skin? Any fever?
[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No weeping. No fever.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Aside from the skin, how's his breathing, tummy, wee and poo?
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): All fine. No wheeze. Eats like a horse. He talked footy the whole way here, drove me mad.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ha, love that. What creams have you got on the go?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Big white tub, thick cream, morning and night. Pink tube once a day on the angry bits. Chemist said the pink one's a steroid. The label's rubbed off though, I think it might be hydrocortazone oh point five, but err don't quote me.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): And does the pink one help him?
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A bit, yeah. Sometimes it stings.
[SEG0022] person_4 (PATIENT): Stings.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. None.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any asthma or eczema in the family?
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad's got asthma. Been on a puffer for years. No eczema in the family.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has a doctor given Ned's rash a name before?
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): GP last year reckoned it looked like eczema. They did a blood test and said it was borderline. I never got the actual number, and I can't remember the month. Just sometime last year.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look, mate. Dry thickened patches behind both knees and in both elbow creases, and a few scratch marks. No break in the skin and no weeping.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Plan for now, keep the white tub morning and night, and we'll bump that pink steroid to twice a day for a fortnight. See how we go.
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Well, actually, it stings him, and we can't read the tube. It's nearly empty too. And that blood test, he screamed the place down, I don't want another one today.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yep, that changes things. Forget the twice a day idea, and stop the pink tube, I'm not happy using an unnamed steroid that stings. I'll start Advantan fatty ointment, methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 percent, a thin layer once a day on the rough patches for seven days, then stop. You can keep the white cream, and please get QV cream and use it four times a day when the skin looks dry.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Looks like an eczema flare to me, not an infection. The nurse takes allergy bloods Thursday morning, no fasting, a normal brekkie is fine. I'll see you in two weeks. If those bloods are borderline we do skin prick testing, and if it hasn't settled by the review we'll swab the skin.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the shoulder pain again, doctor. Eased off for a couple of weeks, then crept back.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come in, sit down. So it settled for a while after last time, and now it's returned. Tell me what it's doing.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Aching, deep inside. Worse at night, lying on it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): That sounds miserable, your sleep must be suffering. Where exactly would you point to?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Here. Top of the arm, at the front, a bit round the back.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Is it the pain that bothers you most, or more the way the shoulder moves?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Stiffness too. In the mornings. Takes an hour to loosen.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): An hour, I see. And how would you rate the stiffness, mild, moderate, or worse than that?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Moderate. Getting dressed is the worst bit.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Getting dressed is a good test, because it needs reaching behind and overhead, which a stiff shoulder hates.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Pulling a jumper over my head.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. And what are you taking for it at the moment?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. When it's bad.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is that helping, or just taking the edge off?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Edge off. That's all.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Any allergies to medicines I should know about, before we talk about anything else?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): None.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And the rest of you, any trouble with your breathing at the moment?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Now let me look at the shoulder. Lift your arm out to the side for me, slowly, and stop when it hurts.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Ow. That's as far as it goes.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your shoulder movement is limited, it stops about halfway and the joint feels tight when I move it for you.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that bad?
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not bad as such, but I can't rule out a frozen shoulder at this stage. Picture the joint capsule like a jumper that shrank in the wash.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. How long does that take to go?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can take months, I'm afraid, but most people get back to normal movement in the end.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Months. Okay.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Meanwhile, keep it moving. Gentle pendulum swings with the arm hanging down, a few minutes each day, and sleep on your other side hugging a pillow.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I can do that.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in six weeks, to check how much it has loosened.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright. Six weeks.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): The receptionist will book that for you on your way out. Have you got any questions for me?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care, and be kind to that shoulder.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah give me a second, this yoke has frozen again. Right. What has you in today?
