[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks. How are you in yourself?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. A bit wrecked, sure, but who isn't. There's nothing wrong with me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? I was half on the screen.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I said I'm fine. Wrecked, but fine. You're not missing anything.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are you sleeping, with the baby?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Sleep's grand. She wakes for the feed and I go straight back off. Not a bother.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever since you got home?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature or anything. I'm grand that way.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And a cough, or anything on the chest?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. Chest is fine.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the appetite?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I don't know. Umm, some days I forget till himself is in. Other days I clear the plate. I couldn't tell you when that started, if it even did.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been tearful at all?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A small bit. I was crying into the tea this morning for nothing. It passes. I'm not going on about it.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Blood pressure on here is one eighteen over seventy six, and the pulse is 82. That's fine.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you still on the iron?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the ferrous fumurate. Err, I nearly said two hundred, it's two hundred and ten milligrams, once a day, by mouth. Since I came home. The iron was low after the birth.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the dose again? The box just refreshed.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Two ten milligrams. Once a day.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is himself with you?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): He's in the chair by the door, pale as anything. Worried sick. I'm telling him there's no need.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I have to ask you straight. Any thoughts of harming yourself?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Absolutely not.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the baby. Any thoughts of harming her?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Don't even say it. She's grand. She's the best thing.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Look, about the sleep, I was brushing you off. I lie awake even when she's out cold, two or three hours, mind going. Since she was born, the whole six weeks. But sure that's just a new baby.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lying awake when the baby sleeps, and crying into your tea at six weeks, I'm thinking a postnatal low mood. I wouldn't call it a firm diagnosis today.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let himself do a night feed if he'll take it, and don't keep this to yourself. I'll see you back here in two weeks.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): If you want. I still think it's a fuss over nothing.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's not a fuss. If you feel worse before then, or if any thought of harm shows up, you come straight back, or out of hours the same day.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send a note to the public health nurse as well, for a bit of support at home. And a blood count, to see where the iron is. Reception will have the form.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Right so. Can I go? He's probably worn a hole in the floor.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): sorry we're late, doctor. the car park was a complete joke, and then my sister rang about her scan, they think it's breast cancer, same as mum had, and I just couldn't cut her off.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, that's a horrible phone call to take. come and sit down. what can I do for you today?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): well, umm, before I get to me, the neighbour said if it's your face you go straight to A&E and not the GP, and the receptionist had written that the dentist is shut all week, so we thought...
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): just tell him about the tooth, love.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): right, yes, sorry. my cheek's come up and the tooth is throbbing. that's why I'm here.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): ok. which side, and how long has it been like that?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): the right one, the upper back tooth, where they put the crown on. err, it started two days... no, three days ago. I was fine the evening they fitted it, and the next night it began to throb, and the cheek came up with it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she was up half the night with it, pacing about.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): yes I was in the kitchen with a cold flannel, then a warm one, neither did much, and I kept telling him it isn't sinus because I've had sinus and this is different. it's in the tooth itself, a deep throb, and the gum feels fat.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): any fever with it, or are you just hot from worrying?
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she felt warm to me this morning, I said so.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): umm I did take my temperature at home, thirty-seven point something, not dramatic. a mild fever I'd say, and a bit achy, though I can still talk for England as you've noticed.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): and right now, any trouble swallowing, or with your breathing?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): no. swallowing's fine, I managed toast, and my breathing's normal. I got a bit puffed walking up from the car park but that's the hill, not the tooth.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. let me look. the right cheek is definitely swollen, tender when I press here, the gum round that crown is red and a bit boggy, but I can't feel a pocket of pus, and you can open your mouth fully.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): it hurts when you press, yes, and when I bite, even soft bread. hot tea sets the throb off, and paracetamol takes the edge off for an hour or two.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): are you taking the paracetamol properly? any other medicines, and any allergies, penicillin in particular?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): paracetamol, the five hundred milligram tablets, two of them so a gram. I nearly said two hundred and fifty then, that was years ago, the little ones. the box says up to four times a day, but yesterday I think I only managed three, I forgot lunch, so I'm not sure I'm doing it right. no other medicines. no allergies, penicillin's been fine.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): you had some for your chest last winter, didn't you, and you finished the lot.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): oh yes, amoxicillin, a week, all done, no rash or anything. that was last winter, not now.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): ok, nothing current except the paracetamol, and no known allergies. let me see what the nurse wrote. blood pressure one oh nine over seventy-seven, pulse seventy-six, temperature thirty-seven point eight. your last pressure was one-forty over eighty-eight, back in March. weight sixty-eight... no, fifty-eight kilos, she's crossed the six out.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): fifty-eight, yes, I've been trying, not that it matters today. uh the tooth though, the dentist filed the crown and said come back if it bit funny, but they're on holiday, nobody answering. I rang four times, left messages, even tried the emergency dental number and it just rang out.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): mm. so, thinking it through, the crown sits over a tooth that can die off quietly, bacteria get in at the root, and I'm thinking this is an infection under that crowned tooth, a dental abscess starting. the throb, the swollen cheek and that mild temperature all fit, and there's no big collection yet, but these can track if we leave them.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): an abscess, right. I was googling at two in the morning, which I know is stupid, and it said Ludwig's something if it goes under the tongue. I checked my tongue and it isn't raised, I don't think.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): let's not jump to Ludwig's. what I want is an antibiotic now, and a dentist as soon as someone is back. I'm going to prescribe amoxacillin, two hundred and fifty... no, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days, by mouth.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): is that the same one she had last winter?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): yes, same drug, and she tolerated it. take it with food if it upsets your stomach. finish the five days even if the tooth settles.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): three times a day, with food, five days, yes. what if, umm, the swelling...
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): if you get difficulty swallowing, or any trouble breathing, or the swelling jumps, or you feel really unwell, you don't wait for me or the dentist. you go to A&E. that's the bit I need you to hear.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. A&E if I can't swallow or breathe, I've got that. and the pain, do I just carry on with the paracetamol?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): yes, stick with the gram up to four times a day, and try not to miss doses, it works better regular. ibuprofen as well if your stomach's alright, four hundred milligrams three times a day with food, but only if you want it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): stomach's fine, I might add it. umm, will you want me back, or is it just the dentist?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you here in three days to check the swelling's going down, whether or not the dentist has rung. reception can book it on your way out.
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): three days, I'll make sure she comes. she was going to wait the weekend.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I wasn't going to wait the weekend, I came today, didn't I. anyway if the cheek gets bigger tonight I'm not sitting on it, I'll go up to the hospital like you said.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): good. so amoxacillin five hundred three times a day for five days, paracetamol regular, back here in three days, and A&E if swallowing or breathing becomes difficult. anything else before you go?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): no, I think that's the lot, thank you. sorry again about being late, and there's nothing you can say about my sister really. we'll ring the dentist again in the morning.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh doctor, sorry, the share auto was not coming and then it started drizzling also. I have come for these cramps in the calf, night time.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Sit. How long has this been going on?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Two months, doctor. Almost every night, both calves, the right one is the bad one, it grabs and I have to stand and stamp the foot.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is up at two, sometimes three. I sleep in the next room and I hear her walking about.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it come in the daytime as well, or only at night?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, only at night. Daytime I am cutting vegetables and doing my work, no cramp.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): My sister-in-law in Pune sent some oil on WhatsApp, I don't even know the name. I tried coconut oil for two nights, nothing, and it stained the bedsheet, my son was annoyed.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you stand and stamp, does the cramp ease off?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, after a minute or two it lets go. If I just lie there it stays.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the feet or the ankles? And pain in the calf when you walk?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No swelling now. Walking is ok, no pain while walking. I go to the temple in the morning, that much I manage.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Breathlessness?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that, touch wood. My husband had a bypass, but that is his story, not mine.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Any burning when you pass urine, or blood in the urine?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No burning, no blood. Just that I go many times because of the water tablet.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she will not drink water. I fill the bottle and it comes back full. Morning one glass, with lunch maybe half, that is her whole day.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): If I drink more I am running to the bathroom, and the bathroom is down the corridor. At night I am scared I will fall, the corridor light fused last week and my son said he will change it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So roughly two glasses in the day, is that all?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, two, sometimes two and a half. Not more than that.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me the water tablet, the name and the dose.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Frusemide. Forty mg, one in the morning after breakfast. They started it for swelling years back. Swelling went, but I never stopped it.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Aunty the strip is twenty mg, I saw it this morning. Last month the nurse at the dispensary also read twenty, not forty.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Err. Forty is the pressure tablet, maybe. I get mixed up. I take one tablet, that much I know, whether twenty or forty I cannot swear.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, we will not lock a dose until we see the strip. Please bring the strip and the old prescription next time.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will put it in my bag tonight itself. It is in the steel dabba near the gas.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): What other medicines are regular?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): For pressure, Mizartan 40 mg, morning. For sugar, Metformine five hundred, twice a day, after food. And Omprazole in the morning, empty stomach, for acidity, the yellow capsule, I don't know the mg.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She also bought magnesium from the medical shop for the cramps. One tablet at night, since one week.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the strength of that magnesium?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, I think two hundred and fifty mg, maybe. The boy at the shop wrote one at night on the cover. I did not bring the bottle.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any painkiller, or anything else now and then?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Sometimes Disprin, if the head is paining. Not daily. Last week two times only.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you ever had a reaction to a medicine? Rash, swelling of the face, trouble breathing?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never. I have taken penicillin and everything, the full course when I had tooth trouble, no problem at all.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, no allergy that you know of. How long have you had the sugar and the pressure?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Sugar, maybe ten years. Pressure longer, fifteen years or so. Both are still there. Metformine I sometimes skip the night dose if I eat late, I am not sure how often.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She skips more than she says. The night Metformine, many nights it is still in the box, I have seen it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): So Metformine is five hundred twice a day on the prescription, but night doses are missed and we cannot say how many. I will record it as not sure.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of. Putting it together, night cramps for two months, very little water, frusemide with the dose not agreed, plus Mizartan, Metformine, Omprazole and the shop magnesium. Let me look at the legs.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Calves are soft, no tenderness, no swelling I can see. Pulses in the feet are present, both sides.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): See, I told you, no swelling. Last year there was, around the ankle, the socks were leaving a mark. That went after the water tablet.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working impression is night calf cramps, possibly from the water tablet and drinking too little. Low potassium is also possible. I am not calling either one confirmed.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Potassium means the blood test, na? My neighbour did so many tests and the bill was high. We are pension people, doctor.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, a blood test for potassium. I will add sodium and the kidney function on the same sample, because of the water tablet. I am booking it today, you can give it tomorrow morning, fasting is not needed.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): For the cramp, stretch the calf before bed, hold for 30 seconds, three times each leg. And in the daytime take water little by little, not one big glass at night.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Thirty seconds, three times, I will ask my son to remind me. Water in the day, ok, I will try. Not at night.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in one week with the blood report and the medicine strip. We will decide the frusemide dose only then. If the cramp becomes constant or the leg becomes red and hot, come sooner, don't wait.

[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, two weeks. No, wait, it's a month. A full month. It's there the whole time, worse when it's quiet, and the radio takes the edge off a small bit.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That radio is on half the night. And the ear defenders I bought him are still sitting in the hall.

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Aye. The plant. Err, machinery roaring the whole shift. They don't give us proper protection so I don't bother with it.

[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Hearing's fine. I can hear you grand.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in six weeks with the result. And if the ringing suddenly gets much worse, or you get discharge or real spinning, don't wait, come straight back.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I was stuck out there watching some cookery yoke on the telly. Waste of time. I'm wrecked already.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Sorry, say that again? I was clicking through a pile of results.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The telly was useless. Can we get on with it, I've no patience left today.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Pain up under the ribs on the right, after anything fatty, a fry or cheese. A bout lasts three or four hours, and it's been a couple of months. Well, maybe six weeks. No, a couple of months.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right side after fatty food. Did you vomit with it at all?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Once. Umm, last week, after a takeaway. Brought the whole dinner back up, and the pain still went on.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with these turns?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No fever.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it shoot through to the back, or up into the shoulder?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. What are you taking when it starts? And the length of a bout, say it again, I half heard.

[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your regular tablets now. The list on screen is half blank. Run through them slowly.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the pressure, 5 milligrams in the morning. The cholesterol one at night, twenty milligrams, I can never remember the name of it. [SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cholesterol one, the dose again, the cursor jumped.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams at night. It's a white tablet. I don't know the name.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): God, the weather. I was meant to bring the grandson to the playground and it lashed rain. He's 6, mad into the hurling, won't sit still.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hurling, is it. My nephew's the same with the football, never in the house. Where were we, it ate a line.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Hurling, not football. Completely different. I'm not here about him.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone belonging to you had the gallbladder out? I'm asking because of the pain after greasy meals.

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking this could be the gallbladder, biliary colic. Can't say for certain until we have a look.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that serious? She was in bits with hers, I remember that much.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't leap to surgery talk. We need the picture first. Sorry, your mother, say that bit again?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Gallbladder surgery. Years back. I already said it.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, got it that time.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): So what are you doing about it. I can't keep missing work.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book blood tests, the liver ones as well, and an ultrasound of the tummy. Reception'll have the forms, both of them arranged.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks for the results. Lay off the fry-ups till then, they set it off.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks, fine. I'll try. I'm too tired to argue about the chips.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good morning. I'll be as precise as I can, because this is a bit unusual. My cousin died suddenly last month, aged thirty-one, and I'd like to be screened.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm very sorry to hear that. Do you know what the cause was?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): They say it was his heart, an arrhythmia of some kind. They're still waiting for the full post-mortem results.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): That must be very hard on the family. And how about you, have you had any symptoms yourself? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Possibly. Now and then I get a flutter in my chest, a sort of skipped beat. But I can't say when I first noticed it.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it when you're resting, or exercising?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Resting, usually. It might have been last year, or the year before, I honestly couldn't tell you.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you ever faint, or nearly faint, with it?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never. I've never fainted in my life.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Do you exercise much?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): I run three times a week, five kilometres, and I've never had trouble with it.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's reassuring. Any allergies I need to know about before I examine you?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): None at all. No allergies.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me take your pulse and blood pressure. ~
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course. ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 62, regular, and blood pressure 118 over 74.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that normal? ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Excellent for a runner. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): So what do you think the flutter is? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): A skipped beat at rest, in someone who runs and has a normal pulse, is most likely ectopic beats, which are extra beats and very common.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Common? So not necessarily a problem? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually harmless. But with your cousin's history, I don't want to rely on that. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Quite. That's why I came. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm going to refer you to the inherited cardiac conditions clinic, and they'll do the right tests, probably an ECG, an echocardiogram, and maybe a heart rhythm monitor.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): And the cousin's results will matter? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Very much. Ask the family to share the post-mortem findings with the clinic, they'll want to see them.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll do that. Is there anything I should avoid in the meantime? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Carry on as normal, and if you ever faint, or get chest pain with exercise, or a racing heart that won't settle, go to the emergency department.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thank you for being so thorough. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): You did the right thing. The clinic will write to you. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What has you in with me today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah thanks. The traffic on the Malahide road was desperate, I was nearly late. It's the ankles, they're swelled up something awful, and I'm forever in the toilet.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the ankles first, in your own words.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Both of them, right up over the sock line. I noticed it, umm, three weeks ago. My neighbour says it's the heat, but sure it's October, what heat.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three weeks, right. Are they sore at all, or is it mostly the swelling?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Not sore, no. Just puffy and tight, the shoes won't go on. I had to wear the old slip-ons in.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And would you say the swelling stays the whole day?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Depends if I've been mooching about the shops.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. And the passing water, what's that been like?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm up twice a night at least, and during the day I'm in and out. I blame the tea, I drink a fierce amount, six mugs easy. My sister says I'm a teapot with legs.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain when you pass water, or any blood?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain and no blood. It's just often, that's all.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What tablets are you on at the minute?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The amlodopine, ten milligrams, once a day, for the blood pressure. And the water tablet, uh, frusimide, forty milligrams in the morning. I've been on the blood pressure tablets for years.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Frusemide forty, every morning. Are you getting that one in every morning?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok, we'll leave that as not certain so. And the readings at home, have you been checking them?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I've the little machine from the chemist. This morning it said 128 over 76. Most days it's around one thirty over eighty. My grandson set the cuff up, he's great with phones, he put an app on it I never open.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's handy to have. Let me take it here. There we are, today in the clinic it's 162 over 94, and the pulse is 74.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): 162? God almighty. It was grand at home this morning. I had a coffee on the bus, maybe that did it, and some fella's shopping bag was on my foot the whole way in.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Different places can give you different numbers, you're not imagining it. Can I have a look at the ankles?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. The right one is the fatter, I think. Or maybe they're the same, I can't see past the belly half the time.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both ankles are pitting, soft swelling up as far as the lower shin. I'm not hearing anything odd in the chest either.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's a relief. I was watching some thing on the telly about hearts and I had myself buried, so I did.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain or tightness with all this?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Breathing is grand too, if you're wondering. I walked from the bus stop no bother.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. I think the swollen ankles are down to the amlodipine, that tablet is well known for it. The pressure is still high in here, so I'd stop the amlodipine and start you on ramipril, two and a half milligrams once a day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril, right so. Will I get that from the chemist on the corner? They were out of the other yoke last month and I had to traipse all the way into town.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor! I'm not sure I'm in the right place, because everyone says my blood pressure's great, but I feel light-headed, especially when I get up quickly, and I wondered if my pressure's too low.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a very reasonable question. When does the light-headedness happen?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): When I stand up from a chair, or the loo, or in the shower. Everything goes sort of fuzzy, and I have to hold on.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, a good while. Months. Maybe since I changed my tablets, or since my holiday, I really can't say when it started.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fainting?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not once. But close.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or palpitations when it happens?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Neither.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any dizziness when you're lying down, or room-spinning?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Only when standing up.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's go through your tablets.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Just the one. Bisoprolol, 5 mg, maybe? For my heart rhythm. Once a day, in the morning.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it 5 or 2.5, do you think?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I think 5. I'd have to check the box.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other health problems?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Palpitations, years ago, which is why the bisoprolol. And an underactive thyroid.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): My appendix, as a girl.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you drinking enough water? ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. Tea and coffee, mostly. Perhaps a litre a day. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check your numbers, first sitting, then standing. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sitting, blood pressure 104 over 64, pulse 58. Standing, 92 over 58, pulse 64.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that low? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's low-normal sitting, and it drops a little on standing, with your symptoms. Let me check your temperature and oxygen as well. ~
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temperature 36.4, oxygen 99 percent.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): All fine? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine. Your pulse is slow, which fits with the bisoprolol. So here's what I think. Your pressure is on the low side, and it drops when you stand, so I'd say this is mild postural low blood pressure, helped along by the bisoprolol and not enough fluid.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): What can be done? ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Drink two litres of water a day, add a little more salt to your food, and stand up slowly, sit on the edge of the bed first.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I can do that. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange a blood test for your blood count and thyroid, and a heart tracing, an ECG, and I'd like to review whether you still need the bisoprolol at that dose.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'd like a 24-hour heart rhythm monitor, to see what your heart's doing during the dizzy spells.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three weeks, with the results.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): morning. she was chatting in the passage. naledi, what number did you tell me?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Nineteen.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): right, we'll see what the scale says. so what's the matter?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eye.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): shame, doc, sticky red eye. the school wants a sick note, otherwise they won't have her tomorrow.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): okay. one eye or both, and how long?
[SEG0007] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): left one first, about four days, thursday. then the right one started, umm, i actually can't say if that was yesterday or the day before. both are red now, stuck shut in the morning.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): this came after a cold?
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ja, last week. snotty nose and a bit of cough. the nose is pretty much gone, the cough still pitches up at night.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): naledi, does the eye hurt?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): itchy at all?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she rubs it the whole time though. and she sleeps badly, tossing for half the night.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): naledi, are you sleeping okay?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): hm. mom says half the night, you say you're fine. were you hot this morning?
[SEG0018] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ja, uh, i thought so. checked with our thermometer.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty eight.
[SEG0020] person_1 (NURSE): she did say thirty eight, that was the home reading. mine just now is 36.8. pulse 104. and she said nineteen, the scale comes out at 19.2 kilograms.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): so 36.8, the fever has settled. any problems with the tummy or the waterworks?
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no, all fine. she's eating.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): what medicine has she had?
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): panado syrup by mouth, the paracetomol. i give 7.5 ml three times a day when she's hot. gave it this morning still.
[SEG0025] person_1 (NURSE): the bottle in the bag, the sticker says 5 ml, not 7.5. i read it twice.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): the sister at the clinic said 7.5 for her weight. so i've been pouring 7.5.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): err, the sticker says one thing, the clinic sister another. i won't pin a dose down off that. does she take it every day?
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): except sundays. she will not take the tablets, ag no, the syrup, she spits it on sundays at her gran's.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Saturday.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ag, saturday, not sunday. gran has her on saturdays. i mixed the days up.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): saturday, got it. any allergy to medicines or eye drops?
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no. nothing.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): chin up, let me look. mm, both whites are pink, left more than the right, with yellow crust on the lashes. the cornea is clear and the lids aren't really swollen. pupils are fine.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Itchy.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): ah, itchy. so it is itchy, even though you said no earlier. the rubbing fits with that.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): oh, and the graze on her knee, from the bike at school. healed in five days, just a mark, no oozing.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): five days, that's normal healing, not a slow healer. i'm thinking viral conjunctivitis after the cold, though i can't completely rule out a bacterial one. no pain, both eyes, clear cornea, so no antibiotic, and chloramphenicol ointment won't hurry a virus.
[SEG0038] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no drops then? what about the school, they were quite sharp on the phone.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): no drops. wash hands, her own face cloth, wipe the crust with cooled boiled water, no sharing towels. i'll do the sick note, keep her home tomorrow, and she can go back the day after if the goo is less. come back if the eye gets sore, if the clear bit goes cloudy, if a lid swells, or if it's not settling in a week.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): okay. the parking was a nightmare, but thanks doc.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Bye.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): cheers naledi. sister will print the note at reception.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, hello, doctor. Gosh, it's the scar, you see, it's been months and it still hurts, and it's right where my skirt rubs, and I told my daughter, she's getting married in June, a lovely lad, a plumber...
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Congratulations to her. Which scar, Margaret, remind me? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): The hip. The new hip, four months ago, on the left. The pain around the scar, it's like a burning, and a bit numb on the side.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the burning been there?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Since about a month after the operation, so, three months, nearly? Though I had the tingling in January too.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the numb patch, is that the same area?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, just on the outside of the thigh. Oh, and the hip itself is stiff in the mornings, I can't get my tights on.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever or sweats?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no fever at all. I took my temperature, I've got that thermometer you put in your ear.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any discharge, any weeping from the scar?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing like that, it's dry as a bone.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Tramadol, 50 mg, twice a day. Paracetamol, 1 gram, four times. Lansoprazole, 30 mg, in the morning, for my stomach, and levothyroxine, 75 micrograms, first thing.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Iodine. I react, they put it on my wristband at the hospital, but I can never remember what it does to me.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, we'll note iodine. What conditions do you have?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Underactive thyroid, acid reflux, and the thin bones, osteoporosis.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations apart from the hip?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): The hip, four months ago, and my cataract in 2019, the left eye.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bone problems in the family?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother broke her hip when she was eighty.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): What did you do for work?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I was a nurse, retired now. Thirty-five years on the wards.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where do you live?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): A second-floor flat, no lift, so the stairs are a battle.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And have you been doing the exercises?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): The physio ones, yes, every morning, apart from when it hurts too much.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me do your numbers. Pulse 72, blood pressure 138 over 84, temperature 36.8, oxygen 97 percent, breathing 16, weight 64 kilos.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? Oh, my daughter's fiancÃ© fixed our boiler last year, that's how they met. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Let's look at the scar.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Mind the skirt. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): The scar is healed and dry, with no redness or swelling. But the skin along it is very tender to light touch.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, that's the burning, even the sheet bothers me. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any problem with your chest or breathing?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, I'm fine in that department.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): The scar looks healed, and I think this is irritation of a small skin nerve, which is common after hip surgery, but I can't completely rule out a deep infection.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh dear, is it infected? ~
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I doubt it, but I'd like to check. I'd like to arrange an X-ray of the hip, and blood tests for inflammation and infection markers.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I carry on with the exercises? ~
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'd also like to do an ultrasound scan around the scar, and a bone density scan, since you have osteoporosis.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): When would that be? ~
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): The bone scan can wait a few weeks. I'd like to see you again in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. I'll put it on the fridge. ~

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja doctor, I'm really worried hey. She's up the whole night, I'm up with her. She's not herself.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. I'm not coping. That's the thing.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Also, I've had asthma since I was small. It's been quiet. I'm not here for that.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame. You've been tearful the whole time, and you look wiped.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any thoughts of hurting yourself?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the baby. Any thoughts of harming him?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Don't even ask me that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She wouldn't, hey. She's a good mom. I'm just, err, I can't switch off, I'm so scared.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tear from the delivery, is it painful now?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not painful.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. What tablets are you actually taking?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Amloc for the pressure, the amlodopine, 5 milligrams in the morning. My sugar tablets for the sugar, metforman, 500 milligrams with breakfast and supper.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The cholesterol one at night, twenty milligrams. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, a teaspoon, from the spice shop. That's all.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I put the morning ones out, she does take them. Eish, that robot outside had us sitting there forever. Sorry.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): No stress. With the asthma, any wheezing?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest tightness?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. No... well, sometimes, when I'm lying awake.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. About three weeks not sleeping even when he sleeps, tearful, ratty, exhausted. No thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, the tear's not painful, no vomiting, no wheeze, no headaches, but sometimes a tight chest when you lie awake. Amloc 5 milligrams mornings for the pressure, metforman 500 breakfast and supper for the sugar, the cholesterol one 20 at night, and a teaspoon of Ayurvedic powder in the morning, asthma since you were small, is that fair?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. That's right. Don't mess with those tablets, I'm not here for the pressure.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, is she going to be alright? I can't think straight, I'm that worried.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is postnatal depression, not only new-baby tiredness, though I'm not fully sure and I'm not starting a mood tablet today. I'll refer you to the postnatal mental health sister, and I want you back here in two weeks. If any thoughts come of hurting yourself or him, go straight to casualty, don't wait. [SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, fine. Casualty if it's bad. Ja, he can do the feed.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Brennan, in you come. I'll grab a blood pressure before the doctor sees you. 136 over 84, pulse 58, and the scales have you at 89 kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Sit yourselves down. What has you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): The tiredness, doctor, though if I start properly I'll wander. I do the accounts at the co-op, the month-end is a killer, I'm 53 in March, and I've been putting the whole lot down to the job and to getting older.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's asleep in the armchair before the nine o'clock news, most nights. I had to drag him in.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I was getting to that. I couldn't tell you when the tiredness began — last winter, or the one before, one or the other. I'm no use after half four, and the backlog at work just sits there.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the fatigue's been there a good while, and you can't pin the start. Are you cold with it as well?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Freezing, even with the heating up and a jumper on in the kitchen. That's been the same stretch of time, whatever length it is, hands worst of all, and the weight —
[SEG0008] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry — the jumper is year-round. He had it on in June.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): The weight, yes. You've me at 89. I was twelve stone a few years back, about 76 kilos, so that's the best part of two stone, and I haven't really changed the eating, only more tea and biscuits at the desk because the days run long.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight up, cold, tired. What about the bowels, any change? And has your mood dipped, or is it just the energy?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): The bowels are a misery. Constipated, every three or four days, hard stools, and I'm after trying prunes and then senna from the chemist. The mood I'll come to, because the senna is a small saga in itself —
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much senna, and how long have you been on it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Two tablets at night, only the last fortnight, and it's done nothing. I read the packet twice so I wouldn't take the wrong amount, and I still feel blocked.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been very flat as well, and the garden's gone to —
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the mood you asked about. I'm low. No interest in the garden and I used to live out there. I don't think I'm depressed, I just put the flatness down to being wrecked from work.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Low, but not depression in your own view. Any thyroid trouble in the family?
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother had the underactive thyroid, for years.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Eltroxin, they called the tablets, right up until she died, God rest her. I think her sister might have had something similar but I never got that straight, so I won't swear to it. I had a blood test myself once and they told me it was borderline.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was that blood test?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): I couldn't date it if you paid me. Before the pandemic, or just after, or somewhere in between. They said borderline, I'm nearly sure of the word.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The letter said normal, Seán. It's in the sideboard at home. You've called it borderline for years and it wasn't.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Was it normal? I was certain they said borderline. Sure maybe I have it wrong — I do mix the old results up.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, we won't hang anything on that old result, since you remember borderline and your wife remembers a normal letter, and neither of you can date it. Let me say back what I have. Tired and cold since last winter or the winter before, weight from about 76 kilos up to 89, bowels every three or four days, mood low but not what you'd call depression, mother with an underactive thyroid, senna two at night for a fortnight with no joy.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the bones of it. I still think the co-op hours are half the story, mind you, and the age.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): They might well be. On examination your hands are cool, the pulse matches the 58 the nurse got, and I can't feel any enlargement or lump in the thyroid itself.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Is a normal feel a good thing? My mother had a goitre late on — or was that someone else. No, it was her, I'm sure of that much.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): A normal feel doesn't rule an underactive thyroid in or out. This could be hypothyroidism, or it could be the workload and age catching you, and I can't tell those apart from the chair.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you'll do a blood test, will you?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will. I'll order a thyroid function test, and a full blood count as well, with the tiredness gone on this long. Not this minute — the nurse will book the phlebotomy.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning is free, if that suits ye. I can put the form through now.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Thursday morning is the audit, I can't do morning, the regional manager is in and I'll be stuck at the desk till lunch. Afternoon I could manage, if there's a slot, though the car park is desperate after three —
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): Afternoon, so. Half two.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Leave the senna off, since two at night for a fortnight hasn't shifted things. Plenty of water, and don't write the whole thing off as age until we have the numbers.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): If it is the thyroid, is it the same tablet my mother was on? I don't fancy being on something for life if I can avoid it, though I know people are, and she managed grand on it for years.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): We don't start any tablet until the result is back, and we'll talk it through then. Come back to me about a week after Thursday, once the results are in.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll root out that old letter so you're not depending on his memory of it.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, that's it. Don't lecture me on the powder. My wife gets it from the shop in town, she swears by it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): No lecture. Did the GP start you on an antibiotic recently?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, four days ago, at the clinic. Amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for this cough. Seven day course, so I've got three days left.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Amoxicillin can push the INR up when you're on warfarin. How's the cough itself?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Still there. Dry, worse at night when I lie down. Been four days.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding? Bruises, nose, gums, blood in the urine, black stools?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I'm not bleeding.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): And greens. Spinach, morogo, that sort of thing. Same as usual?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My daughter said greens are poison with warfarin, so I stopped the morogo and the spinach. Two weeks of nothing, and I used to eat it most days. I miss it, hey.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, that advice has worked against you. Cutting the greens out lifts the INR as well. A similar portion most days is safer than none.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Whatever. Nobody told me that.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any dizziness, or the heart racing?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a clear yes, I won't chase it. Right. Blood pressure is 138 over 82, pulse is 76 and irregular, which fits the fibrillation, and the saturation is 97 percent.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 138 bad? And listen, I said I wasn't bleeding, that was wrong. My gums bleed every time I brush, the last three or four days. There's a bruise on my right thigh that came up from nothing.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): 138 over 82 is acceptable, and the irregular pulse is the old fibrillation, not new. Gum bleeding when you brush, and that thigh bruise, do fit a high INR. Can I look?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Outer thigh. Don't poke.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can see a bruise on the outer right thigh. The gums aren't bleeding while you're sitting here.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, it's when I brush. Ag.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted. Any blood in the urine, or black stools?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Urine's normal. Stools are a normal colour, not black.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None. The amoxicillin hasn't given me a rash or anything.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression, nothing firmer, is that the INR of 4.2 is up because of the amoxicillin and because you stopped the greens. The gum bleeding and the thigh bruise sit with that. I can't prove more today.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So what must I actually do? I've got to fetch my grandson, and the robot by the school is a nightmare now.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): From tonight, stop the five milligrams. Take warfarin four milligrams once a day after supper, still for the fibrillation. Finish the three days of amoxicillin left, and don't take an extra warfarin if you missed one.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Four milligrams, fine. I'm not stopping the powder though. My wife will have a fit.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then keep the powder exactly as it is, and don't increase it. I'd rather you paused it, I don't know what's in it, but I won't fight you today. And put a usual portion of morogo or spinach back most days, the same sort of amount, not a binge.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Steady greens, same powder. Ja. I heard you.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book a repeat INR in a week, and a follow-up with me the same day. Reception will give you the lab form.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): A week. If the gums pour with blood before that, I'm not sitting in this queue for fun.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the gums bleed heavily, or you get a bad nosebleed, go straight to casualties and don't wait. The visit in a week still stands. To say it back, four milligrams from tonight, finish the antibiotic, greens steady, powder unchanged, blood test and review in a week.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, come on through. I'll check your blood pressure before the doctor. Sorry if I seem a bit frazzled, my sister rang at breakfast about her little boy's school concert and I have not quite landed yet.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning. Please do not apologise. I am perfectly happy to wait.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Ta. Blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse 72, oxygen level 98 percent. Have a seat, the doctor will be with you shortly.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Nguyen. Come and sit down. What's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. It is my right heel. For about two months the first steps in the morning have been really quite painful.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Tell me what a morning looks like. When your foot first—
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I have to stand still. It is a sharp pain under the heel, then after a minute or two of walking it eases. By the arvo, on my feet at the shop, it grumbles again. I bought new work shoes just before it started, and I wonder if they are part of it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you still in those shoes most days?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I am. I have not found a replacement. My runners are about a year old, the ones I use for, umm—
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): For your running?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Three mornings a week, about five kilometres. I cut Thursday short and walked the last part home. I did not wish to aggravate it.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the shop, what is the job exactly?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I manage a newsagency. Standing or walking the floor most of the day.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any ongoing conditions I should know about?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I have asthma. I am forty-six, and it has been with me since my twenties. Generally it is well controlled.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you using for the asthma?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): simbicort, the 200/6, two puffs in the morning and two at night. Ventolin as well, two puffs when I need it, though that is rare. I also tried Nurofen for the heel, 400 milligrams twice a day for about a week, and then I stopped. It bothered my stomach.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Any swelling, or any redness there?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not really.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the heel feel warm?
[SEG0021] person_1 (NURSE): Oops, sorry, I left the cuff on the chair. I'll grab it and get out of your way.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. It is no warmer than the other foot.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, pins and needles?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Nothing of that sort.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And pain in the calf, or in your back?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): My back is quite all right. The calf, err—
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It does not go up into the calf.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): With your asthma, any wheeze lately, or does it wake you at night?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes I wheeze if I have been rushing on the shop floor. It does not wake me.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, shoe off if you would. Tender on the inner heel where that band attaches, no swelling I can see, and the ankle moves freely. I reckon this is plantar fasciitis, the plantar fascia tightens overnight when it is irritated and those first steps yank on it, which is why mornings are the worst. New shoes can stir it up as well, and we do not need any scans.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll keep this simple. Stretch the calf and the sole before you get out of bed, and again after a run. Grab some cushioned insoles, or a gel heel cup, from the chemist, and ease the running for a couple of weeks, shorter and slower. If it is not settling in about a month, come back and see me.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I shall do that. I am grateful you explained it.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right so, blood pressure is 118 over 74, and the pulse is 82. You're grand there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that high? I'm all over the place, I hardly slept with the scratching.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're not high. Tell me about the scratching, in your own words.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this itch between my fingers, and around my waist where the jeans sit. I can't stop at it.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And I'm at it too, and the small fella—
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): He's three. Sorry, I talk over people when I'm nervous. He wakes clawing at his tummy.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright. How long has the itch been going on for you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Well I blamed a new washing powder at first. It didn't ease though.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And roughly how long?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): About three weeks. Maybe a bit more. It's desperate at night, I'm still going at two.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it, or feeling fluish in yourself?
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was eating away, grand in herself. My da is on metforman for his sugar, I thought maybe this was a sugar rash.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no fever. And I haven't diabetes. I'm not on any of that.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand. That metforman is his da's, not yours. Any allergy to creams or tablets?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0016] person_1 (NURSE): I'll say, when my own little fella had a dose of this last winter I was up to my eyes in washing. Fierce altogether.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): The itchy rash between the fingers and at the waist, worse at night, and the people at home itching with you, I'd say this is scabies. The mite burrows into the very top of the skin, and the itch is your body reacting to it, not the creature biting you all night.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Scabies? Oh God. Are we dirty? I hoover every day. How did we get it?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): It is nothing to do with being dirty. It passes by close skin contact, it's very ordinary, and it does not mean the house is filthy.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): And the burrowing, does that mean it's in my blood? I'm sorry, I just keep asking.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): It stays in the surface of the skin. It does not get into the blood. The finger webs and the waistband are simply where it likes to sit.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My wrists have been itchy maybe a fortnight. Not a patch on hers.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back to you. Itchy rash between the fingers and round the waist for about three weeks, worse at night, no fever, no allergies, and your partner and the three year old are scratching as well. That is the scabies pattern.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do we actually do? Do myself, my partner, and the small fella all need the cream? We're all in the one house. And do I ring the creche?
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Permethrin five percent cream, for you, your partner, and the child, all on the same night. I'll take you through it step by step.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Is five percent not very strong? I saw a one percent bottle online, permetrin or something.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): That one percent is a different product, not for this. You want the five percent cream. Lyclear is the name you'll see on the box.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): I can show you the putting on of it after, if that settles the nerves.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have a shower first and let the skin cool and dry. Then the cream goes on every inch from the jawline down, between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the belly button, the soles of the feet, and the genitals. Don't skip the skin under rings.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Not the face? What about him, he's only three, what about his face and hair?
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): He's three, so he gets the same as the two of you, jawline down. We only do the scalp and the face in babies under two, or if the head is itchy. Keep it out of the eyes and the mouth.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the face is grand on me anyway. How long does it stay on before a wash?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eight to twelve hours. Overnight is the handy way, then wash it off in the morning. You do the very same again seven days later, even if the itch is easing.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the duvet, she was half saying we should bin—
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't say bin it. I said I didn't know. I trail off when I panic.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't bin a thing. Hot wash the clothes, the towels and the bedclothes from the last three days, at sixty degrees. Anything that won't wash, seal it in a bag for three days. The mite dies quickly once it's off the skin.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty. Right. What about the couch? And can I work tomorrow? I'm on the till in a cafe.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): No spray for the couch. Hoover it if you like, that's plenty. You can go to work the morning after the first treatment, once the cream is washed off. Ring the creche and let them know, and he can go back the day after he's treated.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I've been taking a ceterizine, ten milligrams, in the morning, from the chemist, for the itch. Do I stop that?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the cetirizine. It only dulls the itch, it does not kill the mite. The itch can hang on for two or three weeks after the cream has done its job, because the skin is still reacting.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two or three weeks after? What if it's still as bad? I won't cope.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the itch is still as bad three weeks after the second treatment, come back and I'll look again. No blood tests today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): And you're sure it's not eczema? My cousin had eczema something fierce. Sorry, more questions.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your cousin's eczema is not yours. Looking at the skin, it's dry and scratched between the fingers, with a few tiny burrow marks, and there's a faint rash along the waistband. No weeping, and no sign of cellulitis.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, do we do two nights together or do we wait the week? I get muddled.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): One night now, and once more in seven days. Not two nights running. The prescription will be at reception, enough permethrin for the three of you, two applications each. You'll be grand.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in, Mrs. Keller. I'll grab the vitals before Dr. Shah steps in. Shoes off for the scale if you can manage it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh sure, yes, I can manage, I just go slow with the cane. My daughter Linda drove me, and the parking lot was a complete maze, we circled twice. But I'm fine, really, I am.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mom, just step up. I'll hold the cane.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Weight a hundred and fifty-two pounds. Last time in March you were sixty-eight, that was kilos on the old chart. [SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty-eight point three, is that high? I felt a little warm in the car, but the heater was blasting and Linda had her coat on. I thought it was just the car, you know how those heaters stick on high.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mrs. Keller. Six-week hip check, right?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the right hip, replaced six weeks ago. Well I was going to say eight because the pre-op visits dragged on, no, the surgery itself was six weeks ago Tuesday, at St. Mary's. Dr. Alvarez did it, and everyone there was lovely.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh the hip aches, not sharp like the first week, more a deep ache when I walk to the mailbox, that's maybe forty steps, and at night if I lie on that side. It's better than it was, I can tell. The first ten days I couldn't get comfortable in that old recliner at all.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Scale of one to ten. Now.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): A three. Maybe a four if I've been up awhile. Mostly three, sitting here it's a three.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was worn out after the grocery store yesterday. That lot is uphill.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I was tired, yes, the lot is uphill, that's all, Linda. Not a big setback, I just needed the couch for a bit.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Swelling in the calf?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I look every night, both calves, no swelling, no redness, my neighbor had a clot and she told me to check. So I check, with the lamp on, and there's nothing there.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath? Chest pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain at all. I get winded on the stairs but that's been years, not new, I just pause on the landing. I don't get that tight feeling or anything scary.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The stairs thing is old, Doctor. Since her knees, honestly.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Let me see the wound.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I kept the dressing on till the home nurse said stop, that was week two. I've been washing it with plain soap, not the perfumed one, the white bar, and patting it dry. Someone at church said vitamin E oil but I didn't put any on, I wasn't sure.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Incision is closed. No drainage. No redness. Healed.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh good. I thought that little scab at the bottom might be something, but it's tiny, like a dot.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Using a cane?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the wooden one, it's really just a stick my husband had. A walker is steadier but the cane fits in the car, and Linda's trunk is full of the kids' soccer stuff. They taught me the cane goes in the left hand, umm, because the new hip is the right one.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Aspirin?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, for the clots, the blood thinner one. I take aspirin three hundred and twenty-five, no, that's what my sister takes for her heart, I'm on the eighty-one milligram, once a day. Morning, with breakfast, I don't skip it.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Painkiller?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Tylenol, extra strength, five hundred milligrams, two tablets, three times a day. I was on oxicodone, five milligrams, but I stopped that, umm, about two weeks ago. It made me foggy and I didn't like how the morning felt.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She still has the bottle in the cabinet. I don't think she's touched it since.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't. I don't want it. It's just sitting there behind the band-aids.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm aware of. Penicillin was fine when I had that tooth, years back, no rash or anything.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fever at home? Chills?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't take my temperature, we don't have a thermometer in the house. I felt warm in the car, like I said, but no chills, no shaking. I slept with the one blanket, same as always.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She wouldn't let me buy a thermometer. I offered, twice.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Appetite?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I eat, maybe smaller portions, oatmeal, soup, and Linda brings those casseroles on Sundays. I'm not skipping meals.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Temp's up a little. Wound looks clean. I'm not calling this an infection.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Should I worry, though? My cousin had an infection after her knee and she was in the hospital nine days, and the whole family...
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. Not from what I see. Walk as you are, cane is fine. Keep the aspirin, eighty-one, daily, and the Tylenol as you are, don't go over three thousand milligrams a day.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two tablets three times is three thousand, yes, I counted it on a napkin once. Six times five hundred. I won't add any extra, even if the ache bumps up.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the calf swells, or you get chest pain, go to the ER. We might do a scan if the ache does not settle.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Like an ultrasound?
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): If we need it. Not today. Come back in two weeks. Front desk will book it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, alright. Should I keep checking the calves every night? I set a phone alarm for eight, both legs, and I write it in the little notebook by the phone.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Once a day is enough. Call if it changes. That's it.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. Mom, cane. Watch the rug.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. And thanks for not rushing me on the scale, my balance is still a whole project. We'll be out front if the desk wants the insurance card, it's the blue one, not the expired one.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come on back. You're the ankle, right. Have a seat up here.

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sleeve up for me. Blood pressure first.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure. Practice was a mess, the field was soggy, my cleat stuck and I rolled it, and coach kept the drill going like nothing happened. Then Marcus scored and everybody just moved on.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mm. One eighteen over seventy two. Heart rate 76.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Nice. I run a ton so it's usually low. I'm seventeen, I play midfield, junior year. There's a game Saturday I am not trying to miss, Ridgeview's striker is like a tree.
[SEG0007] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Okay. Sit tight, doctor'll be in.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): What happened.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Twisted my left ankle. Yesterday. Soccer.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swollen?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Puffy on the outside. My shoe barely fit this morning.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bearing weight?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I can. It hurts, but I walked in, four steps across your lobby, no hopping.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Where. Point.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Outer side, under the bump. Not really on the bone, more the soft part. Err, I think.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Numb?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bruising?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Just fat and pink.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Not with this.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): The knee?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not painful. Knee's good.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any medicine for it?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Two advil last night. Four hundred milligrams. Took the edge off. Trainer offered tramadol and I never took that, I don't even like how that sounds.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Daily meds?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Albuterol. My inhaler, two puffs when I need it. Asthma. Had it since I was like eight.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): How often.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm maybe twice a week, practice days. And I stopped monteleukast in March, that was ten milligrams at night. The lung guy said drop it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): The bus smells like old gatorade by the way, which is disgusting, and somebody left a cleat in my bag, not even mine, so my history homework smells like feet now.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wheezing?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. After sprints. Not today.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest tight at night?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cough?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Looking now. Swelling over the outer left ankle. Pressing the back of the outer ankle bone.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): That's alright. Not bad.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Inner ankle bone.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Fine.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Navicular, top of the foot. Base of the fifth metatarsal.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Neither. Hey don't roll it, that part I feel.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ottawa rules. No bony tenderness at the malleoli, you took four steps, no tenderness at the navicular or the fifth metatarsal base. No x-ray unless this gets worse.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So not broken? My cousin had a boot for months and missed prom, whole family group chat was unbearable.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): This is a sprain. Lateral ankle. I can't promise there isn't a tiny crack, but we're not getting an x-ray today.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I play Saturday though. I've been starting. Coach will be so mad if I sit, he already thinks I dog it on defense.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. Rest it. Elevate it above your heart. Ice twenty minutes, a few times a day.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Ice is easy. Elevating in chem class is gonna be a whole scene but okay.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ibuprofen four hundred milligrams by mouth every eight hours, with food, next few days.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Same pills as last night. Alright. Do I gotta come back or what.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it's not better in ten days, or sooner if you can't walk on it. We'll x-ray then if we need to.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry doctor, we got stuck in traffic from the other side of town, and he was getting restless in the car.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That is quite all right, please sit. So, tell me, what brings you in today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): My ankle. I twisted it.
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yesterday evening, doctor, at cricket practice. He jumped for a catch and landed all wrong, and the left ankle twisted under him.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, I see. How has it been since then? Tell me in your own words.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): It is paining. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0007] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Pain is there from yesterday itself, and the swelling came within an hour. He can walk, but limping is there, and it pains when he puts the foot down.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Outer side or inner side, where does it feel worse?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Outside. I think.
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Outer side, just below the ankle bone. That is what he kept saying at home also.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): When it happened, did you hear any pop, or a crack?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0013] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, there was no cracking sound. He just sat on the pitch and held it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. And now, can he take four steps on it, even if it hurts?
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, he walked in from the auto. Slowly, with pain, but he is putting weight, not hopping.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): It hurts when I walk.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or pins and needles, in the toes?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about fever? Shivering, or feeling very hot?
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. He ate his dinner and was chatting, only the ankle was the issue.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has this ankle been hurt before? Any fracture, any plaster cast, anything of that sort?
[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing. First time only.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, good. Any medicine he has reacted badly to? Rash, swelling, trouble breathing?
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. Ibuprofin. When he was small, around five years, we gave ibuprofin syrup for a fever and his lips swelled up, and red itchy rashes came all over the body. The child specialist said never give that again.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I am glad you remembered. We will keep away from ibuprofen, Brufen, and the other pain tablets in that family. Has he taken paracetamol, Crocin, without any trouble?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Many times, for fever. No problem at all with Crocin.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): It tastes bad.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, most syrups do. The nurse has noted the readings here. Blood pressure is one oh nine over seventy-seven. Pulse, err, it looks like ninety-four... no, sorry, I misread the slip, it is eighty-eight.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Last time, in March, the pressure was one-forty over ninety, but he had fever then, so I am not using that figure today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come, hop up, I will be gentle. You tell me if it is too much.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is swelling over the outer left ankle, a bit puffy, no big bruise. I am pressing behind the outer ankle bone and the inner one now.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Not the bone. The soft part. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was crying with it in the night, but since morning he is a little better.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, the soft tissue on the outer side is tender. Along the back of both malleoli I am not finding bony tenderness. Let me check the foot, the navicular area and the base of the little toe bone.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): That is okay.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): No tenderness over the navicular, and none at the fifth metatarsal base. And he has just taken four steps, limping, but bearing weight the whole way.
[SEG0037] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): In the waiting room also he wanted to keep standing. The coach has already phoned about Sunday's match, can you believe.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): The match will have to wait, I am sorry. Let me explain how I am deciding. Using the Ottawa rules, the pain is in the ankle, but there is no bony tenderness behind either malleolus, no tenderness on the navicular or the fifth metatarsal base, and he can bear weight for four steps. Clinically I do not think there is a fracture. My working impression is a sprain of the outer ankle ligaments.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no X-ray today?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the swelling increases, or if he cannot put weight on the foot, then we will do an ankle X-ray. If it is settling, we can spare him that.
[SEG0041] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And at home, what all should we do? Sitting still is not his habit, I am warning you.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Rest is the main medicine, no cricket and no running until the pain settles. Keep the leg elevated on a pillow when he sits or sleeps. Ice inside a cloth for about fifteen minutes, three or four times a day, never straight on the skin.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): No cricket? Umm.
[SEG0044] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will speak to the coach. For the pain, a tablet? I know not to give Brufen.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite right, no Brufen, no ibuprofen, and no diclofenac. Paracetamol, that is Crocin, five hundred milligrams, one tablet by mouth, up to three times a day if the pain is there. Leave four hours between doses, and not more than three tablets in the day.
[SEG0046] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Five hundred, he is fourteen only. Is that not a big dose?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): At fourteen, five hundred milligrams is quite a proper dose. If the pain is only mild, you can skip a dose, no need to give it round the clock.
[SEG0048] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Do we fix a review, or come only if it is not settling?
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): If he is not walking more comfortably in five days, come back and see me. Earlier than that if the swelling suddenly jumps up. Otherwise rest should carry him through. You were right to bring him.
