[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, sorry about the wait. I'm Dr Brennan. What has you in today?

[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): And shaking them brings the feeling back?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Give it a minute. It's driving me up the wall.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's dropping things as well. Dropped a cup of tea on Tuesday, all over the kitchen floor.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): One cup. Don't be making a show of me.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is the job hard on the hands?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm on the packing line all day, gripping boxes. That's not helping, sure.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. About three months. Maybe a bit less.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ah no, Pat. It was on you before Christmas. Five months, easy.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not five months. I'd have said.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. You don't agree, so I'll note it as roughly three to five months and we won't fight the date.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is there pain in the hands, or is it just the numbness?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit of an ache in the right wrist in the morning. Not much. It eases once I'm up and moving.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the neck, or pain shooting down from the neck?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neck's grand.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in the legs, or stumbling?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I'm just tired from being woke up.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks, the bowels, all ticking over?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Yeah. Grand. No bother there.

[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dizzy only on standing?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no pain. Should I be worried about my heart though? My neighbour had a heart attack and she was dizzy.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): No shortness of breath?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, breathing's fine. I am tired though, ever so washed out this last fortnight.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headache? Weakness in one arm?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache, and my arms are alright, both of them. Why, do you think it's a stroke? Please just tell me.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not from what you've said. Tablets. Blood pressure and a sleeping tablet, yes?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, amlodipine, that's ten milligrams in the morning, and the other blood pressure one, ramipril, and zopiclone at night. I do take them. Do I have to stop them all? I won't sleep.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ramipril is five milligrams. Zopiclone is seven point five. She takes the zopiclone every night, doctor, has done for years. The amlodipine she sometimes misses if she's rushing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't miss them. Well, maybe once or twice. Not really.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): So amlodipine ten milligrams most mornings, ramipril five, zopiclone seven point five at night. Any allergies?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I'm allergic to. Is the zopiclone the problem? I read they make old people fall.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Possibly. I'll stop the zopiclone and leave the blood pressure tablets as they are.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been on that sleeping tablet since Dad died, about five-ish years. If you stop it she'll be up all night. The dizziness is in the morning, after she's stood up, not in the night.
[SEG0026] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. Lying blood pressure a hundred and fifty-two over eighty-six, pulse seventy-four. Standing, after a minute, a hundred and ten over sixty-eight, pulse ninety-six.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. That drop changes things. Forget stopping the zopiclone. We'll stop the amlodipine instead and keep the ramipril and the sleeping tablet for now.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop the amlodipine completely? Not just a smaller dose? What if my blood pressure shoots up? And can I still take the zopiclone tonight?
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, stop amlodipine from today. Ramipril five milligrams stays. Zopiclone seven point five you can take tonight. We'll recheck the pressure.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I feel worse before I feel better? I'm really anxious about falling again, even if I say I only slid.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She slid because her legs went. She was on the floor both times. I think you should know that properly.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted. No blackout, you said. Any palpitations?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't race. I just feel panicky sitting here, that's all. Is ninety-six too fast?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): That pulse was on standing. It's acceptable. Drink plenty, stand up slowly, and sit if it swims. Don't drive until this settles.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't drive. Should I get a frame? And what about the chemist, do I just not collect the amlodipine?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't collect it. No frame today. We'll sort a review on the way out.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I go down again tomorrow? Do I ring you or nine nine nine? I need to know which.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you black out, injure yourself, or can't get up, it's nine nine nine. Otherwise ring the surgery the next morning.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll stay with her tonight. She lives alone usually, but I'm there till Sunday.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): You don't have to fuss. I'm fine, honestly, mostly. Will stopping one tablet really fix the swimming feeling?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's the most likely culprit, given that standing drop. Not definite until we recheck. Any questions left that aren't repeats?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Just... if the ramipril is five milligrams, is that a lot? I get muddled with the numbers.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a standard dose. Keep taking it. Reception will book you back in one week.

[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): It just came over me. Tight across the chest, I was shaking, and there was this awful fear. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Had you ever had a turn like that before?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Never. I'm usually grand.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long did it last, would you say?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Err. I don't know, doctor. Maybe ten minutes. The carriage was packed and roasting, sure, but that's nothing to do with it.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. The partner has it at twenty minutes. We'll say somewhere between ten and twenty minutes so.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm. Yeah. Could be.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the chest still tight now, or has it passed?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): It's gone. Chest is grand. I'm just wrecked, I didn't sleep a wink after it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you black out, or feel you might fall?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I stayed standing. Held onto the pole.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did it go down the arm, or up into the jaw?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nowhere else. Just the chest.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you short of breath with it?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. I couldn't get a proper breath. Like a band around me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you clammy, or sick in the stomach?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Clammy, yeah. Not sick. I wasn't going to get sick.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): And was the heart racing?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. It was thumping, going very fast.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on at the minute?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. My sugar tablets, the Metformine, 500 twice a day. And Omprazole 20 milligrams in the morning, for the burn in the stomach.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything for the blood pressure, or an inhaler?

[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's it. I pick them up at the chemist.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take cocaine or any other drugs?

[SEG0034] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Vitals from the cubicle. Pulse 88, blood pressure 122 over 78, and the oxygen is 98 percent.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're not dying. We'll do an ECG this morning and they'll call you down for it.

[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Four, four and six. Of. I'll try. I missed my stop yesterday with the fuss, which was gas afterwards.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks and we'll look at the ECG together. If the tightness comes back and you can't settle it, go straight to A&E, don't be waiting on it.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Grand. Thanks a million.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, mind the step. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, um, thanks. Err, that car park nearly did me in, we went round and round and Sharon almost collected a ute. Anyway, my back's been crook.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We found a spot in the end. She's been shifting about in the car the whole way.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Forget the car park for a minute. Tell me about the back.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's low back pain, and it shoots down my left leg. Three weeks. I was shifting big pot plants and it started that arvo.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three weeks, down the left leg. How sore is it, and what sets it off?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Sitting's the worst, the desk and the driving. Most days it's a 6 out of 10. Lying down eases it. My colleague Dave reckons these cat stretches off the internet, I had a go and the leg just zinged.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She sleeps badly, up and down all night. And she does not take the tablets on Sundays.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah the sleep's right, I can't get comfy. Not Sundays though. I skip Saturdays, after the market I just forget. Sundays I take them.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh. Saturdays, yeah, market day, my mistake.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the missed day is Saturday. Which tablets, and how much?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofin, the nurofen, 400 mg by mouth, morning and night. Been the whole three weeks. Takes the edge off. My sister keeps pushing her biotin gummies for her hair, I've never touched them.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Biotin's your sister's, we'll leave that. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none. My husband Barry's on metforman for his diabetes, he's sweet on it, but that's not mine. Oh, the bakery near here does a lamington that's dangerous.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): His metforman, not yours. Any numbness, or weakness, in the leg?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No numbness. The leg's strong, I can still walk the dog. It's just the pain.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any change with the bladder or the bowels, or numbness in the saddle area?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. All normal, thank goodness.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Weight coming off?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, weight's the same. Apart from that lamington, ha.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cuts or sores that have been slow to heal?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She nicked her shin on the wheelbarrow. Healed in five days, looked ordinary.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah that one closed right up. Did you see the Swans on the weekend? Hopeless.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any old back trouble, or operations?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): First time with the back. Appendix out when I was 20, that's it. Desk job at the council, sitting all day, which is not helping.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking nerve root pain, the way it shoots and sitting sets it off. First plan in my head is an MRI of the lumbar spine, and maybe a short course of prednisolone to settle the nerve. Let me examine you before I commit.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): An MRI, the tube thing? I get a bit funny in small spaces. Uh, Sharon, did I leave the lights on in the car?
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Lights are off. She mentioned at the chemist last week her blood pressure was 138 over 86.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep, that was last week's chemist one, not today. I told her in the car.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll go with today. Blood pressure is 132 over 84, pulse 76. Hop on the couch and I'll do a straight leg raise.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left straight leg raise brings the leg pain on at about 40 degrees. Right side is comfortable to about 70, no pain. Tender over the low lumbar spine. No foot drop, and power's good.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, thinking it through. That straight leg raise fits a left sided nerve irritation, sciatica, my working impression, not a locked-in diagnosis. No weakness, bladder's fine, only three weeks, and the ibuprofen helps. So I'm changing my mind, no scan yet and no prednisolone.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh good. I wasn't keen on the tube. What do we do instead?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to physio, that's the plan. Keep the ibuprofen 400 mg morning and night with food, and try not to skip Saturdays. If you get weakness, bladder trouble, or it's not settling, then we organise an MRI. I'll see you back in six weeks.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Physio, yep. I'll ditch Dave's stretches, they made the leg worse. Six weeks is fine. Short walks with the dog still ok?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walking's good, keep them short. Long sitting loads the lower discs and that's why the leg pain fires, so break it up. If you can't pass urine or the leg gives way, don't wait, go to emergency. Reception will book the physio and the six week review.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her to physio. And I'll nag her on Saturdays about the tablets, market or not.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No worries. Off you go, and mind the step.

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'm the healthcare assistant. Those readings are fine. She'll call you in a minute.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, come on in, I'm Doctor Reilly. Tell me, what's brought you along today?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Eh, my eyes have gone yellow. And the pee is really dark. I'm wrecked, tired all the time.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ah, you poor thing. When did the yellow start, can you place it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Umm. Maybe a week? Could be five days. I can't pin the day down.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the dark urine and the tiredness, did they come on together?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the pee went dark around the same time. The tiredness, well, actually I was already a bit flat on the trip, and then it got worse after I came home.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit about the trip, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Four of us, down the country for a long weekend. We were eating off those roadside stalls, burger vans and that. Two of the lads were throwing up the next day, and one fella said his eyes looked off as well. I don't know if it's the same thing.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): A few of you unwell after the vans. Ok.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): The drive home was brutal though. The M50 was stopped dead, an hour sitting there, and the rain was lashing. You couldn't see the lights in front of you.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Then my brother is on about his new dog, a mad little collie that chewed the skirting the first night. He sent a video of the dog in a raincoat. We were in stitches in the car.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): A dog in a raincoat, I love that. Was the parking here any better this morning?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse. Three laps of the car park, and a jeep nipped into the space. Sure look, that's just how it is. Anyway.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right so, back to the urine. How dark?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Like tea. Dark tea. Not, err, not blood, just brown. I don't know, doctor, is that serious?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): It fits with the yellow eyes. Any pain in the tummy at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. Not that I've noticed, anyway.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been vomiting, or had a fever?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. Fever, I don't know, doctor, I never took it. I felt warm one night but I couldn't say.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any itch in the skin? And the bowel motions, any change in colour?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit itchy, yeah, the last few days. The toilet, I don't know, doctor, I didn't look. Sorry.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you take a drink? Even on that weekend with the lads?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't drink. I never really have. They were on the pints, I was on tea.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about medicines, anything regular?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, omeperazole, twenty milligrams, one in the morning, for the heartburn. That's years now. And if the head is at me I'll take two paracetamol, not every day, maybe once a week. I don't know exactly.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any reactions to drugs, antibiotics, painkillers, anything like that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I'm allergic to it. I came out in a rash all over, and my lips swelled up. They said never take it again. That was years ago, but it's definite, I'm not mixed up on that.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good to know, we'll steer clear of penicillin and the amoxicillin family entirely. Had anyone checked your liver bloods before?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. About three years ago the GP said it was borderline. They never repeated it. I don't know the figures, doctor, they just said borderline.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right, I won't hang any decision on that old comment. Let me have a look.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): The whites of the eyes are yellow, and the skin has a yellow tinge. Tummy is soft. A little tenderness under the right ribs when I press, and no guarding.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. So is it the liver? I don't know, doctor, I keep thinking the worst.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working impression is an acute hepatitis, quite possibly from that roadside food, seeing as the others were sick too. A blockage of the bile duct is still on the list, I can't rule it out properly until the bloods are back. Nothing is confirmed today.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Here's what we'll do. Bloods Thursday morning at half eight, the liver tests and hepatitis serology, A, B and C. No fasting. The nurse will take them then.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): If those liver tests come back borderline, then we do an ultrasound of the tummy. I'm not booking the scan now.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Rest yourself, drink plenty of fluids, stay off alcohol, and keep the paracetamol to the odd dose only. If the yellow deepens or you start vomiting, don't wait for me, come back in.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you here in two weeks with the results. That's a definite slot, not a maybe.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. I'll rest, plenty of fluids, no drink, and I'll go easy on the paracetamol. Thursday at half eight, no fasting. I don't know if work will moan, but I'll be there.
[SEG0042] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll put the bloods in for Thursday at half eight, and the review in two weeks. No fasting, as Doctor Reilly said. You're all set.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back if it is not better in four weeks. If it is easing, no need to hurry back. We can review it then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, my chest has gone all tight and I think it's the pollen. I've got hay fever, you see, and I'm frightened it's turned into something worse.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, deep breath, you're in the right place. Tell me about the tightness. When did it start?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Sunday. So four days ago. I was watching my nephew at a cricket match, sitting on the grass, and I could feel it creeping in.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how would you describe it? A band, a weight, a pinch?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Like someone's pulled a seat belt tight across the front of me.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good picture. Is it there all the time, or does it come and go?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Comes and goes. Worse in the afternoon, and when I'm outside, especially near the park.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does anything take the edge off?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Coming indoors and sitting down helps a bit. But then I sit there and worry, which doesn't help.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very human. Is it actually painful, or just tight?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain. Just tight. Is that better or worse?
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Better, as far as I'm concerned. Now, you mentioned hay fever. How long have you had that?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, years and years. It's the same every summer. I'm used to that part, it's this chest thing that's new.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right. Let me ask about the rest of you. How are your tummy and bowels?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Nothing to report there.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, I keep thinking it's my heart. I lie awake doing the maths on how long I've got.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you said it out loud. Let's check things properly rather than leave you doing sums in the dark. Can I listen to your chest?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, please. Do I need to take my top off?
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just lift it at the back. Breathe in and out through your mouth, nice and steady.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your chest is clear all the way down, and your throat looks completely normal.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Really? Nothing at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing worrying on the listening side. I'll clip this little sensor on your finger as well.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oxygen is 98 per cent and your pulse is 76. Both sit right where I'd want them.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): So it's not my heart.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to put a name on it yet, and I'd rather not guess. Think of your airways as a smoke alarm. Sometimes it's too sensitive and goes off when you've only made toast.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): So the pollen is the toast.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possibly, but we can test it instead of assuming. I'd like to arrange a breathing test, spirometry, which you blow into a tube and it measures how well the air moves.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it hurt?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. It's mostly puffing like you're blowing out birthday candles, as hard as you can, three times.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I can manage a birthday cake. When would that be?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse next door can book it before you leave. I'm not starting any tablets or inhalers today, so you aren't taking anything you don't need.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief, actually. I get nervous about new pills.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. Meanwhile, check the pollen forecast in the morning, keep your bedroom window shut on high days, and change your clothes when you come in from outside.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Change my clothes. I never thought of that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pollen hitchhikes on your sleeves like a stowaway. Little things like that can make the days easier.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll try. And I'll try not to google it tonight.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good plan. Googling at midnight is like asking a stranger for directions in a language you don't speak.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha. Right. Thank you, doctor, I feel less like I'm drowning.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Off you go, and enjoy the cricket from a deckchair next time.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Here.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. How did you fall? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The bike went over a bump, and I put my hand out. ~

[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His grandfather broke his wrist, years ago, but that's all.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Kabir, I'm going to touch your arm very gently, and I want you to tell me when it hurts.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow! Here! ~
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, you're very brave. Mum, the wrist is swollen and tender over the end of the forearm bone, and he doesn't want to turn his hand over. ~

[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't rule out a fracture, which is common at this age, so I'd like an X-ray of the wrist and forearm now.

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Will I need a cast? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it's broken, maybe. A lot of children's breaks are small and heal quickly. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I choose the colour? ~

[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you, doctor. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll come and see you with the picture in a few minutes. If his fingers go blue, cold or numb in the meantime, call us at once.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will. ~
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Mummy, don't leave. ~
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm here, beta. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good boy. See you shortly. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, hello. I've had diarrhoea, I'm sorry to say, for ten days now, since I got back from holiday. It's not stopping.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where were you? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Egypt. A week in Hurghada. I was fine there, mostly, then it started on the flight home.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often are you going?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Five or six times a day. Watery. And I've lost my appetite.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any tummy pain?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Cramping, before I go. Then it eases.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood, or mucus, in the stool?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No blood. Just watery.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever? ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit hot, the first few days. Not now. ~
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Omeprazole, 20 mg, once a day. And loperamide, I think, 2 mg, when I need to go out.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does the loperamide help? ~
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit. For a few hours. ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other conditions?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Acid reflux.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): My gallbladder, in 2016.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you eat anything unusual, salads, ice, or drink tap water? ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Ice in my drinks. And a buffet. I know, I know. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the usual story. Let me press your tummy. Lie back.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft with mild general tenderness, and no guarding. Your mouth is slightly dry. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it serious? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Persistent traveller's diarrhoea after ten days, I'd say it's likely a gut infection picked up abroad, possibly a parasite like giardia, though bacteria are also possible.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): What do I do? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to send a stool sample, to look for bacteria and parasites.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please drink plenty of fluids with some salt and sugar, and eat plain food.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't take the loperamide if you get a fever or blood in the stool.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you get blood, a high fever, severe pain, or can't keep fluids down, come back at once.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. Thanks. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Morning, doctor. Is this the right room?
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright, take a seat. What can I do for you?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It's being confused and drowsy, mostly.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll do your observations first.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep your arm relaxed for me...
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: blood pressure 136 over 86, height 154 centimetres, BMI works out to 31.2, respiratory rate 16, weight 74 kilos, saturation 98 percent, pulse is 108 beats a minute, temp 36.8 degrees. Can you tell me when it first started?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): For one week, I'd say.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Would you say mild, moderate or severe?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, it feels moderate to me. I've been passing huge amounts of urine too, for five days.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed vomiting, chest pain or fever?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No vomiting, chest pain or fever, none of it.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any muscle or joint problems besides this?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, joints are fine.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your medical history?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I've had diabetes for nearly five years now.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I have an irregular heartbeat. My family kept telling me to get it checked.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay. Okay, I can see diabetes in your file as well.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me your medicines, please.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm on Glycomet, 500 milligrams, twice a day. Warfarin. I take it 3 milligrams, in the evening.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not at all.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything relevant on the family side?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): My son has asthma.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your routine, work, habits, that sort of thing.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I only drink at family occasions. My husband and I live above the shop. Not much, I mostly stay in these days. I'm a bus driver, so I sit for long hours.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay as you are for a moment.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): You are very dry and drowsy, and your sugar reading is too high to read.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me tell you where I've got to. I can't pin this down yet. We're looking at a hyperosmolar diabetic emergency or sepsis.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm scared it's something bad. Is it?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's a hyperosmolar diabetic emergency, and we'll know more once the urgent blood tests is back.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sending you for urgent blood tests because of hyperglycaemic emergency. You need hospital now for fluids and insulin. We'll refer you to the emergency team. The thing that would worry me is if the symptoms get worse. If that happens, go to emergency.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll remember that.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else on your mind before you go?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Great, thank you for your help.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, see you soon.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr. Harlan, have a seat. What's going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife dragged me down here. Little cough in the mornings. It's nothing, really.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not nothing. He coughs every morning, and he gets winded hauling groceries in from the car.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're late, he melted down in the parking lot. It's his ear, and he's been up crying at night.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Give me a second, the chart's still loading. Which ear?
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The right. He grabs the right one. It came on after a cold, but I can't—
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Hurts. Go home.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the screen jumped and I lost that. When did the ear pain start?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Mama.
[SEG0007] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can't date it. Not a clean Saturday. Maybe Friday night, or Saturday, after the cold. It all blurs.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the cold still going?
[SEG0009] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Runny nose is mostly done. There's a leftover cough, just a tickle. He's wiped out and cranky.
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): No nap.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He didn't nap, so he's extra mad. Last two nights he wakes up screaming and holds that ear. I rock him or he won't quit.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I was hot. Gamma said hot.
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. My mom, his grandma, swore he felt hot yesterday, but I used the thermometer and—
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hold on, a message just popped up. What did the thermometer say? Repeat that.
[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ninety-eight point six. That's normal. Grandma always thinks he's burning up. He did not have a fever when I checked.
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Hot.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting? Is he pulling at both ears or just the right?
[SEG0019] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Just the right. No throwing up. He picked at some applesauce this morning and that was about it.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Drainage from the ear? Hearing seem off?
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No drainage that I've seen. Hearing seems fine, he snaps to if I say cookie.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Cookie now.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Maybe after. Any trouble breathing, or is the cough what's waking him?
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Breathing's fine. The cough isn't what wakes him. It's the ear.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has he had ear infections before?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): One, I think, when he was smaller. They gave him amoxicillin. That was long ago, last winter, or the one before. I can't tell you which.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did he do okay on the amoxicillin?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Yucky. No.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Well, actually, I'm not sure. I think he got a rash, maybe. Could've been the virus and not the medicine. My sister said something and I—
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): This alert again, sorry. You're not sure there was a rash from the amoxicillin?
[SEG0031] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Right. Maybe a rash, way back. We haven't given it since, just in case. I don't think anyone wrote it down as an allergy.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines is he on now? Any allergy you're actually sure about?
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nothing daily. I gave him children's Tylenol last night, the liquid, just one time, for the ear. It helped a little, then he was up again.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much Tylenol was that?
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Um, the little cup. I think five mils, whatever the box said for his weight. I'm not a hundred percent.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): And allergies you're certain of, food or a drug?
[SEG0037] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nothing I'm certain of. No food allergies. Just that maybe-amoxicillin thing.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'm going to look in his ears. He won't love the light.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Stop.
[SEG0040] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Almost done, buddy. He's been this irritable all morning.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right eardrum is red and bulging a little. Left one looks clear. I don't see any pus in the canal.
[SEG0042] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So it's infected?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Could be an early ear infection after the cold. I'm not calling it definite. He's uncomfortable, not toxic looking.
[SEG0044] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Are you gonna give antibiotics? I don't want to mess with that rash thing if—
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quick, before I answer, any asthma? Does anybody smoke at home? I got pulled off by the screen.
[SEG0046] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No asthma. Nobody smokes. His dad had ear infections constantly when he was a kid, if that matters. We almost got a dog and then we didn't.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): The dog can wait. Chart says four years old, is that right?
[SEG0048] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, four last month.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): He's over two and this isn't severe, so I'd rather watch a couple of days than start an antibiotic today. Keep using the acetaminophen for the pain. You can alternate children's ibuprofen if you want, dose on the box for his weight, with a little food.
[SEG0050] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So we just wait? Even if he screams again tonight?
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Watch him with fluids and rest, nothing in the ear, and no amoxicillin. If a real fever shows up or the pain gets worse, call us. If he's not better in two days, come back and I'll decide on cefdinir as the backup, which you don't start unless we say so.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit her up on the couch. What's brought the two of you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's her eyes, doctor. After the cold they went red and sticky, and the school are looking for a note before they'll have her back.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Sticky. Don't poke.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't, I promise. Which eye was first?
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The right one, four days ago. Yesterday the left joined in. Both of them are stuck shut till I wipe them with warm water.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Gooey. I feel like a wet rag.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): You poor thing. Is there pain in the eye, or is it the stickiness?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): No pain. Itchy.
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she rubs them, no matter what I say.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the light bother her at all?
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Uh she can't bear the light. Sure we've the kitchen curtains half closed.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Light is fine.
[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Well she was squinting at home, whatever she says now.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. I'll not settle the light thing just yet. Tell me about the cold that came before this.
[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A week of a runny nose and a cough. Cough is gone, nose is clear today. She's just flat out of it.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the breathing, or with the tummy, since?
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Chest is grand, and the tummy's fine, she's eating away.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the seeing, books and the telly, same as usual?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Same as usual, yeah. No change.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Stop. I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That baby in the hall is fierce loud, I know. Umm, any knock to the eye, or did anything go into it?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. Thinking it through, I lean to a viral conjunctivitis coming off the cold. A bacterial one isn't fully out with all that stickiness, but I won't call it bacterial on this alone.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Thermometer said thirty seven point eight.
[SEG0025] person_4 (NURSE): That's the reading I took just now, yes. Temperature thirty seven point eight degrees, heart rate 96, regular.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only a touch above. Not a big fever with it. What medicines is she on, if any?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Setirizine, five milligrams by mouth at night, for the hay fever. Only she will not take the tablet on Sundays.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Not Sunday. Saturday.
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Saturday, you're right, I mix the days up. She skips the Saturday one. And paracetamol, 250 milligrams by mouth up to three times a day for the fever, we stopped that when the cold eased.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand, the cetirizine can stay as it is. I'm not reaching for an antibiotic drop.
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She sleeps badly as well, up and down all night rubbing the eyes.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I sleep.
[SEG0033] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You were awake at two, love.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Was not.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that as you don't agree. The cut on the knee, any trouble with healing slow?
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That healed in five days, no bother at all. She's not slow to heal.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Looking now, both whites of the eyes are red, there's sticky stuff on the lashes, the corneas are clear, and there's no sore when she looks side to side.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Itchy. Stop.

[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, come, sit. What is the problem today.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Lower back is paining, and the pain shoots down my left leg. It is there from 3 weeks.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Only while sitting, or all the time.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Sitting only it gets worse. If I stand for a bit it eases. I think I've overdone it, that is all.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Please, I am not in the mood for a lecture.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, not weak. But my feet feel dead, both feet, from about a week. And the whole day I feel like a wet rag.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right leg paining?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Left only.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Trouble passing urine? Any change in motions?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cough, chest pain, breathlessness?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Since yesterday there is a frog in my throat, that is separate. And that drilling outside, uh, I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The throat started yesterday morning only. Back pain is why we came.

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipin five milligram in the morning for the pressure. Metformine 500 milligram morning and night, those are the sugar tablets.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The cholesterol one at night, maybe ten milligram, the name never stays with me. For the pain, ibuprofin 400 milligram twice a day since one week. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, one small spoon.

[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. So pressure, sugar, cholesterol, all ongoing. No new tablet from me today.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank god. I am fed up.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): On the couch please. Straight leg raise.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ugh, slowly.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): That was enough, it is hurting.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Heels and toes. Walk.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Like this?

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): No MRI now. Err, let's see, I am not concluding the exact cause without more. If it has not settled after physiotherapy, then we might think of a scan.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): My colleague already gave exercises and I got worse.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stop those. Do not follow colleague exercises. I am booking physiotherapy, they will show you what to do.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. When.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Reception will fix the physio slot. Meanwhile get up every thirty minutes, do not sit for long stretches. Continue ibuprofin 400 milligram twice a day with food for one more week, then stop if the pain allows.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): One more week, fine. I just want to lie down.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And review?
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks. If the leg becomes weak, or if urine is not passing, come earlier, do not wait for six weeks.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Can we go now.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. Take the physio note from the nurse on your way out.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I will give you the physiotherapy request. Kindly wait two minutes at the desk.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, I've popped the cuff on. Blood pressure is 138 over 84, pulse 72, oxygen 98. Doctor Okonkwo's just washing her hands.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ta love. Um, is 138 decent? Factory medical had me at one fifty over ninety odd, that's why they stuck me on the water tablet.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Today's one is fine. My sister's blood pressure went daft after her third, she's on three different tablets, but that's her not you.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Okonkwo. Come and sit. What's been the trouble?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's me hands. At night the thumb, the index and the middle finger go numb, both sides but the right is miles worse, and I have to shake them to wake them up. Feels like I've overdone it on the packing line.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on, and does it actually wake you?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, maybe six weeks, could be longer, I can't pin it. Wakes me two or three times a night. I flap the hand and it eases off after a minute or so. Daytime I'm mostly alright unless I'm gripping boxes.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been dropping things?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I've started dropping cups. Smashed my Blackpool mug last Tuesday, wife was furious. Nearly lost the kettle as well. Sorry, I'm rambling.
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I've clocked it too. I come three mornings a week for his dad, I'm his dad's carer not his, and twice this month a cup's just gone out of his hand. My own wrists are fine, my daughter's a hairdresser and she's the one always on about her hands.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the numbness travel up the arm at all, or is there neck pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it stays in those three fingers. Neck's fine. Honestly I can't hear myself think on that line, the machines are brutal, but that's just noise, my hearing's alright.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the feet?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, feet are fine. Mornings though I feel like a wet rag, from the broken sleep I reckon. Once I've had a brew I'm alright.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any aching in the hand itself?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, yeah, more of an ache in the right wrist and palm at the end of a shift. I take a couple of Nurofen for it, the 200 milligram ones, not every day.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the water tablet, do you know the proper name and the dose?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, bendroflumethazide, the water tablet. 2.5 milligrams, one in the morning. Little white tablet. Been on it a couple of years for the blood pressure.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bendroflumethiazide 2.5 milligrams, yes. Any other regular medicines?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just that and the odd Nurofen. I pack biscuits, been on that line fifteen years. Oh I used to smoke, packed it in when the factory went smoke free, years back now.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, plasters, anything?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operations on the hands or wrists before?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Closest I've come is a splinter off a pallet. Daft, really.
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I only catch the mornings. My sister had wrist trouble years ago and she still goes on about it, but that's her, nothing to do with him.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look at the hands. No wasting in the palm muscles. I'm going to tap over the wrist.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. That tap on the right sends a tingle into the thumb and middle finger. Left side doesn't. Grip on the right is a little weaker than the left.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah that tap was weird, like a little shock. Reminds me of the static off the shrink wrap, we have a laugh about it on shift.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I think is going on is carpal tunnel. The median nerve runs through a tight tunnel at the wrist, and at night when the wrist bends the pressure squashes the nerve, so those three fingers go numb. Shaking the hand eases it a bit. Working impression, not a definite label yet.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So I'm not falling apart. The lads at work said it was arthritis and I nearly had a panic in the canteen.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't call it arthritis from what I can see. A neutral wrist splint at night, not a tight bandage, often settles this. Buy one at the chemist and wear it every night for the next few weeks.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Every night, even weekends? I sleep with my hands under the pillow. And the dog hogs the bed, useless animal.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, especially then, it stops the wrist curling under the pillow. If the splint hasn't helped, we might send you for nerve conduction tests to check the nerve. Not booking that today.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll nag him about the splint when I'm in with his dad. I forget my own tablets half the time, the blood pressure ones, so I'm a fine one to talk.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's see you back in six weeks either way, and we'll check how the nights are.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, yeah. Should I ease off the Nurofen? They help the ache but I don't want to mess my stomach. Canteen curry is already a gamble.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short courses with food are fine if your stomach stays happy. Don't take them every day for weeks. If you get heartburn or black stools, stop and let us know.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Stomach's been fine, touch wood. I'll grab the splint on the way home. Cheers for not rushing me, I do go on.
[SEG0039] person_1 (NURSE): Chemist on the corner usually has them. My boy wears a wrist support for his boxing, completely different, ignore me.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ha, boxing. Right, I'll leave you in peace.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Take care, and do wear it nightly. See you in six weeks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Hey, come on back to room two. Doctor's a couple minutes out, and the nurse'll grab your vitals.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh thank goodness. Parking was a nightmare, I circled for twenty minutes while some guy in a pickup just sat there with his blinker on. Saturday was worse, my grandson's ball game, hot dogs and everything, he struck out twice and still loved that uniform.
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): That's sweet. My sister's boy plays too, she's at every game and blows up my phone with photos. Arm out. Pressure was one fifty eight over ninety two, ugh the cuff slipped, so it's one forty two over eighty six.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? I've had high blood pressure for years, I check the machine at the drugstore.
[SEG0005] person_3 (NURSE): Doctor'll go over it. Pulse 76, oxygen 95 percent, respirations 18. Excuse the voice, I had a cold last week, my sister brought it home.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): You're fine. The coughing's why I came, every morning I'm hacking stuff up.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning. Dr. Hale. Cough's the main thing?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Morning cough, and the phlegm comes up brown. It's been going on forever.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. How long?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, about a year. No, longer than that, two years easy.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much, soon as I get up. I thought the stuff was yellow sometimes but no, it's brown.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Blood in the phlegm?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fevers?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, weight's been steady. I eat the way I always have. My grandson won't touch a vegetable though, only chicken nuggets, whole drama at their house.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Still smoking?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Quit. Last year... actually it was fourteen months ago. Pack a day for thirty years, wait, thirty five. Thirty five years.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Still on a pill for the blood pressure?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep, lisnopril. Ten milligrams... no, they raised it, twenty milligrams once a day.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Headaches from the pressure?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. Right behind my eyes. I skip the pill now and then.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A little, yeah, on the stairs at the house.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any stomach or bowel trouble?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Belly's fine.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear, I don't hear a wheeze. Years of smoke irritate the lining of the bronchial tubes and they pour out mucus, that's the brown stuff each morning. I think this is chronic bronchitis.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll book spirometry, a breathing test, to measure it. Come back in two weeks with the results. Get the flu shot and the pneumonia vaccine at the pharmacy this week. If you cough up blood or you can't catch your breath, go to the ER.
[SEG0033] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can put that breathing test on the schedule for Thursday morning.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday's good. Appreciate you fitting me in.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, have a seat. What can I do for you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, so the headaches. I've had migraines for years, but lately they're different, worse when I first wake up, and—
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's lately?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and the missus reckons I snore all night and I'm wrecked, but she's—
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): The headaches. Weeks or months?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, sorry. About three weeks. Maybe four. We'd just got back from Merimbula, lovely spot, the bakery there does this—
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three or four weeks. Vomiting with them?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, yeah, twice. Both times first thing in the morning, with the really bad head. I thought it was the prawns from the servo, but—
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only twice?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Twice. Nothing since Sunday.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any change in your vision? Blurring, double vision?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Work's been mental. I'm a chippy, we're short two blokes, and the boss keeps—
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your eyes. Any change?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Nah. Eyes are fine. I can read the plans, no worries.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weakness, numbness, or slurred speech?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Neck stiff at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really, no.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still the old migraine? One side, throbbing?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly the right side, yeah, pounding. Light still bugs me, same as always. Just the mornings are new. And the chucking.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many years have you had migraines?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was about twenty-two. So, twenty-odd years. Mum had them worse, poor thing, she'd be in a dark room for days.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you take?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Sumatriptan. The fifty— wait, no, I thought the chemist gave me the hundred milligram ones, but the box says fifty.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days a week?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days lately. Actually, more like four or five days a week. And Panadol as well, two of the five hundred milligram tablets, sometimes three times a day.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a lot of sumatriptan. Anything else?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah, that's the lot. I was on propranolol years back, for prevention, but I stopped. Made me feel flat as a tack.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did you stop it?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Ages ago. Before covid, I reckon. Couldn't tell you the year.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I can take whatever.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Drink?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Gave up smoking, ten years now. Couple of beers on the weekend, that's it. And I'm not tired, whatever she says. I don't snore.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Recent knock to the head?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Nearly stacked the ute coming off the highway last month, the dog went flying, but I didn't—
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No head injury.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Just a near thing. Shook me up more than anything.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll check the nerves. Follow my finger.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): This the follow-the-finger bit? My brother reckons you lot love that. He had a knee done and they still—
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pupils are equal and they react to light. No double vision looking side to side. Grip's strong, both hands.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): See? I'm fine.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Legs push off normally. Finger to nose is accurate. Reflexes are normal. Neck's supple, no stiffness there.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's not a tumour? I googled morning headaches and it all went a bit—
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I didn't say that. Pattern's changed, worse on waking, vomited twice. Could still be migraine, possibly medication overuse, but I can't exclude something intracranial.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So you're booking a scan?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the morning headaches or the vomiting are still going in two weeks, I'll organise a CT of the head.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. What do I do till then? Because the Panadol's just sitting in the—
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cut sumatriptan to no more than two days in a week. Paracetamol, two tablets, maximum four times a day. And I want you back here in two weeks regardless.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if it's settled by then?
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Two weeks, and reception will book it. If you get weakness, confusion, a sudden thunderclap headache, or vomiting you can't keep fluids down, go to emergency. Don't wait for me.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright. I'll tell her to ease up about the snoring. She's been winding me up all—
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. We're done.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Doctor. They're in room two. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-two.
[SEG0002] person_1 (NURSE): He says the headache is already there this morning. I didn't take a temperature.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Come in, both of you, sit, sit. I'm glad you battled through the traffic to get here.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me, in your own words, what's been happening.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Um. I don't know, doctor. The headaches have been with me for years, maybe five, maybe longer, but it's different now. Mornings are the worst.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Shame, he's really not himself. The morning ones have been this bad for about three weeks. He snores like a tractor all night, and then he's half asleep at work.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag, I don't snore. And I'm not tired. She worries too much. The head just wakes me, that's all.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. How has the morning pain been feeling, when it's there?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): I get sick with it. Properly sick, not just a bit off.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sick as in you've actually vomited?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja. Not every morning. A few times. I don't know when that started, doctor, I really don't.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): And the bad mornings are longer than three weeks. Heavy, right behind the eyes. It was already like that before we went to the coast. Two months? I don't know.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm telling you, three weeks. He only started going on about it after my sister's birthday.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll hold both versions for now. The older headaches, over the years, did someone call those migraines?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, the other doctor said migraine. The light bothers me and I have to lie in a dark room. These morning ones aren't quite the same.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And day to day, how has this been sitting with you?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): The load shedding is what's getting me, hey. The neighbour's generator runs half the night and the bakkie deliveries are all behind.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often are you taking something for the pain?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Two Panados. They take the edge off, then by lunch it's sitting there again.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most days, or only now and then?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Most mornings. Two tablets. Not twice a day, if she's been saying that she's exaggerating.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does take another two after work. And those white tablets in the green box from the chemist, I don't even know the name.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the Imigran. I don't take that every day, only for the old migraine. The strength, I think it's fifty milligrams, or maybe a hundred. I don't know, doctor, the box is at home.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you take the Imigran the way it was intended, right when the attack starts?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I forget, and then I take it late.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And when the Panado runs out he uses Grandpa powders. I saw that last week.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you using the Grandpa as well?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Only if the Panado's finished. Once last week, I think. I don't know.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with all of this?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No fever.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fits, or blackouts, even a short one?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I would remember.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about weakness, or numbness, in the arms or the legs?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Work's been hectic, doctor. I don't even know if the boss believes I'm sick, with all the deliveries piling up.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm, we'll leave work there. Any blurring, or seeing double?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I won't push the eye question. I'm just going to have a quick look at the nerves.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Follow my finger. Pupils are equal, and they both react to light. There's no droop of the face.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Squeeze my fingers. Power is good in both hands. Push the legs up against my hand. Strong, both sides.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now touch your nose, then my finger. That's smooth. Your neck isn't stiff.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Is it bad, doctor? I don't know what you're finding.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm just checking. Nothing on the examination is worrying me.
[SEG0043] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): But the snoring, and him being tired all day, you're leaving that?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm not tired. I told you. The head wakes me, I get up, I drive. That's the whole story.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I hear both of you. Snoring and sleepiness can matter, but you don't feel tired, so I'm not going to hang a label on it today.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working thought is that the old migraine may be changing its pattern. Morning pain with vomiting can also mean a pressure problem, and I can't rule that out from this visit.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): A pressure problem? I don't know, doctor. Like a tumour?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not saying a tumour. Most of this still sits with migraine, but this new morning pattern deserves respect.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the Imigran for a clear migraine attack only, not as a morning tablet. And ease off the Panado every day, because a daily habit can feed the headache.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): So I just stop? I don't know if I can do the mornings without them.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not cold turkey. Use them when it's truly sore, not automatically with the coffee. And the Grandpa counts as the same pain medicine, not a free extra.
[SEG0052] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What about a scan? I told him ages ago we should ask.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the early-morning headache and the vomiting are still there when I see you again, I'll arrange a CT scan of the head. Not today. Only if it hasn't settled.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks either way. If you get a sudden worst headache of your life, weakness, or you can't stay awake, go straight to casualty and don't wait for me.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay. I don't know if it'll be gone by then, doctor.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to lean in. Must I book that two-week visit?
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes please, two weeks, and no scan form for now.
[SEG0058] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put it in the book before you go. We'll leave the blood pressure as it is.
[SEG0059] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. I'll make sure he pitches up, even if he says he's fine.
[SEG0060] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag, I'll come. I just hope it's nothing. That generator was going again last night, but that's another story.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): alright, before the doctor comes in I'm just gonna check your pressure. arm out for me, palm up.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): oh yeah sure, of course. I rolled the sleeve in the waiting room already, these offices are always chilly so my hands get cold, hope that doesn't throw the number off.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): you're fine. 128 over 78, pulse 76, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): 128, okay. the pharmacy machine said something like 150 over whatever last spring when I was late, but that was months ago and I don't count it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): mm. he'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll sit over here, I drove her. her husband's pills are in a different bag so nobody mixes them, he takes metformin, a thousand milligrams, and those aren't hers.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): hey, I'm Dr. Patel. what's been going on.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): well, um, it's my stomach. err, I've been getting these cramps low down and they ease off once I pass stool, plus the bloating, and my bowels have been switching around for about a year.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): okay, let me get that. cramps that settle after a bowel movement, bloating, bowels changing for about a year. what does the switching actually look like.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): so some days I'm constipated, I sit there and nothing happens. then other days it's loose and kind of urgent, I have to find a bathroom, and it goes back and forth. I even keep a note in my phone, not perfect, but most weeks I write something down.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): she's been on about it at home since last year, yeah. and she skips lunch when the meetings stack up.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): any blood in the stool?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): no. no blood. I check, I know it's not pleasant, but I look pretty much every time, and I have not seen blood on the paper or in the bowl.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): have you lost any weight?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): no, I haven't lost weight. the scale at home is the same, I weigh myself Sunday mornings, and the number hasn't dropped. the jeans feel tight when I'm bloated but that's the bloat, not a real change on the scale.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): alright, no blood and no weight loss. how often are the cramps, and where do you feel them.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): most days, uh, five days a week, especially after lunch. they sit low, both sides but more the left, and once I go they fade. not sharp like a knife, more a crampy squeeze that kind of rolls.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): and the bloating, what sets that off.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): stress, honestly, and big meals. work has been a lot, I'm a project coordinator at a logistics company and the deadlines pile up, and when I'm stressed the bloating gets worse. I skip lunch when meetings run long and then I eat a huge one, which doesn't help. I don't smoke, and I'll have a glass of wine on a weekend sometimes, that's it.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): so work stress and large meals make the bloating worse, and lunch is hit or miss. are you taking anything for the bowels?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): umm, myralax, the powder. one cap in water, a couple times a week, only when I can't go, not every day. I tried imodium once when it was loose and it bunged me up, so I left that alone.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): one cap of MiraLAX a couple times a week for constipation, and you stopped the Imodium after a single try. any other medicines that are actually yours?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): no, that's the only thing I take. my sister keeps telling me to try biotin, she takes 5000 micrograms, those gummies, for her hair. I don't take biotin, that's her thing, not mine, even though she texts me about it constantly.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): biotin stays your sister's. any drug reactions, anything you've ever reacted to?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): no, never. I have taken penicillin and everything. amoxicillin when I had strep a few years back, the whole course, and I was fine, no rash, no swelling, nothing.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): no reactions, including a penicillin-type antibiotic. outside the gut, any trouble with urination?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): no, peeing is totally normal. no burning, I go a regular amount, that's never been the problem, it's all the bowels and the cramping.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): okay. I'm going to feel your belly, if that's alright.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah go ahead. I had a bagel this morning so it might be a little full, sorry. the sore spot is usually the left lower bit, I can point if you need, it's about where my hand is now.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): soft. tender on the left lower side when I press. no guarding.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah that's the spot, that's exactly where the cramp sits. it eases when you let go, same as after I use the bathroom. I've poked it myself at home which probably isn't useful but it feels the same.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): she holds that left side in the car sometimes. I wasn't sure if I should even mention it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): it matches what I'm finding, so yes, worth saying. let me put it together. about a year of crampy lower pain that gets better after you pass stool, bloating worse with stress and big meals, constipation and loose stools alternating, no bleeding, no weight loss. this sounds like it could be irritable bowel, and that's my working impression, not a final label.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): irritable bowel, okay. I've read about that online at midnight, which I know is a bad idea, and some of it fit and some of it scared me. I wanted an actual person to say it instead of a webpage.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): understandable. I'm going to order bloodwork today, a blood count and a celiac screen, so we're not missing something that can look similar.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): blood count and the celiac one, okay. err, do I need to fast, because I already ate the bagel, and if I have to come back I can do tomorrow morning before work, I start at eight.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): no fasting for these. on food, smaller meals, add fiber gradually, not all at once, and keep that phone note going. ease off the huge lunches when you can.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): smaller meals, fiber slow, keep the note, I can do that. the fiber thing, like oats or a powder, because the powder makes me more gassy if I jump up too fast, I learned that in a meeting once, very embarrassing. so food first is better for me.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): food first, oats, fruit, not a big jump in any powder. we might do a ct scan of the belly if it does not settle. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): a scan only if it doesn't settle, okay. I'd rather not unless we need it, those machines make me a little claustrophobic if I'm honest. if you say later that we should, I will.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): let's see you back in two weeks with the blood results and the food note. reception can put that on the schedule on your way out.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): two weeks, yeah. I'll bring the note, and I'll try not to google the whole time. thanks, really, both of you.

[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What's brought you along today?
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah it's nothing really. The heel's a bit sore first thing, that's all. I'm only here because herself booked it.

[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Overdone it how? Tell me a bit more, in your own words.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Like there's a pebble stuck under the heel when I get out of the bed. Two steps of that and it's gone. It's two months, maybe. I couldn't tell you the date, sometime after the new year or before it, I've no notion.

[SEG0011] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he's still out running on it, which is pure mad, three times a week.

[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): New shoes in the mix at all?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeh, new runners. Fierce stiff. Got them, ah, I don't know when, a while back.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or pain shooting up the leg, or a sore back with it?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I can't hear myself think in the shop some days but that's the radio blasting, not me.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or did you twist it or stand on something?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever, no twist. I'm on my feet in the hardware shop all day, that's the job.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all, or take a drink?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Never smoked. A pint at the weekend, that's it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any medicines at the minute, or anything you've stopped?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): The odd ibuprofin. Four hundred, no wait, the two hundred milligram ones, one or two of them, when it's being a nuisance. Not every day. And I had that voltaral gel, gave it up, useless.

[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I had a bad do with penicillin myself years ago, but sure that's me, not him.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations in the past, or diabetes, that sort of thing?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No operations. No diabetes. Fit as anything.

[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Yerra I'll do them. Can we go, the shop's short today.

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): it's this rash, doctor, and she's been burning up. a boy in her class had measles and the school sent a letter.
[SEG0004] person_4 (PATIENT): good afternoon, doctor. i feel like a wet rag.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): shame. tell me about the rash. where did you first notice it?
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): on her face two days ago, and now it's down her chest and both arms. little red spots, some of them running into each other.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): and the fever, when did that—
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ag, sorry. the n1 was a proper mess, hey. we sat at that robot by the mall forever, the petrol light blinking, i thought the bakkie was going to die on us.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): ja, that stretch is awful this week. catch any of the cricket?
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): only a bit, on the radio. the proteas were batting and i lost the score completely. anyway.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): right. which day did she first feel hot?
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): umm. her granny phoned about the church fete, of all things. sorry, doctor.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): sorry. the fever, i really can't say which day it started. it just crept up.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): that's all right. any cough, a runny nose, anything with the eyes?
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): a cough for about three days, and she's sniffly. both eyes have gone red.
[SEG0016] person_4 (PATIENT): there is a frog in my throat, doctor. and my feet feel dead.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): mm. any vomiting?
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no. no vomiting, and she is still drinking.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): good. any diarrhoea? any trouble with her breathing?
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no, neither. no runs, and the breathing is fine.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): and otherwise, her tummy, passing water, any pains in the joints?
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no, nothing like that. she's normally well, apart from the eczema on her file.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): yes, the eczema, we'll leave that. any operations in the past? allergies to medicines or food?
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no operations. and no allergies, doctor.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): what have you been giving her for the fever?
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): paracetomol, the panado syrup. i nearly said ten mils, sorry, it's five mils on the syringe, every six hours since yesterday. umm i might have missed the night one, i'm not sure.
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): i can't hear myself think in that classroom, doctor. the children are very loud.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): classrooms get like that, hey. there's a red blotchy rash on the face, chest and arms, the eyes are pink and the throat is red. i don't see koplik spots. chest is clear, neck is soft, and the pulse is one hundred and twenty.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): about the jabs, doctor. she had the baby ones, but the measles, err, i'm not sure she got both doses. the card is in a drawer at home.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): bring the road to health card next time and we'll check it. counting the days, the rash for two days after being hot, plus that classmate, this could well be measles. i can't confirm it sitting here. it might still be some other viral rash.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): i'm sending blood today for a measles igm, and i must notify the health department. keep her at home, away from other children, for four days from when the rash started.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): carry on with the panado and plenty of fluids. i'll see you back in three days. if she turns drowsy or struggles to breathe, come straight back, don't wait.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): we will, doctor. thank you.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, the kidney bloods are up. Creatinine is 168, and the eGFR is down at 36.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Last year your one in the hospital said the kidney blood was borderline. I don't know if 36 is desperate, doctor.

[SEG0008] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He lives on his own. I call in the mornings and do the tablet box. The numbers do upset him.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. The tablets, what are you on? Slowly, I'm still catching the screen.
