[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Err I don't know, doctor. The white one.
[SEG0013] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Amlodipine 5 milligrams every morning. Metformin 500 with breakfast and with the tea. Ramipril 5 milligrams at night.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): And the cholesterol one at night. A small yellow yoke. I don't know the name of it, doctor.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yellow cholesterol tablet at night, name unknown. Any herbs, or stuff from the shop?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Only the ayurvedic powder in the morning. A spoon of it in the tea. My sister sends it over.
[SEG0017] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He's buying ibuprofin in the shop though. Two of the 400s when the knee is at him. I told him to leave them be.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Again, two of the what? The screen ate that.
[SEG0019] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Two 400 milligram ibuprofen. Most days, when the knee pains him. From the shop, not on a prescription.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): The knee is desperate, doctor. I'm after overdoing it in the garden, that's all. Sure I can't hear myself think with that radio outside.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Any chest pain?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I'm not breathless.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the ankles, any swelling?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are the bowels? And the waterworks?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Bowels are grand. I get up once in the night to pass water. I don't know, doctor, does that count?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Once is nothing unusual. How's the energy in yourself?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): I feel like a wet rag. No energy at all. And I've a frog in my throat this week, croaky as anything.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again. A frog in the throat?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Croaky all this week. And my feet feel dead, both of them, like they're not mine.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Numb, the two feet. How long would that be?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh I don't know, doctor. A long while. I can't give you a date.
[SEG0035] person_1 (CAREGIVER): First I heard of the feet. The ankles swell every evening though, I've seen them myself.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): You said no swelling a minute ago. Is it every evening or not?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Well actually they come up of an evening, like sausages. I put the feet up and it eases. I forgot, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm looking. Both ankles are puffy and the thumb leaves a little dent, mild enough. Blood pressure today is 146 over 82.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Is that the tablets doing it? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working impression is the shop ibuprofen is pulling the kidney function down, with the diabetes and the ramipril in the mix. Creatinine 168 and an eGFR of 36 would fit that. It's not confirmed.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): So do I stop the ramiprill?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Continue the ramipril, 5 milligrams at night. Stop the ibuprofen, nothing from the shop or the chemist, none of that family.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): What about the knee then, and the powder? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Start paracetamol, two 500 milligram tablets up to four times in the day. Leave the ayurvedic powder off, there's no telling what's in it. I'll book repeat creatinine and eGFR in two weeks, and I'll see you back in a fortnight.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): And if the knee is still desperate?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the paracetamol isn't holding the knee, we might do an x-ray. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0047] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Can I say, I'm not sure he takes the ramipril every night. Some mornings the tablet is still in the blister.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ramipril. Say that again?
[SEG0049] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He misses nights. I can't say he takes it the way it's written.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Most nights I do. Sometimes I forget. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Try for every night, the kidneys need it. If the ankles get worse or you get breathless before the fortnight, come back sooner.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand so. I'll do my best.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, sit yourself down. You look a bit washed out, so what's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm just wrecked. That's why I'm here. I can't even do the stairs at home without stopping halfway.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wrecked as in tired, or is the breathing the bit that's worrying you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The tiredness, mostly. I'm snapping at my flatmate over nothing. And yeah the stairs, one flight and I'm gasping.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you been this tired?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I keep eating ice. Like proper cubes out of the freezer, all evening. It's ridiculous, I know.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, the ice, we'll come back to that. The tiredness, how long is it actually going on?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I haven't a notion of the exact day. A couple of months, anyway. It just crept up.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the gasping on the stairs, did that come on around the same time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Flat ground I'm grand. On the stairs I have to stop and hold the rail, and it eases if I stand still a minute.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough with it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No cough.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had a fever?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I am freezing all the time though, even with the heating on I'm in a jumper.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight dropped at all?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Well, actually, I think it has a bit. My belt's on a tighter hole. I couldn't tell you how much, uh, I don't own a scales.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand, we won't hang anything on a number we haven't got. Your periods, are they heavy or all over the place?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): They're normal. Why, did someone say they weren't? Every twenty eight days, five days, not heavy, same as always.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nobody said a word. I'm only asking because heavy periods can leave you drained. The ice, then, how long have you been at that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks. Err, maybe three. I go through a whole tray a night. My flatmate thinks I've lost the plot.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you eat meat or fish at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm vegetarian, strict, six years now, no meat and no fish. Pasta, cheese, beans sometimes, and a fierce lot of tea.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets or vitamins on the go at the minute?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I got ferrous sulphait tablets from the chemist, uh, maybe 200 milligrams, once a day. I only lasted three days, my stomach was in bits, so I stopped. That was last month.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped completely? Nothing else, no iron water, no multivitamin?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else. And I'm not starting them again, they were brutal.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't push a tablet that turned your stomach, not before we know what we're at. Did the stomach settle once you stopped?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, grand after a day or two. Can we hurry this on, I'm on an early shift tomorrow and I'm wrecked sitting here.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep it moving. I'm just thinking out loud, err, tiredness, the ice craving, breathless on the stairs, strict vegetarian, it lines up with low iron. That's a working impression, not a fact yet.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm anaemic. Brilliant.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Maybe. I can't call it anaemia until the bloods are back. Low B12 can look similar enough if you don't eat meat, so I wouldn't rule that out either.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat cheese. Does that not cover it?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cheese has a little B12, not always enough, and it does nothing for the iron. Tea with your meals actually blocks the iron you do get from food. That's the bit I'd like you to change.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Change how. I'm not going back to meat, if that's where this is heading.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): You don't have to. Lentils, beans, the greens, have them with orange juice or a bit of fruit, and leave the tea for an hour either side of the meal.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Whatever.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a quick look at you before you head off. Sleeve up there, please.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is 112 over 70. Pulse is 98, a touch fast for sitting still. Oxygen is 99 percent.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 98 bad?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not dangerous, just quicker than I'd like in a young one at rest. The inner eyelids are pale. Chest is clear, no wheeze. Heart sounds are normal, I don't hear a murmur.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Pale. So it's the iron thing again.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): It fits, it doesn't prove it. I'll send bloods today, a full blood count, a ferritin, and B12 and folate as well.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Today? I have a bus to get.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Phlebotomy is just down the corridor, a few minutes and you're away. The results should be back for a visit in a fortnight.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Can you not just ring me?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd rather see you. Two weeks, here, and we'll go through the numbers properly. If you feel faint, or the breathing gets markedly worse before that, don't sit on it, come back or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Two weeks. And the tea thing.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Food first, and no new tablet from me today. If the ferritin is low we can talk about a gentler iron then, but I'm not starting one now.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. I'm going before I fall asleep on this chair.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Get the bloods done on your way out, and mind yourself on those stairs.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. I heard you the first time.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your sister's coconut oil stays out of Leo's plan. [SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. None that we know of.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, I'll mute this. Go ahead.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Temperature right now is ninety eight point six fahrenheit and his pulse is 92. Let me mirror the story so we're aligned. [SEG0038] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, that's the shape of it. What if the skin gets oozy or infected?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it oozes, the redness spreads, or he gets a fever, call the office. Otherwise I'll see him back in two weeks, just to look.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks? You promise it won't hurt? Can I still play soccer?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Promise, nothing we do today hurts, and soccer is okay. We'll check the patches in two weeks.

[SEG0001] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hello! This is Bella, she's six, and she gets tummy aches before school, every morning, and I'm at my wits' end.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello Bella. Can you tell me about your tummy? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It hurts. Here.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When does it hurt?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Not at school. ~
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She means weekdays, doctor. Monday to Friday, before school, then it goes by the time we get there, and she's running about by break.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): And on Saturdays and Sundays? ~
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Fine. Never a problem. ~
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bella, do you like school? ~
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. I love it. ~
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She says that, but she cries when I leave her at the gate, doctor.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't cry.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do, sweetheart, you cry every morning.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll write down that Bella says she doesn't cry and Mum says she does. Bella, is there anything about school that's difficult, or any person who's unkind?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No. ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does your tummy ever hurt when you do a poo, or when you eat? ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. ~
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her bowels are regular, and she eats breakfast, if she can. ~
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me feel your tummy, Bella. Lie back, it'll tickle. ~
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Hee hee.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Her tummy is soft, and there's no tenderness anywhere, even when I press deep.
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is it something physical? ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing here worries me. Children often get a real tummy ache in the morning when they're a bit anxious about separating from you, and it goes once they're distracted. ~
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I feel terrible. ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't. It's very common at this age, and it's not your fault. ~
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What can I do? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): A calm, consistent goodbye routine, and a firm, kind drop-off. Don't linger. And talk to her teacher so they can greet her at the gate.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I do linger. I give her a hundred cuddles. ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): One big cuddle, a quick wave, and off you go. ~
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Mummy, I'll be good. ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): You are good, Bella. And I'd like to arrange a urine test, just to rule out a simple infection that could be causing tummy aches.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. Can she do it here? ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, the nurse will give you a little pot. ~
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three weeks, to see how the mornings are going.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, I've got your obs. Blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse is 74. Your partner was filling me in out there while you were in the loo.

[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grab a seat. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my jaw. It hurts when I chew, like a deep ache, and it clicks. Right side mostly.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. When did the click start?
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, she got in first out there. She told me the clicking's been about three months, and that you've been getting headaches with it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months? No. Umm, the click started about three weeks ago, after that stupid deadline. And I haven't had headaches, she's the one with the migraines, she gets mixed up.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so I'm hearing three weeks from you and three months from her. I'll park the click as somewhere between three weeks and three months. You don't go along with the headache.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. The chewing pain, that's more like a fortnight. Toast is the worst, and it's heaps worse when I'm stressed, like this stocktake at the bookshop. On the weekend when I'm pottering it's milder.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the grinding, is that you noticing it or just her?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): She hears it at night, wakes her up. I'll give her that one, I do grind. I don't hear it myself, obviously.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and she keeps waving her metformin at me. Metforman, err, whatever, for her sugar, telling me to lay off the biscuits. I don't take any of her tablets.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's hers, we'll leave it right out of this. The stress and the clenching, that actually fits what the jaw joint does.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Work's been mad. We watched this terrible renovation show on the weekend too, I don't know why we bother with it. Anyway.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature, I feel fine in myself.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has your weight shifted at all lately?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't think so. Maybe I've been snacking a bit more, hard to say, the jeans still fit. I wouldn't call it a change. Or maybe a tiny bit, I dunno.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing chesty. Lungs are good.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you been using for the pain?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Nurofen. Four hundred milligrams when it's bad, maybe two or three times in a week, by mouth with food. My sister's mad on biotin gummies for her hair and she keeps offering them. I had one once to shut her up, did nothing, they're hers.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): So nurofen four hundred as you need it, not the biotin. Let me feel the joint.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Open slowly... yep, there's a click right over the joint on the right when you open, and the muscle here is tender. Left side is quiet, no click there.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the spot. Ow, sorry. She reckons I should give up crusty bread forever, she's dramatic.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking this is the jaw joint, the temporomandibular joint, stirred up by the clenching and the grinding. The click is the little disc in there slipping a bit as you open. I don't reckon it's an infection, not without a fever. That's a working impression, I haven't proved it on a picture.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I need a scan then? My uncle waited ages for a knee scan, totally different, I know, he still brings it up at Christmas.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't scan this now, a picture wouldn't change the first step. Soft foods for a couple of weeks, nothing chewy, and a mouth guard at night. Start with one from the chemist. If you want a fitted one later your dentist can make it, but I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Soft food, soup and eggs, I can do that. Will the guard make me dribble? Sorry, dumb question.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Most people settle with it after a few nights. Keep the nurofen as you have been, with food, and don't go over the packet dose. Try not to chew gum or pen lids, that loads the joint.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I do chew pen lids. Caught. Ok I'll stop.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back if it's not settling in about four weeks. Sooner if you can't open properly, or the pain goes sharp and constant.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks, yep. If I can't open I'll come in. Tell her the headaches were a false alarm, she'll hate being wrong.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you back out. I think she's still in the waiting room.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): And just so my note's straight, the click we're calling roughly three weeks to three months, and no headache as far as you're concerned. Look after the jaw.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Morning. It's these patches. Itchy ones, on my elbows and knees. I've had them a few months.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me more about them. What do they look like?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Red, with a silvery flaky bit on top. They look daft.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do they flake a lot?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Aye, I find bits in the bed. And they itch like mad, mainly at night.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you ever had anything like it before? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No. First time. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any changes to your nails, pitting, ridges, anything?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nails are fine.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And are your joints okay, any pain or stiffness, especially in the morning?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Joints are fine.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What work do you do?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a scaffolder. I'm outdoors most days, and gloves and knee pads, so the knees are rubbed a lot.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): That could be making them sorer. Let me have a look. Roll up your sleeve, and your trouser leg.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): There you go. ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. I'm not going to put a label on it today. I'd like to treat them first and see how they respond. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Fair enough. What's the treatment? ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to start you on a steroid cream, betamethasone, apply it to the patches once a day for two weeks, thinly.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Just to the patches? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just the patches, nowhere else. Wash your hands afterwards. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Does it stop the itch? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): It usually does within a few days. And I'd like to arrange a skin scraping from one patch, to make sure it's not a fungal infection.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): A scraping? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): A tiny bit of the flaky skin, painless. I'll do it now. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on then.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Done. You'll hear if anything shows. Moisturise every day, with a plain thick cream, even when they're better.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm not much for creams. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): It makes a big difference. Try it for a fortnight. ~
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. And if it doesn't work? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then come back and we'll think again. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm very sorry to be late, Doctor. The bus from Terenure was held up at Rathmines, and I do hate to keep you waiting.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand. Sit down. What brought you in?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): My neighbour was quite sure it was nothing and told me to stay at home. I nearly took her advice.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. What is actually the matter?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The room spins when I turn over in the bed, or when I look up. It only lasts a few seconds.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Since when?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, since last week. It began last Tuesday, as I was sitting up.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nausea with it?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. A wave of nausea each time. I have not vomited.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any hearing loss?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. My hearing is quite normal.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ear pain?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none at all.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I have not felt feverish.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cough, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Nothing of that sort.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight up or down?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm not altogether sure. Perhaps a pound or two lighter, but I haven't been on the scales.
[SEG0020] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry. Observations. Blood pressure 146 over 88, pulse 72.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Medicines on the chart?
[SEG0022] person_3 (NURSE): Uh, amlodopine, 10 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm afraid that is not correct. I take 5 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure. I have never been on the 10.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll not lock the dose in until the pharmacy checks it. Still taking it?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, every morning. I have had the high blood pressure for about five years.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. I'm not calling this Meniere's. Hearing is intact, the spins last seconds, and they come with turning in the bed or looking up. That is usually benign positional vertigo, a loose crystal in the ear. Vestibular migraine is still possible, but less likely.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I understand. Is it serious?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not this pattern. Positional test now. When I say, lie back quickly, head turned to the right.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now. There is a short burst of nystagmus to the right. It fades inside a minute. The left side is quiet.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): That was the very same spinning.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ears are clear. Drums look normal. No scan today.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): That is a relief. Thank you.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll teach you the Epley exercise. Do it at home twice a day until the spinning stops. Sit, turn the head, lie back, then roll onto the side. I'll write the steps for you.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Twice a day. Yes, I can do that.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sleep propped up for two nights. Don't drive if a spin comes on. Come back in three weeks.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): I shall book it. Thank you for seeing me, and sorry again for the delay.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not a bother. Reception will put you in for the three weeks.

[SEG0054] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll talk it over at home. He hates the idea of a needle, but the stairs are the real problem.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the pain is no better in six weeks, come back to me and we'll pick one. Mind the stairs in the meantime, one step at a time.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, sorry we're late. The car park was an absolute shocker and she wouldn't undo her seatbelt.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No worries, you're here. Come and sit. How old are you, love?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Five. Um. Are we in trouble for being late?
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's just turned five. Wound up all morning, sorry about that.
[SEG0005] person_4 (NURSE): Got the obs while you were coming through. Temp's thirty six point seven, pulse a hundred and eight, sats ninety eight percent, blood pressure ninety six over sixty two. Wriggly, but the numbers are decent.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, all of that looks fine. Mia, what's been bothering you?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): The car was hot. And I don't like those chairs.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): They are a bit scratchy, hey. Is it just the chairs, or is something else itchy?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): My knees are itchy.
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, that's why we're here. Itchy dry patches behind both knees and in the elbow creases. She's scratching them raw, worse at night, and it wakes her up.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's this been going?
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Six weeks. It faded for a couple of days, then came straight back.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): It wakes me up. I scratch and scratch. Will I have to have a needle? Is that bad?
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): No needle today, promise, and it's a nuisance not an emergency. Mum, any weeping, or yellow crusts on the patches?
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Mostly just dry and she picks at it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I won't call that an infection. Any cough, or trouble with her breathing?
[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough. Breathing's been fine, she was tearing around the park yesterday.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone at home with asthma, or eczema?
[SEG0019] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her dad's had asthma since he was a kid. I get a bit of hay fever in spring, nothing else.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): So will I get daddy's asthma? Is the itchy thing forever?
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not automatically, sweetheart. They can run in families, but lots of kids only get the skin part. What creams have you been using?
[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A big white tub a few times a day, and a little yellow tube at night that the chemist gave us. I can never remember the names, we just go by the colour.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know if the yellow one was a steroid?
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, someone said hydrocortazone, the one percent one, but I wouldn't swear to it. Might be wrong.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): The yellow one stings a bit. Do I have to keep using it? What if it stings worse?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): We can stop anything that stings. Any allergies to creams or medicines?
[SEG0027] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing like that. She's never reacted to a medicine.
[SEG0028] person_4 (NURSE): She was picking at both elbows in the waiting room. I left the skin alone, didn't put anything on.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good to know. Mia, can I have a look at your knees and elbows? I won't do anything that hurts.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Ok. But will it hurt? I don't want it to hurt.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just eyes, no poking. Skin behind both knees and both elbow creases is dry and a bit thickened, with scratch marks. No weeping, and it's not hot.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I look weird? Are they gonna laugh at me at kindy?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): You don't look weird at all. From those dry itchy patches in the creases, I'd call this eczema, atopic dermatitis. That's my working impression, not a final stamp.
[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. So do we chuck the yellow tube? And is the white tub even doing anything? Google's been no help.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the yellow tube, and stop the white tub too, we don't know what's in it. I'll prescribe methylprednisolone aceponate ointment, zero point one percent, that's Advantan, a thin layer once a day on the patches only, for two weeks. And QV cream, the plain moisturiser, at least three times a day, plus straight after a bath. Steroid first, give it a minute, then the QV.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Three times? That's heaps. Will the new cream sting me?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ointment's usually kinder on cracked skin than a cream is. Thin smear only. If a patch gets redder, or hot, or starts weeping, stop and ring the clinic.
[SEG0038] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Baths though? A mum at playgroup reckons no soap and oats in the water. Is that actually right?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short lukewarm baths are fine. No soap on the sore patches, pat dry, moisturise straight away. Oats are optional, not the treatment, and please don't put the steroid on her face.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Can I still swim? What if the pool makes it bad?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Swimming's fine. Rinse the chlorine off and put the moisturiser on after, or the skin will dry out.
[SEG0042] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should we do a blood test, or those allergy pricks? Her cousin had the whole lot.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the patches aren't settling after the two weeks of ointment, we can look at allergy testing then. No pricks this visit.
[SEG0044] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And follow up, do we come back only if it's worse?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks either way so I can check the skin. Reception will book it as you leave.
[SEG0046] person_4 (NURSE): I'll walk you out and get that two week review in the book. You were brave, Mia.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Ok. Bye. It still itches.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Alright, I weighed him just now. Seven point six pounds, heart rate a hundred and forty-two. He stayed pretty calm.

[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): How was the drive? I was stuck past the mall forever, rain coming sideways, and my defroster is basically decorative.
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Quite slow, I'm afraid. We sat at the river bridge nearly twenty minutes with the windshield completely fogged. I apologize if that put us behind.
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My husband argued for the back roads, and I overruled him, which was foolish. He is home with the dog, who has taken up residence in the laundry basket.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ha, the laundry basket always wins. I'm Dr. Ellison, by the way. This rain is meant to sit all weekend, just gray and heavy.
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. My mother will not stop texting about her tomato plants drowning. I told her the tomatoes can wait.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): They can. So, what brought you in with him today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His skin has gone yellow. That is why we came.
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Mm.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yellow. When did you first notice it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. I cannot really date it. It crept up on us, maybe a few days, but I am not certain.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright. A lot of this age is hard to date. How have the feeds been?
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He takes the breast, and we give formula too. I nearly said every three hours, well, actually it is every four. The nursery doctor also said he has eczema on his cheeks.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eczema, okay, noted. Is he hard to wake for a feed?
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He wakes quite reliably on his own.
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): Ah.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not really.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): And diarrhea?
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Never.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): With the eczema, does the skin weep or ooze?
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not that either.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does he seem itchy? Scratching at the cheeks?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No... well, sometimes he rubs his cheek against my shoulder.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sometimes, then. Any cough, or breathing that seems too fast?
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Not the cough, and not the fast breathing either.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does his belly hurt him, do you think?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, he is not in pain.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Looking at digestion more broadly, anything else with his belly that worries you?
[SEG0033] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing else there.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have the wet diapers dropped off?
[SEG0035] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. My sister's boy was yellow last spring, and she still texts me at odd hours about those blue lights. He's chubby now, so, uh, that's her story, not advice.
[SEG0037] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Of course. Thank you, that is kind to mention.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any medicines at home?
[SEG0039] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, Doctor. We give d-vysol, vitamin d drops, four hundred units once a day by mouth. Err, I think we missed yesterday. The bottle stayed in the other bag.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Four hundred units a day, and yesterday is a maybe. Any allergies?
[SEG0041] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. None.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look him over. You can keep a hand on him.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): The eyes are yellow, and the color comes down across his chest and belly. Belly is soft, and I don't feel an enlarged liver.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): The soft spot is flat. He seems comfortable enough.
[SEG0045] person_4 (PATIENT): Uh.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): That yellow is bilirubin. At ten days the liver is still maturing, so pigment from old red cells builds up and stains the skin. Breast milk can slow the clearing a little. I think this is ordinary newborn jaundice.
[SEG0047] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I understand. I appreciate you explaining it plainly.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd like a blood test for bilirubin today, before you leave. The lab down the hall can draw it.
[SEG0049] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. Today is quite alright with us.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the level is high, we might start phototherapy. I won't decide that until we see the number.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Either way, I want to see him back in three days. We'll call you this afternoon with the result.
[SEG0052] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will be by the phone. Should feeding change at all?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the breast milk and the formula, and try not to go much past four hours. Wake him if you have to. Call or come sooner if he's hard to wake, if the yellow reaches his legs, or if the wet diapers thin out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Morning, doctor. Lovely to meet you.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, it's been about three months now. And pain at night when I lie on it, too.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How troublesome is it day to day?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Severe, really. I've also had an ache down the upper arm, for nearly five years. As for ache down the upper arm, I'd say a couple of times a week.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had difficulty combing your hair before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a similar thing about six months ago. It went away.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing like fever?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Not at all, no fever.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any neck pain, swelling or chest pain?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't had any of them.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the waterworks?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No changes there.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about smoking?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I've never touched a cigarette.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything you do to stay fit?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I do a yoga class on Thursdays.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your eating.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you on your own at home?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I live with my elderly mother.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm on metoprolol, 50 milligrams, twice a day. Simvastatin. I take it 20 milligrams, at night for my cholesterol.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I follow.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Clopidogrel, 75 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any health conditions I should have on record?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, high blood pressure. I've had high cholesterol for two years now. I didn't want to make a fuss, you know.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And besides that?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got gout. I've had heart disease, yes.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, high blood pressure and gout are known to us, good to have that clear. Anything surgical in your history?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Just a triple bypass, eight years ago.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me get the readings out of the way.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bear with me while this finishes...
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: pulse 64, blood pressure 119 over 74, temperature is 36.7 degrees, saturation 97 percent.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the area, I'll be gentle.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, raise your arm for me.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is pain when you lift the arm out to the side between about sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees, and the grip strength is normal.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, no problem.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, good, you can sit up again. Putting it all together, I think we're dealing with a rotator cuff tendon problem at this stage.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, what are the odds it's serious?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's a rotator cuff tendon problem, and we'll know more once the an ultrasound of the shoulder is back. Stop me if I've got anything wrong. You've had difficulty combing your hair for about three months, and no fever or chest pain.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): That's it, yes.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll request an ultrasound of the shoulder, it'll help with shoulder pain. I'll request a shoulder X-ray, it'll help with shoulder pain. For this, naproxen, 250 milligrams, twice a day with food, for one week. That should help with shoulder pain.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I carry on if I feel better?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the shoulder moving gently within comfort and avoid heavy overhead lifting. Please take the tablets with food so they don't upset your stomach.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay. Let's get you seen by physiotherapy, I'll arrange the letter.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Sure, where do I go?
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in four weeks. Right, that's the plan. Do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, thanks, take care.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Just get me the cream. I need to sleep.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Ready for you, doctor. I'll stay in case you need anything.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, thanks. Hi, how can I help today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Mainly wheezing. There's a couple of other things, but that's the main one.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): About... well, two days. And a sore chest from coughing, too. With sore chest from coughing, I'd say once or twice a day.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, and what about weight loss, ankle swelling or coughing up blood?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): I haven't had weight loss, ankle swelling or coughing up blood, no.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pins and needles or loss of strength anywhere?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing odd there.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me ask about allergies, anything at all?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't think I have any, no.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any long-term conditions?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I've got COPD.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, tell me your medicines, please.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): It's Tiotropium inhaler, once a day.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): I only drink at family occasions.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): How active are you?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): I hardly move around during the day.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you work outside the home?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm a hairdresser, on my feet all day.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): What operations have you had, if any?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Just part of my thyroid removed, years back.
[SEG0024] person_1 (NURSE): Okay, so the vitals from earlier. Pulse is 98 beats a minute, temperature is 37.6 degrees, oxygen saturation is 89 percent. Respiratory rate 21, blood pressure 141 over 90.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, noted.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll need to examine you for this, it won't take long.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm just checking this side.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): There are scattered wheezes on both sides and no crackles.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, so my impression is this: The most likely explanation is an infective exacerbation of chronic lung disease.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, is this serious, doctor?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with an infective exacerbation of chronic lung disease do well once it's treated properly. I'd like to arrange a sputum sample for purulent sputum. It's a routine test and it'll give us a much clearer picture.
[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, I did a chest X-ray before they came in, the result's on your screen.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that helps. Let's use doxycycline, 100 milligrams, twice a day, for five days. It's for chest infection. Keep using your inhaler as before and drink plenty of fluids. If you become more breathless or your lips turn blue, that's the point to come in urgently.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, uh, I know what to watch for.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's plan a check in two weeks. That's everything on my side. Anything you're unsure about?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Erm, good, thanks, I'll see you then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, sit him up there. What's the problem today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's his skin, doctor. The backs of the knees and the elbows, dry and itchy, and he's scratching the life out of himself at night.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah the itchy bits. They go all scratchy and I can't leave them, it feels like little ants walking under the skin when the light goes off, and I scratch and scratch even when mam says stop.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long is this spell?
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sure he's had the dry skin since he was a baby. This bad bit is about six weeks. Umm, maybe a bit more.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waking with it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah. He wakes himself scratching. The sheets are a state in the morning.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): And then in the morning I feel like a wet rag, all floppy and heavy, because I was scratching all night and I didn't really sleep, and school is hard when I'm sleepy, but the itchy bits are why we came, not the school, the school is grand mostly.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any oozing? Yellow crusts?
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No crusts. Just dry and red.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. He's grand in himself, apart from the itch.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wheeze? Any trouble with the breathing?
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, not a bother with the breathing. Himself, his dad, has the asthma. Finn doesn't.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tummy pain? Runny eyes?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. My tummy is fine, I had porridge and it was grand. I can't hear myself think when the telly is loud in the kitchen but that's just the telly, not a sore thing. And my eyes don't run, they just blink normal.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What creams are on him?
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A grand big white tub, no smell on it, the label's worn off so I couldn't tell you the name. And a little pink tube for the sore patches.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Name or strength on the pink one?
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I don't know it. The chemist just said use the pink one. We put it on the elbows and the backs of the knees.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): The white one is cold, I do it myself sometimes, two squirts, and I rub and rub till it's all gone in, and the pink one is only a tiny dot, mam does that because she says I've overdone it if I squeeze too much out.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often, the white tub?
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most days. Well, when I remember. Some mornings we're out the door and it doesn't get done.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the pink tube?
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The pink tube, once a night on the patches, these last few weeks. Not every single night, if I'm honest.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything by mouth for the itch?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We had cetirizene. I think it was 10 mg, no, he's small, it was the 5 mg, one at night. I stopped it in March. It made him dopey for school.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you were given and didn't use?
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, they gave us fucidin last winter for a spot on his chin and I never opened it. Never gave it to him.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies? Medicines or creams?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing that I know of.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Elbows up. Let me see.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dry thickened patches, both elbow creases and the backs of both knees. No ooze. Skin's not hot. No infection that I can see.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): They look like maps, all pinky and wrinkly, and when you press them it doesn't really hurt, it just itches after, like the ants come straight back, and the left knee is the worse one I think, or maybe the right, I forget which I scratch more.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is his eczema flaring. I'm changing the steroid.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the pink tube. I'll give you clobetasone, 0.05 percent, a thin layer twice a day on the patches only, for seven days, then stop it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a day, seven days, then stop. Grand.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep a plain moisturiser, lots of it, all over, three or four times a day. The white tub is fine if it's a plain one. Steroid on first, wait twenty minutes, then the moisturiser.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No soap in the bath. Nails short. Cotton at night.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. No soap, short nails, cotton.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Can I still have the blue bubbles? I like a big pile of them and then my skin goes all tight after, and mam says that's why the patches get cross with me, but the bubbles are the best bit of the bath.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No bubbles. They dry the skin.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll live. And if the seven days doesn't clear it?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it's not settling, or if it starts to weep, we might swab it then. Not today.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see him back in three weeks anyway.
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks. Do I book that at the desk?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Reception will put the three weeks in. If it weeps before that, ring us.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Will the ants go if I do the new cream and I don't scratch, because I try not to but then I forget and I do it in my sleep and I wake up and the skin is sore from me, and I don't mean to, it just happens.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): The itch should ease. Hands off it if you can.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks, doctor. Seven days of the new one, the white tub, and back in three weeks.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Off you go.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): hello, sorry about the delay, do sit
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Hello. I hope I'm not late.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, um, I'll sit in if that's okay, I know what's been happening.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please do. Extra information is always welcome. Tell me what's brought you in.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We came cos of a chronic cough with lots of phlegm.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was the first time you noticed it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): about three weeks, give or take
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was closer to a month, doctor.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, so roughly three to four weeks. Is that right?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, somewhere around that.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It's severe, honestly. It happens on and off. I'm hoping you can tell me something definite.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): and the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): So, tell the doctor about the other thing, that's what worries me.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I was getting to that! I've also been getting out of breath. I've also had green phlegm lately, since yesterday.
[SEG0016] person_4 (UNKNOWN): Yes, that's right, that's how it was.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you got any known allergies?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I've never had an allergy.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hold on, doctor, I think she reacted to naproxen once. I'm not certain, though.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember that
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, so that's unclear. I'll record what each of you said. Have you been to theatre before?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I had keyhole surgery on my gallbladder, two years back.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's on your current medicine list?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I take omeprazole, 20 milligrams, once a day. I take hydrocortisone cream, when needed.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What conditions have you been treated for in the past?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): yes, migraines. I looked a few things up online, and that probably didn't help
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, acid reflux. I kept putting it it off, which I know isn't sensible.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): is that everything?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Eczema, for five years. My neighbour said I should get it looked at. I didn't want to make a fuss, you know. I've had depression, yes.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, right. Okay, I can see acid reflux and eczema in your file as well. Has anyone in your family had anything serious?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): My aunt has rheumatoid arthritis.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I used to drink heavily but I stopped four years ago.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything you do to stay fit?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I do a yoga class on Thursdays.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you work outside the home?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm a hairdresser, on my feet all day
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain or coughing up blood?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no chest pain, no coughing up blood. I did have tiredness at one point, but that went away on its own.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead. Have you noticed fever or weight loss?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): no, none that I've noticed
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): what about your tummy and bowels, anything unusual there?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No, um, all normal there.
[SEG0045] person_5 (NURSE): Okay, so the vitals from earlier. Temperature 36.7, BP is 126 over 77, oxygen saturation is 97 percent, respiratory rate 18, pulse 65.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, noted.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you in a second, make yourself comfortable.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): let me feel here
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): There are coarse crackles at both bases and the fingers are slightly clubbed.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): thank you, you can get dressed
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): let me tell you where I've got to. It's hard to say. A flare of bronchiectasis is one possibility and a chest infection another, and I'd rather not commit yet
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Do you think it's something serious?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's reasonable to be concerned, but right now a flare of bronchiectasis is my leading thought, not anything worse.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's book a chest X-ray to to look into bronchiectasis flare.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, so how long will it take?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sending you for a sputum culture cos of purulent sputum we'll begin with clarithromycin, 500 milligrams, twice a day, fourteen days that should help with bronchiectasis flare keep up your airway clearance exercises twice a day let's get you seen by the the respiratory clinic, I'll arrange the letter please don't wait if the symptoms get worse that's when to be seen urgently let's plan a check in two weeks
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, that's all from me. Any questions?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, so alright, thanks, take care.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Look after yourself.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): The N3 was a car park this morning. Was it as bad coming in from your side?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I wasn't counting the cars. I'm on my lunch, can we start.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Go on then. What's brought you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The hand goes dead on me at night. And I dropped a cup this morning, smashed it all over the kitchen. That's the reason I'm here.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dead, as in numb, or is it sore?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Numb. Umm, pins and needles in the thumb, the index and the middle finger, right hand mostly, and the left only if I lie on it. It's been about four months, since February.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waking you from sleep?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Every night nearly, two or three in the morning. I have to shake the hand to get it going again. I barely sleep and I'm wrecked the next day, so don't tell me I look tired.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't. The cup, is the grip going in the daytime as well?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Well actually the phone as well, a mug at the desk yesterday, and the cup this morning. The grip just goes and the thing is on the floor.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the hand with it, or only the numb feeling?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. Just dead and tingly. I already said numb.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry. Pain in the neck, or does it shoot down from the neck?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neck's grand.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any numbness in the feet?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Feet are fine.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath, or chest tightness when you're walking about?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I'm not here about my chest.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Give me the ordinary life in one go, would you, the job, the hours, the food, exercise, drink.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm in the office at the furniture factory in Navan, accounts, on the computer the whole day, hours half seven till half four, five days, and the odd Saturday if the invoices pile up. Diet is sandwiches at the desk and a takeaway most evenings, and a fry on the Sunday, and I don't exercise, the walk from the car park is the height of it. Four or five pints of a Friday, well actually it's four, and I don't smoke. There, happy?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'll do. In the family, diabetes, blood pressure, heart trouble, any of that?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my other sister is grand, and another sister has pressure but no sugar. I haven't got sugar myself, if that's the next question. Can you look at the hand.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): In a second. What tablets are you on?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, two tablets, if the hand is at me in the morning, not every morning. I was on naproxin five hundred milligrams twice a day for the hand and I stopped it in March, it did nothing and it turned my stomach. Amitriptaline got mentioned and I never took it, not once.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol when you need it, naproxen stopped since March, amitriptyline never started. Any vitamin or blood pressure tablet hiding in the press?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. That's the lot. Are we examining or chatting.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Examining. Both hands on the desk.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): They're there. The right is the one, obviously.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thenar bulk is preserved both sides, no wasting. Grip is a little weaker on the right than the left.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): What's thenar even mean.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Err, pad of muscle under the thumb. It's not shrunk, that's the good bit. Tell me what you feel when I tap the right wrist.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's the buzz, yeah. Don't keep doing it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Positive Tinel's on the right. Left wrist, no tingle when I tap. Light touch is duller on the right thumb, index and middle finger than on the ring finger.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. I could have told you the fingers. Are you done.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Done with the hands, err, let me think this out loud. Little finger is spared so I'm not chasing the ulnar nerve, but night waking, the three fingers and the positive tap, my leading thought is the median nerve squeezed at the wrist, carpal tunnel, and I am not concluding it today. A root in the neck could still do this, and off sugars or a lazy thyroid can copy the whole picture. I will not put a final name on it yet.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): After all the poking you still don't know. For god's sake.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know what leads the list and what I won't cross off. Let's see what the tests say before anyone stamps it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. So what do I actually do.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Get a neutral wrist splint off the chemist and wear it on the right hand at night for the next two weeks. It stops the wrist folding up in your sleep. You can still shake it out if it goes dead, but the splint is the thing that might settle it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): A splint in the bed. I'll look an eejit. The invoices won't do themselves either if I'm messing about with appointments.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): The lads don't need to see it, it's for the night. Bloods are booked, not a maybe. The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, fasting glucose and a thyroid test. Nothing but water from midnight, in at half 8, and you eat straight after.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday, half 8, fasting. I'll tell them at the office. This is eating my week.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, the B12. I'm not booking that unless they come back borderline.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): And the nerve test, is that today or what. Someone said nerves.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it does not settle with the splint, then we do nerve conduction studies. Conditional, not arranged.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it's the neck you were on about?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it does not settle, a scan of the neck, only in that case. I'll see you in two weeks with the bloods either way, that visit is booked.

[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had a blocked nose before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): I, I had a similar thing a couple of years ago. It went away.

[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, joints are fine.

[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.

[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I have thin bones, for nearly five years.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sure.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, heart failure, that matches what I have here. Right, are you allergic to anything? Any allergies to medicines or foods? Just so I get the full picture.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): I've never had an allergy.

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, that's all I needed to check.

[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, I'll look out for that.

[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Look after yourself.

[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Confused, the once. It cleared.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Once.

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning. Fasting from midnight, and don't take the morning gliclazide till after the bloods and you've had the breakfast. We'll do a fasting glucose and the hba1c.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in two weeks with the results. Eat the breakfast every morning, don't be skipping it, and take the gliclazide with the food.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ms. Harlan, come on in and have a seat. What brings you by?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, hi. Um, I'm just exhausted. And cold, cold in my bones, even with the thermostat sitting on seventy-two. It's been going on for months.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Months is a big range. Closer to two, or more like half a year?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I almost said since Christmas, but no, it started before that. Fall. I keep pinning it on work. I'm fifty-two and the office has been a complete circus.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Dana, I live in the spare room and help with the house. She's been dragging since September, easy. Gets home, drops the bag, and just sits.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Appreciate that, Dana. So tired and cold since the fall. What else have you noticed?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The weight. I've put weight on, my work pants won't button. And, this is kind of gross, I'm constipated.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not gross at all. About how much weight, and what's the bowel pattern?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe twelve pounds. I didn't exactly weigh myself. I go every three or four days now, hard stools. I used to go every morning.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been safety-pinning the waistband. That's new for her.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's your mood been with all this?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I don't cry or anything, I just don't care about stuff I liked. I figured that's the job and getting older, you know?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any hair loss, dry skin, a lump in the neck, or changes with your periods?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Periods stopped a couple years ago, menopause. Skin's dry, yeah. No lump. Hair's thinner, though I color it, so it's tricky to judge.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or feeling like you might pass out?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She nods off on the couch after dinner. She never used to.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): That's true. Oh, and my mom had thyroid trouble. Took a pill for it her whole life. They checked mine once and it was borderline, they said.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline. Any sense of when that was, or what the number was?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I want to say two years ago? No number stuck. They said borderline and left it. I never started a thyroid medicine.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): I had the old note up. March of twenty twenty-three, the TSH was normal. It wasn't marked borderline. So the chart and what you remember don't line up.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Huh. I would've sworn they said borderline. Anyway.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her sister sent iron tablets in the spring. Bottle's still sealed in the cabinet. She never took a single one.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the iron was never taken.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Right, never. The senna I did use, one tablet at night for the constipation. I stopped it in March because it was cramping me up.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Senna, one tablet at night, stopped in March. Anything you take now? Any allergies, to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Just a multivitamin, one a day. No allergies that I know of. Oh my gosh, though, the drive over was ridiculous.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): We sat on the bridge forty minutes, and a guy in a pickup had the country station so loud the windows buzzed. Then a huge flock of geese went over, hundreds of them, heading south.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Made me think of my granddaughter's school play last month. She was a tree, construction-paper leaves and everything. I teared up, the happy kind. Sorry, I wander off.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Paper leaves in the cup holder for a week. Weather's been the same way, coat on, coat off.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): No harm done, geese aside. You've been tired and cold since the fall, up about twelve pounds, with hard stools every three or four days, a flat mood, dry skin, thinner hair, and naps after supper. Your mother had thyroid disease, the twenty twenty-three TSH was normal on the chart, and you never started thyroid medicine or the iron. Senna stopped in March, you take a multivitamin daily, and you have no allergies.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's the picture. I still think it's just the job and my age, though.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Work and age can absolutely wear you down. I'm also thinking this could be an underactive thyroid, and I'd rather check than guess. I want a TSH, a free T4, a blood count, and a basic metabolic panel.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Can they stick me today?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the lab has a slot when we're done, yes, otherwise tomorrow morning. You don't need to fast. Coming before breakfast is fine if it's easy, not a requirement.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I start the senna again, and when am I supposed to come back?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't restart the senna. If the constipation is really bothering you before the labs are back, psyllium once a day is fine to try on your own, and I'm not prescribing it. Ease up at work a little this month if you can, and I'll see you in two weeks for the results either way. Call sooner if you get chest pain, if you start vomiting with the constipation, or if you feel markedly worse.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, got it. I'll try to leave the geese out of it next time.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning, Mr Brennan. I'll take your readings before the doctor sees you. Sleeve up there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, yeah. I was ages in the waiting room. Nearly nodded off.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Blood pressure is 138 over 82. Pulse 74. Oxygen is 96 percent on room air.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. That finger yoke always feels odd. Grand so.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): All done. Doctor will call you in a second. Have a seat.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr Brennan. What brought you in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the cough, doctor. Well, actually it's every morning. I wake up coughing. The wife said I was to stop ignoring it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been there.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Years. Five years easy, maybe longer. I couldn't put a date on when it actually started, to be honest.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Phlegm.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Brown phlegm. Well, actually it's a dirty brown, not bright or anything. Most mornings, and not a lot of it.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blood in it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I'd have come in a lot sooner if there was.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. None.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short of breath.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): A wee bit if I'm hurrying on the stairs. Not when I'm sitting. I can still walk the dog grand.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Weight's been steady. Same belt hole as last year. The good trousers still fit.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever or night sweats.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neither of those.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Not anymore. I quit last year, around Paddy's day, so March. Twenty a day before that, for about thirty years. The lads gave me fierce stick over quitting.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah sure speaking of the lads, the grandson had a hurling match on Sunday out in Kilmacud.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The weather was wicked. Horizontal rain. We were soaked on the sideline, the whole lot of us.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the M50 on the way home was a car park. An hour, easy. He's only seven and he still got a score. Chips after, the car all steamed up, and he was delighted with himself.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): The cough.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. I do go on. Yeah, the cough.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril, 5 milligrams, one tablet every morning, for the blood pressure. Been on it a few years. And I had the brown inhaler, beclamethasone, two puffs twice a day, but I stopped it in March.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Beclometasone. Stopped in March. Not using it now.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Not a puff since. Once I was off the cigarettes I thought I was grand. Oh, the chemist handed me amoxicillin last winter for a cold. I never took it, the box is still in the press.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit of a wheeze in the morning, yeah, with the cough. It eases once I'm up and moving.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bowels or waterworks.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No, they're grand. No trouble there at all.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to the chest. Deep breaths.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Your hands are freezing, doctor, I'll tell you that for nothing.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Expansion is equal. Breath sounds reduced at both bases. A few crackles, they clear when you cough. No wheeze just now.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Crackles. That sounds worse than it feels, to be honest.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm calling it chronic bronchitis for now. COPD is still possible with that smoking history. Spirometry will sort which.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): COPD. God. That's what the neighbour has, and he's forever at the clinic.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm booking spirometry for Thursday week, to see if this is COPD.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday week. Do I have to do anything special for it.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): No inhaler the morning of the test. Get the flu vaccine and the pneumococcal vaccine. Stay off the cigarettes. Come back in three weeks.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): The jabs. I keep putting them off. The chemist on the corner does the flu one anyway. Three weeks, right.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Three weeks. We'll go through the result then.
[SEG0048] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I have the spirometry down for Thursday week, and your review in three weeks. Thursday morning for the test, is that alright.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday morning is grand. Nothing else on, unless there's hurling, and I'll shift that.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's everything from me.
[SEG0051] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): You're booked in. The slip will be at the desk on your way out.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Lovely. Mind yourselves. That rain is not letting up.

[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anything else changed down there over those months? Any other symptoms you've noticed?

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very useful to know. So the dryness is constant, and the pain with intercourse comes on at the start and lingers a little afterwards.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, that's exactly what it's like.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for telling me, I know that wasn't easy. Now, let me ask about your general health. Any long-term conditions I should know about?

[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the only one. I'd know, I do the pill organiser.

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now, with your permission, I'd like to examine you gently. Dilys, would you mind passing me that curtain?
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Of course, doctor.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Seun, that's all done and you can get dressed. The skin around the opening is thin and pale, and it looks dry, with a little redness but no sores or lumps.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it something serious? I was so worried it might be something nasty.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't see anything that worries me. Honestly, what you describe, together with the dryness and given your age, most likely points to thinning and dryness of the tissues from lack of oestrogen.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): So it's the change, even this long after?

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. In the meantime, go slowly, take your time and stop if it hurts, there's no pressure to try at all.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): My husband is very understanding. It's me that's been... avoiding it.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very common, and nothing to feel guilty about.
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And if it's still sore, doctor?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't eased within a month, come back and see me and we'll go through the choices properly.

[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Wonderful. Thank you both for being so open with me today.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. That's a weight off.
