[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good afternoon, how are you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, I'm just here to help with the details.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, that'll be useful. Pull up a chair. Start wherever you like, I'm listening.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): I mean, honestly, it's sore knees, and my family pushed me to come.
[SEG0005] person_4 (NURSE): Okay, so the vitals from earlier. Weight 80 kilos, height 162 centimetres, pulse 74, temperature 36.7, blood pressure 152 over 97.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you. Can you tell me when it first started?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Erm, I'd say three days, maybe.
[SEG0008] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hm, I'd say more like five days.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, so roughly three to five days. Is that right?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): So, you know, yes, somewhere around that.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often do you get it?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): It happens a few times a day.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): And, And the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Erm, tell the doctor about the other thing, that's what worries me.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Erm, I was getting to that! Let me think, and I've been snoring as well.
[SEG0016] person_5 (UNKNOWN): Yes, exactly like that.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): A few quick ones: chest pain, low mood or high thirst?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah, no, no chest pain, no low mood, no high thirst. I was putting on weight over the years at one point, but that went away on its own.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm, okay. Did you notice any palpitations?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Not at all, no palpitations.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the waterworks?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing there, no.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, any change in your bowel habit or your stomach generally?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing unusual, no.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything in your past medical history I should know?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): I've got high blood pressure. My neighbour said I should get it looked at. I didn't want to bother you but it keeps coming back.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): I've got thin bones.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): I've had an irregular heartbeat, yes. High cholesterol, for nearly five years. I've been reading about it online and it worried me. Work has been very busy so I kept ignoring it.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, what else?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): I have an underactive thyroid.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I follow. Okay, I can see thin bones and an irregular heartbeat in your file as well. Does your family have any medical conditions?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh, um, my grandmother had dementia.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you allergic to anything? Any allergies to medicines or foods?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, no, not that I know of.
[SEG0037] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Actually, I remember she had some kind of reaction to diclofenac before. I couldn't swear to it.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't remember that.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll note both of those. Are you taking anything regularly, including from the pharmacy?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): I take amlodipine, 5 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Roughly how long on that one?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): For nearly five years. It's alendronate, 70 milligrams, once a week for my bones.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Roughly how long on that one?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): About about three months. It's bisoprolol, 2.5 milligrams, once a day for the heart rhythm.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): It's a... um, I can't remember what it's called. It's a small white one.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): For my cholesterol, I believe. My daughter sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's your work?
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm a plumber, lots of bending and kneeling.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold that for a second.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your weight and waist measurement are both above the healthy range.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): All finished, thank you.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, so my impression is this: This is probably obesity with weight-related symptoms. Another possibility is an underactive thyroid. Let's book a thyroid test to look into weight gain. I'm going to order a cholesterol test, for obesity. I'd rather check than guess, and this is the quickest way to know more. Aim for a loss of half a kilo a week with smaller portions and a daily thirty-minute walk.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think the weight management service should see you too.
[SEG0056] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright, thank you.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please don't wait if the symptoms get worse. That's when to be seen urgently. See me again in three months.
[SEG0058] person_3 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, good, I'll return then.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else on your mind before you go?
[SEG0060] person_3 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): come on in, either chair is fine. i'm doctor ellis. that hallway is a maze, huh?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): uh, yeah. i almost bailed in the parking lot. my sister's the one who wanted this.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): because you promised, after my endo appointment. i'm jenna.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): glad you both made it. what's been going on, from your side?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): it's not a big thing. i've lost a bit of weight and my heart speeds up sometimes. she panicked 'cause of her thyroid, not 'cause i'm sick.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): okay. walk me through the weight, however it looks to you.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): umm, maybe a month. and i eat more than usual, second helpings, so i'm not dieting or anything.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): a month? no. she's been dropping since april, that's three months, and the home scale said 128 this morning, down from 142.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): i'm not fighting the 128. the three months is her story, not mine.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): alright, i'll hold the weight change as roughly one to three months, since you're not landing in the same place. we can leave the exact start open.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she sweats through her shirt by lunch too. even at the library desk.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): okay, i sweat more than i used to. it's summer. can we not make it a whole thing?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): tell me about the fast heart. what does it feel like?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): pounding. comes and goes. the machine out front said 124 and everybody freaked. i was just sitting there.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): any chest pain with it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): no. none.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): shortness of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): mm. no, breathing's fine.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): her hands shake. her coffee was rippling this morning, i watched it.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): only a little, and only after coffee. it's not a disease.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): when did the pounding start? even a rough guess.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): err, i don't know. i can't put a date on it. it just showed up.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): and she sleeps badly. up at two, up again at four, i hear her.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): i do not. i sleep fine. you just wake up easy and blame me.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): so you two don't agree about the sleep. i'm leaving that one unsettled.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): oh, she sliced her thumb on a cat food lid last week. healed in five days. looked totally normal.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): any cuts that have been slow to heal?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): no. that one closed in five days. it was nothing.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): what medicines do you take? only yours, not someone else's.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): um, sertraleen, fifty milligrams, every morning, for the anxiety. been a couple years.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she skips it on sundays. sunday in the pill box is always still full.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): no. saturdays. i miss saturdays when i'm off work. not sundays. she got the day wrong.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): fine, saturdays then. and just so it's not on her chart, the biotin gummies are mine for my hair, and my methimazole is for my graves'. she's never taken them.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): right, her thyroid, not mine. i don't take her stuff.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): good. biotin and methimazole stay jenna's. your anxiety has been going those couple of years, and the sertraline is every morning except the saturdays you forget.
[SEG0036] person_4 (NURSE): sorry, quick interrupt. i'm nia from triage. heart rate 124, blood pressure 132 over 78, temperature 98.4, oxygen 99 percent. that's the same 124 she saw out front.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): thanks. that lines up with what you said. hands out flat for me.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): they're gonna be normal.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): there is a fine tremor. your neck doesn't feel big. heart is regular, just fast. skin's warm and a little damp.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): any fever lately?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): no.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): besides the bigger appetite, anything with your stomach or bowels?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): no. bowels are normal.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): smoke at all? how about alcohol?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): never smoked. a beer on the weekend. coffee is three cups a day, well sometimes four, no, three.
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she works the desk at the county library. we also got lost in your parking garage, which i'm still mad about, but that's not why we're here.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): thinking out loud, the things on my list are an overactive thyroid, especially with jenna's graves' in the family, or anxiety breaking through the sertraline, or the coffee pushing your pulse. i am not going to conclude this is graves' today. i won't pick one of those until the tests come back.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): so i'm ordering a tsh, a free t4, and a cbc, plus an ecg before you leave today. those are set, not a maybe.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): front desk will book you back in two weeks for the results. try to ease off the extra coffee till then. if you get real chest pain or you pass out, go to the er instead of waiting.

[SEG0057] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, that's fine.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can sit up now.
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): Taking everything into account, my working impression is tonsillitis. I'd also keep a viral sore throat in mind.

[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like tonsillitis, but I'd like to confirm. Let's book a throat swab to look into recurrent tonsillitis. Plenty of fluids and soft foods, and he can return to school when the fever has gone.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't skip meals, and try to eat smaller portions more often through the day. I'm going to send a referral to the ENT clinic. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0063] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, I'll bear that in mind.
[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the symptoms get worse, or you feel really unwell, please come to the emergency department.
[SEG0065] person_4 (PATIENT): Um, I know what to watch for.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): See me again if recurrent, tonsil review. Does all of that make sense?
[SEG0067] person_4 (PATIENT): Okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're late. The dog got out, and then the ring road was an absolute car park.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, sit yourselves down. How are things generally?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Bit quiet, that's all. His brother Dave had a melanoma cut out last spring and it's been on our minds.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry about your brother. What did you want me to see today?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Mole.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Whereabouts?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Back.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which side?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Left.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Left shoulder blade. I've watched it for months. The colour's gone darker and blotchy, not the flat brown it was.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has it bled at all?
[SEG0013] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Once. In the shower, about 3 weeks back, just a spot.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Only the once?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any itching, or is it sore?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the mole on the left shoulder blade has gone darker and uneven, bled once about 3 weeks ago, not itchy, not sore. Fair?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the sun. Shocking burns in his twenties, Spain every summer, peeling for days.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Severe sunburns on holiday in your twenties. Do you still burn easily?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other moles worrying you?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Just this.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you date when the colour started changing?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. I couldn't put a date on it. Months, not years.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the start date open then. Err, nurse, have you the numbers?
[SEG0028] person_4 (NURSE): Blood pressure today is 152 over 88, and his weight is 94 kilos.
[SEG0029] person_4 (NURSE): Repeat script, Omprazole 20 milligrams for his acid, Metformine 500 twice a day for his sugar, and Mizartan 40 milligrams for the pressure.
[SEG0030] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mizartan isn't 40. He takes eighty. The chemist box says eighty.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Eighty.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): The list says 40 and you both say eighty, so I won't pin a dose on the Mizartan. The Metformine is for the diabetes and the Mizartan for the blood pressure, both ongoing?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been on the Metformine a couple of years. The Omprazole longer, for the acid.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else, a water tablet?
[SEG0036] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. The water tablet, little white one, every morning. I can never say the proper name.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can't name it?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Of. Just the water tablet.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No known allergies noted. Shirt up, I'll have a look.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Left scapula, a mole about eight millimetres, irregular edge, brown with a darker black patch, and a small crust.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is that the one you've been watching?
[SEG0045] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. It used to be smaller and all one colour.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so it has changed in colour and in size, it bled once, and today the edge is irregular with two colours and a crust.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't rule out a melanoma. This needs dermatology, not reassurance from me.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll send an urgent referral on the two-week pathway. If it bleeds again before they see you, come straight back.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep it out of the sun, factor fifty, and don't pick the crust. Bring the Mizartan box in so we can check that dose.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, sit. We've got a short slot, so what brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's nothing, really. I'm tired. Who isn't, right?
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Months. Um, since last winter, or the one before, I couldn't tell you. It kind of snuck up.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every day?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. I crash around three. It's the job, and I'm fifty-two, so, you know.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Office manager at a dental clinic. Phones, payroll, people calling out. My sister thinks I should get checked, she makes a federal case out of everything.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you feel cold when other people don't?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I live in a cardigan, even in July. Well, our AC is set to meat locker, so I wouldn't call it a real problem.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight up or down?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Up a little. Ten pounds, well, actually maybe fifteen. I don't own a scale, so don't write that in stone. It's the snacks at the front desk.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Same stretch of months?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I guess. Jeans got tight after the holidays and just stayed tight.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are your bowels?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): They're fine. Well, actually, I'm a bit backed up. Every two or three days instead of every morning. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any straining or blood?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): A little straining. No blood. I don't take anything for it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is your mood down?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I mean, I'm flat, kind of blah, but that's the schedule, not... I'm not depressed. I'm not crying in the car or anything.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hair thinning, dry skin, or a change in your voice?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no, and no. My husband would've mentioned the voice. He narrates my life.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): None of that. I can cross the parking lot just fine.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any thyroid disease in the family?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): My mom. She was on thyroid pills her whole adult life. Underactive, I think, or Graves. I always mix those two up.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ever had a thyroid blood test?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, once. They said it was normal.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): When?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, I don't know. Five-ish years ago? Could've been longer. It was that clinic on Maple, before they closed. I don't have a date.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Wait, no, I'm remembering it wrong. They didn't say normal. Borderline, they said. I never kept the number.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicines, including over the counter?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the water pill. The little white one, for my blood pressure. That's the only real medicine.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure's still the reason, got it. Which water pill, and what dose?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): HCTZ. Twenty-five milligrams, every morning. Been years. I don't miss doses, before you ask.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else? Pain pills, vitamins?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Advil, sometimes, for my knees when I've been on my feet. Two of the brown tablets. Not every day.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thyroid isn't enlarged. No puffiness in the face. Pulse is seventy-six and regular. Pressure today is one thirty over eighty-six.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Nothing dramatic. I almost canceled and went back to the desk.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is an underactive thyroid. It might just be the hours and getting older. I can't call it yet.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll order a TSH and a free T4. Get the blood drawn this week, lab downstairs.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to? If it's borderline again they'll just shrug, and I'll have wasted a morning.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, you have to. Come back in two weeks and we'll go over the results. Keep taking the HCTZ, and don't start any thyroid pills off the internet.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this screen just froze on me again. Okay, Mr. Hale, what brings you in?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): A few months at least. I can't pin the start down.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm with it, or is it dry?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings there's some gunk. It was yellow for a bit after that chest thing, but now it's mostly clear, I think.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): The chest thing, when was that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): About three weeks ago. Urgent care told me it was a chest infection and handed me antibiotics.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which antibiotic? I'm not seeing it on here.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the pink pills. Azithromycin, I think. Five days, and I finished the pack.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the cough, did that clear after the pills?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The heavy part eased off. The morning cough is still there, though, and so is getting winded.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the breathlessness new, or has it been around?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, it's been creeping up. Stairs are the worst. I have to stop halfway up.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with that?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about fever or night sweats?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not now. I had a fever with the infection, but that's gone. No night sweats.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you wheeze?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, yeah, in the morning. I don't know if you'd call it wheezing. More like a little whistle.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): About ten a day. Well, actually, maybe twenty. Depends on the day. I've smoked since I was a teenager, so, what, forty years?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, something just pinged. Was that ten or twenty?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Closer to twenty, I guess. I don't know, doctor. I don't really count them.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any inhalers?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The rescue one, albuterol. Two puffs when I need it. And they gave me fluticasone, but I don't use that one much.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often for each? Sorry, say it once more, I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Albuterol, some days twice, some days not at all. The steroid one I forget. Maybe a few times a week if I remember, and I don't know the dose.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me pull up this morning's spirometry. One second. FEV1 is one point seven two liters, 61 percent predicted. FVC is 3.05 liters, and the ratio is 56 percent.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? Last time, a couple years back, they said it was borderline. I don't know what the numbers were.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Say that again? Borderline when?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe two years ago, at the other clinic. They just said borderline and to cut back on smoking. I didn't.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Looking at today's numbers, this is an obstructive pattern. I'm thinking COPD, with the smoking and that morning cough. It could still be leftover from the infection, though. I don't want to lock that in today.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I need more medicine, or what?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I want you using the fluticasone, two puffs twice a day, every day, not just when you remember. Albuterol stays two puffs when you're short of breath, up to every four hours.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, I'll try. The quitting thing, I don't know, doctor. I've said I would a hundred times.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to the smoking cessation clinic. They can go over patches or whatever fits. And I'm ordering a chest x-ray to be sure that infection cleared.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I gotta come back for all this?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in three months. If the breathing gets worse before then, come in sooner.

[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Doctor Maseko. Sorry about the wait. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my skin, mostly. The acne on my face just won't quit, and my periods are all over the show.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm her mother. She's been stressing about the photos. Her cousin's wedding is in Durban and she keeps plastering on makeup.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, Mom, the wedding isn't why we're here. It's the spots and the periods that are actually bothering me. We nearly missed the turnoff as well, the sign is tiny.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. The periods. How long have they been irregular?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, about two years now. I'll skip a month, sometimes two. The last one was, I think, six weeks ago? Ja, more or less.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the acne, did that start around the same time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh the lady at the salon was on about a charcoal mask, shame. She wanted four hundred rand a session. I told her no ways, I'm not made of money.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ja, the salon can wait. When did the acne itself start?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, sorry. Same sort of time, about two years. It's the chin and the jaw, and a bit on the cheeks. It gets worse just before a period, when I actually get one.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any hair where you wouldn't expect it, on the face or the chest?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, a bit of hair on the chin and the sideburns. I pluck it in the car before work. I work at the clothing shop in the mall, and the lights in there show everything.
[SEG0015] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's put on weight as well. She still stays with me, so I see it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mom, please. I have put on weight, ja, maybe ten kilos over those two years. I'm not sitting eating koeksisters every day. I even tried the gym for a month and then the shift times got silly.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud, so stop me. Err, spots, cycles all over the place, a little facial hair, weight up. That cluster makes me wonder about polycystic ovaries, but it might also just be the weight and the cycles nudging each other. I don't want to put a label on you until we've looked properly.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with all of this?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about a cough, or being short of breath?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, my chest is fine. Nothing like that.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): And headaches?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, not really. Not proper headaches. Sometimes after a long shift my head feels a bit tight, but I wouldn't call it a headache. I don't know, it's vague.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay, we'll leave that one. Are you using any medicines at the moment?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I put benzoyl peroxide gel on at night, the 5 percent, just on the spots. And if the period cramps are bad I take ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, maybe two days in the month.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't forget the antibiotic. The GP gave her doxycycline last year and she stopped it.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the doxicycline. It was 100 milligrams once a day. I did about three months and it made my stomach horrible, so I stopped. That was last year. The GP's rooms didn't even have aircon, I remember that more than the tablets.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any diabetes in the family? With the weight and the cycles I always ask.
[SEG0031] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja, I've got type 2 diabetes. Diagnosed about eight years back. Her father doesn't have it.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke? And alcohol?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. I'll have a cider at a braai, not every weekend, one or two. My uncle braais every second Saturday and he always offers, hey.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. I was going to start you on a combined pill today, Yasmin, one tablet a day. It often settles the skin and the cycle.
[SEG0035] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She gets those bad headaches with the flashing lights. Migraines. I told the other GP, it happens.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Mom, that's like twice a year, with the zigzags in my eyes. I didn't think it was a big deal.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ah, that changes it. If there's migraine with the visual aura, I'm not happy putting you on a combined pill today. Scratch the Yasmin. We'll park the pill completely, and rather do bloods and a pelvic scan before we pick any treatment.
[SEG0038] person_1 (NURSE): I can book the bloods at the lab downstairs, and radiology has a pelvic scan slot on Thursday if you want it.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ja, let's do that. Hormone bloods, a fasting glucose because of your mom's diabetes, and the pelvic ultrasound on Thursday. Come back in three weeks and we'll go through the results. Keep using the ibuprofen the way you have been if the cramps bite, and don't start any contraceptive pill in the meantime.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. Dr Shah will see you in a minute. I'll just pop the cuff on for your blood pressure, alright?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, yes. Sorry, that telly out there, I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Loud, isn't it. Right, 132 over 84, pulse 78. Through you go.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Have a seat. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my skin. I've got this awful itchy rash between my fingers and round my waist, where the waistband rubs. It's been about three weeks, maybe a bit longer, and it's driving me mad.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. When you say three weeks, has it been there the whole time?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, yes, the whole time. I kept thinking I've overdone it at the cafe with all the hand washing, but this isn't just dry skin.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): And is there a time of day it's worse?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Nights. After tea I'm climbing the walls. It's like something's crawling under the skin between my fingers, and there's a bit on the inside of my wrists now too. I barely sleep.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Can you see spots, or is it only the itch?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Little bumps, and I've scratched it raw in places. Same along the waist.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is anyone else in the house itching?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. My partner Tom is scratching his wrists. And our little boy, he's four, he's itchy at bedtime as well. I'm frightened I've given it to them. We keep the place clean, honestly.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hmm, let me think this through. Fingers, waist, wrists, worse at night, and the people you live with itching too. That is very likely scabies. The mite sits in the skin, which is that crawling feeling.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Scabies? Oh god. Does that mean we're dirty? I hoover every single day.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, it doesn't mean that at all. It spreads by close skin contact, and tidy houses get it just the same.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I still work? I'm in a cafe, hands on everything. And can he go to nursery, or do I have to keep him off?
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): After the cream has gone on, you can be back at work the next day, and he can be back at nursery the next day. We'll go through it step by step so it isn't a muddle.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Is it that permetrin cream I read about? How do I even put it on?
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Permethrin five percent cream, often sold as Lyclear. You apply it from the neck downwards, all over, and leave it on for eight to twelve hours.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not my face? What about under my nails, I bite them. And, umm, down below, do I have to?
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leave the face unless it's itchy there. Do go under the nails, between the fingers, the soles, the groin and the bottom. Is your scalp itchy?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Scalp's fine. Face isn't itchy either. It's the hands and the waist.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Have a shower, dry off, then put the cream on cool skin. Leave it overnight and wash it off in the morning. Everybody at home should do it on the same night.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Even a four year old, the same night? Is that safe? I've read scary things online.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, it's the treatment we use from two months of age. You or Tom put it on him, neck down. Then all of you repeat the exact same thing seven days later.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I miss a patch, say behind a knee? Does it all fail? And does it sting? I'm going to mess it up.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can tingle a little. Try not to miss hands, wrists, waist, feet and the groin. If you've been careful, you don't throw the whole thing out over one small gap.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the bedding? There's a mountain of it. I'm all over the place trying to think it through.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wash clothes and bedding from the last three days at sixty degrees. Anything that won't wash, bag it for seventy-two hours. Don't buy insecticide sprays for the sofa, they aren't needed.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-two hours for his rabbit as well, the soft toy? And all the towels?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, bag the soft toy or hot wash it. Towels from those three days too. The mites die off the body quite quickly, so it isn't the whole house.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I did try Canesten from the chemist last week, the antifungal one. I thought it was a sweat rash. It did nothing at all.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's clotrimazole, so it was never going to clear this. You can stop it. Anything else you've put on the skin?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I put the yellow steroid cream on, the hydrocortisone, twice last week, then I stopped because it wasn't doing much. And I take my water tablet every morning, the bendro, two point five, for my blood pressure. Years, that's been.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the bendroflumethiazide as usual. Hydrocortisone might ease the itch a touch but it won't kill the mites. Any allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Oh, and last autumn they did a cholesterol blood test, and the nurse said it was borderline. They never started me on anything.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't go into that today, I haven't got a figure in front of me. Any fever while this has been going on? Any cough, or trouble breathing?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No cough. Breathing's alright actually. I just feel like a wet rag from not sleeping.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. Yes, small burrows between the fingers, and scratch marks where the waistband sits. No sign of a spreading skin infection.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Are those little lines the burrows? If I'm still itching in a fortnight, has it failed? I can't keep going like this.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): The itch often carries on for two or three weeks after the mites are dead, so a fortnight doesn't mean it failed. If the rash is still spreading after the second treatment, or if you see pus, or you feel feverish, come back sooner. Otherwise I'll see you in four weeks.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. And Tom and our boy definitely treat the same night, even if his spots are tiny? How much cream do we get?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Same night, all three of you, whether you can see much or not. I'll prescribe three tubes of permethrin five percent to start with. You repeat it on day seven, so check with the chemist whether you'll need more cream for that second go. Reception can book the four week visit.
[SEG0045] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Pop out to me when you're done and I'll book the four weeks. The prescription usually hits the chemist next door within the hour.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Sorry for firing questions. I'll write every step down so I don't lose them.

[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And it's so muggy my glasses fogged in the parking lot. Her brother's T-ball got rained out this morning, field was a swamp, then the coach tried to move it to four and bailed.

[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr. Shah. Sorry you had to wait. What brings you in?
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This rash. She woke up with it a couple of days ago, on her belly and both arms, red and bumpy.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Maya, does it itch?

[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever, vomiting, or trouble breathing?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Got it. Anything new around then, a medicine, a cream, something she ate?
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's the messy part. Um, she started amoxicillin four days ago, four hundred milligrams twice a day, the pink liquid, for an ear infection. I also started a new cream, hydrocortisone one percent, twice a day, three days ago, 'cause her arms were dry. And Saturday she had shrimp at her uncle's, first time ever.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, she doesn't know if it was the shrimp or the cream or the antibiotic, and honestly neither do I. The rash was there Sunday morning.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): So all three land in the same couple of days. Any allergies?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Well, actually, when she was about two she got penicillin for an ear infection and broke out in hives. We stopped it. I've always said she's allergic.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No I didn't.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Honey you were two, you don't remember. Hives, all over. The pediatrician told us to stop the penicillin.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Red raised bumps over the abdomen and both forearms, plus a few scratch marks. Lips and tongue aren't swollen. Lungs sound clear.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. It itches. Bad. At night.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): There it is. She told me that at three in the morning and then told you no. Worse at night.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the itch is real, nights are worse. Thinking out loud, this could be a drug rash from the amoxicillin, or something in the new hydrocortisone cream, or the shrimp. Early on those can look alike, and I can't separate them today.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you don't have a name for it.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): No firm diagnosis. I'd stop the amoxicillin and stop the hydrocortisone starting today. Four days is a reasonable pause for a simple ear infection, but call if the ear pain comes back.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm tired.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): I know. For the itching, let's start cetirizine, five milligrams by mouth once a day. Children's syrup is one milligram per milliliter, so that's five milliliters once a day.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Like Zyrtec. What if the rash just stays?
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it's still there in two weeks, we can arrange patch testing for the cream and related stuff. Not something I'm ordering today.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And a follow-up visit?
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. I want to see her back in two weeks either way. Emergency room if her lips or tongue swell, if she wheezes, or if the rash takes off fast.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Stop the antibiotic, stop the cream, cetirizine once a day, back in two weeks, ER if she swells or wheezes. Okay.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's it. We'll just watch the ear unless it flares.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Can we go?
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We can. Thanks, doctor.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): The dose, sorry. I lost you, the screen's jumped again.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The vet can't fit her in till Thursday. Her nails are a disgrace, honestly.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, breathing. Sorry. I'm alright unless I rush, then I'm a bit puffed. I'm sixty-two, I put that down to age.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you on a cholesterol tablet?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Was. Rosuvastatin. I stopped it in March, the muscle aches were shocking.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength was that?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? Or twenty. Don't remember. They also wrote ezetimibe and I never filled the script, never took it.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So not the ezetimibe. And the rosuvastatin, you—
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Stopped in March, yeah. Knees have been niggly for years from the gardening, both of them, though I'm not here about that.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Achy with the gardening, comes and goes, been years. Not why I came in, mind you.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Back to the chest. You said there was no pain. What about climbing stairs, or walking fast?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, there's a tight feeling. Not pain exactly. Like a band around the chest. Only on the stairs at home, or if I'm legging it for the bus.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's that tightness been there?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't put a date on it. Maybe a month. Could be longer. I honestly don't know.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it go if you rest?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, a minute or two and it's gone. If I dawdle up the stairs it doesn't come on at all.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sweating with it? Jaw pain, or pain down the arm?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweating. Jaw's fine. Arm, no, I don't think so.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most times you hurry, or just occasionally?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Most times, if I don't take it slow. The 412 is hopeless, you get halfway down George Street and it sails past, so I'm forever—
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? The chart's flicked over.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Most times when I'm rushing. Not when I go slow. That was it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I've cut the wine right back. None on weeknights. My husband still has a beer with dinner, that's his business.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking, I meant. Not the wine.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. Can't stand the smell. The wine is one glass on a Saturday if we go out.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm aware of.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heart disease or diabetes in the family?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Dad had a heart attack at about seventy. No diabetes in the family, far as I've heard. Mum's ninety-one and still attacking the crossword.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure's 152 over 88, pulse 78. Heart sounds are normal and regular, no murmur, and the lungs are clear.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 152 bad? And the tight feeling, what do you reckon that is?

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina. That's a bit of a shock.

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): What if it keeps happening?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled, we might do a scan, a CT of the arteries. Not today, only if it's still going. I'll see you in a fortnight with the results either way.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it comes on and doesn't go when I stop?
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it stays after you've rested, or you get proper pain, sweating, or it starts while you're sitting, ring an ambulance. Don't drive. Take the aspirin every morning, not just when you remember, and keep the perindopril going as you are.

Transcript (encounter 00504)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I'm so sorry, doctor, I'm dreadfully late. The bus just sat there outside the library and I nearly got off and walked, but then I thought I'd be even later.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't worry, we've plenty of time. Sit down, catch your breath. Now, what's been going on with your eyes?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the left one. I keep seeing these little floaters, like specks of dirt or tiny cobwebs drifting about. About two weeks now, I think.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): And are they there all the time, or do they come and go?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly they're there. They float off when I look at them, which is rather maddening. And then there are the flashes, as well. Little flickers of light at the side, like someone taking a photograph. That began last Tuesday.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Tell me more about the flashes. Are they in the same eye?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, the left. Is that terrible? It sounds terrible. My friend Pauline said a flash can mean you're going blind.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know it's frightening to hear, so let me ask a few things to put it into context. Has a dark curtain or shadow come across any part of your vision?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no curtain. Nothing like that. It's all still there, just with the specks in it.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And any pain in the eye, or redness?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain at all. No redness either, I looked in the mirror this morning, twice.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite right to look. Now, I'm going to ask a wider question. Any problems with your nerves or your head, like weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that, I'd have gone straight to A&E, wouldn't I?
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): You would, and that's exactly the right instinct. Let's go through what you're taking, so I've got the whole picture.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I take atorvastatin, 20 mg, in the evening. Ramipril, that's 5 mg, in the morning. And levothyroxine, 50 micrograms, first thing before breakfast. For my underactive thyroid. Have I forgotten anything? I think that's all of them.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): That sounds right. And with the thyroid, anything else I should know about your health generally?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's the only thing really. I had a rash with penicillin when I was a child, my mother always told me. I haven't touched it since, so I suppose I'm allergic.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's useful and I'll note it down. Do you smoke, or drink at all?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I've never smoked, never even tried it, my father would have had a fit. And I have a glass of wine on Fridays, sometimes two if Pauline's visiting.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very moderate. Let me read your numbers, now that you've cooled down from your bus dash. Blood pressure is 148 over 90, a little higher than usual.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh dear. Is that because I rushed? It's usually fine at home.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite likely. Your pulse is 78, oxygen saturation is 98 percent, temperature 36.6, and you weigh 71 kilos.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Goodness, am I meant to weigh less? I was seventy-three at Christmas.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, you're perfectly fine. Now, I'll tell you what I think. What you describe, floaters and flashes arriving in one eye with no curtain and no pain, most likely means the jelly inside the eye is shrinking and pulling away from the back of the eye. It's called a posterior vitreous detachment, and it's very common at your age.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it dangerous? Pauline said it was dangerous.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually it's harmless. The worry is that occasionally the pulling can tear the retina, which is why I take the flashes seriously.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Will the floaters go away?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Often they fade or you simply stop noticing them over a few months. The flashes tend to settle sooner.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): What should I do if it gets worse?
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you notice a lot more floaters suddenly, a curtain or shadow, or your vision going blurry, come straight to the eye casualty that same day. Don't wait for an appointment.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. A curtain, a shadow, a lot more floaters. I'll write that on my hand.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): A sticky note on the fridge might be kinder to your hand. And I'd like to see you again in two weeks to check how things are changing.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Shall I pop in at the desk on my way out and pick a time, or do they ring me?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): The desk will sort that out for you while you're there. No need to rush, they're friendly.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Lovely. And next time I'll be early, I promise. Thank you ever so much, doctor.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're quite welcome. Mind how you go.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): right, before you start, blood pressure today is 152 over 84, pulse 72. last time it was 164 over 90, just so you've got it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): that's fine though. I feel alright. bit of a waste of a morning if you ask me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): mm. and the bloods I asked for this morning, can you read me the kidney ones?
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): yeah. creatinine is 174, eGFR 34. back in the spring the eGFR was 41.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): thanks. so this is your diabetes and kidney review. how have you been in yourself?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine. err, they just sent the letter for the kidney thing. bit of an ache in the knee, few months, nothing really. comes on if I walk to the shops, goes when I sit down.
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): he wouldn't have come if I hadn't pushed. my sister's been on dialysis three years now, and I can't stop thinking about it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): oh leave off. I'm not like that. I'm fine.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): you've got type 2 diabetes, and the chronic kidney disease we've been following. still on the ramapril, and the metformin?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah both by mouth. ramipril five milligrams in the morning, metforman for the sugar, five hundred twice a day. diabetic fifteen years. the kidneys, they told me a couple of years back.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): anything from the shop, for pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): just ibuprofen. four hundred milligram tablet, by mouth, when the knee niggles. not every day. hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0013] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Mm. he gets them by the till at the shop. I did say.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd rather you weren't on those with these kidneys. any chest pain?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): no.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): and breathlessness, walking about?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): not really.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): any vomiting?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): never.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): with the diabetes, any numbness or tingling in the feet?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): no.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): getting thirsty, drinking more?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): not that either. well, actually, a bit in the evenings. nothing much.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): up in the night to pass water?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): no... well, sometimes. just the once.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): and your bowels, any trouble there?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah, fine. no trouble.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): let me check. ankles are soft, no swelling. the knee isn't hot, and it isn't swollen.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): so, just to say it back. mild ache in the knee for a few months, worse on walking, eases when you sit. shop ibuprofen now and then, ramipril five milligrams, metformin five hundred twice a day, type 2 diabetes for fifteen years, kidney disease a couple of years. today the pressure is 152 over 84, creatinine 174, eGFR 34.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think the ibuprofen has nudged the kidney function down, on top of the kidney disease we already know about. that's my working impression, not the final word. the repeat bloods will tell us more.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): the way it works, ibuprofen narrows the little vessels into the kidney filters, and ramipril drops the pressure on the way out, so together they can push the creatinine up. and diabetes can dull the nerves in the feet, which is why I asked about the tingling, even though you're not getting that.
[SEG0032] person_4 (CAREGIVER): so those tablets go in the bin? I had a stomach ulcer myself years ago from ibuprofen, I won't touch the stuff.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): yes, please stop the ibuprofen, don't buy any more. we'll keep the ramipril at five milligrams, that's for your blood pressure and the kidneys. metformin stays at five hundred twice a day while your eGFR is above 30. for the knee, paracetemol by mouth, one gram up to four times a day.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): paracetamol doesn't do anything. uh, fine, if you say so. the ibuprofen was barely anything anyway.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll book repeat kidney bloods in two weeks, creatinine and the eGFR again. if those haven't settled we might arrange a kidney ultrasound, but not just yet.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in six weeks with the results. if the knee gets properly worse before that, come sooner.
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): I'll sort the blood form at the desk. mind the step on the way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, both of you. I'm Dr Shah. Lovely to see you — what's been going on?

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): The legs. How are you feeling in yourself?
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Swollen.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both sides, or just one?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Both.
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, he won't give you a paragraph. Last couple of weeks, and by evening his shoes won't go on. We nearly missed the bus, the 47 was late again.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): The shoes are useful to know. Any breathlessness with the swelling?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Stairs.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the stairs. And sitting quietly — breathless then, or no?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He stops halfway up now. He never used to.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain while that's happening?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about a cough, or a wheeze?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He still sleeps flat. No extra pillows. I'd have noticed, I'm in the next room.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's good to hear. How's your energy, and your appetite?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Tired.
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He eats everything I cook. It's the tiredness. And he nods off in the armchair after lunch, every day lately.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): You sort the pill box, don't you? Talk me through it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sunday nights. The water tablet first — box says furosemide. Forty milligrams, one in the morning.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And he actually takes that one?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I put it out and he swallows it. I haven't seen him miss it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What else sits in the morning compartment?
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Bisoprolol, two and a half milligrams. His heart tablet. Then the little white one.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any name on the little white one?
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nothing I can read, it's tiny and round. I think it's the blood pressure tablet, maybe five milligrams? I binned the box, which was stupid of me.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): White.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no name we can trust. Is bisoprolol separate from the heart tablet, or have you counted one tablet twice?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh. Um. I've double-counted it. The heart tablet is the bisoprolol. There's only one.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll log it once, then. Two and a half, mornings. Did another doctor stop anything?
[SEG0033] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Atorvastatin, the cholesterol one. Hospital doctor stopped it in March. His legs were aching.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): And he's stayed off it?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes.
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. They wrote naproxen for his knee as well, but we never collected it. He never took one.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Naproxen never started, so I'll ignore that. Any shop-bought pain relief?
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol, when the knee grumbles. Not daily.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Roughly how much, and how often?
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two tablets, maybe two or three times a week. Five hundred milligrams each, I think. Boots own.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Knee.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the knee still play up?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0044] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Old arthritis, years of it. Not why we're here. His brother had a knee done — oh, ignore that, not relevant.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Consider it ignored. The heart failure and the blood pressure — those are still the diagnoses you've been living with?
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. Heart failure a few years back, and high blood pressure. Both still going on.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at those ankles and listen in.
[SEG0048] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Worse on the left, I reckon. Or — actually, maybe not. Hard to tell in the morning.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both ankles are puffy and they pit with pressure. Chest is clear, no crackles. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Pulse is seventy-two, regular.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the blood pressure?
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): One hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-two. Oxygen saturation is ninety-six percent.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think the puffy ankles and getting breathless on the stairs mean the heart failure is a little less settled. I'd like to change the water tablet. Forty milligrams once a day isn't holding the swelling, so we'll give forty milligrams in the morning and another forty at lunchtime.
[SEG0054] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So two of them?
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two doses, yes — not both at once. Leave the bisoprolol as it is. And I won't guess at the little white one. Bring the tablet itself, or a clear photo, before we touch it.
[SEG0056] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll photograph it tonight.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the breathing gets worse, or he can't lie flat, or the swelling shoots up, come straight back, don't wait. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks to see if the extra dose has done the job.
[SEG0058] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks is fine.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): Ta.

[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been pacing the flat all week, doctor. I had to nearly drag him down here.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the aunt why you're in, or is there something on you.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the lump. I've a painless lump in my neck. I'm after having it two weeks, uh, no, three weeks.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which side.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): The right, just under the jaw. It doesn't hurt one bit, and that's what frightens me. Painless is bad, isn't it?
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bigger since you noticed it.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Like a marble, maybe. Umm, I spotted it the night of the hurling, so yeah, three weeks.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Night sweats.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Once. Just the one night I woke drenched. Not since, thank God.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever now.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I felt grand this morning. No temperature that I could tell.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight loss. Cough. Sore throat.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No weight loss. No cough. Throat's been fine. Err, I did get a scratch off the cat though, about two weeks back, on the left hand. It's nearly healed.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The cat's mine, she sleeps on my bed. My sister's allergic so she won't come near the place. She takes biotin for her hair, swears by it. Would biotin shrink his lump?
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Biotin does nothing for a node. A lymph node swells when the body is fighting an infection. A cat scratch is a common reason.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): So is it cancer then? My aunt's started in the neck. Will I need a biopsy? How fast would you know?
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not calling it cancer. Most likely a reactive node. I can't fully rule out lymphoma from the chair, so we'll get a scan.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok. Ok. Umm, last year in student health they did bloods and said the white cells were borderline. They never repeated it. Does that change things?
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll note it. Any tablets.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing regular. I don't even take paracetemol.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I take sertaline myself, fifty milligrams, but that's for me. He won't go near it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0027] person_4 (NURSE): Err, I'll grab his obs. Temperature 36.7, pulse 88, blood pressure 118 over 76, sats 99 percent.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, on exam there's a right neck node just below the angle of the jaw, about 2 centimetres, mobile and non-tender. No other nodes. Throat clear, ears clear.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Two centimetres, is that huge? What if the scan is bad? Should I be getting rid of the cat? I'm really not able for this.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): No surgery today. Bloods today, full blood count and CRP, and an ultrasound of the neck. Back here in two weeks for the results.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks is ages. What if it grows, or I get a fever before that? Does the ultrasound hurt?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): The scan doesn't hurt. If the lump grows quickly, or you spike a fever, or the sweats come every night, come back sooner or go to emergency. Stay off the lymphoma pages tonight.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch him. I mind my own mother as well so I'm well used to checking for fevers. We'll be here in two weeks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Nora's in the chair whenever you're ready. I've the obs done, she's a bit warm. Parking was a nightmare, just so you know.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): The face of me. It's swelled up and the tooth is throbbing. I'm after a crown and I'm destroyed with it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which side, and when did the crown go on?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Left. And I'm not sleeping with it, it's just... ugh.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry doctor. The crown was Thursday, so that's three days. The dentist is away till next week, that's why I brought her.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Three days of this on the left. Throbbing, worse at night. I can't even lie on it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any temperature with it?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm roasting in the bed. Umm. A bit of a fever, nothing mad.
[SEG0010] person_1 (NURSE): Temp is 37.8, pulse ninety four, pressure 136 over 84, sats 98 percent. Respirations 16.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Open a small bit... the left cheek is warm, swollen, tender along the jaw. No obvious collection I can feel. Mouth opening is a bit tight.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah will you stop. That hurts. Don't be poking at it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry. Any trouble swallowing your spit or your food?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Swallowing is grand.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the breathing, any tightness or...
[SEG0016] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She was up half the night pacing. I nearly rang the out of hours, I didn't know whether...
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Breathing is fine. Not a bother. I'm wrecked and cranky, leave the pacing out of it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. What have you had for the pain?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Paracetamol from the chemist. Two tablets. Doesn't touch it.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It's a gram, four times a day, I set them out. She missed the lunchtime one yesterday, and I'm not sure she took the evening one, she was dozing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other regular tablets?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): The sugar ones. I forget the... err. The name of them.
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Metformin. Five hundred milligrams twice a day, for the diabetes. She's been on it years.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so the diabetes is ongoing. Anything else in the gut, or with the waterworks?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Can we get to the tooth.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking amoxacillin, five hundred three times a day for five days, and I'll see you in a fortnight. That should cover it.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Hang on, penicillin. I can't have penicillin.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): What happened when you had it?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Years ago, for a chest thing. A rash all over me and my lips swelled up. They told me never again.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The lips were bad that time. She's stayed away from it since.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, scrap that. No amoxicillin, nothing in that family. We'll use clindamicyn, three hundred milligrams four times a day for five days, by mouth.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Four times. I'm tired just hearing it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know. And a fortnight is wrong as well, err, now I'm thinking about the diabetes and the fever and the cheek still coming up.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She's been a bit higher on the sugars the last day or two too.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): That settles it. Nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, a full blood count and a CRP. No fasting, you can eat, just come at half eight.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday half eight is free. I'll book her in.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'll see you here Friday morning, not in two weeks. We'll look at the swelling and the bloods.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Friday. More waiting. That telly outside is brutal, cookery on a loop.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the swelling hasn't settled by Friday, or if you're worse, then we do a scan of the face. Not booking it now. If those bloods are borderline I'll add a swab of the gum, only if they're borderline.
[SEG0040] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And if she goes downhill before Friday?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): If swallowing gets hard, or the breathing gets difficult, or the swelling runs to the eye or down the neck, straight to the emergency department. Don't wait for me.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): I hear you. I'm not deaf. I'm sore and I want the bed.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Soft food only. Keep the paracetamol going the way it's set out, and finish every dose of the clindamycin even when the tooth eases. Ring the dentist when they're back next week.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Fine.
[SEG0045] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Will the tablet fix the crown, or is the tooth gone?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Working read, it's an infection under the crown, a dental abscess, and the antibiotic should knock it back. Could also be cellulitis of the cheek without a pocket of pus, I can't separate those fully today. Prescription is at reception, Thursday half eight for the bloods, Friday morning with me.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Four months. Perhaps a little more. I hoped it would settle by itself.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does it happen every time, or only now and then?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Nearly every time. A glass of milk in the evening, or ice cream when the grandchildren visit. Within an hour the tummy is full of gas, and the stools become loose.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any pain with the bloating?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not sharp pain. A heavy, stretched discomfort. It eases once the loose stool has passed, mostly.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blood in the stool? Or black stools?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Nothing I could point to.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. So nothing definite. Any loss of weight?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. Weight is unchanged. My clothes fit as they did last year.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever? Any vomiting?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, and no vomiting.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you cut out the dairy at all?

[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And in that week, did the bloating and loose stools settle?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I suppose, a little. Sometimes, not really. We were at my sister's, so the meals were different. I cannot be sure.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): We will leave that as unclear, then. What medicines are you taking regularly?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipin in the morning for the pressure. I nearly said ten milligrams, but it is five milligrams. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, one small spoon stirred in warm water.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go on.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The cholesterol one at night. I think ten milligrams, though, err, the name has slipped my mind, the strip is at home. And my sugar tablets, metforman, 500 milligrams morning and night, for the sugar.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me set that out. Amlodipine five milligrams each morning for the pressure, and an Ayurvedic powder, one small spoon every morning. A cholesterol tablet at night, possibly ten milligrams, name forgotten, and metformin five hundred morning and night for the sugar. Is that fair?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. That is correct. I do not miss them.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to medicines or foods?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None that I know of.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Family history — bowel disease, coeliac, or sugar?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had sugar, later in life. No bowel disease in the family, and I have not heard of coeliac among us.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Alcohol?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. Alcohol, only a small peg at weddings, not a habit.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still in work?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Retired now, from the accounts department of the electricity board. I live with my wife.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any burning or frequency when you pass urine?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Urine is quite normal.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, breathlessness?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Neither, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the couch for a moment. Abdomen is soft, bowel sounds are present, no tenderness, and I do not feel a mass.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Provisionally I would call this lactose intolerance, as it follows milk and ice cream and you have not lost weight. I still cannot rule out coeliac disease.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Please tell me what I should do.

Carry on limiting milk and ice cream, but do not stop wheat or roti before the blood test, and do not stop the Ayurvedic powder.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bring the cholesterol strip next time, so we can check the name and the dose. We will review in two weeks.
[SEG0044] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can book that blood test downstairs just now, and the review appointment in two weeks. I will put the form in the queue.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you very much. I shall go down directly.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): In you come. I'll do the checks before Dr Keane sees you. Have a seat there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I hope I am not inconveniently early.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're grand, sure. My sister had a wicked dose of back pain after her little lad was born, and she couldn't sit in the car for months. Different story to yours, mind. Cuff's going on.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Right. Blood pressure is 132 over 78, pulse 74, oxygen 98 percent. That's all fine. He won't be long.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Keane. Sorry, the morning list ran over a bit. What brings you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor. I have a pain in my lower back which shoots down my right leg, from the back past the knee into the calf. It has been three weeks. Sitting at my desk brings it to seven out of ten, and walking eases it a little.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the pain reach the foot?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It stops in the calf, and it does not go into the toes.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): How did it start? Was there a lift, or did it just arrive?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I lifted a box of files at the office. The ache began that evening. Well, actually, the shooting began the next morning.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Umm. Are you taking any tablets for the pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Ibuprofin, four hundred milligrams, three times a day, by mouth, with food, for the past two weeks.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ibuprofen, four hundred milligrams three times a day for the pain. Grand.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. That is correct.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has someone been at you about exercises?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A colleague at the office showed me some stretches. I have been doing them in the evenings, as she advised.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do they help at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I would not wish to say they have made a difference.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not had a fever.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any trouble passing water, or with the bowels, or numbness where you sit?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you lost any?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I have not weighed myself, so I cannot say.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you had the back imaged before, an x-ray or a scan?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): About two years ago they did an x-ray of the lower back. They said it was borderline, a bit of wear and tear. I was not given a figure.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Err, a borderline remark on an old x-ray isn't something I'd hang a diagnosis on. Lie back there. I'm going to lift the leg, a straight leg raise.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right leg, the pain comes on at about forty degrees. Left side is clear to seventy degrees, no pain. Tender over the lower lumbar spine, and no weakness in the foot that I can find.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I think is happening, thinking out loud, is the disc is irritating the nerve going down the right leg. Sitting tugs on that nerve, which is why it shoots. Your body isn't fighting an infection here, and the bone isn't the main event.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Thank you for explaining it so carefully. Would a scan be required?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not for now. I won't order an MRI yet. If it hasn't settled with the physio, we might do a lumbar MRI then. I'll refer you to physiotherapy, and I'll see you back in six weeks.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep moving, don't sit for hours, carry on with the ibuprofen with food, and only do those stretches if they don't stir the pain. If the leg gets weak, or you cannot pass water, don't wait the six weeks, come straight in.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly, doctor. I shall follow that, and I will not ignore a change of that kind.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll send the physio form from the desk. Mind the step. My sister swears by her physio, but that's her own business.

[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not the same illness. PCOS can affect sugars down the line though, so your mom's diabetes is worth knowing, and I'll check a fasting glucose.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or feeling short of breath?

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, a bit hit and miss then. Any burning when you pass urine?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp, thanks doc. We'll pitch on Thursday.

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Niamh, book those. Bloods Thursday morning with the nurse. First scan slot you have. And back to me in two weeks, not six.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ease off the fizzy drinks and the late takeaways. It helps the weight. That's the lot.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not that heavy. A stone is hardly a crisis.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're 79 kilos and it's up. The bloods will talk.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): And the wet rag thing is only the exams. I'm grand.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Noted. It still goes down.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the spots even go? Feels like a waste of a morning.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): No promises till the results. Questions?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've a lecture at four, so I need to hop.
[SEG0052] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): All booked, Aoife. Half eight Thursday, don't eat, water is fine. Scan Friday week at two. Back in two weeks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): On you go.
