[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was Saturday night, a few hours after the meal. That's three days now, not two. She's losing track of it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right so. And the vomiting, is that still going on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's stopped. I haven't got sick since yesterday evening.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She did, doctor. She vomited this morning in the bathroom. I had to clean it up.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think that was this morning. I don't know, maybe I'm wrong, but I don't remember it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. How many times have you been to the toilet with the diarrhoea?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A good few. Six, or eight? I lose count once I'm going all the time.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nearer ten, I'd say, since yesterday morning. Watery, every time.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in it, or anything black?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Just water, nearly.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the tummy itself, is there pain?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Cramps, low down. They come on fierce before I have to run, and they ease a small bit after.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you managing to drink at all?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): A small bit of water. I'm thirsty the whole time. I don't know if it's enough, doctor.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she's hardly passed urine. A small drop this morning, very dark, and nothing much since yesterday.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone else from the wedding taken bad?
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her sister, and two of the cousins. Texting this morning, the same thing, runs and getting sick. They all sat at our table.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I had the fish, though, not the chicken. I don't know if that even matters.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): It might not be the one plate, so, if the whole table is down with it. Any fever, or shivers?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. I feel a bit cold now and again, but I haven't a clue, really.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I took her temperature this morning before we came out. It was 36.8, normal.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking these days?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure tablet, the little white one, every morning. And I've been taking the Imodium for the runs.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Imodium is loperamide. How many of those have you had?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't know, doctor. Maybe two after each time I go? Or, well, actually, was it one. The box said two to start. I'm not sure I did it right.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been taking them since Sunday, and the chemist told her not to, if it was a bug off the food. She took them anyway.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd stop the Imodium now. If this is a tummy bug, better to let it out than cork it up.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. I thought I was doing the right thing. Sorry, doctor.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're grand, no harm done yet. Do you know the name of the little white tablet?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. It's just the blood pressure one. I've been on it for years.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril, five milligrams, one every morning. She doesn't miss that one.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lovely, stay on the ramipril. Any water tablet, or anything for the sugar?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just that, and the Imodium I was telling you about.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a quick look at you now, if that's alright. Pulse, pressure, and your tummy.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 98, blood pressure 112 over 68, and the temperature here is 37.1.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your tongue is dry, and the skin on the back of your hand is a little slow coming back. Tummy is soft, tender low down, no guarding.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that serious, doctor? I don't know what any of that means.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's mild dehydration, that's all. Not severe. My first thought was to send a stool sample off today and maybe give you a tablet for the infection.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Would a sample not be the sensible thing, with so many of them sick?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was leaning that way, but actually, no. Others are ill the same way, there's no blood, and it's only a few days. I won't send a sample today.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled in three or four days, then we might send a stool off. No antibiotic either, I changed my mind on that. It should be a short food bug or a virus.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do I do, just wait? I don't know if I can face food.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sip Dioralyte, little and often, even a teaspoon every few minutes. Flat 7-Up if the Dioralyte turns your stomach. Plain food when you fancy it, nothing greasy, and leave the Imodium in the press.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know if I'll keep the Dioralyte down, doctor.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tiny sips all the same. If you can't keep any fluid down, or you go dizzy, or you see blood, or the urine dries up completely, come straight back or go on to the emergency department.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Will you want to see her again this week?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not booking a routine visit. If you're not clearly better in three or four days, come back and we'll see about that stool test then.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I hope I'm not being a bother over nothing.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a bit of it. Mind yourself, and Nuala will keep an eye. You'll likely turn the corner shortly.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Her car's been making this awful noise, that's why we were late. I've just been living in the recliner.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. No, I don't think so.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Burning when you pee?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): The incision itches under the tape. That's what makes me nuts.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the bladder alone, then. What medicines did they send you home with? Antibiotics?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): The pink capsules. I took them five days... or was it seven? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Cephalexin. He's been on it. I'm not sure about the midday one, he sleeps right through it.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. There might be two pills left. Or I'm done. I don't know.

[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the oxycodone was never started. Any allergies to medications?

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I remember.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): No known allergies. I'm going to look at the incision myself.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Same as the nurse said. Warm, red, a little yellow drainage, and it's still mostly closed. This is most in keeping with a superficial wound infection.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): A deep abscess is unlikely while it's holding together, but the exam doesn't fully rule that out. We'll swab the drainage.

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice a day I can probably remember. I think.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll put an alarm on my phone so we're not guessing.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Keep it clean and dry. Showers are okay if you pat it dry, no baths. Dry gauze once a day.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it gets bad tonight? I don't know what counts as bad, doctor.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads, the drainage increases, or the fever comes back, call or go to the ER. Otherwise I want you back here in two days to recheck it.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two days works. I'll get him here.
[SEG0058] person_1 (NURSE): I'll lay a dry dressing on once that swab is collected.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the new one gonna burn my stomach like the ibuprofen did? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): It can. Take it with food. And don't restart the ibuprofen.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. No more pink capsules. Two days.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's the plan. Stop the cephalexin, start the new antibiotic today, culture goes to the lab, and I'll see you in two days.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, sorry we're late. The robot by Checkers packed up and we sat in the queue for ages.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ag, that's fine, you're here now. Have a seat, both of you.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm shattered. I hardly slept.
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been grumpy the whole morning, shame. Sorry about the mood.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): No stress. What brings you in today?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): My cheek's all swollen and the tooth won't stop throbbing.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which side, and how long's that been going?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Right bottom one. Three days. It's the tooth with the crown.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): And when did they put the crown on?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, I can't date it. Last winter, or the one before. I honestly don't know.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her dentist's away in Durban this whole week, so we couldn't get seen there.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. The pain, is it a throb or a sharp jab?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Throbbing. The whole time. It's bad. Keeps me awake.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has the swelling got bigger since yesterday?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not sure then, we'll leave that. Any bad taste, like pus coming out?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I can't say.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja. A bit warm since yesterday. Mild, nothing hectic.
[SEG0020] person_4 (NURSE): Obs are in, doctor. Temperature 37.8, pulse 96, blood pressure 128 over 82, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta. Any trouble swallowing?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Swallowing's fine.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): And breathing, any difficulty there?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's fine. I'm just sore and irritable, can we move on.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, wheeze, other chest stuff?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for the pain?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Panado. Paracetamol. Two of the 500 milligram tablets every six hours. Takes the edge off, only a little.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She had a Brufen as well, yesterday.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, one 400 milligram ibuprofen, then my stomach burned, so I stopped. Not again.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, penicillin, anything?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Diabetes, high blood pressure, heart problems, anything ongoing?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She teaches grade four at the primary, she had to phone them this morning.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, I'm a teacher. I should be in class. Can we just get on with it, I'm exhausted.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja. Let me look. Open slowly for me.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Ow. That's the one.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right cheek is swollen, warm, tender when I press. No pointing abscess. Mouth opening is limited. Throat is clear and the airway looks fine. There's a gland up under the right jaw.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Well it hurts if you press it, obviously.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, this is a dental infection, probably an early abscess around that crowned tooth. That's my working impression. Swelling plus the mild fever fits, though I can't lock it down without a dental x-ray.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Dentist's not even in town. So now what?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll prescribe amoxicillin, by mouth, 500 mg, three times a day, for five days.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Amoxacillin. Okay. Does that actually fix it?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): It should settle the infection in the cheek. It won't sort the tooth. See the dentist the day he's back.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the paracetamol, same dose you've been using. Don't restart the ibuprofen, your stomach didn't like it.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine. Whatever.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Warm salt water rinses, gently, a few times a day. Soft food, and don't poke at the gum.
[SEG0049] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What if it gets worse in the night, though?
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): If swallowing becomes difficult, or you battle to breathe, or the swelling jumps, go to casualty. Don't wait.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back if you're not better by Friday.
[SEG0052] person_4 (NURSE): I'll get the script printed at reception so you can fetch it on the way out.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Good. I need to lie down. This has wiped me out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, I am not able to put the drops properly. Half goes on my cheek, half goes on my saree, and I am sure nothing goes in the eye.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, very common problem, and nothing to be embarrassed about. Sit comfortably and tell me what happens when you try.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I tilt my head back, I hold the bottle high, and then at the last second I close my eyes. My grandson laughs at me, he says I am blinking before the drop even leaves the bottle.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): So you are flinching. Everyone does it. The eye is very protective, like a goalkeeper, it shuts the gate when anything comes close.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Exactly like that. And my right eye has also started watering a lot, ever since I started struggling with this.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the watering been going on?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten days, I think. Yes, ten days, because it began just before my sister's housewarming and she said, why are you crying at my party.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. Is it only watering, or does it also hurt? Any pain in the eye?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain, no. Only watering, that is all, but it is very irritating.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And has the sight changed at all, any change in your vision, blurring or anything?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, vision is the same as always. I can still thread a needle, that is my test.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good test. Is that for work?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I stitch blouses at home for the ladies in our colony. Forty blouses before Diwali, last year, I did. So my eyes are very important to me.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can see that. And you have glaucoma, if I read your file correctly. How long has it been?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Two years now. The earlier doctor told me, pressure in the eye can damage the nerve silently, so I must be regular.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): He told you right. That is why getting the drops into the eye matters so much. Let's fix your technique today, instead of me just telling you to try harder.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Please. My neighbour says she puts them lying on the sofa, and her husband holds the bottle.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): That works for some people, but you don't need a husband. Think of your lower eyelid as a little pocket. Put your finger just under the eye and gently pull the skin down, so the pocket opens.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Like this? My finger is shaking a little.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. Now look up at the ceiling, and bring the bottle close, not so high. Imagine you are watering a tiny plant, you don't pour it from the roof.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I am looking at the ceiling. There is a spot on the ceiling, by the way. It looks like a map of Sri Lanka.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll mention it to the maintenance team. Now squeeze one drop only, into the pocket, and keep looking up while it lands.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): One drop. Oh! It went in. I felt it go in. It was cold.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's it. Now close your eyes gently, don't squeeze them shut, and press lightly with one finger in the inner corner near your nose for a minute.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Why the nose corner? Is that a secret?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not a secret. It is like putting your thumb over a tap, it stops the drop draining away down the little channel into the nose, so it stays in the eye longer and does its work.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I never knew. My drops were running down my own nose all this time.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite likely. Wait five minutes between two different drops, if you ever use more than one, and wash your hands before you start.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Wash hands, pocket, one drop, press the corner. I will write it on a card and stick it on the bathroom mirror.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Excellent idea. Practise a few times in front of the mirror with your grandson watching, and let him be the judge.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): He will love that, he has been a judge of my cricket also. The watering, will it stop?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sure better technique will help a lot with the cheek, and if you blink less, you'll waste less. Let's see how it goes.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, doctor. Should I come back to show you?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, I'd like to see you in three weeks. Bring the bottle, and I'll watch you put one in on your own.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. I will practise every morning, like a homework.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do that. And no stitching blouses until the drop is in, or you will be telling the blouse about your eye.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha, ha. Thank you, doctor. I will not close my eyes this time, I promise.

[SEG0002] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Thank you. I'm Denise, I look after Mr Lindsay on weekday mornings. ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Good morning. I should say that I'd like this to be accurate, so I shall be precise. ~

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very clear, thank you. Was it just the one eye?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. When I covered the right eye, I could see nothing. When I covered the left, the right was normal.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He phoned me straight away. I think he was shaken. ~
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has it happened before or since? ~
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Not before. Not since. ~
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the eye, headache, or flashing lights?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain. No headache. No flashes.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in your face or limbs, or any trouble with speech at that time?

[SEG0016] person_3 (NURSE): I've got the list, doctor. Aspirin, 75 mg, once a day. Atorvastatin, 40 mg at night. And amlodipine, 5 mg, once a day.

[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your vision, pupils and eye movements are normal, and the back of the eye looks healthy. There's a swishing sound, a bruit, over the left side of your neck.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Madam, I have taken the vitals. Blood pressure is 142 over 88, pulse 78, temperature 36.8, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry doctor, we got late. The auto was stuck near the sabzi market.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): That is fine. Sit, both of you. What brings you?
[SEG0004] person_4 (PATIENT): Doctor, I have high BP since many years, but today I came for this pain. Right upper stomach, it comes after fatty meals, and it stays two or three hours.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. We will come to the pressure. Since when is this pain?
[SEG0006] person_4 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Umm, maybe three weeks, I cannot say the day. It has come two or three times, only when the food is oily.
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Worst was the wedding biryani. She would not even lie down, just sat holding her side.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you vomit that night?
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): Once only. I vomited. Not again after that.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0011] person_4 (PATIENT): No. No fever.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yellow in the eyes, or the urine turning dark?
[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Loose motions?
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): Never. Motions are normal only.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the pain go to the shoulder or the back?
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): No. It stays here only.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which tablets are you on?
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): Digene, uh, the white chewable ones, two tablets when the pain starts. And for pressure, my BP tablet, amlodopin, five milligram, one every morning.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergy?
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operation in the past?
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): Never. Is it something bad? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me press here. Tender under the right ribs. The belly is soft, no guarding. Eyes are not yellow.
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her mother had the gallbladder surgery for stones, years back. She is thinking it is the same.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): That is useful. With your blood pressure, any chest pain?
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): And shortness of breath?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. Climbing stairs, a little. I don't know, doctor, whether it is the pressure.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swelling in the feet?
[SEG0031] person_4 (PATIENT): Not that either. Feet are fine.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Err, thinking aloud. Right upper pain after oily food, for hours, mother had stones. I am keeping gallstones with biliary colic, and also simple gastritis, both open. I will not conclude which today.
[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): Gallbladder, like my mother? I am scared, I don't know.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): I am not saying it is that for certain. Heart pain is less likely, but I will not rule it out fully. We will see what the tests say.
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): Ok doctor. What to do?
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I am booking blood tests, liver function, full blood count and serum amylase. And an ultrasound of the abdomen, for this week.
[SEG0037] person_4 (PATIENT): The scan, will it pain? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): No pain from the scan. Avoid oily and fried food, and continue Digene when the pain comes. Come back in one week with the reports. If the pain comes with fever or you vomit again, come earlier, do not wait.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, hello. I think I might have broken my ankle? I came down the stairs wrong about an hour ago.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oh dear, let's have a look at it in a second. Tell me what happened. ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I missed the last two steps, I think, and I landed on the side of my foot. It sort of folded under me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you hear or feel anything crack when it happened?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I felt something, a sort of pop. I'm not sure if I heard it. Is that bad?
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can mean different things, so don't read too much into it. Can you put weight on it at all?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. I tried to hobble and it hurt too much. I'd say it's severe when I stand.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where exactly is the pain?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Outside of the ankle, down towards the little toe side. And it's swollen, it's gone puffy already.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else? Numbness, tingling, anything odd in the foot?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): My toes have been tingling a bit, but I can't say when that started. Maybe in the car, maybe before.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll test that properly in a moment. Any pain in your knee?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my knee's fine. Foot's just a bit stiff.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you bang your head or hurt anywhere else when you fell?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I only fell the last bit. Just the ankle.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Have you hurt this ankle before?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): A few years ago I twisted it playing netball, but nothing like this.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Let me check your pulse and so on first. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 84, blood pressure 124 over 76, temperature 36.7.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? I feel a bit shaky. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfectly fine, the shakiness is just the shock. Now I'm going to press along the bone gently, and tell me when it hurts. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow, right there! ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's tender over the outer ankle bone and there's swelling around it. Your toes are warm and pink and you can feel me touching them.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): So is it broken? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It could be a fracture, or a bad sprain, and I can't tell which by looking. That's why I'd like an X-ray of the ankle now.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh. Right. How long will that take? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll take you straight there. Meanwhile keep the foot raised on this stool.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Raised. Okay. Can I walk on it to the toilet? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't put any weight through it at all. Ask a nurse for a wheelchair if you need to go.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): No weight. Right. And what happens after the X-ray? ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll come and tell you what it shows, and we'll plan from there. ~
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you. Sorry, I'm very nervous. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfectly understandable. You've done the right thing coming in. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hello, take a seat, I'll be with you in a second.

[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine, sit down. We'll go through it together. What's been worrying you?
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's pain under my right ribs after fatty meals, doctor. She didn't want to come, but I insisted.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been? These questions might sound routine, but they matter.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's been going on for about a week.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you describe it a bit more for me? How strong it is, what the pattern is, what helps. It helps to be thorough at this stage.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, fatty meals. That makes it worse. Only lying still, and it's not much. Honestly, a couple of times a week. I've been feeling sick too. I mean, as for feeling sick, it's mild, honestly. It comes and goes. I had pain going to my right shoulder before. That's settled now, though.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any dark urine, yellow eyes or pale stools?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't had dark urine, yellow eyes or pale stools, no.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, go on. Did you notice any fever?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Definitely no fever.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Actually, doctor, I did notice fever. She doesn't always say.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't think I did. Maybe a little, I'm not sure.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll note both what you've said and what you've noticed. Neurologically, anything strange?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your breathing, any trouble there?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Breathing's normal.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's talk a little about your daily life and habits.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I do a yoga class on Thursdays. Lots of rice, lentils and some fruit. My partner and our baby.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any health conditions I should have on record?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I have anxiety, for about a year. I've had high blood pressure for five years now.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, any other things?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I have heart failure.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so anxiety and high blood pressure are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. Is there anything relevant on the family side?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): My son has asthma.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's on your current medicine list? These questions might sound routine, but they matter.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She is on escitalopram, 10 milligrams, once a day for the anxiety, I give it to her. She is on lisinopril, 10 milligrams, once a day for my pressure, I give it to her. She takes metoprolol, 50 milligrams, twice a day.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm-hmm.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's an antacid, 10 ml, when needed, doctor.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, no, I've never been operated on.
[SEG0034] person_4 (NURSE): Doctor, I've got the readings for you. BP is 126 over 78, saturation 97 percent, pulse is 82 beats a minute, temperature 36.5.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, let's have a proper look at you.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's fine.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to your chest now.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is tender under the right ribs and you stop breathing in when I press.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's fine.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, you can sit up again.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, based on the history and the examination, this looks most like gallstone-related pain. That's my thinking for now, and it may change as we learn more. A stomach ulcer is also on my list.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm scared it's something bad. Is it?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like gallstone-related pain, but I'd like to confirm. Let's book liver blood tests to look into biliary pain. I'd like to arrange an ultrasound of the abdomen for biliary pain. I'll start you on paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day when needed, one week. That's for pain. Avoid fatty and fried foods until the scan. Please take the tablets with food so they don't upset your stomach.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's get you seen by the surgical clinic, I'll arrange the letter. Let's plan a check after the scan. I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, thanks, I'll see you then.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): All the best.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you notice the yellow?
[SEG0005] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, umm, day four, maybe day five. I can't really pin the day down.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Wah.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breast or formula?
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Both. Breast milk, and we give some formula after. He feeds about every four hours.
[SEG0009] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My sister keeps texting that four hours is too long. He just knocks out though.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0013] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grunts when he's on the breast. I wouldn't call it a cough. Maybe a tiny bit. I don't know.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Vomiting or diarrhea?
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting. And the poop is that yellow seedy stuff, not diarrhea. He does spit up a little after the bottle.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Mmm. Wah.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight from the nurse is seven pounds 1 ounce.
[SEG0018] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was seven pounds six ounces when he was born, so he's down a bit.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Skin is yellow from the face onto the chest. Sclera are yellow. Belly is soft, no masses.
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been so fussy, doctor. Barely naps, and I am wiped. We had the baseball game on at two a.m., don't ask.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): This is newborn jaundice. Could be ordinary physiologic jaundice or breast milk jaundice. I'm not locking that in.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll draw a bilirubin today.
[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): In the hospital they said the bilirubin was borderline. They didn't give me a number.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Discharge sheet?
[SEG0025] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's on the counter at home. Of course.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Medicines?
[SEG0027] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You mean me, I'm the one nursing. Amlowdipine, uh, ten milligrams, no, five milligrams, for the pressure, every morning.
[SEG0028] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cholesterol one at night. It's atorva-something, forty, wait, 20 milligrams. Sugar tablets too, metforman, five hundred twice a day.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, the one from the shop. I stopped the iron in March, killed my stomach.
[SEG0030] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A friend said gripe water. We never gave it to him.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't start that. Keep breast and formula, and wake him if he goes past four hours.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I read the yellow can hurt their brain. Is that what's happening?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's what the level is for. I'm not saying that from a look.
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Right.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Wet diapers?
[SEG0037] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah. Plenty, pretty much every feed.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Be back tomorrow morning and we'll go through the result.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if he looks worse tonight?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the yellow spreads to his legs or he stops feeding, come in sooner.
[SEG0041] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Drop the formula?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Keep both. Just feed him.
[SEG0043] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Neighbor's kid got some light-up blanket. We doing that?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not booking phototherapy right now. Depends on today's number.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Mmph.
[SEG0046] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's rooting again. Figures, right in the office.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lab will draw him before you go. Tomorrow morning, this clinic.
[SEG0048] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. Thanks.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): This sounds like an enlarged prostate slowing the flow. That's only provisional until the tests come back. I'm sending a PSA blood test and a urine test, you can do both at the lab today.

[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, sister. Oh, Doc, my father had prostate trouble as well, not cancer, just the enlargement. Does that run in the family?

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): It's pantoprazole, 40 milligrams, before breakfast for my acidity. I'm supposed to take it regularly, but I don't always manage.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, have you had any chest pain or fainting?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none of those at all.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What can I do for you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the knee, doctor. I'm worried sick about it, I really am.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which knee?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh the rain was pouring and the bus was jammed, I was ages getting across, and then—
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which knee?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The right. Sorry. Um, going down the stairs it catches me, and at night it's wicked.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months... no, nearer five months. It came on after the new year.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I end up like my mother? She had the two knees done. I'm not able for an operation, I just—
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop there. Morning stiffness?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, about ten minutes till I get going. Is that bad? Should I be worried if it's only—
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Locking? Giving way?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It doesn't lock, and it hasn't given way.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hips or back?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just the right knee. Nothing else.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Could it be a clot though? I was reading last night and I haven't slept... well, I do sleep, but then I'm googling like a mad thing.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a clot. Stairs and night pain is the joint. What are you putting on it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac gel from the chemist. I rub it on twice a day. One percent, I think... maybe. I never properly looked at the tube.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tablets?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother takes metformin for his sugar, the diabetes, and he says tablets wrecked his stomach, so I got nervous, but—
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your tablets.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac, the tablets, from the chemist as well. Only sometimes, when the pain is bad. Not every day.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Strength?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams... no, seventy-five. The box says seventy-five. One of them, maybe two or three times in the week.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach problems?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No stomach problems. None.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yes. A small bit of heartburn if I take the tablet late in the evening. I couldn't tell you when that started. I didn't think it counted.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that dangerous? Do I stop the tablets altogether? The gel is the same drug, isn't it, will that burn me too? I've been fretting all week.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gel is grand. If the heartburn comes, leave the tablets off. If you take one, take it with food, not on an empty stomach.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Eleven stone... no, sorry, twelve stone four. I always mix it up. They weighed me in the surgery last month.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): That weight is loading the knee. Cut the biscuits. Short walks.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister is on biotin, big tablets, for her hair. Would that do the knee any good? She keeps telling me to try it. Is it safe with the diclofenac? How many would I even take?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. That's your sister's. Biotin will not fix the knee. Don't start it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair enough. God, the weather though. I was telling my granddaughter, she's seven, she had camogie on Saturday and the rain never stopped. They were out on the pitch the whole hour. She thought it was brilliant, of course.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): They were soaked, and she lost one sock in the dressing room, just one sock. The cars around the school were bumper to bumper. We laughed the whole way home on the bus.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The knee.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. So what will you do? Physio? Someone said an injection. I'm terrified of needles, but if it works I'll do it. Does it work? How sore is it? Can you walk the same day?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Physio is one option. A steroid injection into the knee is another. I am not booking either today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Which is better though? If I try the physio first, can I still have the injection if it's no good? And how long are people waiting? The lists are a fright, aren't they?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either can wait. We decide next time, if the pain is still there.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it arthritis? Please say it straight. I've had myself in a wheelchair by Christmas, which is ridiculous, I know, but at three in the morning it doesn't feel ridiculous.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most likely osteoarthritis of the right knee. I can't confirm that without an x-ray, and I am not ordering one today.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No x-ray? Is that safe? What if it's something else, a tumour or that? I know I sound mad.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing suggests a tumour. Osteoarthritis fits. Come back in six weeks.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. And if it gets worse before that, the stairs are a killer, what do I do? Ring you? Go back to the chemist?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ring the surgery if you cannot walk on it or it swells right up. Otherwise the gel twice a day, the tablets only now and again with food, and keep moving.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the heartburn go if I ease off the tablets? And should I be on something for the stomach? I don't want an ulcer. My head is racing.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off and it should settle. No stomach tablet from me today. Six weeks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. I'll try to stay off Google. Thanks a million.

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, since two nights he is just crying and crying, holding the ear. It started after the cold only.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which ear is he holding, the right or the left?

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Arjun, beta, can you show me where it is hurting?
[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): Ear.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): This right one?
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it paining the whole day, or more when he lies down?
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Daytime he plays, then suddenly cries. Night time only he is screaming, we were up till two.
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): Hurts.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the crying been, and the cold before that?
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Crying is two nights. Cold was there from last week, runny nose and a little cough. Cough is almost gone now.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever in these days?
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. I checked yesterday night, thermometer was ninety eight point four Fahrenheit. My mother stays with us, she said he was hot to touch in the evening, but I don't agree, the reading was normal.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is he taking food and water?
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Water he is drinking. Food, only two spoons, he pushes the plate. Morning he wanted biscuits though, then he left them.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Arjun, tummy pain?
[SEG0020] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pus or watery discharge from the ear?
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing coming out. I checked with the torch.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any medicines he takes regularly, or anything from before I should know?
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No regular medicines. Um, long ago, when he was a baby, the child specialist gave amoxicillin. I think he got a rash, maybe. I'm not sure, could have been the viral only.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember if the rash started after the syrup?
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not really. My husband says there were some red spots, I only half remember. It is all mixed up.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, we will be careful with that. Let me look in the ear, just a small light, beta, you can sit on Amma's lap.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right drum is a bit pink and dull, not bulging badly. Left ear is clear. Throat is mildly red, chest is clear, and he is in no distress.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So it is an infection, doctor? His nursery teacher also had sent a note, but that is a different thing, about the fancy dress.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely a mild ear infection after the cold, or just the tube blocked from the cold. I am not fully sure, and I don't want to start an antibiotic today.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was inconsolable at two in the morning. I felt terrible, actually.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nights are the worst, I know. For the pain, give paracetamol, the two hundred and fifty milligram syrup, six ml every six hours if he is hurting. That comes to three hundred milligrams.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We have Crocin at home, the two-fifty one. Same, no?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, use that Crocin. If the pain is still there after two days, or if you measure a real fever, then we start an antibiotic, cefpodoxime, not amoxicillin, because of that maybe rash. I am not giving it today.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if even that doesn't settle? My mother will ask me all this.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it does not settle, we might do a scan, though I doubt we will need it. Let's see him in two days.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two days, alright. Should I put warm oil in the ear? My mother was insisting.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't put oil or anything inside the ear. Keep offering him water, and if he turns very drowsy or the pain becomes severe before those two days, come sooner, don't wait.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): come on back. I'll grab a couple numbers before dr. patel steps in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): ok. um. sorry, the parking lot had me going in circles.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): ha, that lot eats people's mornings. you're alright.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): blood pressure is 118 over 76, heart rate 78, temp thirty six point eight, oxygen sat 98 percent.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): my sister had a miserable itch last winter, her little boy too, and folks blamed her housekeeping. drove her nuts.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): oh. yeah. I don't know.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): hi, I'm dr. patel. those numbers look steady. what brought you in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): the itching. between my fingers, and right where my jeans sit on my waist. it's driving me nuts.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): itching between the fingers and along the waistband. when did that start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. maybe two weeks, could be three. I can't pin the day down. and it's way worse at night, I wake up scratching.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): roughly two or three weeks, no clear start, worse at night. anybody else at home itching?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): my partner, and our little boy. he's four. they're both scratching. we all live in the same apartment.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): partner and your four year old, same apartment, both scratching. what have you put on the rash?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): um some hydrocortazone cream, the one percent from the drugstore. used it a few days. didn't really help, so I stopped.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): over the counter hydrocortisone one percent for a few days, then stopped, not much help. anything else you take regularly?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): just vitamin d. a thousand units, I think, once a day. the bottle's at home, so I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): vitamin d, about a thousand units daily, and you're unsure of the number. any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. years ago some pill gave me a rash. I can't remember what it was called.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): a rash from a pill you can't name. we won't guess. have you had any fever with this?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): mm, I suppose. sometimes, not really.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave fever as a maybe, not a yes. any cough, or trouble breathing?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): no. nothing like that.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): and your stomach? nausea, diarrhea?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): no. stomach's been fine.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): joint pains, or swelling in the hands?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): uh, no.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): any blood tests you remember?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): last spring they did cholesterol. they said it was borderline. I don't know the actual number. I never went back.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): cholesterol called borderline last spring, no number, not followed up. let me look at your hands and your waist.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): scratch marks in the finger webs, a few small bumps along the waist. no pus, and no big blisters.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): is it bad? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think this is scabies. a tiny mite burrows in the top layer of skin, and the itch is your body reacting to that mite. that's why it flares at night, and why people in the same home get it together.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): scabies? that sounds dirty. I don't know.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): it isn't about being dirty. it spreads by close skin contact and by sharing bedding.
[SEG0035] person_1 (NURSE): mm. my own kid's daycare sent a note about this once, and my sister caught all that shame. wasn't about her floors.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): we'll treat you with permethrin five percent cream. the same night, your partner and your son get treated too, even on skin that isn't itching.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): permathrin? I don't know how you even put that on.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): permethrin. tonight, after a cool shower, dry off, then coat every bit of skin from the neck down. between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the belly button, the groin, the soles. don't skip the creases.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): wait, my face too? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): not your face. you're an adult, so neck down is enough. the scalp and face are only for your little boy, and you keep it out of his eyes and mouth.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): neck down for me. ok. how long does it stay on?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): eight to fourteen hours. overnight is easiest. wash it off in the morning. then do the exact same thing again in 7 days.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): and they do it the same night?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): same night, same routine. the pharmacist can show you how much cream for a four year old.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): what about the sheets? do I throw them out? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): don't throw them out. wash the clothes, bedding, and towels from the last three days in hot water and dry them on high. anything you can't wash, seal in a bag for three days. vacuum the couch and the mattress.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): hot wash, bags, vacuum. will the itching stop tonight though?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): the mites should die from the cream, but the itch can hang on for two or three weeks while the skin settles. stop the hydrocortisone. I won't add a pill for the itch, because we don't know which pill gave you that rash.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): ok. um. do I have to come back?
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): yes. I'll have the desk book you in two weeks so I can check the skin again. if it spreads fast, or you see pus, or someone at home gets much worse, call us before that.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I can print the cream steps and the laundry list for you on the way out.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): thanks. I still feel kind of embarrassed, but alright.

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the dose?

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): When it starts I tend to get being short of breath on slopes as well.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often do you get it?

[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): no, nothing to report there

[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, is your urine normal, no changes?

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'm just after your blood pressure before you go in. Left sleeve up for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The left is better anyway. The right was bruised after the bloods last month, and I've been favouring it, though that's nothing to do with why I'm here.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. 138 over 84, pulse 76, temperature 36.6.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): 36.6, yeah, that matches the little thermometer at home. I kept checking because my mother always said a jaw ache might be a temperature coming on.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Grand. The doctor will see you now.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, the two of you, sit in. What's brought you along today?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the jaw, doctor. When I chew there's a pain just in front of the ear, and it clicks, a little pop, and I have to stop mid-bite.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): That sounds miserable. How does it behave through the day?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings are rotten, like I've been clamped shut all night. If work is mad it comes back in the evening, a sharp ache, not really a throb.
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And there's grinding. I hear the teeth going most nights. He sleeps through the whole thing.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't feel it myself, but I believe him. He's not one for making things up, and some mornings the jaw is already tired before I'm even out of the bed.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the click every time you open, or mainly when you're eating?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, mainly with food. A crust, an apple, a chop, the right side clicks, and for a second the mouth won't open the full way, then it gives.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this, or have you felt unwell in yourself?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): The stress has been desperate. We've a new accounts package and I'm on the laptop till half nine, and the face tightens when I'm staring at the screen.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll come back to the stress. On the fever, though, any temperature, or feeling hot and shivery?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever at all. I haven't felt hot once.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has the jaw been at you?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Err. Last winter, or the one before. I couldn't put a date on it. It just crept in.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He only said it out loud when the clicking got loud at dinner. Before that he'd just go quiet over the food.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What eases it, if anything at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A warm cloth helps a small bit, and the soup days are grand. Paracetamol takes the edge off, but I don't like swallowing it every single day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): What regular medicines are you taking?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformine for the sugar, 500 milligrams twice a day, for years now. And Mizartan for the pressure, 40 milligrams every morning.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else from the chemist?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Omprazole, 20 mg, once a day before breakfast, for the acid. I never miss that one, because the heartburn is rotten if I do.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the evening Metformine, does that actually get taken?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, not always. If I'm home late I forget it, maybe two or three evenings a week.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are the teeth themselves sore, or is it the joint?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): The teeth are fine, the dentist went over them and found no holes. I had a crown put on a back tooth years ago after it cracked on a mint, but that side is quiet now. It's the joint that clicks, not the tooth.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He rubs the right side of the jaw in the car. I see it at the lights, every time the traffic stops.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the stress, you feel that makes the pain worse?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, definitely. A deadline and that evening the pain is sharper and the click is louder. A quiet Saturday it's only a niggle, unless I chew a steak.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the jaw ever lock and stay shut? Any swelling, or a bad taste?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No locking that stays. No swelling I've seen. And no bad taste, I was watching for that in case a tooth was going off.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): How is the sleep, apart from the grinding he hears?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. I wake once or twice and roll over. It's not a proper insomnia.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all, or take a drink in the evenings?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I gave up the cigarettes eight years ago. A glass of wine at the weekend, and not through the week.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you doing for work these days?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm an accounts clerk, screens all day. I jam the phone between the ear and the shoulder, which is probably stupid for this jaw.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me feel the joint and have a look in the mouth, if you're alright with that.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, it's the right one, just there. Go easy though, it gets very tender if it's pressed.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tender over the right jaw joint as you open, and I can feel the click. No swelling. Teeth look fine, and the throat is clear.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's the exact spot. It hops a little toward the ear, not down into the neck at all.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think this is the jaw joint itself, a temporomandibular problem, with the grinding and the stress feeding it. I don't think it's an infection.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): That's a relief. My uncle had a jaw infection after a tooth came out, and I had myself half convinced, even with the dentist saying the teeth were sound.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Soft food for a couple of weeks, nothing chewy or crusty. And get a boil-and-bite mouth guard from the chemist for the night.
[SEG0049] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll stand over him until he wears it. He'll say it's uncomfortable after one night, I know him.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I will wear it, I promise, even though I hate plastic in the mouth. I'll do the soups and the scrambled egg and leave the crusts, and I'll keep a note of the bad evenings the way I do with the sugar readings.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Paracetamol is grand when you need it, up to one gram four times in the day, with a bit of food. No chewing gum. If it's not easing in three weeks, come back and we'll think about the dental hospital. If it locks solid before that, ring us.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Keane, before the doctor comes in, I've your blood pressure at one thirty eight over eighty two, and the pulse is 76. You can stay where you are.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I'm seventy four and I'm wrecked, so the sooner this is done the better.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello there, I'm Dr Brennan. Come on in, the pair of ye. What's been troubling you, in your own words?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The legs. At night they seize up in desperate cramps, and stretching or walking it off only helps a small bit. Next day I'm like a wet rag.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's roaring the house down some nights. Mam, tell her how long it's been.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, two months, maybe longer, I haven't a notion exactly. Both calves, the right is worse, and I'm too tired to be counting.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is it just the calf, or does it run up into the thigh as well?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the calf. I get up and stamp around the kitchen and—
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she won't drink. I put a glass by the chair and it sits there all day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Will you let me finish. Then I can't get back to sleep, and I'm fit to be tied.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): The sleep is broken after them, I hear you. How much are you actually drinking in the day?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, I don't... uh, the tea goes cold half the time.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Go on, Mam.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): A cup of tea in the morning and a sup of water with the tablet. That's the height of it.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the ankles, pain in the chest, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Don't be adding things on me.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand, I won't pile on. What tablets are you taking at the minute?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet. I call it frusamide, forty milligrams every morning, years now, for the blood pressure I think. And I got magnesium in the chemist for the cramps.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Frusemide forty milligrams each morning for the blood pressure, yes. The magnesium, what strength, and how often?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): One at night. The dose, err, I haven't a notion, the bottle's at home.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She doesn't always take that magnesium either. And Auntie Brid keeps pushing her biotin, the hair tablets, as if that'd fix cramps. Brid's the one on the biotin, not Mam.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it most nights. I can't hear myself think with the two of ye going on. Brid's tablets are her own business.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else, even now and again?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Two paracetamol, the 500 ones, if the legs are sore after a bad night. Not every day.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any reactions to medicines at all? Anything that didn't suit you?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not... look, I'm wrecked, can we not—
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has to ask, Mam.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. I've taken penicillin and everything, the amoxacillin one years back, and not a bother.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good, so nothing that disagreed with you. I'll have a look at the calves. They're soft, there's no heat, no swelling, and the pulses in both feet are there.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): They feel grand sitting here. It's only in the bed they go mad.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Apart from the legs and the tiredness, any bother with the tummy or the waterworks?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. That's all grand. It's the cramps and being wrecked, nothing else.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think these night cramps may well be tied to the water tablet and you drinking so little, but I won't change the frusemide until we see the salts. I'll book bloods for the potassium, and the kidney numbers with them.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): More bloods. Brilliant. That's all I need.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I know it's a nuisance. Stretch the calves before you get into bed, and try for more than that one cup of tea, even a glass with the dinner. We'll see you back in a fortnight with the results.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the bloods for tomorrow morning at the desk, and the review for two weeks. Mind yourselves.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Morning doctor. I'm his mother. This is Arjun, he is having fever and cough, please see him, he was up half the night.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hmm, one second, this screen has frozen again... sorry, what is the child's name? I didn't catch it.
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Arjun. He turned four in January.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Arjun, four. Ok. Tell me, what brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The fever, and the cough with it. He is just not himself.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Fever is there from four days, doctor. I am the grandfather, I stay with them in the same house.
[SEG0007] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Papa, no. It started day before yesterday, so two days, not four.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, can you repeat that? I was typing the registration. Two days or four days?
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I am saying four days. From Sunday night he was warm, I remember, because the match was on.
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Today is Thursday, no? Um, well actually I first checked the thermometer on Tuesday morning. So two days. You are mixing it with that cold he had last week.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so we are not sure, somewhere between two and four days. Arjun beta, how are you feeling?
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it the throat, or the cough that is bothering you?
[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): Cough. Mama.
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cough is wet, more in the night, and the fever comes and goes. In the day he is a bit better.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): How high has the fever been? The number, if you have it.
[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Around midnight I thought the thermometer said one hundred and three... no, sorry, I looked again, it was one hundred and one point four Fahrenheit.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Before that, when I checked around ten, it was one hundred and three Fahrenheit. I saw the reading myself, doctor.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): So one hundred and three at ten, and one oh one point four around midnight. What medicine did you give?
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Crocin. I gave two spoons... no, no, one spoon only, the 5 ml spoon. It is Crocin DS, so one spoon is two hundred and fifty milligrams.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Two fifty milligrams, one spoon. How often? Say it again, I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three times yesterday and once this morning, by mouth, every six hours. Not closer than that.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Morning I also gave Brufen, the ibuprofen, one spoon... wait, no. I am getting muddled. The pink bottle was Crocin only. I did not give Brufen.
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Correct, only Crocin. We have not given ibuprofen at all this time.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting? Any loose motions?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting, and no loose motions.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is he breathing fast? Any rash on the skin? Pulling at the ear?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, no, nothing like that. He is playing a little in the afternoon. Only he is eating less.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, appetite is down since yesterday. He took some milk, that's all. He didn't want rice.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any old problems? Asthma, hospital admission, anything on the file? The file is slow to open.
[SEG0031] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No asthma, no admission. Last winter he had a bad cough and they did a chest X-ray. They said it was borderline, but they didn't start any medicine for it.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was going to have his tonsils out... ah no, that was his cousin in Pune. Arjun himself has not had any operation.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): No surgery then. Any allergy to a medicine or anything else?
[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No allergies that we know of.
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): I don't know.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, beta. Come, let me look in your mouth. Big open.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Throat is a bit red. Chest is clear, I don't hear any wheeze. Both ears look normal. Tummy is soft, no pain when I press.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temperature now is thirty eight point two degrees Celsius. Heart rate one hundred and eighteen beats per minute. Breathing is twenty six a minute. Oxygen is ninety eight percent.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, is it pneumonia? They had said that X-ray was borderline, no?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't think it is pneumonia. My impression is a viral fever with a cough, provisional, from what I see today. That old borderline X-ray doesn't mean he has a chest infection now.
[SEG0041] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So, antibiotic or we just wait?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No antibiotic now. Continue the Crocin, 5 ml, that is 250 mg, up to four times in a day if the fever is there, with at least six hours between doses. And plenty of fluids, water, buttermilk, whatever he will take.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You want a blood test? We can go to the lab downstairs itself.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the fever is still there after three days, we might do a blood count.
[SEG0045] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if he becomes worse before that, what to do?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): If he is breathing fast, or very dull, or the fever is just not settling, come earlier, don't sit at home. Otherwise, if he is not better in three days, come back and see me.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You know the traffic from our side was terrible, we left at seven itself and still... anyway. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0048] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you doctor. We will do as you said. Arjun, say thank you.
[SEG0049] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): And walking is excellent. Keep it up. If you get sudden severe back pain, or you fall, come in the same day.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor. I do apologise for troubling you, but my voice has gone. It's been a little over a week now.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good afternoon. Not at all. Let me hear you. Can you say your name and where you live? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Margaret Ashworth, number twelve, Birch Road. You can see it's quite croaky. ~
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can hear it, a bit husky. When did it come on, exactly?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten days ago, rather suddenly. I woke up and it simply wasn't there, I could only whisper.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Had you been ill, a cold or a cough, beforehand? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing at all. I'd been to my choir the night before, mind you, and we did the whole of the Messiah. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah. Enthusiastic singing could do that. And how has it been since? Is it improving or staying the same? ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A little better in the mornings, but by the evening it's worse again. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any pain in your throat, or difficulty swallowing? ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain to speak of, and I can swallow perfectly well. It's just the voice. ~
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. You're not on any regular treatment I should know about? ~
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I'm very fortunate. I take nothing at all, except a vitamin on Sundays. ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any other health conditions?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I have a touch of acid reflux, nothing major.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's useful. Open wide and say ahh for me. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Ahh.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Throat looks fine. The vocal cords are inside, so I can't see them from here. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Quite so. What do you think it is? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): A sudden husky voice after heavy use, with some reflux in the background, looks most like laryngitis.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Laryngitis. Is that serious? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not usually. The cords are inflamed, like a sprained ankle, and they need to rest. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I see. Then I shall be silent on the subject of Handel. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exactly, no singing, and avoid whispering too, which strains the cords just as much.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Whispering is bad? ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, doctor. The number 19 sat behind a bin lorry and then I came in the wrong door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, Mr Hale. Have a seat. Were you rushing?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit. I was up the allotment at half six staking beans, and next door's cat was in the compost again. Filthy animal.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite a start. What did you come in for, though?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah. Right. It's the waterworks. I'm up three or four times a night for a wee, the stream's gone weak, and I dribble after.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So night-time trips, a poor stream, and dribbling at the end.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. I stand there and it just trickles. Takes forever, and then there's a little bit more in the pants.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, did I even lock the shed. I keep seeing that fork left out in the rain, and if it rusts...
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry. Umm, I couldn't put a date on it, it's been months but it crept up, and I really don't know when it started.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. No clear start, then. Is the dribbling the same, or newer?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): The dribbling's the newer bit. Last few weeks. The getting up and the weak stream, that's the one that's been months.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Blood? God no. My brother, he had a thing with his...
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay with you a second, sorry. No blood that you've actually seen?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): None. Not once. I would have noticed, I'm sure.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Burning or pain when you pass water?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No burning, no pain. It's just slow.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Through the day, are you rushing, or is it mainly the nights?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Mainly the nights. I do go more in the day than I used to, but I'm not dashing for it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you drinking in the evening?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Tea. Always a pot while the news is on, 2 or 3 mugs, and another if the football's on. Can't drop the evening brew.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): That late fluid will keep waking you. It isn't the whole reason for a weak stream, but it piles on the night trips. Think of the bladder as a tank you're topping up at bedtime.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): I did wonder. My dad was the same, ended up having the prostate out when he was about seventy. I sit there at night and I think of him.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, thank you. Medicines, what are you on just now?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Ramipril. Five milligrams, mornings, for the blood pressure. Been on it years. Nothing else, uh, far as I remember.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ever had a PSA, the prostate blood test?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): They did one at the hospital, three-ish years ago. They said it was borderline. I never got a number, and nobody chased me, so I let it lie.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Borderline, and no figure. Alright. Thinking it through, weak stream, dribbling, up at night, in a chap your age, this is most likely the prostate enlarging in the ordinary benign way.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't properly exclude a cancer from the story alone, so I don't want to call it that, but it isn't what the pattern is shouting.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the bit I didn't want to say out loud. The cancer word.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. What I am going to do is book a PSA blood test and a urine sample, today. The urine is to look for blood we haven't seen and for infection. The PSA is the fresh prostate check.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I fill the pot here?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, before you go, if you can. Reception will hand you the bottle. I'll put both requests in now, so they're arranged, not a maybe.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): And if the PSA's up?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we talk about what it means. It isn't a diagnosis on its own. There's also a tablet I want to start, called tamsulosin.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Never heard of it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four hundred micrograms, one capsule by mouth at night. It eases the muscle at the neck of the bladder so the stream often picks up. First few doses can make you light-headed if you stand up fast, more so with ramipril on board, so take it once you're in for the night.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Tamsolosin, right. Will it fight with the ramipril?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tamsulosin. Not a fight, but both can drop the pressure a little, so if you feel faint you sit down and you tell me. I'd like you on it starting tonight if the chemist has it. I'll send the prescription.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright. I'll try it. Nights are grim enough already.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): And ease off that evening tea. Half a mug, earlier if you can. Don't stop the ramipril.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Half a mug. The football will feel all wrong, but fine.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bowels been alright, any change?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Bowels are fine. Clockwork. Sorry, I do rattle on about nothing.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright. I've felt your tummy, it's soft, and I can't feel the bladder. I'm leaving the prostate examination today, the blood test is the useful bit first.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Soft is good, is it?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is. Come back and see me in about four weeks, results in hand, and we'll see if the tamsulosin suits you. Put it on the calendar so it doesn't drift.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still come in two weeks. Yes, bring the notes.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister wanted me to ask if she should stop lisinopril also. She coughs in the winter sometimes.

[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where exactly is it itchy?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Between the fingers, and a small bit at the waistband. Only a nuisance.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): When is it worst?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Night time, I'd say. In the day I'm grand.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The little fella scratches his tummy in the bed too, and my wrists are at me as well.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Two days. A couple of days, maybe. Nothing at all.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two days my eye. It's three weeks, since before the Easter break at school.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): We won't pin the start today. Let me look at the hands and the waist.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. There are little tracks between the fingers, and a few raised bumps along the waist. It doesn't look infected.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No fever. Not a bit sick.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you lost any?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Maybe a pound, maybe I haven't. No scales in the house. I'm grand.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's the tummy? Any upset?

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on, so I know what we're working around?

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): That helps. With the night-time itch, the webs of the fingers, and the whole house scratching, I'd say this is scabies. I wouldn't fully rule out eczema, but I won't park it as eczema and leave it. We don't need blood tests for this.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): The same night, everyone in the house gets it, you and your partner and the child, even if you think the itch is small. Hot wash the sheets, towels and clothes at 60 degrees, and bag whatever won't wash for three days.

[SEG0029] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he actually uses the cream. He'd skip it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in a fortnight and we'll have another look at the skin.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Right so. Seems a lot of fuss, but grand.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's fine, sit down. We'll go through it together.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's no appetite, doctor. She didn't want to come, but I insisted.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the timeline, when did it begin?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): it's been going on for four weeks. Oh, and pain that started around my belly button then moved to the right. That's been about the same, two months
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): okay, can you describe it a bit more for me? How strong it is, what the pattern is, what helps
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I notice it more with moving and and coughing. Honestly, once or twice a day. Oh, and a low fever. Ah, as for low fever, moderate, I'd say.

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, something like this happened last year, and it went away on its own.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): so, a few questions about your lifestyle now
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll have a glass of wine with dinner. I've never touched a cigarette. I'm vegetarian and have been for years
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been to theatre before?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I had a triple bypass, eight years ago.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me ask about allergies, anything at all?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Hmm, um, there was some antibiotic, I was told I was allergic. But I couldn't tell you what it was called or what it did.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm on paracetamol, 650 milligrams, when needed. Clopidogrel. I take it 75 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): how long has that been going on?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Nearly five years now. I'm, I'm on something called simv... simvastatin, 20 milligrams, maybe, at night.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you happen to bring the box or the paperwork?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, it's at home. Eltroxin I don't take anymore.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does your family have any medical conditions?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): My grandfather had a stroke. Sorry, you know, what was I saying, my cousin has psoriasis.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): has anyone ever diagnosed you with something?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Arthritis in my knees, for nearly five years.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): is there anything more?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got gout. I've never really been one for hospitals. Okay, so I've had heart disease for nearly five years now. An underactive thyroid, for about ten years. Yes, high cholesterol.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so arthritis in your knees and gout are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few quick ones: urinary symptoms, diarrhoea or cough?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Nope, uh, nothing like that.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): anything unusual with passing urine?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): No changes there.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pins and needles or loss of strength anywhere?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing odd there.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): going by what you've described, it points towards possible appendicitis. A urine infection is also on my list. Gynaecological pain is still possible. Let's get an ultrasound or CT scan, for possible appendicitis
[SEG0038] person_4 (CLINICAL_STAFF): We have a slot Thursday at 10 am, if that works.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Thursday, that works for me.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sending you for urgent blood tests because of abdominal pain. You need to go to hospital now and not eat or drink. The surgical team would be the right next step, I'll refer you.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.

[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, will do.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): do get help quickly if the symptoms get worse we'll catch up straight away that's all from me any questions?

[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): look after yourself
